text:
2027: A WARNING TO UNIVERSITY VICE-CHANCELLORS WHO MAY SERVE AS INEC RETURNING OFFICERS

1. For years, INEC has relied on university vice-chancellors as returning officers during Nigerian elections.

2. The assumption is that these individuals possess the intellectual capacity, independence and integrity required to oversee electoral collation.

3. But academic qualifications alone cannot guarantee electoral integrity.

4. Consider Professor Peter Ogban of the University of Calabar.

5. During the 2019 senatorial election involving Godswill Akpabio, Ogban, serving as returning officer, falsified results in Oruk Anam and Etim Ekpo local government areas to favour the APC candidate.

6. In March 2021, he was sentenced to three years' imprisonment. 

7. The Court of Appeal upheld that conviction in April 2025.

8. Yet, a subsequent investigation revealed that he was walking freely after serving only a fraction of his sentence.

9. What does that tell Nigerians about electoral accountability?

10. As 2027 approaches, university vice-chancellors who may be appointed returning officers must understand something.

11. The title of vice-chancellor is not a guarantee of integrity, and a professorship cannot turn fraudulent figures into legitimate votes.

12. If your father, mother, husband or wife is a vice-chancellor likely to undertake electoral duties, speak to them.

13. Remind them that their academic reputation, professional career and personal liberty are worth more than whatever inducements politicians might offer.

14. There have been allegations of electoral manipulation involving university academics.

15. Every credible allegation deserves investigation, and every proven offender deserves punishment.

16. Nigerians must also understand that they have the right to scrutinise election results, document discrepancies and demand accountability.

17. No vice-chancellor should be intimidated for performing their duties honestly.

18. But no returning officer should expect academic prestige to shield deliberate electoral fraud.

19. In 2027, let the figures announced at collation centres reflect the votes cast by Nigerians, not the interests of politicians.

text:
A Tale from the Subconscious: Reflections on Humanity, Greed, Slavery and Freedom

Tuesday, 17th November 2026

A tale from the subconscious, a thought for humanity to ponder.

How can one give what they do not have?

I often wonder about the nature of humanity. What makes a person so consumed by greed, hatred and selfish ambition that they consciously choose to destroy another human being? What gives one person the courage, or rather the cruelty, to take another person’s life, dignity, happiness or freedom?

How can you look at a fellow human being and despise their happiness? Do you not appreciate their smile? Do you not marvel at the wonder of human existence?

Consider the human brain, the imagination, the complexity of thought, the ability to dream, to reason, to create something from nothing but an idea. A thought conceived in the mind can become an invention, an artefact, a discovery or a reality that transforms generations.

What a magnificent being humanity is!

And yet, what a contradiction we have become.

Is it because human life begins through the seemingly ordinary biological union of sperm and egg that we have forgotten how extraordinary life truly is? Have we become so accustomed to existence that we no longer recognise its value?

Sometimes, I sit in silence and ponder the darkest chapters of human history.

Slavery.

How did humanity descend to such depths of wickedness?

How could one human being look upon another, possessing the same capacity to think, love, dream, suffer and hope, and decide that this person should become property?

How could men, women and children be torn from their homes, separated from their families, chained, transported across oceans, sold and subjected to unimaginable suffering?

The transatlantic slave trade remains one of history’s most horrifying demonstrations of organised human cruelty. For centuries, millions of Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic, while countless others suffered or died through capture, displacement and exploitation.

I struggle to comprehend the magnitude of such suffering. I cannot imagine enduring those horrors. The thought of being stripped of one’s freedom and dignity is almost unbearable.

And then my mind travels to my ancestry.

I am proudly Igbo, from Eastern Nigeria.

My identity carries a history that I must never forget.

In 1803, a group of enslaved Igbo Africans resisted their captors near St. Simons Island, Georgia, in what became known as Igbo Landing.

Historical accounts and oral traditions recount how some of these captives entered the waters of Dunbar Creek and drowned rather than submit to continued enslavement.

Their story has endured for more than two centuries as a symbol of resistance, dignity and the human longing for freedom.

Whenever I reflect upon Igbo Landing, I am reminded of the terrible choices oppression can impose upon human beings.

What kind of world forces people to confront such a choice?

What kind of humanity creates a system in which freedom becomes so distant that death appears to offer the only escape?

And yet, slavery happened.

Colonial exploitation happened.

Apartheid happened.

The systematic degradation of human dignity happened, often justified by those who considered themselves civilised, enlightened or superior.

And I wonder: Have we truly learned from history, or have we merely changed the methods through which human beings oppress one another?

Today, my thoughts turn towards Africa.

A continent blessed with extraordinary human talent, fertile lands, natural resources, cultural richness and immense possibilities.

Yet, across many African nations, millions continue to struggle with poverty, corruption, insecurity, unemployment, weak institutions and failures of leadership.

How can a continent so richly endowed continue to experience such widespread deprivation?
How can leaders entrusted with the welfare of their people knowingly pursue personal enrichment while communities suffer?

Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

text:
By the time the mat is finished, it will be spread across a yard, covered in wet rice, and walked past by people who will never ask who made it.

That is the part that stayed with me.

I watched a two-minute video of a man making one of these mats by hand, and I went in expecting a craft clip. Nice textures, satisfying hands, a pleasant way to lose ninety seconds. What I got instead was a quiet argument about what kind of work gets seen and what kind does not. And the strangest thing is that the video never makes that argument out loud. Nobody speaks to the camera. There is no caption explaining what to feel. A man kneels on a concrete floor, and a pile of raw bamboo slowly becomes a flat, tight, patterned surface, and the whole case is made by the pile and the surface and what happens in between.

So, let me start where the video starts, because the beginning is already a small mystery.

The first image is a floor covered in long yellow-green strips. Hundreds of them, maybe more, laid out in lines like a field that has been combed. They are not sticks and they are not planks. Each one has been split down to something thin, flat, and flexible, with the glossy outer skin of the bamboo still on one face. In the first seconds a man is crouched in the middle of them, gathering a handful, tapping the ends straight against the ground the way you would square a stack of paper.

Here is what I could not stop wondering. Someone had to turn a hard, hollow, stubborn pole into hundreds of identical ribbons before this scene could even begin. That work is not in the video. It happened before the camera started, and it is the reason everything else is possible. The clip opens in the middle of a story whose first chapter we are not shown.

Hold on to that. It comes back.

The next thing the video does is odd. It stops showing the floor and cuts to a round black opening in a tiled counter, the kind of built-in cooking pit you find in a kitchen where a large wok sits sunk into a stove. Inside it, bundles of bamboo strips stand upright, packed together, each bundle tied near the top with a loop of yellow strip. A dark ladle tips into the frame and water pours in.

This is a small detail, and I think it is the most important one in the whole film.

Because up to this point, a viewer could assume the man is simply weaving dry material, and that the skill is all in the fingers. The wok tells you otherwise. Before a single strip is woven, the material has been prepared, soaked, and heated. I cannot tell you from the footage exactly how long the strips sat in that water or why this particular water temperature, and I will not pretend to. What I can say is that the people who make these things clearly do not trust raw bamboo to do what they want. They change it first. They make it forgiving.

Think about what that means. Bamboo wants to be straight. It is a plant that grows in tall, rigid lines, and its fibers run the length of the stem like a bundle of taut cables. If you try to bend a dry strip sharply, it can split or snap. To weave it over and under hundreds of times, in a tight pattern, you need it to give. The pot is where it learns to give.

And notice who is not in that shot. There is no one standing over the stove performing for the viewer. The bundles just sit there in the dark, tied up neatly, waiting. The cut is brief, and then we are back on the floor, and the tone of the whole thing has already shifted. This is no longer a man handling a pile of sticks. This is a man handling a process, and the process has stages, and some of those stages happen out of sight.

I find that more moving than any dramatic reveal.

The room itself deserves a mention, because it tells you things the video never states. It is a large, bare space with a grey concrete floor, pale blue-green walls, a dark wooden door with worn paint, and a low table along the wall holding a few household objects, including what looks like a woven basket. It is not a factory. It is not a studio built for filming. It looks like part of an ordinary house, perhaps a ground floor or a hall that has been cleared so that there is room to lay out something big. I am describing what I can see, not claiming anything about where it is or who owns it. But the scale of the empty floor is itself a clue. You do not clear a room like this for a small object.

You clear it for something that needs to be as large as a rug, or larger.

That brings me to the first real surprise of the weaving, and it is a surprise of scale.

Most woven things we know are made at the size of a hand or a lap. A basket. A placemat. A hat. You hold them while you work, and they grow toward you.

This one does not grow toward him. He grows around it.

In the footage he works on his knees, on his haunches, sometimes nearly lying alongside the weave, because the thing he is making is larger than the reach of his arms. He does not sit at a bench with a frame. The floor is the frame. The strips run out in front of him and beside him in a wide fan, and the finished part of the pattern spreads behind and beneath his knees like a tide coming in. As the weave advances, he moves with it. He is not building the mat in front of himself. He is walking it into existence.

I keep coming back to how physical that is. Every bend of the strip is a bend of the body. When he leans, the whole line of his back leans. When he needs to pull a long strip through, he does not use a tool that hangs off the hand like a needle. He uses his arm, and then his shoulders, and then his weight.

And the first few weaving shots are almost chaotic to look at. This is the second small mystery, and I want to be honest about it, because I misread it the first time.

Around the middle of the area, there is a great loose tangle. Long curved strips arc up off the ground in loops, overlapping, bowing in every direction, like the ribs of something enormous. At a glance, it looks like a mistake, or like the moment before everything gets thrown out and restarted. A viewer who is used to tidy craft videos might wince. It looks like trouble.

It is not trouble. It is the opposite of trouble.

Those arcs are what happens when you have a lot more strip than you currently need. The strips are cut long, and the weave is only partially built, so the unwoven lengths spring and curl until it is their turn. What looks like disorder is stored material. It is the future of the mat, held in the air, waiting to be pulled down into place one row at a time.

That is a lovely thing to realize, because it flips the emotional reading of the scene. You thought you were watching someone fighting with the material. You were actually watching someone who has made a great deal of preparation, and who is now spending it carefully, row by row.

The second thing I noticed, once I stopped panicking about the loops, is the rhythm.

If you watch his hands closely, there is a repeating motion that the clip returns to again and again. A strip goes under, and the next goes over, and then the pair shifts by one position, and the pattern advances a tiny step. In the close shots you can see the result forming under his fingers: small interlocking rectangles in alternating light and dark tones, tight against one another, as though someone had drawn a grid and then pulled all the lines closer together until no gaps were left.

Look at the surface long enough and a second pattern appears inside the first. The rectangles do not just sit in rows. They slope. They form diagonal runs that point in one direction, then hold, and then reverse direction, creating a kind of zigzag that travels across the whole width of the mat. I am not a weaver, and I cannot give you the formal name for it with confidence. But I can tell you it looks like the chevron of a herringbone cloth, and that on a surface this large, it reads like a path.

Some of the strips still carry the green of fresh-cut bamboo. Others have gone pale gold. The colors are not random decoration. They come from the two faces of the strips, the skin side and the inner side, and from where each strip was cut along the stem. That mix of green and gold is what gives the finished surface its depth. It is the plant's own coloring, rearranged.

Now think about what weaving at this scale demands of attention.

On a small basket, if you make one mistake, you can see it right away and undo a few rows. On a surface this wide, a mistake in the pattern can drift. If a strip is placed one position off, the slope of the whole diagonal tilts. The error does not stay put. It travels outward with every row that follows. The person doing the work has to hold a picture of the entire surface in mind while his hands are focused on one tiny crossing.

That is the part no camera can capture. We can only see him do it. We cannot see him know it.

And he does seem to know it. He moves along the weave as if he is reading the whole surface, not just the crossing under his fingers, the way a sailor reads a horizon. His hands do the local work, and the rest of him keeps checking that the local work agrees with the whole.

I cannot tell you how many years of practice produce that habit. The video does not say, and I am not going to invent a number. But if you have ever watched someone who is truly good at something, you know the signature of it. The movements are not hurried, and they are not hesitant. They are economical. There is nothing in them that is not needed.

There is also a moment, partway through, when he changes position and goes low, almost flat against the concrete, with one forearm braced on the finished part of the weave. The sleeves on his arms are a deep navy blue, a separate pair of cuffs worn over a green work jacket. They are the kind of detail that makes you suddenly understand the nature of this job. Split bamboo has edges. Pulling strip after strip across a forearm for hours would be punishing. My guess, and it is only a guess, is that the sleeves take the abuse so the skin does not have to.

That is craft knowledge too. Not just the pattern, but the protection.

Then comes the third act, and it is the one I did not see coming.

For a long stretch, the video is about the weave. You settle into it. You start to think the film is simply going to keep showing you the pattern advance until it fills the floor. And then the attention moves to the edge.

At the boundary of the finished weave, the loose ends of the strips still fan out into the open, long and unruly, like the fringe of something half-made. Anyone who has ever woven, knitted, or sewn will know what this means. A woven surface is only as strong as its borders. The middle can be perfect, and it will still unravel from the margin if the margin is not secured. The edge is where weaving either becomes an object or goes back to being a pile.

What he does next is, to me, the most beautiful sequence in the film, and it is made almost entirely of small things.

He lays a thick, flat length of bamboo along the margin, a kind of rail, green and glossy on its outer face. He feeds a cord around it and through the weave. In some shots the cord is a twisted reddish rope, and in others there are narrow red bands, bright against all that gold. Then, with a thin curved strip held between his fingers, he starts to bind the rail to the mat, passing the strip through and around, again and again, drawing it tight. A short blade lies on the concrete nearby, the sort of thing you reach for without looking. At one point it is the only tool visible in an entire frame.

Pay attention to how few tools there are in this film. There is no machine. There is no loom. There is a knife, some cord, a wok, and a man who knows what the next step is.

And yet the edge, once bound, changes the whole character of the object. Before, the weave was a sheet of strips that happened to be held together by their own crossings. After, it has a frame. It has a spine along one side. It can be lifted, carried, dragged, rolled, and hung on to without coming apart.

This is where I want to pause on something, because it is easy to rush past.

The red.

Almost everything in this video is a shade of yellow, green, grey, or brown. It is a muted palette, earthy and quiet. Then, along the finished edge, a thin line of red appears. It is a very small amount of red. You could easily miss it. But once you see it, you cannot unsee it, because the eye goes straight to it, and then it follows the line down the whole length of the mat.

I do not know what the red means. It may be purely practical, the kind of cord that was simply available. It may be a habit, or a tradition, or a matter of taste. The video does not say, and I would be making things up if I offered a story about luck, or ceremony, or family. What I can tell you is what it does. It marks the border. It tells you where the object ends and where the room begins. After minutes of looking at texture, you are given a single clean line, and it makes the whole mat look finished in a way that the weave alone never did.

Sometimes a very small decision is what turns a thing into something that looks like it was made on purpose.

I want you to picture the moment next, because the video lingers on it just long enough.

He has finished the border. The mat lies flat on the concrete, a long rectangle of patterned bamboo with a green rail and a thread of red down its side. And in a few quick shots, we see it from a distance, from straight above, almost like a map. The herringbone runs across it, perfectly regular, edge to edge. It is clean, and tight, and entirely uniform. If you had come in at that moment, without having seen anything that came before, you might believe it had been made by a machine.

You would be wrong, and the video has just spent most of two minutes proving it.

The last stretch is the quietest. He kneels at one end, takes hold of the finished edge, and begins to roll. The mat lifts off the floor and folds over itself into a long cylinder, and as it turns you can see both faces of the weave at once: the glossy skin side, the pale inner side, the pattern winding around and around like the rings of a tree. The roll gets thicker as it goes. He is not hurrying. He does it carefully, with both hands, keeping the edge straight.

Then the camera pulls back, and for the first time you see the whole room again. A man on his knees, a long roll of bamboo extending from his hands out of the frame, a door, a table, a patch of bare floor where, a couple of minutes ago, there was a field of loose strips.

The floor is empty now.

All of that material has become one object.

I have to tell you what the object is for, because it is the detail that rewrites everything above. According to the title of the video, this is a traditional mat used for drying rice. I am taking that from the title, not from anything shown on screen, so treat it the way you would treat any caption. But if it is correct, it means the whole sequence we have just watched, the cutting, the boiling, the bundling, the weaving, the binding, all of it, is in service of something that will spend its life underneath grain.

Think about what a drying mat actually does.

It is a surface that holds food up to the sun and the air. The grain is spread across it, turned, gathered, spread again. The mat takes the heat, it lets moisture escape, it carries a weight that is small in each grain and enormous in total. It is walked on, swept, stored, brought out again. In the process, the mat is basically invisible. You do not look at a drying mat. You look at the rice.

And that is exactly the point I started with. The mat is the thing that does the most and is noticed the least.

So let me go back to the missing first chapter.

Remember the strips on the floor at the very start. Hundreds of them, thin and flat and uniform. I said someone had to turn a stiff pole into all of those ribbons, and that the video begins after that work was done. I want to take that seriously now, because it changes how you read everything else.

A strip like that is not a natural thing. Bamboo does not grow in ribbons. A grower has to cut a stalk at the right moment, split it lengthwise, and keep splitting until the pieces are thin enough to bend. Then the strips have to be brought to a consistent width and thickness, because a weave this tight depends on every piece being nearly the same. If one is too thick, it will not lie flat. If one is too thin, it will gap. The mat's regularity does not begin at the weaving. It begins long before, in the dozens of small decisions that produce a pile of near-identical strips.

I do not know from the footage who did that work, or whether it was the same man, or how long it took. I want to be clear about that. It may have been him. It may have been a neighbor, a relative, a supplier. The video is silent. But the structure of the scene tells you something true regardless: what we watch is the final third of a much longer journey, and the part we see is the part that is easiest to film.

That is true of nearly everything we admire. We see the weave and not the splitting. We see the finished edge and not the preparation. We applaud the visible stage, and we forget that it stands on a heap of invisible ones.

And there is a second compression I should mention, because it matters for honesty.

The clip lasts a little over two minutes. A mat this size does not get made in two minutes. The video is cut and sped, and each jump hides hours of repeated, tiring labor. I cannot say how many hours, and I will not guess at a figure, because any number I gave would be invented. But when you watch the pattern leap forward between shots, remember what the cuts are covering. Every one of those leaps is a stretch of kneeling, reaching, pulling, and checking, done over and over by one person on a hard floor.

I think this is why the video is so satisfying and also quietly sad. The editing delivers all the pleasure of the result and almost none of the cost. You get the pattern without the aching knees.

Now, a skeptic might say: so what? It is a mat. It is a rice mat. Plenty of people make them. Why dress it up as something profound?

Fair question. Let me answer it with the one thing I find hard to argue with, which is the herringbone.

A machine can make a herringbone. In fact, a machine is very good at it. A machine can produce a perfect, endless, flawless weave without a single stray fiber. If all you wanted was uniformity, you would not need this man at all.

So why does the handmade version matter?

Because the uniformity on screen is not the uniformity of a machine. It is the uniformity of a person who has decided, thousands of times in a row, to place the next strip exactly where the last one told him to. Every crossing is a small act of judgment. Every judgment is correct, or he corrects it. The perfection is not a property of the material. It is the accumulated residue of attention.

That sounds abstract, so here is the concrete version. Look at the strips where the weave meets the loose fan of unwoven material. On one side of that line there is order, and on the other there is a spray of material pointing in every direction. The line between them is where he is working. It moves a few centimeters at a time. Everything behind it is decided, and everything ahead of it is still possibility. He lives on that line. He is the person standing at the edge of what has been settled.

There is a kind of courage in that, though it is not the dramatic kind. It is the courage to commit to a pattern knowing that any error will be carried forward into every row you have not yet made.

Now let me return to the wok, because I have not finished with it.

I said the pot was where the material learned to give. I want to push on that, carefully, because it is a good image and I do not want to lean on it harder than the footage allows.

Everything else in this film is about order imposed on material. Strips laid straight. Strips woven over and under. Strips bound to a rail. It is a story of discipline. The wok is the one place where the story admits that the material has its own nature, and that you cannot simply force it. A dry strip resists. It wants to be what it was. The way you get it to cooperate is not by pushing harder, but by changing the conditions so that cooperation becomes possible.

That is a better description of skilled work than most things I have read about skilled work.

The man on the floor is not overpowering the bamboo. He is working with a cooperation that has been arranged in advance. The heat did the persuading before he ever touched a strip. His job is to use that window well, to weave while the material is willing, and to bind it before it hardens into the shape it has been given.

Which raises a question I find myself unable to answer, and I would rather admit that than pretend. How does he know how long the window lasts? The video does not tell us. A strip pulled from hot water changes as it cools and dries, and a worker with enough years behind him presumably senses that change through his fingertips. But I am inferring, not reporting. All I can say is that the film shows a man who never seems to be fighting the clock, and also never seems to be wasting time.

There is one more thing about the ending that I keep turning over.

When he rolls up the mat, he is hiding it. The moment it becomes a cylinder, the pattern disappears into itself. You can see an edge of herringbone along the outside, but the full surface, the field of crossing rectangles that took all that labor, folds out of sight. The most finished version of the object, the version that was visible to the camera from above, lasts only a few seconds before it is gathered up.

That is not a flaw in the film. It is the nature of the thing.

A mat is made to be rolled, carried, unrolled, covered, and used. It is not made to be admired flat on a clean floor with a camera overhead. The few seconds of that flat, perfect view are, in a sense, an accident. They exist because someone chose to film the moment between making and using, the brief gap when the object belongs to its maker and not yet to the world.

Then the roll goes out of the frame.

I want to come back now to the sentence I opened with, because it means something different than it did at the start.

By the time the mat is finished, it will be spread across a yard, covered in wet rice, and walked past by people who will never ask who made it.

At first, that sentence sounded like a complaint. It sounded like a small injustice, the sort of thing you say about unseen labor in order to make the viewer feel guilty. But after watching the whole film, I do not read it that way anymore. I read it as a description of how well the work was done.

A good mat does not announce itself. It lies flat. It does not tear. It does not shed splinters into the grain. It holds its pattern through seasons of use, and because it does, nobody has any reason to think about it. The very invisibility that we are tempted to pity is the proof that the work succeeded. If a mat is noticed, something has gone wrong with it.

That is a strange standard to hold yourself to. You labor over every crossing, every strip, every border, and the reward for getting it right is that nobody looks. The reward for getting it wrong is that everybody does.

And yet the man in the video works as though this is entirely normal. There is no performance in it. He does not glance up to see whether the camera is watching. He does not slow down at the impressive parts or speed up at the dull ones. The border gets the same care as the field. The wok gets the same care as the weave. The last strip gets the same care as the first.

I cannot know what he feels about it, and I am not going to put thoughts into his head. What I can do is describe what the footage shows: a person doing a long job from beginning to end with a steadiness that does not depend on being seen.

Maybe that is the real reason this video holds attention. Not the satisfying patterns, not the texture of the bamboo, not even the surprise of watching a mess of loops become a clean grid. It is the sight of someone who treats an unobserved task as if it deserved his full attention, because it does.

So here is the picture I am left with.

A yard in the sun. Rice laid out across a broad, golden surface. Someone turning the grain with a rake, and someone else carrying a basket, and nobody looking down. Beneath all of it is a herringbone of green and pale gold, a red line along one edge, a rail bound in with a thin curved strip, and, somewhere under the weave, the memory of a floor in a bare room where a man knelt and walked a pattern into existence one crossing at a time.

The rice will be gathered. The mat will be rolled again.

And the only evidence that anyone was ever there will be the fact that nothing broke.

𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗟𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱: 𝗤2 & 𝗛1 𝗙𝗬27 𝗘𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘆 🚀:

Premier Explosives Limited showcased a robust recovery in its Q2 FY27 performance, with significant year-on-year growth in revenue and profitability. The company is strategically expanding its defense capabilities and progressing with its acquisition plans.

𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀:

- 𝗤2 𝗙𝗬27 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲:
  ▸ Revenue from operations surged by 92% YoY & 42% QoQ to ₹1,452.8 million.
  ▸ EBITDA increased by 161% YoY & 193% QoQ to ₹172.3 million.
  ▸ EBITDA margin improved to 11.9% from 8.7% in Q2 FY26 & 5.7% in Q1 FY27.
  ▸ Profit After Tax (PAT) stood at ₹119.7 million, a 33% YoY decline, but a 295% QoQ increase.
- 𝗛1 𝗙𝗬27 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲:
  ▸ Revenue from operations grew 13.8% YoY to ₹2,478.4 million.
  ▸ EBITDA declined 15.9% YoY to ₹231.1 million, with margins at 9.3%.
  ▸ PAT declined 54.8% YoY to ₹150 million.

𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗸 & 𝗕𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁:

- 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵: The outstanding order book stands at ₹16,420 million as of October 2026. 📈
  ▸ The Defense segment constitutes approximately 96% of the total order book, ensuring strong revenue visibility.
- 𝗔𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗼 𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗔𝗰𝗾𝘂𝗶𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: The 26% open offer has been successfully completed. The acquisition of an additional 41.33% promoter holding is in progress. This association is expected to enhance capabilities for larger defense programs.
- 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 & 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻: Focus on strengthening manufacturing capabilities & expanding product portfolio in high energy materials, countermeasures, rocket motors, & ammunition.
- 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗳𝗳𝘀 & 𝗙𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗲𝘀: Expected revenue contribution of ₹200 million from chaffs & flares in FY27 based on current orders.
- 𝗥𝗗𝗫/𝗛𝗠𝗫 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Water trials for RDX/HMX have commenced, with commercial production expected by mid-to-end December 2026. Initial production is targeted at ~30 tons in Q4 FY27, with potential revenue of ~₹200 million. Expansion of capacity from 100 to 600 tons per annum is underway.
- 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 & 𝗪𝗮𝗿𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘀: Land mines are closer to commercialization. Warheads are already being produced & exported. Bombs are in early tender stages.
- 𝗗𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗱𝘀: Currently supplying on a trial basis; awaiting qualification by the Air Force & Army for larger quantities.
- 𝗡𝗶𝗽𝘂𝗻 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿: Order for over 1 lakh pieces received; production with incorporated changes has restarted, with bulk supplies expected within FY27.

𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 & 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰 𝗨𝗽𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀:

- 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁: Significant improvement in supply chain for components, with supplies resuming.
- 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻 𝗙𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀: Efforts are underway to improve gross margins, particularly in bulk explosives & service contracts, targeting 20-25% for defense products.
- 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗟𝗶𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗲𝘀: Applications for export licenses are in process for multiple orders, with some expected in the next month. The process is order-specific & can take 3-4 months.
- 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗲𝘅: ₹11 crore capex incurred in H1 FY27, with the remaining planned for H2 FY27, primarily for RDX/HMX capacity & reconstruction.

𝗤&𝗔 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀:

- 𝗖𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀: Delivery period extensions are being sought for pending orders, with completion expected within the current financial year.
- 𝗕𝘂𝗹𝗸 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀: Existing Singareni order extended; participation in future tenders planned for growth.
- 𝗥𝗗𝗫/𝗛𝗠𝗫 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁: Production & sales are contingent on receiving export licenses from the government, with potential for ~300 tons in FY28.
- 𝗗𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗱 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲: Quantities are small currently, awaiting armed forces qualification.
- 40𝗺𝗺 𝗔𝗺𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Development is stalled due to non-availability of raw materials & propellants from MIL; import efforts are ongoing.
- 155𝗺𝗺 𝗔𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗦𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗹𝘀: No current facility or plans to produce 155mm artillery shells.
- 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀: Collaborations with IIT Madras & BITS Pilani are currently in the research stage, with no commercialization yet.
- 𝗔𝗣 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗱: Policy formulated by Andhra Pradesh government for defense industry; company has selected an option, awaiting progress.
- 𝗕𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘁𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Expected in December following the completion of the Apollo acquisition.

The company expressed confidence in its long-term growth potential, driven by a healthy order book and India's focus on defense indigenization. 🇮🇳

text:
The World Ahead 2027

1. The post-Trump era.
As the dust settles from the midterms, the race to succeed Donald Trump will begin. But he won’t be a lame duck—more like a destructive Angry Bird. Expect more executive orders, legal spats, sudden renamings, grandiose building projects and military adventures as he furiously tries to retain his influence and shape his legacy. Meanwhile, the world will start to wonder what a post-Trump America might look like.

2. Aftershocks from Iran.
A clean-cut resolution to the conflict seems unlikely, so uncertainty will persist. But Mr Trump’s ill-advised war has reduced America’s stature; its allies no longer trust it and its enemies no longer fear it. The war’s consequences will ripple throughout 2027, reshaping regional politics, reconfiguring energy flows and threatening food security, with fertiliser in short supply. In Iran itself, the regime will tighten its grip.

3. Hottest year ever, again.
2027 is expected to be the hottest year on record. A “super El Niño” will offer a preview of the warmer, more volatile future that awaits, with more droughts, heatwaves, wildfires and extreme weather, unless emissions are cut quickly. But Mr Trump has unwittingly become the world’s greatest salesman for renewable energy. It’s the best way not just to address climate change, but to escape from the ups and downs of global energy markets.

4. The AI backlash grows.
The risks of AI are under scrutiny. The danger of a crash will rise as AI firms take on more debt in complex, opaque deals. Whatever happens in markets, more capable models will power a spate of cyber-attacks. Companies and governments will worry about political risks to AI supply chains. But concerns about job losses, or the energy and water use of data centres, are not backed by data. The backlash reflects fears over imagined impacts, not real ones.
It may be 50 years old, but “Star Wars” seems more relevant than ever in 2027

5. Europe’s populist right.
Right-wing populism has been on the rise around the world for some time. But in 2027 all eyes will be on France, where Marine Le Pen of the populist-right National Rally has a good chance of winning the presidency. That would throw a spanner into the Franco-German engine that powers the European Union—and heighten concerns about debt-laden France’s precarious public finances.

6. Bond-market pressure.
But it’s not just France that has the bond markets on edge. Fiscal profligacy, the AI construction boom and renewed inflation (from higher energy prices) are raising governments’ borrowing costs across the rich world. Higher rates are squeezing companies and households, too. This can’t go on for ever. Something, somewhere, has to break.

7. Taiwan’s deadline.
Technology has changed the nature of war, making it easier for smaller powers to fend off larger ones, as seen in Ukraine and Iran. What does that mean for China’s designs on Taiwan? Xi Jinping is said to have set a deadline of 2027 for China’s armed forces to be ready to capture the island. America is distracted. Will China make a move, or await the outcome of Taiwan’s elections in 2028? The next two years will be perilous.

8. The Ozempic effect.
As well as helping people lose weight, slimming drugs are changing consumer behaviour, as the newly slender, granted a new lease of life, engage in “revenge shopping”, splurging on clothes, cosmetics and fitness. The drugs’ success has also rejuvenated interest among pharmaceutical companies in therapies to boost longevity.

9. Cheaper space launch.
SpaceX’s huge Starship will start making regular satellite launches. Chinese rocketry firms will demonstrate reuse of boosters. Cheaper launch will pave the way for private space stations and, yes, building data centres in orbit, which may not be as crazy as it seems.

10. Rebooting Hollywood.
“Star Wars” is re-released for its 50th anniversary, and a new film. The Avengers return, again, and a new James Bond."

text:
The Speedway Murders: 48 Years Without Justice

On November 17, 1978, four young employees working the closing shift at a Burger Chef restaurant in Speedway, Indiana, disappeared during what appeared to be a robbery.

They were:

Jayne Friedt, 20
Ruth Shelton, 18
Daniel Davis, 16
Mark Flemmonds, 16
Two days later, their bodies were discovered in a wooded area of Johnson County. All four had been murdered.
What began as roughly a $500 restaurant robbery became one of the most notorious unsolved crimes in Indiana history.
The investigation was troubled almost immediately. Police initially considered the disappearance a possible prank or case of employees leaving without permission. The restaurant was cleaned and reopened before investigators fully understood that it had been the scene of an abduction. Evidence that might have identified the killers was therefore disturbed or lost.

Jayne’s car was later found abandoned near the Speedway Police Department. Investigators came to believe that more than one offender was involved and eventually focused on people connected to a group committing restaurant robberies at the time. Yet despite thousands of investigative hours, numerous suspects, confessions and reported leads, no one has ever been charged. https://t.co/iaKiOs00TO

In 1984, prison inmate Donald Forrester claimed involvement and reportedly supplied details that investigators considered significant. But information about his cooperation leaked, Forrester recanted, and prosecutors ultimately declined to charge him. Whether he had participated, learned details from someone else or constructed an elaborate story remains unresolved.

The case is still officially open.

Modern forensic science offers a measure of hope that did not exist in 1978. Indiana State Police now has a formal investigative genetic-genealogy program that is helping reopen cases dating back to the 1970s. Authorities have not publicly confirmed that usable DNA exists in the Burger Chef case, so it would be wrong to promise that genealogy will solve it. But every improvement in extracting and analyzing old evidence creates another possibility. WRTV

After 48 years, memories have faded and many of the people involved may have died. But someone may still know something—an old confession, an unexplained absence, a weapon, a car, or a story that never quite made sense.

The case should not be remembered merely as “the Burger Chef murders.” A restaurant did not die that night. Four young people did.

Jayne Friedt.
Ruth Shelton.
Daniel Davis.
Mark Flemmonds.

Indiana State Police continues to request information concerning the case. The Indianapolis District can be reached at 317-899-8577 or 800-582-8440. https://t.co/iaKiOs00TO

🔵#DRC: Washington’s Mineral Appetite Overshadows Its Commitment to Peace and Stability

The Democratic Republic of Congo is increasingly becoming a strategic mining battlefield for Washington, where access to mineral wealth appears to be taking precedence over the country’s long-term political stability.

The latest controversy surrounding American analyst Michael Rubin, who reportedly argues that President Félix Tshisekedi should face exile or imprisonment, raises an uncomfortable question: Is Washington genuinely interested in restoring peace in Congo, or primarily interested in securing access to its enormous mineral resources?

Rubin’s position, as reported by AXE Media on 16 November 2026, exposes the divisions within American thinking about the Congolese crisis. His criticism of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and American envoy Massad Boulos centres on what he sees as Washington’s pursuit of mining contracts at the expense of its diplomatic approach to the conflict.

The evidence of Washington’s priorities is difficult to ignore. The US-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement, signed in December 2025, establishes preferential opportunities for American investors, including rights of first offer on strategic mineral projects and access to Congolese mineral exports. The agreement also explicitly links mineral cooperation to American supply-chain security and competition with China.

Reuters further reported in April 2026 that American companies were showing significant interest in Congolese mining assets, including copper, cobalt, lithium, gold and tantalum projects.

This is where the contradiction becomes particularly important. Washington presents itself as a diplomatic actor seeking peace in eastern Congo, yet its economic strategy is inseparable from securing strategic resources and limiting China’s influence.

The question is not whether American investment can benefit the Congolese people. It certainly can, under transparent and mutually beneficial arrangements. The real question is whether peace and political stability are independent American priorities or merely conditions Washington considers necessary to protect its commercial interests.

When mineral access becomes the central measure of a country’s strategic importance, the Congolese people risk becoming secondary to the competition between foreign powers.

Congo needs more than foreign investors competing for its underground wealth. It needs lasting peace, accountable institutions, sovereignty over its natural resources and a future in which its mineral riches translate into prosperity for its citizens.

Until those priorities are demonstrably placed at the centre of American engagement, Washington’s commitment to Congolese stability will remain a legitimate subject of scrutiny.

text:
Luna Lovegood was often treated as the strangest student at Hogwarts, but she became one of the most loyal and courageous witches of her generation.

Luna was the daughter of Xenophilius and Pandora Lovegood. Her childhood changed dramatically when her mother died in an experimental spell accident while Luna was still very young. She witnessed the tragedy herself, leaving her with the ability to see Thestrals, creatures that can only be seen by people who have witnessed death and understood it.

After losing her mother, Luna was raised by her father, who edited a magazine called The Quibbler. Xenophilius encouraged her curiosity and taught her to question things, even when other people thought her beliefs were unusual.

At Hogwarts, Luna became known for her unusual personality, strange theories and willingness to believe in creatures that most witches and wizards dismissed as imaginary. Other students frequently mocked her, but she rarely seemed interested in changing herself just to gain their approval.

Her friendship with Harry Potter, Hermione Granger and Ron Weasley gradually gave her a place where she was accepted. She became an important member of Dumbledore's Army and helped Harry understand that he wasn't alone in being able to see Thestrals.

Luna also played a significant role in the fight against Voldemort. She fought alongside Harry and his friends at the Department of Mysteries and later became involved in the resistance at Hogwarts.

During the Second Wizarding War, she was kidnapped by Death Eaters and imprisoned in the Malfoy Manor because of her father's support for Harry. Even under those circumstances, she remained remarkably composed and helped encourage the other prisoners.

After the war, Luna went on to become a naturalist, travelling around the world to discover magical creatures. She eventually married Rolf Scamander, the grandson of the famous magizoologist Newt Scamander. Together, they had twin sons named Lorcan and Lysander.

Perhaps the most beautiful part of Luna's story is that she never had to become someone else to find happiness. The same girl who was laughed at in the Hogwarts corridors eventually built a life around the curiosity and imagination that made her different.

Luna Lovegood proved that being misunderstood doesn't mean you have nothing valuable to offer the world.

text:
In the latest @AusForeign, I respond to David Kilcullen’s June essay, Plan B: How to defend Australia without submarines.

David is right that Australia needs contingency planning. All good militaries undertake contingency planning, they just generally don’t do it in public.

But there is no simple Plan B for AUKUS. It is a multi-phase capability program, and the response depends on what has failed and why. A delay in the Virginia-class transfer is a very different problem from the US ultimately refusing to transfer submarines.

I also question how far other capabilities can compensate for the loss of submarines. David canvasses options including the B-21, long-range strike, drones, surface ships and a larger army. All may have value, but none replicates the full range of roles submarines perform.

Likewise, the frequently cited idea of simply returning to France is not a straightforward alternative. France faces many of the same industrial and timeline challenges, with its nuclear-submarine construction concentrated at Cherbourg alongside its own substantial submarine program.

The broader point is that Australia needs a balanced force regardless of what happens with AUKUS. The capabilities David identifies should be pursued because they strengthen the ADF, not because they offer an easy replacement for submarines.

Correcting the Historians: Abū al-Yusr ʿĀbidīn on the Early Fitnahs

An examination of Aghālīṭ al-Muʾarrikhīn (أغاليط المؤرخين) — “The Errors of the Historians”

This is an examination of Abū al-Yusr ʿĀbidīn’s views on the early Islamic civil wars, *NOT* a reflection of my own.

Shaykh Muḥammad Abū al-Yusr ʿĀbidīn (1889–1981) was a Syrian Ḥanafī jurist and Grand Mufti of Syria. 

Descended from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī رضي الله عنه, he was a relative of the renowned Ibn ʿĀbidīn, author of Radd al-Muḥtār, and the son of a former Mufti of Syria.

In his work, he challenges historical accounts concerning the Companions and Umayyads that he considers unreliable or influenced by sectarian prejudices.

The First Fitnah:

Abū al-Yusr defends Ahl al-Jamal, particularly ʿĀʾishah, Ṭalḥah, and al-Zubayr رضي الله عنهم, arguing that their departure to Baṣrah was intended to reconcile the Muslims and seek justice for ʿUthmān’s murder, not to rebel against ʿAlī.

According to his account, both parties were approaching reconciliation when the murderers of ʿUthmān, fearing its consequences, deliberately provoked fighting.

He writes concerning ʿĀʾishah:

ولم تكن معتدية ولا عادية ولا محاربة رضي الله عنها وأرضاها

“She was neither an aggressor, nor a transgressor, nor one seeking war. May Allah be pleased with her.”

He also explains ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir’s criticism of ʿĀʾishah as a misunderstanding of her intentions.

He ultimately endorses an account that:

ويدفع اللوم عن الطرفين رضي الله عن الجميع

“Removes blame from both parties, may Allah be pleased with them all.” [1]

His treatment of Ṣiffīn is more critical of ʿAlī’s political judgment. He describes him as exhibiting insistence.

He argues that ʿAlī’s refusal to heed advice contributed to the bloody conflict with Muʿāwiyah. [2]

The Second Fitnah:

Abū al-Yusr defends Yazīd’s caliphate, arguing that his established allegiance was legally binding regardless of whether others were more virtuous.

He writes:

فبيعة يزيد إذن شرعية ومن خرج عليه كان باغيا

“Thus, allegiance to Yazīd was legally valid, and whoever rose against him was a rebel.”

He compares Yazīd’s defence of his allegiance to that of ʿAlī:

فقام أيضا يدافع عن بيعته كعلي ابن ابي طالب

“He too stood to defend his allegiance, just as ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib did.” [3]

He also rejects accusations that Yazīd personally ordered al-Ḥusayn’s killing, questions reports condemning him, and cites the prophecy concerning the first army to attack Constantinople in his favour. [4]

Abū al-Yusr recognises the sincerity of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr رضي الله عنه, maintaining that his actions arose from ijtihād for the sake of Allah and His Messenger rather than worldly ambition.

Nevertheless, he criticises Ibn al-Zubayr’s political judgment, describing him as uncompromising and lacking certain qualities necessary to maintain authority. 

He compares his religious steadfastness to that of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, suggesting that these very qualities made governing difficult under the circumstances of his time. [5]

Abū al-Yusr also defends Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam against reports claiming that the Prophet ﷺ cursed him.

He likewise presents ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān favourably, citing his knowledge, jurisprudence, and devotion to worship, while acknowledging his struggle against Ibn al-Zubayr for the caliphate. [6]

Even concerning al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf, he highlights his prayers and religious devotion, though this does not necessarily imply approval of all his actions. [8]

Conclusion:

Abū al-Yusr offers a notably nuanced reading of these events. He vindicates Ahl al-Jamal, criticises ʿAlī’s political decisions at Ṣiffīn, defends Yazīd’s legitimacy, and challenges accusations against several Umayyad rulers. 

Throughout his work, he distinguishes political errors from sinful intentions and questions the reliability of historical narratives surrounding the early civil wars.

Allah knows best.

The Door That Only Banks Can Open

While most of the market is still arguing over whether a stablecoin should be allowed to pay anything at all, one institution quietly built the only structure that can still answer yes.

eUSD is not another token sitting in a wallet hoping for a yield program. It is a bank-issued dollar, created under a Nebraska Digital Asset Depository Institution charter. That single fact changes the rules. When the GENIUS Act and related efforts began closing the door on passive “rewards” for non-bank stablecoins, Telcoin’s CEO Paul Neuner noted the practical difference: as both a bank and an issuer, they retain the ability to offer yield even if pure stablecoin rewards are restricted elsewhere. Official statements confirm the plan: Telcoin Digital Asset Bank intends to provide GENIUS Act-compliant yield on eUSD, subject to regulatory requirements.

The distinction is not marketing. Non-bank issuers are largely limited to the narrow lanes the new rules allow. A chartered bank operates under a different license. It can take deposits, manage reserves under banking supervision, and structure offerings that remain inside the regulated system rather than outside it. That is the narrow door most projects never walked through.

No one has promised that simply holding eUSD in a wallet today already earns interest. The product is still subject to final regulatory steps. But the architecture was designed so that, when those steps are cleared, the yield does not have to come from a loophole. It can come from the same banking framework that already governs the dollars behind it.

While others debate whether the door should stay open, Telcoin built the only key that still fits the lock.

In his reading, Brazil was not a normal election but a hybrid war: the State Department, the "techno-feudalists" of Silicon Valley, Wall Street and Brazil's own comprador elite on one side; on the other, a digital army built on WhatsApp — from 50,000 subscribers to ten million in a matter of days — and a student mobilization in the streets. Why Brazil, of all countries? Gas, oil, water, the world's second-largest rare earth reserves — and a number one trading partner, for fifteen years, named China.

The second half turns to what the midterms have produced: a president humiliated at the ballot box, "like a cornered animal," with a window that closes on January 3, when the new Congress is seated — and a war with Iran that, by his account, the United States has already lost. Two against one — with Moscow and Beijing holding the only off ramp Washington has left.

The question he leaves the room with is not whether Lula won, but whether a government can govern when the right still holds both houses and the old money keeps a penthouse in New York and a house in Miami.

text:
“The Boy Called, Miracle”
(A Civil War story by Lisa Nazzaro)

Cody sat with his back against a wagon wheel, the letter paper balanced on his knee, trying to write by the light of the fire. 

The ink froze in the nib if he paused too long. Around him the battalion had settled into the low talk that comes after a day of marching, boots drying, cards being shuffled, someone humming the same three notes over and over because he had forgotten the rest of the song.

He had already told his wife the weather and the distance and that the new boots had not yet split. He was searching for something truer when the boy stepped into the circle of light.

No one heard him approach. One moment the fire showed only the faces they knew; the next, a child stood just outside the reach of the flames, dressed entirely in white. 

The cloth was clean enough to hurt the eyes, as if it had never touched mud or woodsmoke. He was small, barefoot, and very black against the pale linen.

For a second no one moved. Then Sergeant Hale, who had three boys of his own back in Ohio, shifted on his haunches and said, “Come on in, son. Fire’s free.”

The boy came. He sat where they made room for him, knees drawn up, and accepted the tin plate of beans and hardtack that was passed to him without a word. 

He ate the way hungry children eat…quickly, carefully, eyes lowered. When the plate was empty he wiped his mouth with the back of his wrist.

“What’s your name?” Hale asked.
The boy looked up. His voice was soft and clear. “My mama calls me Miracle.”

Someone laughed, not unkindly. Someone else offered him coffee. He shook his head. He sat a little longer, watching the sparks climb, and then he stood and said, “Thank you.”

The white gown caught the firelight and seemed for an instant brighter than the flames themselves. He walked three steps toward the dark between the tents and was simply gone. 

No sound of bare feet on frozen ground. No outline against the trees. The men stared at the place he had been until the sergeant cleared his throat and said, “Well.”

Cody finished the letter that night. He did not mention the boy.

“Dearest Ellen,
We are camped above a river that still has ice in its middle. The men are well enough. Corporal Briggs found a nest of eggs yesterday and shared them round; we pretended they were from your hens. I keep the ribbon you sewed into my coat. 
When the wind is right, I can almost smell the lavender water you put on it. Tell Mother I will write her next. Tell the children their father thinks of them at every creek we cross. I am still yours.
-Cody”

In the weeks that followed, the story of the boy in white traveled the company the way all strange things travel…quietly, then louder, then quieter again. Some said he was a runaway. Some said he was a spirit. 

Cody said nothing. He had seen the boy’s eyes when he gave his name, and they had not looked lost. They had looked as if they were exactly where they meant to be.

He wrote again from a pine woods after a skirmish that had cost them two men and a mule.
The nights are the longest part. I dream of the kitchen table and the way you set the lamp so it doesn’t smoke. 

Last night, I woke thinking I heard the baby crying, but it was only the wind in the canvas. If you can spare the paper, send me the words the children are learning. 

I want to hear their voices even if I have to imagine them. We are still moving. I will come home when the thing is finished.
Spring came in mud. The roads turned to rivers of their own. Cody’s boots rotted at the seams. 

He cut new ones from a dead man’s saddle blanket and wrote to Ellen about the lilac bush that had somehow survived in the yard of a burned house. 

He asked her to press a blossom if the one by the back door was blooming, and to send it inside the next letter so he could hold something that had grown while he was gone.

text:
Conclusion

Deuteronomy 27:1–10 reveals the remarkable seriousness with which the LORD prepared Israel to enter its promised inheritance. Great stones were to be erected and covered with plaster so that the words of the law could be written plainly. Mount Ebal was appointed as the location where the written testimony and altar would stand. The altar was to be constructed from whole stones without the use of iron tools. Burnt offerings and peace offerings were to be presented, and the people were commanded to eat and rejoice before the LORD. Moses and the priests then called Israel to recognize its covenant identity and obey the commandments of God. The nation was not instructed to establish its authority over the land by announcing the greatness of its own accomplishments. It was commanded to acknowledge the greatness and authority of the LORD. The written law, altar, sacrifices, and public confession belonged to the covenant relationship governing Israel’s life within Canaan.

The passage also demonstrates the danger of allowing outward religious accomplishments to replace actual obedience. A man may construct an impressive monument, participate in a solemn ceremony, and speak enthusiastically about God’s commandments while privately rejecting the authority those commandments possess. Israel was not permitted to make that distinction. The law was to be written plainly because it was to govern the nation’s conduct. The altar was to be constructed according to revelation because worship belonged to the LORD rather than to human imagination. The sacrifices were to be presented according to the appointed order because religious enthusiasm could not replace obedience. A monument to God’s word becomes a testimony against the very people who erect it when they refuse to obey what the monument declares. The same warning reaches every generation tempted to substitute religious appearance for righteousness. Scripture does not become less authoritative because a man has discovered a more entertaining way to disregard it.

Finally, the Christian must recognize the difference between Israel’s national covenant and the eternal redemption secured through Jesus Christ. The Church is not commanded to cross Jordan as a nation, erect plastered stones upon Ebal, or offer animal sacrifices upon an altar of unhewn rock. Salvation is by grace through faith in the Saviour who died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures. Galatians 3:13 declares that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us. Ephesians 2:8–9 establishes that eternal salvation is the gift of God, not the accomplishment of human works. The stones of Ebal testified to the law God had given Israel, but the cross of Calvary declares the finished sacrifice by which sinners may receive eternal redemption. The altar on Ebal belonged to Israel’s appointed worship, but the blood of Jesus Christ accomplished what the blood of bulls and goats could never accomplish. The nation was required to write the commandments plainly, and the Christian is required to receive the word of truth without twisting its meaning. The Israelites were commanded to remember that the land came from the LORD, and the believer must remember that salvation comes through Christ alone. No military victory can purchase righteousness. No beautiful monument can erase sin. No elaborate ceremony can improve the finished work of the Saviour. And no amount of human religious enthusiasm can replace obedience to what God has actually revealed. The final lesson is unmistakable: The LORD did not command Israel to build a monument to human greatness. He commanded a witness to divine authority. The stones declared His law. The altar acknowledged His appointed worship. The sacrifices testified to the seriousness of approaching Him according to His instructions. And the nation was commanded to hearken unto His voice.

In Arabic, Sibel can be linked to the term for "sister" or "female companion," adding layers of familial and social significance to the name.

Culturally, Sibel holds particular importance in Turkish society. It is a name that is often chosen for girls and is appreciated for its melodic sound and meaningful essence. Over the years, Sibel has been embraced by various forms of art and literature, further embedding it within cultural narratives. Its usage extends beyond mere naming conventions, as it symbolizes a connection to one's heritage and the values associated with femininity and companionship.

Historically, the name Sibel can be traced back to ancient roots, with connections to the Sibyls of Greco-Roman mythology. These figures were known as prophetesses or oracle-like women who communicated divine messages, often embodying wisdom and foresight. Though the direct link between the name Sibel and the ancient Sibyls may not be explicitly documented, the thematic resonance of prophecy and femininity may have influenced the name's popularity and meaning in contemporary contexts.

In modern times, the name Sibel has gained recognition through various notable figures, particularly in Turkey and among Turkish-speaking communities. One of the most prominent individuals bearing this name is Sibel Can, a celebrated Turkish pop music singer and actress born in 1970. Her work in the music industry has made her a household name in Turkey, and she is often regarded as a cultural icon. Another notable person is Sibel Kekilli, a German-Turkish actress known for her roles in films and television, including her acclaimed performance in the series "Game of Thrones." The name Sibel is also prevalent in various forms of popular culture, including literature and television, where characters named Sibel often embody traits such as strength, intuition, and compassion. Its appearances in various narratives reflect the ongoing relevance of the name in different contexts, illustrating how it resonates with different audiences.

Despite its popularity in certain regions, the name Sibel may not be as widely recognized outside Turkish-speaking populations, which may limit its cultural significance in a broader international context. Nevertheless, its rich etymological roots and the historical narratives associated with it contribute to a deeper understanding of the name's significance.

In summary, Sibel is a name steeped in cultural and historical richness, with origins that span multiple languages and traditions. It embodies themes of femininity, companionship, and subtlety, making it a cherished choice among parents in Turkish culture. The name's association with notable figures and its presence in contemporary media continue to enhance its legacy, ensuring that Sibel remains a relevant and meaningful name in various contexts.

The Sibylline Oracles (Latin: Oracula Sibyllina) are a collection of oracular utterances written in Greek hexameters ascribed to the Sibyls, prophetesses who uttered divine revelations in a frenzied state. Fourteen books and eight fragments of Sibylline Oracles survive, in an edition of the 6th or 7th century AD. They are not to be confused with the original Sibylline Books of the ancient Etruscans and Romans which were burned by order of the Roman general Flavius Stilicho in the 4th century AD. Instead, the text is an "odd pastiche" of Hellenistic and Roman mythology interspersed with Jewish, Gnostic and early Christian writings and thinly veiled references to historical figures such as Alexander the Great and Cleopatra, as well as many allusions to the events of the later Roman Empire, often portraying Rome in a negative light.[1]

The Sibylline Oracles are a valuable source for information about classical mythology and early first millennium Gnostic, Hellenistic Jewish and Christian beliefs. Some apocalyptic passages scattered throughout seem to foreshadow themes of the Book of Revelation and other apocalyptic literature. The oracles have undergone extensive editing, re-writing, and redaction as they came to be exploited in wider circles.

One passage has an acrostic, spelling out a Christian code-phrase with the first letters of successive lines.

Introduction
The Sibylline Oracles in their existing form are a chaotic medley. They consist of 12 books (or 14) of various authorship, date, and religious conception. The final arrangement, thought to be due to an unknown editor of the 6th century AD (Alexandre), does not determine identity of authorship, time, or religious belief; many of the books are merely arbitrary groupings of unrelated fragments.[2]

These oracles were anonymous in origin and as such were apt to modification and enlargement at pleasure by Hellenistic Jews and by Christians for missionary purposes. Celsus called Christians Σιβυλλισται ('sibyl-mongers' or 'believers in sibyls') because of prophecies preached among them, especially those in the book of Revelation. The preservation of the entire collection is due to Christian writers.[2]

Sources for the Sibylline texts
The oldest of the surviving Sibylline oracles seem to be books 3–5, which were composed partly by Jews in Alexandria. The third oracle seems to have been composed in the reign of Ptolemy VI Philometor. Books 1–2 may have been written by Christians, though again there may have been a Jewish original that was adapted to Christian purposes.

All the oracles seem to have undergone later revision, enrichment, and adaptation by editors and authors of different religions, who added similar texts, all in the interests of their respective religions. Some have suggested that the surviving texts may include some fragments or remnants of the Sibylline Books with a legendary provenance from the Cumaean Sibyl, which had been kept in temples in Rome. What is a prophetess in the Bible?

Thus, prophets and prophetesses are to say whatever message God has given them before the person or people for whom the message is intended. Prophets and prophetesses sometimes foretold future events, but most often they forthtold, proclaiming God’s truth, warning people of judgment, and calling them to repentance. Throughout history, God has used His Spirit to relay messages to female prophetesses, who were responsible to speak forth His Word to the people.

from the old testament
Sometimes, the message of a prophetess was a comforting encouragement (Haggai 1:13). Sometimes, it was a convicting warning (Jonah 3:2).
From time to time, it was a prediction of far-off future events (Zechariah 2:10–12).
A prophet or prophetess was responsible to share exactly what the Lord had given them (Deuteronomy 18:18). Samuel was taught to share the message in full, even if it was an uncomfortable truth that might not be well received (1 Samuel 3:17–18). When Jeremiah tried to stop sharing God's messages, he said, "If I say, 'I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name,' there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot" (Jeremiah 20:9). Thus, prophets and prophetesses bore great responsibility in relaying God's Word to its intended audience.
God declared, "And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Even on the male and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit" (Joel 2:28–29). In this statement, God specifically mentioned daughters who prophesy and His Spirit being poured out on female servants.
The first woman to be identified as a prophetess in Scripture is Moses's sister, Miriam, in Exodus 15:20. Her words were recorded in Scripture as she led the women in worship after God's miraculous rescue at the Red Sea.
The female judge who ruled over the Israelites, Deborah, was introduced first as "a prophetess," then "wife of Lappidoth," and finally in her role as "judging Israel at that time," perhaps implying that her primary role and legacy was as a prophetess who spoke the Word of the Lord (Judges 4:4). from the new testament

And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. By embracing this responsibility, we honor the legacy of these women and ensure that God's message continues to reach those who need it. In our daily lives, this means being attentive to God's guidance, knowing His Word, and being courageous in our communication. We can be consistent in sharing His love and wisdom with those around us, knowing that the Spirit can speak through anyone, regardless of gender, age, or status.

(F) Pope Saint Damasus I

“Likewise it is decreed . . . that it ought to be announced that . . . the holy Roman Church has been placed at the forefront not by the conciliar decisions of other churches, but has received the primacy by the evangelic voice of our Lord and Savior, who says: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it; and I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven . . . ’ [Matt. 16:18–19]. The first see, therefore, is that of Peter the apostle, that of the Roman Church, which has neither stain nor blemish nor anything like it” (Decree of Damasus 3 [A.D. 382]).

(G) Saint Jerome

“‘But,’ you [Jovinian] will say, ‘it was on Peter that the Church was founded’ [Matt. 16:18]. Well . . . one among the twelve is chosen to be their head in order to remove any occasion for division” (Against Jovinian 1:26 [A.D. 393]).

(H) Pope Saint Innocent I

 “In seeking the things of God . . . you have acknowledged that judgment is to be referred to us [the pope], and have shown that you know that is owed to the Apostolic See [Rome], if all of us placed in this position are to desire to follow the apostle himself [Peter] from whom the episcopate itself and the total authority of this name have emerged” (Letters 29:1 [A.D. 408]).

(I) Saint Augustine

“Among these [apostles] Peter alone almost everywhere deserved to represent the whole Church. Because of that representation of the Church, which only he bore, he deserved to hear ‘I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’” (Sermons 295:2 [A.D. 411]).

“Some things are said which seem to relate especially to the apostle Peter, and yet are not clear in their meaning unless referred to the Church, which he is acknowledged to have represented in a figure on account of the primacy which he bore among the disciples. Such is ‘I will give unto you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,’ and other similar passages” (Commentary on Psalm 108 1 [A.D. 415]).

“Who is ignorant that the first of the apostles is the most blessed Peter?” (Commentary on John 56:1 [A.D. 416]).

(J) Council of Ephesus 

“Philip, presbyter and legate of [Pope Celestine I] said: ‘We offer our thanks to the holy and venerable synod, that when the writings of our holy and blessed pope had been read to you . . . you joined yourselves to the holy head also by your holy acclamations. For your blessedness is not ignorant that the head of the whole faith, the head of the apostles, is blessed Peter the apostle’” (Acts of the Council, session 2 [A.D. 431]).
“Philip, the presbyter and legate of the Apostolic See [Rome] said: ‘There is no doubt, and in fact it has been known in all ages, that the holy and most blessed Peter, prince and head of the apostles, pillar of the faith, and foundation of the Catholic Church, received the keys of the kingdom from our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior and Redeemer of the human race, and that to him was given the power of loosing and binding sins: who down even to today and forever both lives and judges in his successors’” (ibid., session 3).

(K) Pope Saint Leo I

“Our Lord Jesus Christ . . . has placed the principal charge on the blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles, and from him as from the head wishes his gifts to flow to all the body, so that anyone who dares to secede from Peter’s solid rock may understand that he has no part or lot in the divine mystery. He wished him who had been received into partnership in his undivided unity to be named what he himself was, when he said: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ [Matt. 16:18], that the building of the eternal temple might rest on Peter’s solid rock, strengthening his Church so surely that neither could human rashness assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it” (Letters 10:1 [A.D. 445).

The Sibylline Oracles (Latin: Oracula Sibyllina) are a collection of oracular utterances written in Greek hexameters ascribed to the Sibyls, prophetesses who uttered divine revelations in a frenzied state. Instead, the text is an "odd pastiche" of Hellenistic and Roman mythology interspersed with Jewish, Gnostic and early Christian writings and thinly veiled references to historical figures such as Alexander the Great and Cleopatra, as well as many allusions to the events of the later Roman Empire, often portraying Rome in a negative light.[1]

The Sibylline Oracles are a valuable source for information about classical mythology and early first millennium Gnostic, Hellenistic Jewish and Christian beliefs. Some apocalyptic passages scattered throughout seem to foreshadow themes of the Book of Revelation and other apocalyptic literature. The oracles have undergone extensive editing, re-writing, and redaction as they came to be exploited in wider circles.

One passage has an acrostic, spelling out a Christian code-phrase with the first letters of successive lines.

These oracles were anonymous in origin and as such were apt to modification and enlargement at pleasure by Hellenistic Jews and by Christians for missionary purposes. Celsus called Christians Σιβυλλισται ('sibyl-mongers' or 'believers in sibyls') because of prophecies preached among them, especially those in the book of Revelation. The preservation of the entire collection is due to Christian writers.[2]
