John endeavored to describe the same, that he might both be known of the godly in that age, and be further observed and marked of posterity afterwards. This delineation hath one type, that is, his heads, but a double description or application of the type: one permanent from the nature of itself, the other changeable, by the working of men. The description permanent, is by the seven hills, in this verse, the other that fleeteth, is from the seven kings, verses 10, 11. And here it is worthy to be observed, that one type hath sometimes two or more applications, as seemeth good unto the holy Ghost to express either one thing by divers types, or divers things by one type. So I noted before, of the seven spirits, Rev. 1:4. Now this woman that sitteth upon seven hills, is the city of Rome, called in times past of the Greeks, … i. of seven tops or crests, and of Varro, septiceps, i. of her seven heads (as here) of seven heads, and of others, septicollis, i. standing upon seven hills.
Revelation 17:9 The beginning of these Kings or Emperors is almost the same with the beginning of the Church of Christ, which I showed before, Rev. 11:1. Namely from the year 35, after the passion of Christ, what time the Temple and Church of the Jews was overthrown. In which year it came to pass by the providence of God that that saying The beast was and is not, was fulfilled before that the destruction of the Jews immediately following came to pass. That was the year from the building of the city of Rome, 109, from which year S. John both numbered the Emperors which hitherto hath been, when he wrote these things, and foretelleth two others next to come: and that with this purpose, that when this particular prediction of foretelling of things to come, should take effect the truth of all other predictions in the Church might be the more confirmed. Which sign God of old mentioned this in the Law, Deut. 18, and Jeremiah confirmeth, Jer. 28:8.
Revelation 17:10 Whose names are these: the first, Servius Sulpicius Galba, who was the seventh Emperor of the people of Rome, the second Marcus Salvius Otho, the third Aulus Vitellius, the fourth, Titus Flavius Vespasianus, the fifth, Titus Vespasianus his son of his own name.
Revelation 17:10 Flavius Domitian son of the first Vespasian. For in the latter end of his days S. John wrote these things, as witnesseth Irenaus, Lib. 5 adversus hareses.
Revelation 17:10 Nerua. The Empire being now translated from the family of Flavius. This man reigned only one year, four months, and nine days, as the history writers do tell.
Revelation 17:11 This is spoken by the figure synecdoche, as much to say as that head of the beast which was and is not, because it is cut off, and Nerua in so short time extinguished. How many heads there were, so many beasts there seemed to be in one. See the like speech in Rev. 13.3
Revelation 17:11 Nerua Traianus, who himself in divers respects is called here the seventh and the eighth.
Revelation 17:11 Though in number and order of succession he be the eighth, yet he is reckoned together with one of these heads, because Nerua and he were one head. For this man obtained authority together with Nerua, and was Consul with him, when Nerua left his life.
Revelation 17:11 Namely, to molest with persecutions the Churches of Christ, as the histories do accord, and I have briefly noted, Rev. 2:10.
Revelation 17:12 The third place of this description as I said, verse 18, is a prophetical prediction of things to come which the beast should do, as in the words following S. John doth not obscurely signify, saying, which have not yet received the kingdom, etc. For there is an Antithesis or opposition between these kings, and those that went before. And first the persons are described, in this verse, then their deeds in the two verses following.
Revelation 17:12 That is, arising with their kingdoms out of the Roman beast: at such time as that political Empire began by the craft of the Popes greatly to fall.
Revelation 17:12 Namely, with the second beast whom we called before a false prophet, which beast, ascending out of the earth got unto himself all the authority and power of the first beast, and exerciseth the same before his face, as was said, Rev. 14:11, 12. For when the political Empire of the West began to bow downwards, there both arose those ten kings, and the second beast took the opportunity offered to usurp unto himself all the power of the former beast. These kings long ago, many have numbered and described to be ten and a great part of the events plainly testifieth the same in this our age.
Revelation 17:13 That is, by consent and agreement, that they may conspire with the beast, and depend upon his beck. Their story is divided into three parts, counsels, acts, and events. The counselors some of them consist in communicating of judgments and affections: and some in communicating of power, which they are said to have given unto this beast in this verse.
Revelation 17:14 With Christ and his Church, as the reason following doth declare, and here are mentioned the facts and the events which followed for Christ’s sake, and for the grace of God the Father towards those that are called, elected, and are his faithful ones in Christ.
Revelation 17:15 This is the other member of the narration as I said verse 7, belonging unto the harlot, showed in the vision, verse 3. In this history of the harlot, these 3 things are distinctly propounded, what is her magnificence in this verse, what is her fall, and by whom it shall happen unto her, in the two verses following: and lastly, who that harlot is, in the last verse. This place which by order of nature should have been the first, is therefore made the last, because it was more fit to be joined with the next Chap.
Revelation 17:15 That is, as unconstant and variable as the waters. Upon this foundation sitteth this harlot as Queen, a vain person upon that which is vain.
Revelation 17:16 The ten Kings as verse 12. The accomplishment of this fact and event, is daily increased in this our age by the singular providence and most mighty government of God. Wherefore the facts are propounded in this verse, and the cause of them in the verses following.
Revelation 17:17 A reason rendered from the chief efficient cause, which is the providence of God, by which alone S. John by inversion of order affirmeth to have come to pass, both that the Kings should execute upon the harlot, that which pleased God, and which he declared in the verse next beforegoing: and also that by one consent and counsel, they should give their kingdom unto the beast, etc., verses 13, 14. For as these being blinded have before depended upon the beck of the beast that lifteth up the harlot, so it is said that afterward it shall come to pass, that they shall turn back, and shall fall away from her when their hearts shall be turned into better state by the grace and mercy of God.
Revelation 17:18 That is, Rome that great City, or only City (as Justinian calleth it) the King and head whereof was then the Emperor, but now the Pope, since that the condition of the beast was changed.

This book examines the relationship between temple architecture and religious practices in South India, particularly during the Vijayanagara and Nayaka periods (fourteenth–seventeenth centuries). Branfoot explores temple design, processional rituals, royal patronage, and the role of temples in the religious and social life of the region. After Steyr Motors $4X0, another takeover bid for a rare listed European defense asset. Finnish - Polish satellite maker ICEYE is bidding €41/share for Italy’s Avio $AVIO.MI.  ~20% premium means ~2.4x EV/Sales, 40x EBITDA.

The big question is political now - will Italy let it happen? Watch the Italian government and Leonardo $LDO.MI, which controls 19% of the voting rights. Either way, another scarce European defense asset, AVIO is behind Vega rockets and key Ariane components, has attracted a strategic bid.

I think several obvious targets are still hiding in plain sight, trading for peanuts despite unique technology and European military contracts:

• 4C Group $4C.ST — defense software, with strategic value to major primes that can integrate it in the offers like $RTX
• Ceotronics $CEK — Military communications, obvious one for soldier equipment primes like Rheinmetall or Thales
• Wallix $ALLIX.PA & CY4Gate $CY4.MI — Cyberwarfare and cybersecurity targets for primes and IT groups
• Bittium $BITTI.HE — Tactical comms, potentially attractive to the same buyers as Ceotronics
• MilDef $MILDEF.ST — Rugged military IT, a valuable capability for larger defense players...

European defense M&A to continue.

The question isn't whether more of these niche players will attract bids. It's who's next. And how much longer they'll remain this cheap with all money flowing into AI on markets?

text:
Over the summer I talked to the CEO of Springboards, a startup building an LLM that’s designed to come up with a wider variety of responses than its mainstream rivals do. At the start of the call, he said something that’s been stuck in my head since: “We often say that we’re a self-loathing AI company. We don’t know if we really like what we’re doing.”

“I guess that makes me a self-loathing AI journalist,” I replied. It was a joke! I love my job. But I do not love many of the things the technology I write about has become: warped by hype, steered by zealots, inescapable.

The CEO of Springboards and I are far from alone. Around the world, a love/hate attitude toward AI is very much the vibe right now.

On the one hand, public feelings are souring fast. According to the Pew Research Center, more adults in the US think AI will have a negative impact on them personally, and on society in general, than expect a positive one. The pessimism is strongest among the young.

More than half of people worldwide say that AI products and services make them nervous, according to a report from Stanford University. In a Gallup poll in May, 71% of US adults said they would oppose construction of a new AI data center in their area, far more than the 53% who said they would oppose a new nuclear power plant. And in an NBC poll in March, AI was less popular than ICE.

Yet the number of people using AI is still skyrocketing. ChatGPT hit a billion monthly users in May, according to the market analysis firm Sensor Tower. Google DeepMind’s Gemini is close behind, logging 950 million users in July.

According to Pew, half of US adults now say they use a chatbot, more than twice the number who said they did in 2023. One in four people say they do so every day. And it’s a global habit: More than a third of adults across all 38 OECD countries (a group of the world’s wealthiest democracies) report having used generative AI tools in the last three months.

All these surveys paint a picture of two contradictory truths: A lot of people really do not like AI and a lot of people cannot get enough of it. What’s going on?

It’s possible that these are two distinct groups, but I doubt it. The numbers don’t add up unless the Venn diagram is on its way to being a circle.

It’s also possible that the more people use AI, the more negative their opinions about it will be. There’s at least a correlation to back this up: The Global North, where adoption is highest, skews pessimistic. In the Global South, where adoption levels are lower, people are more optimistic.

But here’s what I really think is going on: When people say they hate AI it’s not the technology they dislike but, rather, the relentless drive of the companies behind it to push the tech upon us in as many ways as possible. They’re telling us to brace for the biggest social and economic upheaval in generations. How do they expect people to feel?

In many ways, we’ve been here before. We saw a similar dynamic play out with social media over the last 20 years. Billions flocked to Facebook and Twitter despite mounting techlash against the companies that ran those services. Ditto for Google search.

With social media there wasn’t much anyone could do. Quitting a platform meant losing all your content and connections, giving you the choice to suck it up or start over. But with AI there’s still a chance for people to have some sway. There’s certainly more political appetite for regulation this time around. All 50 US states have either passed or proposed laws governing the development and deployment of AI, creating a patchwork of more than 2,100 bills across the country—a tenfold increase in three years. 

And with a number of top-class open-source alternatives to Google and OpenAI and Anthropic already on the market, there’s also (for now, at least) the potential for more consumer choice and the market pressure that goes with it. 

I don’t want to be naïve. Trillion-dollar companies are hard to move. But what comes next is not as inevitable as those companies often imply. When I asked the Springboards CEO why his firm was developing a new model if he didn’t really like AI, he told me there was no walking back from LLMs—but you could still make them do something different. 

Here’s hoping we see a lot more of something different: Clarity about what AI can and cannot do and, crucially, a technology that’s not sold as if it’s about to take over the world.

The Trump administration plans to advance restrictions on new Chinese optical transceiver models despite lobbying from major U.S. technology companies, Reuters reports.

Executives warned that compliance could take 𝘂𝗽 𝘁𝗼 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲, highlighting the industry’s reliance on Chinese suppliers.

👉 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀

➤ 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗣𝗢𝗦𝗘𝗗 𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦: The FCC is seeking to block U.S. imports of new Chinese optical transceiver models over national security concerns. These components transmit data through fiber-optic cables inside data centers.

➤ 𝗕𝗜𝗚 𝗧𝗘𝗖𝗛 𝗣𝗨𝗦𝗛𝗕𝗔𝗖𝗞: Amazon, Google, Meta, CoreWeave and Cisco joined Microsoft in a meeting with White House officials, warning that companies could need up to 10 years to comply.

➤ 𝗠𝗘𝗔𝗦𝗨𝗥𝗘 𝗔𝗗𝗩𝗔𝗡𝗖𝗘𝗦: Despite doubts raised by the lobbying, three sources told Reuters the initiative is moving forward. The report does not establish that a final ban has taken effect.

➤ 𝗖𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗔’𝗦 𝗠𝗔𝗥𝗞𝗘𝗧 𝗦𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗘: China accounts for roughly 𝘁𝘄𝗼-𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗱𝘀 of the global optical transceiver market, according to Counterpoint Research. Eoptolink and Zhongji Innolight supply major U.S. hyperscalers.

Sharing a new essay from @FengmingLuPE and me on what makes tech transfer work, vs what sounds good on paper but is unlikely to deliver…

As APEC approaches, with the G20 coming up next, there's a window to put some meat on the bones of the Board of Investment (currently just words).

Many dismiss it as unrealistic in the current political climate, but we think there's a promising way to make it work for both sides. The question is how.

And to start, what do we get wrong about tech transfer? One common misperception is that we underestimate how much heavy lifting domestic suppliers, engineers, and firms have to do.

In the piece, we discuss some of these ideas focusing on China's auto industry and what its experience with foreign automakers, e.g., Tesla, can teach us about doing tech transfers.

Our argument is that so-called tech transfer isn't a one-off transaction, or even necessarily a transfer at all... It's a process of iterative capability building. It often starts with much less glamorous legacy tech, followed by the right incentives and sustained capacity building over time.

The recipient country (in the BOI case, the U.S.) needs to think carefully about which legacy technologies to transfer that would be realistic starting points for domestic capability building, then how to iteratively build up domestic suppliers, engineers, etc., and develop the capacity to absorb, adapt, and eventually improve on those technologies.

Also, how to tie deals into Chinese incentives (which tech they are open to transfer, and for what in return?) and critically, build institutions that are independent of political climates, which change fast.

China's experience offers some surprisingly (or unsurprisingly) relevant lessons for how the U.S. might approach this today!

 🏗️REBUILDING TRUST COULD TAKE YEARS

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🤝 A partnership doesn't guarantee adoption
📈 Adoption doesn't guarantee profitability

💰 AND PROFITABILITY DOESN'T GUARANTEE THAT YOUR FAVORITE TOKEN WILL CAPTURE ANY OF THAT VALUE

🚨 THAT'S THE PART CRYPTO HYPE KEEPS SKIPPING
🏦 Banks can benefit from blockchain technology without creating meaningful demand for publicly traded cryptocurrencies
💸 And even when a token benefits, investors can still overpay for that growth

🎯 A BIG NAME IN A PRESS RELEASE ISN'T A BUSINESS MODEL
💰 SHOW US THE USERS, THE REVENUE AND WHO ACTUALLY CAPTURES THE VALUE

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🌍 9) THE ECONOMIST'S 2027 COVER — LOOK FAMILIAR?

⚔️ Geopolitical tensions
🤖 Artificial intelligence
🏦 Financial instability
⚡ Energy and climate pressures
🇪🇺 Political uncertainty

🚨 SOUND FAMILIAR?
💰 These are many of the same forces we've been tracking for months — from energy disruptions and government borrowing to AI financing and pressure on global liquidity

🔍 THE COVER ISN'T A SECRET PROPHECY
🌍 It's an illustration of the risks and questions shaping the year ahead

🎯 AND THAT'S WHAT MAKES IT INTERESTING
👀 THE WORLD'S BIGGEST STORIES ARE INCREASINGLY CONNECTED BY ONE QUESTION: 
💰WHO WILL PAY FOR WHAT COMES NEXT?

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
10)🔮 WHAT COMES NEXT?
🙉STOP WATCHING THE SYMPTOMS
👀WATCH THE CAUSES

🤖 NVIDIA — Are investors paying for revolutionary technology, or have names like Jensen Huang and Sam Altman become an enormous part of what they're actually valuing?

🏦 FED — Rate cuts can make money cheaper. 
But can they rebuild destroyed refineries, secure shipping routes or end wars?

❗️DON'T CONFUSE THE RESPONSE WITH THE SOLUTION

🌍 GEOPOLITICS — Even if peace agreements arrive tomorrow, roll up your sleeves. 
Infrastructure must be rebuilt, assets secured and credible guarantees established.

🛢️ ENERGY — Stop looking at oil supply alone. 
The Middle East and Europe need functioning, secure energy systems — not just more barrels on paper.

🟠 BITCOIN — Until global conditions improve and sustained spot buying returns, crypto risks continuing to recycle the same liquidity.

🚨 AND HERE'S THE BIGGER PICTURE
❗️THE MARKET ISN'T REJECTING THE FUTURE

💰 IT'S REPRICING THE COST OF BUILDING IT
- 🤖 AI needs financing
- ⚡ Energy needs rebuilding
- 🛡️ Peace needs security guarantees

text:
Every few decades, someone announces that science has reached its end. In 1903, the revered physicist Albert Michelson wrote that the “facts of physical science have all been discovered.” In the 1980s, Stephen Hawking predicted that theoretical physics might be finished by the end of the century. With the explosive arrival of artificial intelligence, the feeling is in the air again—this time accompanied by a Nobel Prize.

In 2024, Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind were awarded part of the Nobel in chemistry for their neural network AlphaFold, which predicts the three-dimensional structures of proteins by learning from thousands of experimentally measured shapes. This devilish problem had resisted systematic attacks for half a century; AlphaFold seemed to have solved it once and for all, and the world became fixated on the promise of its approach. Hassabis and his team called AlphaFold “the template for how AI can accelerate all of science to digital speed.” A wave of startups building foundation models for biology, chemistry, and materials discovery raised billions of dollars, buoyed by DeepMind’s success. AlphaFold had shown that the combination of AI and sufficient data could make groundbreaking discoveries (even if we did not understand the underlying mechanisms involved), and it seemed, once again, that a path through the rest of science was laid out before us. 

To be sure, AI will bring extraordinary changes to science, but it has become increasingly clear that AlphaFold, and things like it, may not be the best template for that metamorphosis. Though it is a profound achievement, the conditions that produced the likes of AlphaFold are rare, and the time it will take to meet those conditions in other fields will be measured in decades, not years. Instead, the acceleration of science will come about thanks to another approach: AI agents. 

The primary condition for AlphaFold’s success was the existence of the Protein Data Bank, a data set of roughly 170,000 experimentally validated protein structures on which DeepMind’s team could train its model. The creation of the Protein Data Bank was not simple: It took 53 years of international scientific cooperation and, by a recent estimate, roughly $21 billion worth of experimental work to assemble. Efforts of that scale are infamously difficult to fund, next to impossible to coordinate, and hugely time-consuming to execute; they have often been unsuccessful as a result. 

But even in fields with the requisite cohesion and resources, and where the relevant data are not rendered inaccessible by commercial ownership, another barrier is too little discussed: the scientific impossibility of generating comparable data. In the case of protein structures, the key experimental technique—protein crystallography—is an unusually replicable and dependable tool, so much so that over 25 Nobel Prizes have relied on it. But in most of experimental science, results vary more often than not. Cell lines drift. Chemicals have trace contaminants. Lab humidity changes. The creation of measured datasets that will be consistent enough, accurate enough, precise enough, and scalable enough to train a modern neural network in biology or most of chemistry would require new kinds of measurement and new standardized approaches—none of which will be ready anytime soon. 

Of course, there are a handful of fields where these requirements are met: weather forecasting, much of genomics, very limited areas of chemistry. These may see AlphaFold-style breakthroughs soon, if they haven’t already. Government support for the production and coordination of those datasets will be critical, as the US National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology has argued. But for most open questions in science, we will need a different plan, at least in the short term. Luckily, something quieter and more modest has begun to show promise.

Scientists have always reasoned under uncertainty. Biologists working to identify new drug targets have never had perfect datasets. Instead, they combine docking calculations and known structures, factor in molecular dynamics, run a handful of binding assays, and use their judgment to weigh each method according to its particular strengths and points of failure. The skill of science is not in any single tool; it is synthesizing what many tools produce, and revising the results as the evidence comes in. This is how most working research actually proceeds. But until very recently, no software could do it.

Agents now can. Simply put, an agent is an AI reasoning engine that has been given access to tools—digital or physical—and the capabilities to use them. Over the last few years, a fundamental architectural shift in AI has enabled the rapid proliferation of these programs, which are powered by large language models, dramatically reducing the need for scientifically specialized datasets. For science, this technological advancement represents a foundational change: it has allowed us to create digital tools that can mimic the iterative, highly contingent process of actual research. While tools like AlphaFold apply a powerful approach to a limited question, agents are inherently generalists. They do not represent a new way to do science—instead, they digitally model the human process of discovery. 

Consider Google’s AI Co-Scientist, announced in May. Researchers gave it a one-page brief and a goal: Figure out how antibiotic resistance spreads between bacterial species, a key driver of drug-resistant infections. The system spun up sub-agents. One drafted hypotheses from the literature. Another picked them apart like a peer reviewer. A third ran tournaments to rank the strongest candidates. A fourth refined the winning hypothesis. The agent concluded that resistance genes were hitching rides on bacterial viruses, borrowing whichever virus could ferry them into a new host. The hypothesis was correct. Researchers at Imperial College London had spent a decade reaching the same conclusion through painstaking wet-lab work; their paper, previously unseen by Co-Scientist, was still in peer review.

Agents like Co-Scientist are still novel tools, and there are real challenges to overcome before they become a ubiquitous part of the scientific process: They are still liable to hallucinate, their judgment is not consistent, and they have memory and input constraints that limit the time they can run autonomously. But these technical barriers will fall away, and as they do we will begin to notice the compounding effects of scientific agents on the reliability, consistency, and velocity with which science is done.

Perhaps most notably, agents offer a structural fix for science’s “reproducibility crisis,” the widespread problem of researchers’ inability to replicate each other’s results. For decades, the scientific community has begged researchers to share their raw data and exact code in an effort to standardize experimental processes. But researchers have long resisted this tedious administrative work, which happens after the interesting science is already done. Agents, in contrast, automatically log every move they make, creating an exact record of the method that led to their results and allowing for precise replication. 

A second consequence will be an amplification of scientific memory. The transfer of knowledge between researchers is a famously murky process; if it isn’t done over years of training and observation, graduate students are left to pore through the messy lab notebooks kept by decades of predecessors, looking for the details that will make or break their protocol. As agents become an increasingly large part of the scientific process, though, a lab’s entire scientific history will be recorded in a central, standardized repository of institutional knowledge.

But the most important impact of agents will be speed. In any field, when testing an idea takes less time than arguing about it in a meeting, people stop debating and just run the test. An agent that can read a thousand papers in an hour, design 500 molecules, and learn from its failed tests by morning will bring down the cost of experimentation and fundamentally change the pace at which science gets done. It will also give researchers the freedom to chase bold, strange questions they never would have risked their time on before, opening scientific doors we have yet to imagine.

While the AlphaFold template will certainly be key to incredible discoveries, it alone will not bring us to the end of science. Instead, the shift toward agentic AI represents a much rarer tier of breakthrough: a tool that envelops every field of science at once. Historically, tools of such scope have arrived just a handful of times: calculus, statistical inference, spectroscopy, the computer. Each revealed a world of problems no one had thought to formulate, and those problems, in turn, defined their fields anew. With agents, another such transformation is upon us.

Eric Schmidt was the CEO of Google from 2001 to 2011. In 2024, with his wife Wendy, he co-founded Schmidt Sciences, a philanthropic venture to fund unconventional areas of exploration in science & tech. 

Suhas Mahesh leads AI for Science work at the AI Center of Schmidt Sciences. He is a specialist in AI for materials discovery.

text:
🗞️17 November 2026 | Daily Edition: Pre-Market

Washington Licensed the Venue, the Bid Still Hasn't Shown Up

The CFTC cleared a blockchain-built perps exchange, Wells Fargo's clients became the biggest Bitcoin ETF holders on paper and Solana's foundation took control of a top crypto data site, while Bitcoin slipped back toward $64,000 and Nvidia's results loom.

Prepared around 5:50 AM EST on Tuesday 17 November. This edition picks up from Monday's US Close, prepared at 4:05 PM EST, and only adds what happened since: the evening session, Asia and the first hours of Europe. Crypto prices are live prints as of about 5:45 AM EST, and futures, oil, Treasury, dollar and gold figures are live overnight prints.

1⃣ Bitcoin poked above its weekly close after the bell, then bled through Asia

Bitcoin carried Monday afternoon's higher lows into the evening and printed about $65,475 in the 5:00 PM EST hour, briefly above the $65,315 weekly close. It could not hold it: Monday's daily candle closed near $64,815 at 7:00 PM EST. Asia bought one dip to about $64,320 in the 9:00 PM EST hour and pushed it back to $65,120 to $65,150 in the 10:00 PM EST hour, but every bounce after midnight made a lower high. The low so far is about $64,080 at 5:15 AM EST, as Europe opened, and it trades near $64,190, about 1.3% below last night's edition and about 0.5% lower over 24 hours.

🖊️ Market significance: The weekly close has now rejected price twice in under a day, once at Monday's open and again after the bell.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The afternoon divergence from the Nasdaq did not carry into Asia. Price is back above Monday's $64,030 post-open low, but only just, and that is the level I watch into the US open.

2⃣ Ether lost $1,800 again, Solana and Zcash held up

Ether reached $1,842 at 12:15 AM EST, matching Sunday night's overnight high, and was turned back for a second time. It fell to about $1,788 at 5:15 AM EST, under the $1,801 and $1,808 afternoon lows, and trades near $1,793, about 1.4% below last night's edition. Solana went the other way, up about 1.3% overnight to near $72.25, and XRP is near $0.957. Zcash is near $924, up about 3% to 4% since last night's edition, and Hyperliquid's HYPE is near $68.70.

🖊️ Market significance: Ether failed at the same $1,835 to $1,842 band that has capped it since the weekly close, and now sits just above Monday's $1,785 low.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Solana's strength during its own conference week is real but small. Ether is the weak leg of the majors this morning, and I would not call it a base until $1,785 holds on a retest.

3⃣ Shorts reloaded overnight as the big short book left

Bitcoin open interest on the largest on-chain perps venue rose about 2.7% since last night to about 38,750 BTC, and on a large offshore exchange it rose about 4.0% to about 31,850 BTC, while price fell about 1.3%. Bitcoin funding is flat, between about -0.001% and +0.001% per eight hours on the big offshore venues, and Ether funding has slipped slightly negative again. Meanwhile, on-chain trackers show Abraxas Capital, which one researcher linked to Monday's leaked API keys without confirmation from the firm, has closed almost all of its Hyperliquid shorts, leaving about $11.6 million open, with its account value down about $161 million in 24 hours to about $22.4 million.

🖊️ Market significance: Rising open interest into falling prices with flat funding means new shorts, not new longs, did most of the overnight positioning.

🗨️ My viewpoint: One large short seller left the market and others replaced it. That keeps squeeze fuel in place above $65,315, but it also tells me the marginal trader still leans bearish.

4⃣ ETF selling slowed to a trickle outside IBIT

Monday's spot Bitcoin ETFs other than BlackRock's IBIT lost about $68.6 million, led by Grayscale's GBTC and Fidelity's FBTC. IBIT's own Monday number is still not confirmed by two trackers, so I am leaving it out for now. Spot Ether ETFs lost about $8.4 million, while Solana ETFs took in about $11 million to $12 million, mostly into Bitwise's BSOL. Hyperliquid ETFs saw about $7.9 million of outflows.

🖊️ Market significance: After $1.065 billion of Bitcoin ETF outflows last week, Monday's selling outside IBIT was a fraction of the recent daily pace.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Slower selling is not buying. The IBIT figure decides whether Monday was the first flat day in more than a week or just a quieter red one.

5⃣ Wells Fargo's clients now hold the biggest Bitcoin ETF stake on file

Wells Fargo's third-quarter 13F, filed Monday afternoon, lists 49,577,094 IBIT shares at 30 September, worth about $2.35 billion, up from 24,396,222 shares in June. That makes it the largest reported institutional IBIT holder, ahead of Jane Street, Morgan Stanley and Bank of America. About 85% of the shares sit in its two brokerage arms, so these are client positions rather than the bank's own trading book. Harvard's endowment held 3.04 million IBIT shares, about $144 million, at quarter-end.

🖊️ Market significance: The largest US wealth platforms are now the main channel for Bitcoin ETF ownership, not hedge funds.

🗨️ My viewpoint: These are 30 September positions, taken with Bitcoin near $83,700, and Bitcoin is about 23% lower today. Advisor-held money is usually patient, but this is the cohort the next few weeks will test.

6⃣ The CFTC cleared its first blockchain-built derivatives exchange

At about 4:30 PM EST on Monday, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said the agency had approved the first exchange and clearinghouse applications for a firm using blockchain-based architecture to execute and settle derivatives. Backpack confirmed at 4:58 PM EST that it is the firm: its TLD Markets unit was designated a contract market on 16 November, and its TLD Clearing unit was registered as a clearinghouse on 13 November. Backpack plans leveraged crypto perpetual futures for US users, with crypto collateral, cross-margin, 24/7 trading and one global order book.

🖊️ Market significance: Onshore, leveraged, 24/7 crypto perps were the product US traders had to go offshore for. A regulated route now exists.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is the CFTC doing by licence what Congress has not done by statute. It lands hours before today's 3:00 PM EST Senate hearing for the CFTC nominees, which will test whether that approach has bipartisan support.

7⃣ The Binance hackers started moving their Ether

After selling down most of their smaller tokens, the wallets tied to the 29 October Binance theft moved about 74,880 ETH, roughly $137 million, across new addresses early this morning and began swapping it into Bitcoin through THORChain, according to on-chain trackers. They still hold more than 600,000 ETH and about 18,360 BTC that have not been laundered. Separately, the wallets behind Bitget's $387.5 million September hack have moved about 2,267 BTC, about $161 million, mostly into mixers over the past 11 days. Binance co-founder He Yi said frozen funds are controlled by law enforcement, not the exchange, and stay untouched unless a court orders a transfer.

🖊️ Market significance: More than $2 billion of stolen Bitcoin and Ether is still sitting in attacker wallets, and it has started to move.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Swapping Ether into Bitcoin through cross-chain routers is a laundering step, not open-market selling, but it adds steady supply into thin overnight liquidity. I watch the size of each batch.

8⃣ A web-testing tool planted address-swapping code on 178 sites, Ledger among them

An attacker abused a flaw in Optimizely's account signup on 16 November to inject code into customer pages at 178 organizations, including Ledger, HSBC, the BBC and Salesforce. The script swapped Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Tron and other wallet addresses in forms and in copied text for the attacker's own, and also skimmed card numbers. Optimizely said it removed the code and fixed the flaw. Wallets linked to the attack had received only about $7,040 by Monday evening, and Ledger said its devices' private keys were not affected.

🖊️ Market significance: The attacker never touched Ledger's servers or wallets. One vendor's script was enough to reach a hardware wallet maker's website.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The small haul is luck, not design. Checking the full address on the device screen before signing is the habit that defeats this kind of attack.

9⃣ A judge cleared the MEV brothers, a Robinhood engineer pleaded guilty

On Monday afternoon, Judge Jessica Clarke acquitted Anton and James Peraire-Bueno of wire fraud over the 12-second, $25 million Ethereum MEV trade of April 2023, ruling that prosecutors had not shown material misrepresentations. A first trial ended in a hung jury in November 2025. Separately, former Robinhood engineer Huaisong Xiang pleaded guilty to wire fraud in Manhattan for using confidential information about upcoming Robinhood crypto listings to trade Hyperliquid perps, and agreed to forfeit $125,523.

🖊️ Market significance: Courts are drawing a line between exploiting code, which this ruling did not treat as fraud, and trading on stolen information, which still is.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The acquittal will be read across DeFi as a green light for aggressive MEV. I read it more narrowly: wire fraud was the wrong tool, and that puts more pressure on Congress to write market-conduct rules for on-chain trading.

1⃣0⃣ Twenty-two fund managers signed up to sell tokenized funds on Solana

Project Harmonia, run by Allfunds Blockchain and the Solana Foundation, named a first cohort of 22 asset managers on Monday, including Apollo, Fidelity International, Schroders, Franklin Templeton, Wellington, AllianceBernstein, Janus Henderson, WisdomTree and Galaxy. Their tokenized funds will be distributed both through Allfunds' network of more than 3,300 asset managers and institutions and on Solana itself. The first funds are due to go live on Allfunds in the first quarter of 2027.

🖊️ Market significance: Fund distribution, not fund creation, has been the bottleneck for tokenized products. This plugs Solana into an existing wholesale fund network.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Harmonia matters more than most conference headlines because it comes with a launch quarter and named managers. I will judge it by the assets that arrive in 2027, not by the logos.

1⃣1⃣ Solana's foundation took a majority stake in a top crypto data site

The Solana Foundation's chief product officer said overnight that the foundation now holds a majority interest in CoinGecko, the crypto price and data platform. CoinGecko described the deal as backing from the foundation and plans wider coverage of stocks, real-world assets and derivatives, plus on-platform trading powered by Solana. No price or stake size was disclosed, and CoinGecko said its site, app and data feeds will keep running as usual.

🖊️ Market significance: One of the industry's most used neutral price references is now majority-owned by the foundation behind one blockchain.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The growth logic is clear, since a data site with tens of millions of monthly users is a trading funnel. The question the market will ask is whether rankings and listings stay neutral, and only a published governance setup can answer that.

1⃣2⃣ Holders took their biggest loss since July, one buyer kept stacking Ether

Bitcoin holders realized a net loss equal to about 25,800 BTC, the largest since 13 July, according to on-chain data. On the other side, wallets linked to Erik Voorhees bought another 13,134 ETH overnight and now hold about 84,840 ETH bought over six days at an average of about $1,931, with about $13 million of stablecoins left. At $1,793, that buyer is about 7% under water. Supply of the two largest stablecoins was steady, with USDT near $175.3 billion and USDC near $69.1 billion to $69.4 billion.

🖊️ Market significance: Capitulation-style loss taking on Bitcoin and steady dip buying on Ether are happening at the same time, and the dollar float on the sidelines is not growing.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Large realized losses often appear near local lows, but they confirm a bottom only after price stops falling. The Voorhees-linked buyer is close to spending its last stablecoins.

1⃣3⃣ Treasury buyers kept adding small amounts

Twenty One Capital bought 154.32 BTC on Monday for about $10 million in cash at an average of $64,801, taking it to about 43,668 BTC. The Smarter Web Company added 55 BTC this morning for 2,905 BTC in total. Strategy added a "USD Strength" measure to its dashboard and said its dollar reserves can pay 3.4 years of interest and dividends, about 41% of the weighted duration of its preferred stock, which it calls Digital Credit. In mining, Bitdeer said in an SEC filing that its chief technology officer, Yuling Ma, will step down on 30 November for personal reasons.

🖊️ Market significance: Treasury buying is continuing, but in sizes of tens of millions of dollars, not the billions that moved the market last year.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Strategy's new metric is aimed squarely at the forced-selling fear. Three years of cash cover makes a forced Bitcoin sale to pay dividends much less likely in the near term, which takes one tail risk off the table.

1⃣4⃣ Kalshi bought a stock broker, the CFTC nominees face the Senate today

Kalshi bought New York broker-dealer FB Securities in July and plans to offer stock and ETF trading within about two months, according to reports late Monday, building on the crypto, metals and single-stock perps it added this year. In Washington, the Senate Agriculture Committee holds its confirmation hearing for CFTC nominees Nathan Anonick and Matthew Rowland at 3:00 PM EST today.

🖊️ Market significance: Prediction markets are turning into full brokerages at the same time as the CFTC, their regulator, fills its empty seats.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Event contracts, perps and stocks in one app is the Robinhood model built from the other end. Today's hearing is the first public read on how a full commission would treat that bundle.

1⃣5⃣ Tether backed a Brazil dollar app, Korea's top exchanges shrank

Tether's investment arm put $15 million into Nomad to expand dollar accounts and stablecoin payments in Brazil. In South Korea, customer deposits at Upbit and Bithumb fell by about ₩2.5 trillion, roughly $1.87 billion, this year through the third quarter, and the value of crypto the two exchanges own fell 11.4% and 26.7%.

🖊️ Market significance: Dollar stablecoins keep expanding into emerging-market payments, while Korea's retail exchange money keeps leaving.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Brazil is where stablecoins are winning on usefulness, not speculation. Korea's shrinking deposits are a reminder that the retail bid that drove past altcoin rallies is much thinner this year.

1⃣6⃣ Asia sold chips on new US curbs, Nasdaq futures dipped about 0.3%

Asian stocks fell after Washington moved on Monday to close a loophole that let Chinese firms rent Nvidia computing power from data centres in other countries. South Korea's Kospi fell about 2.6% and Japan's Nikkei about 1.3%, and Europe's main indexes are down about 1%. At about 5:35 AM EST, S&P 500, Nasdaq 100 and Dow futures were each down about 0.3% to 0.4%. Nvidia's board set up a national security and export control oversight committee overnight, ahead of quarterly results after today's close.

🖊️ Market significance: Futures point to a fourth straight losing day for tech, but a mild one so far, which leaves Nvidia's results as the session's main risk event.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Bitcoin only managed to break from the Nasdaq for one afternoon. If Nvidia's numbers steady tech, I expect crypto to get a relief bid. If they don't, Monday's lows are the first test.

1⃣7⃣ Two more ships hit mines, oil barely moved, yields eased

Iran's navy said two vessels, an LNG carrier and an oil tanker, caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. Brent is near $92.40 and WTI near $85.65, both roughly flat after Monday's 3% drop. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5.10%, about 2 to 3 basis points lower, the dollar index is flat near 103.6 and gold is up about 0.15% near $3,859.

🖊️ Market significance: The oil market is shrugging off ship strikes in Hormuz because it is pricing a supply surplus, which keeps inflation pressure from energy contained.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Yields easing is helpful, but at 5.10% the 10-year is still a headwind, and rate futures still price a December hike.

1⃣8⃣ Retail sales at 8:30 AM EST, Nvidia after the close

October retail sales are due at 8:30 AM EST, and the homebuilder sentiment index follows at 10:00 AM EST. Fed Governor Christopher Waller, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem and New York Fed President John Williams all speak today, and the Fed minutes follow on Wednesday at 2:00 PM EST.

🖊️ Market significance: A strong spending print would add to the case for a December hike, the one macro outcome crypto has struggled with all month.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The order of events matters: data at 8:30 AM EST, the CFTC hearing at 3:00 PM EST and Nvidia after the 4:00 PM EST close. Any one of them can move Bitcoin by 2%, so I keep size small until the evening.

🗨️ My Overall Viewpoint:
The overnight session gave back Monday afternoon's progress. Bitcoin tested the $65,315 weekly close after the bell, failed, and drifted to about $64,080 by the European open, while Ether was rejected again at $1,842 and lost $1,800. Positioning tells the same story: open interest climbed while price fell and funding stayed flat, so fresh shorts replaced the large short book that Abraxas closed. Holders realized their biggest loss since July, and the Binance hackers started moving their Ether. Yet the structural news was some of the best of the month. The CFTC licensed a blockchain-built perps exchange onshore, Wells Fargo's clients emerged as the largest Bitcoin ETF holders, 22 asset managers committed tokenized funds to Solana and ETF selling outside IBIT slowed to about $69 million. The building continues. The buying does not, yet.

For the US session, my Bitcoin support is $64,030 to $64,080, Monday's post-open low and this morning's low, then $63,830 and $63,725, Monday's and Sunday's lows, with $61,950 behind them. Resistance is $64,815, Monday's daily close, then $65,150, the Asia bounce high, $65,315, the weekly close, and $65,475, last night's high. A close back above $65,315 would turn this into a range with an upward bias, while a break of $63,725 puts the $62,000 area in play. For Ether, support is $1,785 to $1,788, Monday's low and this morning's low, then $1,772 and $1,709. Resistance is $1,808, then $1,818, last night's edition level, and $1,835 to $1,842, the band that has capped every bounce since Sunday. I stay defensive. text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the evening of November 17, 1973, Richard Nixon walked into a hotel ballroom at Walt Disney World in Orlando and faced four hundred Associated Press managing editors with the cameras already rolling. He had come up from Key Biscayne carrying the weight of the Saturday Night Massacre that had detonated only weeks earlier. Attorney General Elliot Richardson and Deputy Attorney General William Ruckelshaus had resigned rather than fire Special Prosecutor Archibald Cox. Solicitor General Robert Bork had carried out the order. The special prosecutor’s office, the Senate Watergate Committee, the federal courts, and the major newspapers were all in full pursuit. The press had already decided the presidency was finished.

For more than an hour Nixon stood at the podium and took their questions. They pressed him on the break-in at the Democratic National Committee headquarters, on the cover-up, on campaign financing, on his personal taxes, and on whether he had ever profited from public office. He answered that he had made his mistakes, that he had not supervised his campaign as closely as he should have, but that in all his years of public life he had never profited from public service and had never obstructed justice. He had earned every cent he possessed. Then he looked into the cameras and said the words that would outlive the night:

“People have got to know whether or not their president is a crook. Well, I’m not a crook. I’ve earned everything I’ve got.”

He also delivered a grim piece of dark humor that only a man under that kind of pressure would offer. Asked why he was flying without a backup aircraft, Nixon replied that by taking only one plane he was saving energy and taxpayer money—and possibly time on the impeachment process—because if that one plane went down, “they don’t have to impeach me.” Those who were in the room said he looked tense. The editors did not let up. The networks did not let up. The phrase was already being written into the next day’s headlines before he left the hall.

What followed is known. The tapes continued to surface. The legal pressure mounted. On August 9, 1974, Nixon became the only president in American history to resign the office. Yet the night in Orlando remains a study in a president standing alone against a press corps, a special prosecutor, and a political class that had already rendered its verdict. He did not plead. He did not apologize for the declaration itself. He told the country, in plain English, that he was not a crook. Whether one accepts the claim or rejects it, the moment revealed the raw condition of the modern presidency once the institutions and the media decide a man must be driven from office. The fight is rarely limited to the evidence alone.

text:
Socialism Versus Capitalism, It’s A 2016 Referendum
by Greg Allen
Published Oct 1, 2016 

I’ve heard many say the 2016 presidential election is the most important one they can recall in a lifetime.  Why are so many individuals saying that?  Without articulating it, I believe a score of people believe the very existence of the United States is at stake.  Many believe “The American Dream” is threatened.  

Hundreds of elections have been held through the annals of time, so what makes this one so different?  Simply put, I believe 2016 will go down in history as a national referendum on socialism versus capitalism and many believe whoever the winner is the country will either wither or bloom once more.

An estimated 100 million Americans watched the first presidential debate between Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton.  Both candidates have extremely poor approval ratings, some speculate the lowest in history, so why is this election so important when so many distrust these individuals?

Dissatisfaction in the electorate, at an all-time high, may explain why.

Donald Trump, a capitalist, claims he’ll make America great again and explained how he’d accomplish that during the debate.  Hillary Clinton, a liberal, is of the opinion more socialism is best.  During the debate she said she would excessively tax the rich.  How does one define what rich is?  I may be one of modest means, but I’m an American who cherishes freedom and that indeed makes me a rich soul.  The American Dream can be defined by many things, but prosperity is most certainly at the top of the list.  Hillary Clinton, by making that statement, is essentially saying she wants to attack the American Dream and penalize those who live it.  I see failure in that type of logic.

The Nation’s 20 trillion dollars in debt and a record number of Americans are on disability and food stamps now – I find that frightening.

Public perception used to be it was shameful to be on welfare or food stamps, but financial mediocrity doesn’t seem all-that-unusual anymore.  Has the American Dream been overhauled?

Is a mediocre pursuit of happiness the new norm for Americans?

Is trifleness a new low when it comes to education too?  Is it to be expected that half of all college grads can’t find work even though they’ve spent thousands of dollars, and went in debt to do so, to obtain a degree that may or may not suffice anymore?

What does it say about our culture when Rutgers University offers a course in “Underwater basket weaving,” that Montclair State University offers a class titled “How to watch television,” or that Occidental College offers credits for attending a course called “Stupidity?”

Society has fallen prey to a progressively bent logic, which isn’t really progressive at all but regressive.

Many have failed to recognize the socialist plight that plagues us.

For many Americans it’s not in their DNA to do just enough to get by.  Yet for many more they see life as mediocre at best and the entitlement stigma they feel they deserve has attached itself.  For many, to just exist in life is fine and it can become a reality if they only relent to the entangling dependence government offers.

With what we see manifesting itself in Washington, D.C. one can only conclude that mediocrity is the new norm – if that’s so, the American Dream is dead.  However, I believe there are scores of those who won’t allow that idealization of what America is to just go away.

The American Dream imparts that hard work and determination isn’t some novelty and success can be accomplished by anyone.  American Pride resides in many, still, and to embrace an ideology that’s counterintuitive to that is something that will be pushed back by those who wanna dream.

America is truly an astonishing place and although she may have lost her way that fair Lady has by no means doused that flame of liberty in a muddied pond of hopelessness.

Socialism or Capitalism?  Mediocrity or Prosperity?  It’ll be interesting to see who walks away with all the marbles come November.

Greg Allen’s column, Thinkin’ Out Loud, was published bi-monthly from 2009 to 2017.  He’s an author, a former nationally syndicated columnist and the founder of Builder of the Spirit Ministries in Jamestown, Indiana.  He can be reached at https://t.co/9QdchPfdBy.

text:
People who argue for reduced police funding usually mean one of three things: modest cuts and reallocation of some budget, narrowing what police are asked to do, or (more rarely) near-total replacement of traditional policing. Here are the main reasons commonly offered for wanting less funding:
1. Reallocate money to other priorities
Police departments often consume a large share of municipal general-fund budgets—frequently in the 20–40% range in many U.S. cities, and sometimes higher for public safety overall.​ Advocates argue that this crowds out spending on education, housing, mental-health services, job programs, or youth programs. They claim these address root causes of crime more effectively over the long term than additional officers or equipment.
Readsludge
2. Police handle too many non-crime problems
A large share of police calls involve mental-health crises, homelessness, substance issues, noise complaints, or welfare checks rather than violent or property crime. Proponents of “unbundling” say specialized responders (clinicians, social workers, or unarmed crisis teams) could handle many of these more effectively and at lower cost, shrinking the need for a large armed force. Some cities have piloted this for certain call types.
3. Reduce police–civilian contact to lower harm
Critics point to racial disparities in stops, use of force, and fatal shootings (Black Americans are about 13–14% of the population but a higher share of people killed by police). They argue that less contact automatically means fewer bad outcomes. Some also cite the historical origins of modern U.S. policing in slave patrols and enforcement of segregation-era laws, claiming the institution is structurally biased and cannot be reformed sufficiently.​
Britannica
4. Past reforms have not delivered
Body cameras, de-escalation training, civilian oversight boards, and consent decrees have not eliminated high-profile incidents or changed the overall pattern of outcomes enough for some advocates. Their conclusion is that the only reliable way to reduce police violence is to reduce the size and role of police departments rather than trying to improve them.
5. Libertarian / limited-government version
This approach focuses on the laws police are required to enforce rather than on race or reallocation to social programs. Repealing or deprioritizing “victimless” offenses (drug possession/sale, prostitution, loitering/vagrancy, many minor traffic stops) would eliminate a substantial share of arrests—over 20% in some years for drugs, alcohol, prostitution, and vagrancy alone. The argument is that this would:
Free officers to focus on crimes with clear victims (homicide, robbery, burglary, assault).
Reduce high-risk encounters and discretionary enforcement that drives racial disparities.
Allow smaller police budgets (or the same budgets used more efficiently) without increasing serious crime.
Cato Institute and similar groups have made this case explicitly, noting that drug-prohibition enforcement alone costs tens of billions annually while generating underground markets and additional violence.​
Cato
Evidence and practical outcomes
The empirical record is mixed and contested. Quasi-experimental studies generally find that increases in police numbers reduce crime (especially violent crime) in the short-to-medium term, though the size of the effect varies. The large 2020 homicide spike was real (roughly +30% nationally), but research indicates most cities did not permanently cut police budgets; the sharper change was “de-policing” (fewer proactive stops) amid protests, low morale, and staffing losses. Crime rates later fell substantially in 2023–2025 in many places, often alongside restored or increased funding and staffing recovery. Cities that made deeper or longer-lasting cuts (e.g., certain cases in Austin, Portland, Minneapolis) generally saw larger crime increases before later reversing course, though COVID-era disruptions, gun purchases, and other factors complicate simple causation.
In short, the most common rationales are resource reallocation toward social services, narrowing police responsibilities, reducing contact to limit harm, skepticism that reforms work, and (from a different direction) simply enforcing fewer laws so that fewer police are needed. These are the main ways someone might arrive at wanting police funded less; the strength of each depends on how one weighs the trade-offs around crime, liberty, equity, and government scope.

text:
IF I WERE YOU, reading that a Milan court has put Revolut's Italian business under judicial administration, I would skip the mafia headlines and the €76.5 million. I would look at one number: 265 to zero.

Revolut is not under investigation. Its operating model is. Facts first, with their sources. My reading after, and I will say where it begins.

On Monday, Italy's financial police executed a decree of the Milan court's preventive-measures section. It places Revolut Bank UAB, the group's Lithuanian bank, under judicial administration for one year. The order is limited to the Italian business.

The timing is hard to miss. Twelve days earlier, on 4 November, Revolut closed a secondary share sale that values the group at $115 billion, 53% above the $75 billion of a year ago. In October its Italian arm announced that it had passed 6 million customers, more than one Italian in ten by its own count, and its general manager said the ambition was to become the first bank in the country.

So Europe's most valuable private technology company now has two court-appointed administrators sitting beside its managers in its fourth-largest market.

What the court did

The legal basis is Article 34 of Italy's anti-mafia code. It is a preventive measure, not a penalty. It applies to a business that, through negligence rather than intent, ends up making life easier for people under investigation or convicted for serious crimes. Milan prosecutors have used it in recent years on fashion houses and logistics groups. In October 2024 they used it on a bank, Banca Progetto, and the court lifted that measure early, nine months later.

The state does not take over. Management stays. Two administrators work alongside it with wide powers of access and inspection and a 15-point remediation plan, according to Reuters, which reviewed the 39-page ruling. Revolut has five days to name a liaison officer and 60 days to present an action plan. The administrators owe the judges a first report within 30 days, a full assessment of the anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer controls within 90, and progress reports at least every quarter. Italian media report a hearing on 25 February 2027. By law the measure runs for up to a year and can be extended to two. It can also end sooner if the work is done.

Because Revolut operates in Italy through a branch and not a subsidiary, the order is formally addressed to the Lithuanian bank, while the oversight covers only Italy.

What the court did not do

It did not open a criminal case against the bank. Neither Revolut nor its managers are under investigation. The judges found negligence, not complicity. Accounts, cards and payments work as before, and deposits remain covered up to €100,000 by the Lithuanian guarantee scheme.

The people whose accounts are described in the decree are suspects or defendants in other proceedings, and some have been convicted. Those who have not are presumed innocent. I will not name them here.

Revolut says it acknowledges the decision, will cooperate fully with the Italian authorities, takes its anti-money-laundering obligations extremely seriously and keeps investing in its controls. It does not comment on individual accounts.

What the court found

The case has two origins. The first is a 2024 inspection by the Milan financial police of Revolut Digital Assets Europe, the Cyprus company that runs crypto services for the group's European customers. It produced a report in December 2024 alleging more than one million breaches of the rules on customer due diligence and record keeping, and 60 suspicious transactions that were not reported. The second is a tax-fraud investigation opened in Milan in 2025, in which Revolut accounts kept turning up.

From there the investigators built a sample: 24 people living in the Milan district, each under investigation or already convicted. According to the ruling, they concealed financial flows of €41.9 million through Revolut accounts between 2021 and 2026. In the same period other banks filed 265 suspicious-transaction reports on those same 24 people. Revolut filed none.

The prosecutors' total is larger: €76.5 million of transfers, concealment or diversion of funds. They also cite more than €4.6 million that was already subject to seizure orders and moved without being caught in time. Italian press accounts of the decree add texture: accounts opened days after a seizure, a company account with some €7 million of turnover and a balance close to zero, transfers abroad in slices of €12,000 to €26,000. The customers include people whom investigators tie to 'ndrangheta clans, to the Milan inquiry known as Hydra, to the Equalize data-theft case and to an alleged underground bank serving organised crime.

There is one more detail, and it may be the most telling. In September the prosecutors served the bank with an order to produce records. According to the Italian news agency ANSA, the decree says the answers were partial. One of the fifteen tasks now given to the administrators is to audit how Revolut retrieves data and hands it to law enforcement.

The conclusion is that none of this was episodic. Milan's chief prosecutor called it a "stable management model". In their filing, as quoted by Reuters, prosecutors wrote that the bank had become a "financial reservoir" for serious criminals, and that this gave it an unfair advantage over competitors with adequate controls.

Keep that last clause in mind. It is an argument about competition, made by a prosecutor.

The wrong number

Here the interpretation begins.

€76.5 million over five years is not a large sum. Revolut held £50.2 billion of customer balances at the end of 2025. Italy's financial intelligence unit received 162,059 suspicious-transaction reports in 2025, covering operations worth about €100 billion. Danske Bank's Estonian branch handled some €200 billion of payments between 2007 and 2015, much of it suspicious by the bank's own account. ING paid €775 million to Dutch prosecutors in 2018 and ABN Amro €480 million in 2021.

Measured by volume, this is a footnote. Nobody is claiming that Revolut is a mafia bank, and anyone who writes that headline has skipped the court's own finding of negligence.

The right number

The number that matters is 265 to zero.

It matters because it is a controlled comparison. Same people. Same years. Same country. Different banks. The incumbents, with their branches and their legacy systems, saw something 265 times. The bank whose pitch is superior technology saw nothing, or saw it and did not report it. I do not know which, and either answer is uncomfortable. The first is a failure of detection. The second is a failure of reporting.

And these were not invisible customers. Several were named in court papers and in newspapers. That is why the remediation plan requires the screening of adverse media, with human review behind the automated tools.

A third of the workforce

Now set that against what the company says about itself. In its 2025 annual report Revolut states that its systems analysed more than 10 billion transactions during the year and that over one-third of its global workforce works in financial crime prevention.

One-third of the workforce. Zero reports on 24 suspects.

I do not think the two statements contradict each other. I think they describe two different jobs.

Fraud and money laundering are different economic problems. Fraud costs the bank money: refunds, chargebacks, complaints, lost customers. A bank that fights fraud is defending its own income statement, and it will invest in that without being asked.

Laundering is the opposite. A customer who launders does not complain. He funds the account, pays the fees and moves volume. Reporting him produces a cost, loses a client and earns nothing. The benefit goes to the state. Suspicious-transaction reporting is a public good that private firms are required to supply, and a system left to optimise its own losses will find fraud and miss laundering.

There is a hint of this in the official statistics. Italy's financial intelligence unit says the 11.5% rise in reports in 2025 came largely from newly registered reporters, online banks in particular, and was mostly linked to scams and cyber-fraud. That is consistent with my reading. It does not prove it.

Too strict and too lax at once

A second fact points the same way. In April this year Italy's competition authority fined Revolut companies more than €11 million for unfair commercial practices. Part of it, €5 million, concerned the way accounts were suspended, limited and blocked, and how little customers were told about it. Revolut rejects the findings, has said it will appeal and argues that account checks are mandatory.

Put the two decisions side by side. In the same country, in the same year, one authority says the bank handled account freezes aggressively and without clear information, and a court says it let through people whose names were in case files.

That is not a staffing problem. It is a calibration problem. A monitoring system produces false positives and false negatives together when it does not know enough about who the customer is. Which is what the December 2024 report alleged: more than a million gaps in customer due diligence and record keeping. Transaction monitoring built on thin customer knowledge can block the student who receives an unusual transfer and wave through the shell company with a tidy pattern.

Speed is the product

Why would a bank know too little about its customers? Because knowing them is slow, and the product is speed.

Revolut added a million Italian customers between the five-million mark earlier this year and October. Group-wide it went from 68.3 million retail customers at the end of 2025 to more than 80 million by early November, roughly twelve million in ten months on my arithmetic. Revenue rose 46% in 2025 to £4.5 billion and pre-tax profit 57% to £1.7 billion.

Look at the Italian numbers more closely. Savings held with Revolut in Italy passed €1.2 billion in October, almost four times the level of a year earlier. That is about €200 per customer, on my arithmetic, and it covers savings products, not current-account balances. Still, it describes a bank that is for most Italians a second account: small balances, frequent movement. That is a fine business. It is also the setting in which a pass-through account looks like everyone else's.

Accounts opened in minutes, from a phone, without a branch: that is the cost advantage over the incumbents, and it is a legitimate one. But part of that advantage is the cost of the checks. Every bank that filed one of those 265 reports paid for an analyst to write it, and may well have lost the customer afterwards. The bank that filed none kept both the saving and the client.

This is the prosecutors' competition argument, and I think it is the most important sentence in the case. Compliance is a cost of production. A firm that does not bear it underprices those that do.

Who captures the value, who pays, who absorbs the risk

The value is captured by shareholders and employees. The November transaction was a secondary sale: existing holders sold stock at a $115 billion valuation and no new money went into the company.

The cost is paid by the state, when assets under seizure move before anyone notices. It is paid by competitors that fund the controls. And it is paid by ordinary customers, who meet the system at its bluntest when an account is frozen without explanation.

The penalties so far do not change the arithmetic. The Bank of Lithuania fined Revolut Bank €3.5 million in April 2025 for failings in the monitoring of business relationships and transactions. It was the largest fine that central bank had ever imposed, and the bank noted that no confirmed case of laundering had been identified. Add the Italian competition fine and the total is roughly €15 million, well under 1% of one year's pre-tax profit on my arithmetic. The Milan measure carries no fine at all.

The risk sits somewhere else: in the licences.

Who supervises a bank that is everywhere?

Count the authorities. The group is run from London. The bank has been licensed in Lithuania since 2021. Since the start of 2025 its European holding company has been supervised directly by the European Central Bank, which set its Pillar 2 capital requirement for 2026 at 4.5% of risk-weighted assets, the highest of any bank under its direct supervision, according to Bloomberg. Press reports in 2025 said the ECB had asked for stronger controls after a review. Anti-money-laundering supervision is national: the Bank of Lithuania at home, the Bank of Italy and its financial intelligence unit for the Italian branch. Consumer protection sits with the competition authority. The crypto arm is in Cyprus. A second bank was licensed in France in August, and Western European customers, Italians included, are due to move to it over time.

With all those supervisors, the first authority to act decisively in Italy was a criminal court, using a statute written for companies infiltrated by the mafia.

The supervisors are not absent. Reuters reports that the financial intelligence unit has completed an inspection of the Italian branch and that its findings are expected shortly, and that Bank of Italy inspectors are separately examining transparency and customer protection. But the order of events says something. A prosecutor with a sample of 24 names moved faster than the architecture built to prevent the problem.

There is a precedent for what a supervisor can do. In March 2022 the Bank of Italy barred the Italian branch of N26, the German online bank, from taking on new customers after an inspection found serious anti-money-laundering shortcomings. N26 began onboarding again, partially, at the end of June 2024. Two years and three months without growth in a market.

So which is harsher? The Milan measure sounds dramatic because the word mafia is in the statute. In practice it is therapeutic: Revolut can keep opening accounts every day of the year it lasts. A supervisory ban sounds administrative and stops the engine. What the Bank of Italy does with its own findings will matter more for the business than Monday's decree.

One practical question follows from the group's reorganisation. The court's order is addressed to the Lithuanian bank. If Italian accounts migrate to the French one, the remediation has to travel with them, and a third national supervisor enters the room. I would want to know how the court, the central banks and the ECB intend to coordinate that.

Europe's answer is on its way, slowly. The new Anti-Money Laundering Authority will select up to 40 cross-border groups in 2027 and supervise them directly from 2028. Until then a bank with one licence and dozens of markets answers to each national regime separately, and to any prosecutor with jurisdiction over a branch.

The passport is European. The enforcement is national.

Why $115 billion is exposed

A valuation like that is a price on licences. Since the start of 2026, by its own account, Revolut has launched banks in the United Kingdom, Mexico, Australia and New Zealand, and it has conditional approval for a banking charter in the United States, where it plans to open in 2027. Every one of those is a regulator's judgment on the quality of controls.

The company understands this. The head of its American unit said at a Reuters event on Monday that a serious problem in one market has consequences in others, the United States included.

Compliance debt behaves like technical debt. It is cheap to accumulate while you grow and expensive to repay at scale, and it is repaid on someone else's timetable. A bank adding more than a million customers a month cannot remediate customer files faster than it creates them unless it slows down or spends heavily. Either choice shows up in the numbers that support the valuation.

What the incumbents should not conclude

It would be easy for the traditional banks to read 265 to zero as a certificate of virtue. I would not.

A count of reports measures activity, not quality. Italy's financial intelligence unit itself tracks the share of reports that carry little or no laundering risk. And the largest laundering scandals in Europe happened inside old banks with marble lobbies. The difference is one of kind. For Danske or ING, the failure was a scandal inside the model. For a bank whose product is automated onboarding, it is a test of the model.

Six million Italians did not open a Revolut account by mistake. I assume they did it for price and convenience, and the incumbents had decades to offer both. The right conclusion is not fewer challengers. It is the same rule, priced into every business model.

What it means for a customer

Today, nothing changes. The measure does not touch accounts, cards or payments.

What will change is the questions. The plan requires a review of customer due diligence, beneficial ownership and risk profiles, and of digital onboarding and card issuance. Expect requests for documents, and expect some accounts to be reviewed or closed. That is the remediation working, not the bank failing.

The honest caveats

Three of them.

First, I have not read the decree. I have read Reuters' account of the 39-page ruling, the prosecutors' statement as reported by Italian agencies, and Italian press coverage.

Second, the figures do not fully reconcile. The ruling attributes €41.9 million to 24 people; the prosecutors speak of €76.5 million in total. Reuters reports 265 reports by other banks over 2021 to 2026; Italian newspapers cite 112 for a narrower window, from January 2023 to July 2024. The prosecutors count about 5 million Italian customers and 50 million worldwide; the company says more than 6 million and more than 80 million.

Third, a preventive decree is not a judgment. It was issued on the prosecutors' request, the standard is negligence, and Revolut has not yet argued its case before a court.

What I would monitor

The administrators' first report, due within 30 days, and the full assessment at 90. Revolut's action plan at 60 days. The hearing reported for 25 February, and whether the court ends the measure early, as it did for Banca Progetto.

The findings of Italy's financial intelligence unit, and whether the Bank of Italy restricts new customers, as it did with N26.

Whether prosecutors or supervisors elsewhere in Europe run the same test: take a list of known suspects and count the reports each bank filed.

The American charter and the timing of any listing.

The appeal against the competition fine.

And one disclosure Revolut could make tomorrow: the number of suspicious-transaction reports it files, by country and per million customers, next to its peers.

That is the criterion. Not the share of the workforce assigned to financial crime. Not the billions of transactions analysed. Reports filed on the right people, and the time it takes to answer a prosecutor's request.

Count the reports, not the staff.

An account can be opened in minutes. A customer cannot be known in minutes.

Roberto Balbino | Founder & CEO, Fintech SCB
