text:
🌌 100 FACTS ABOUT AURORAS: THE NORTHERN AND SOUTHERN LIGHTS

☀️ HOW AURORAS WORK
𝟏. Auroras are light given off when charged particles from the Sun collide with gases in Earth's upper atmosphere

𝟐. The particles travel on the solar wind, a stream of plasma that flows out from the Sun at roughly 400 to 800 km per second

𝟑. Earth's magnetic field steers the particles toward the polar regions, which is why auroras gather around the poles

𝟒. The particles excite oxygen and nitrogen atoms; when those atoms relax, they release light

𝟓. Most auroras glow at altitudes of about 100 to 300 km, far above clouds and planes

𝟔. The lower edge rarely dips below about 80 to 90 km

𝟕. The tops of red auroras can reach 400 km or more

𝟖. Auroras form in ring-shaped belts around each magnetic pole called auroral ovals

𝟗. The ovals are centred on the geomagnetic poles, not the geographic North and South Poles

𝟏𝟎. The northern lights are the aurora borealis; the southern lights are the aurora australis

𝟏𝟏. Northern and southern auroras often happen at the same time and can look like near mirror images

𝟏𝟐. Auroras happen during the day too, but sunlight usually drowns them out

𝟏𝟑. Much of the energy comes from Earth's magnetotail, the long stretched-out tail of the magnetosphere on the night side

𝟏𝟒. Sudden releases of that stored energy are called substorms, when the sky can explode with fast-moving light within minutes

𝟏𝟓. A large aurora can dump hundreds of gigawatts of power into the upper atmosphere

🎨 THE COLOURS
𝟏𝟔. Green is the most common colour, from oxygen at around 100 to 250 km, at a wavelength of 557.7 nm

𝟏𝟕. Red comes from oxygen higher up, usually above about 250 km, at 630 nm

𝟏𝟖. The red oxygen glow takes up to about 2 minutes to emit, so it only survives in the thin upper air where collisions are rare

𝟏𝟗. Blue and violet come mostly from nitrogen

𝟐𝟎. Pink or magenta fringes along the bottom edge are typically nitrogen glowing low in the atmosphere

𝟐𝟏. Yellow and orange tones can appear where red and green light overlap

𝟐𝟐. Our eyes are most sensitive to green, which is one reason it dominates what we see

𝟐𝟑. Phone and DSLR cameras often catch colours the eye cannot, because they collect light for several seconds

𝟐𝟒. Faint auroras can look grey or white to the naked eye, since our colour vision weakens in the dark

𝟐𝟓. All-red auroras are rare and are often seen far from the poles during strong storms

🌀 SHAPES AND TYPES
𝟐𝟔. Auroras can appear as quiet arcs, rippling curtains, rays, spirals, patches or a glowing diffuse haze

𝟐𝟕. A corona forms when rays seem to burst from a point directly overhead; it is a perspective effect of parallel rays

𝟐𝟖. Pulsating auroras switch on and off every few seconds like a slow heartbeat

𝟐𝟗. Flickering auroras can shimmer several times per second

𝟑𝟎. Black auroras are dark gaps or shapes within the glow where no light is emitted

𝟑𝟏. STEVE (Strong Thermal Emission Velocity Enhancement) is a narrow purple-white ribbon studied with help from citizen scientists from 2016

𝟑𝟐. STEVE is technically not an aurora, as it is not produced by the usual particle rain

𝟑𝟑. STEVE is sometimes joined by a 'picket fence' of short green stripes

𝟑𝟒. Auroral 'dunes' are wave-like green stripes in the upper atmosphere that were first described in 2020 thanks to amateur photographers

𝟑𝟓. Proton auroras, caused by incoming protons, are usually faint and diffuse

🌍 WHERE TO SEE THEM
𝟑𝟔. The best latitudes for the northern lights are roughly 65° to 72° north

𝟑𝟕. 🇳🇴 Tromsø in Norway, about 350 km north of the Arctic Circle, is one of the world's most popular aurora cities

𝟑𝟖. 🇮🇸 Iceland lies close to the auroral oval and sees aurora on many clear, dark nights

𝟑𝟗. 🇫🇮 Finnish Lapland, including Rovaniemi and Saariselkä, offers glass igloos for sky-watching from bed

𝟒𝟎. 🇸🇪 Abisko in Sweden is famous for a 'blue hole' of clearer skies created by the surrounding mountains

𝟒𝟏. 🇨🇦 Yellowknife in Canada is often called one of the best aurora spots on Earth thanks to flat terrain and dry winter weather

𝟒𝟐. 🇺🇸 Fairbanks in Alaska sits under the auroral oval and has run aurora forecasts for decades

𝟒𝟑. 🇬🇱 Greenland offers auroras over icebergs and fjords

𝟒𝟒. 🇷🇺 Murmansk is a well-known aurora destination in Russia's far north

𝟒𝟓. 🇬🇧 Scotland's far north, including Shetland, sees the 'mirrie dancers' several times a year

𝟒𝟔. 🇦🇶 Antarctica gets the most aurora australis, but few people are there to see it

𝟒𝟕. 🇦🇺 Tasmania is the most popular place to see the southern lights from a big populated landmass

𝟒𝟖. 🇳🇿 Stewart Island in New Zealand has the Māori name Rakiura, often translated as 'land of glowing skies'

𝟒𝟗. 🇦🇷 🇨🇱 Southern Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego can see the aurora australis during strong activity

𝟓𝟎. Dark skies far from city lights make a huge difference

𝟓𝟏. The aurora season in the far north runs roughly September to March, when nights are long enough

𝟓𝟐. In summer, the Arctic has midnight sun, so the aurora is there but invisible

𝟓𝟑. Activity often peaks within an hour or two of local midnight, though shows can come at any time of night

𝟓𝟒. Some studies suggest more geomagnetic activity near the spring and autumn equinoxes, linked to the Russell-McPherron effect

🌞 SOLAR STORMS
𝟓𝟓. Big auroras follow solar storms, especially coronal mass ejections that hurl billions of tonnes of plasma into space

𝟓𝟔. A coronal mass ejection can reach Earth in about 1 to 3 days

𝟓𝟕. The Kp index rates geomagnetic activity from 0 to 9; the higher the number, the farther from the poles the aurora can be seen

𝟓𝟖. NOAA's G-scale ranks geomagnetic storms from G1 (minor) to G5 (extreme)

𝟓𝟗. The Sun goes through an activity cycle of about 11 years, and auroras are most frequent near and just after solar maximum

𝟔𝟎. Solar Cycle 25 reached its maximum around late 2024, according to NASA and NOAA

𝟔𝟏. The Carrington Event of 1859 is the most famous geomagnetic storm on record

𝟔𝟐. During it, auroras were reportedly seen as far south as Cuba and Hawaii

𝟔𝟑. Gold miners in the Rocky Mountains reportedly woke up and started making breakfast, thinking it was morning

𝟔𝟒. Telegraph lines sparked and some operators said they could send messages with the batteries disconnected

𝟔𝟓. A storm in May 1921 also pushed auroras to unusually low latitudes and disrupted telegraph and telephone systems

𝟔𝟔. In March 1989 a geomagnetic storm caused a 9-hour blackout across Québec, Canada

𝟔𝟕. On 10 to 11 May 2024 the first G5 storm in more than 20 years painted skies across much of the world

𝟔𝟖. In May 2024 auroras were photographed from places as far apart as Mexico, northern India and southern Europe

𝟔𝟗. A strong storm in October 2024 brought another round of low-latitude auroras

𝟕𝟎. The US Space Weather Prediction Center issues forecasts and alerts so grid operators and satellite teams can prepare

📜 HISTORY AND MYTH
𝟕𝟏. The name 'aurora borealis' is often credited to Galileo in the early 1600s

𝟕𝟐. Aurora was the Roman goddess of the dawn; Boreas was the Greek god of the north wind

𝟕𝟑. Captain James Cook is credited with naming the aurora australis in 1773 after seeing it in the Indian Ocean

𝟕𝟒. Some of the oldest possible aurora records come from ancient Mesopotamian astronomical texts

𝟕𝟓. In some Finnish folklore, a fire fox swept its tail across the snow to throw sparks into the sky

𝟕𝟔. The Finnish word for aurora, revontulet, is often translated as 'fox fires'

𝟕𝟕. Some Sámi traditions say you should not wave, whistle or sing at the lights

𝟕𝟖. In some Inuit stories the lights are spirits playing a ball game in the sky

𝟕𝟗. A popular modern tale links the lights to the shields of the Valkyries, though historians doubt it comes from Norse sources

𝟖𝟎. In medieval Europe, red auroras were sometimes read as omens of war or plague

𝟖𝟏. Kristian Birkeland, a Norwegian scientist, argued around 1900 that auroras are driven by electric currents from the Sun

𝟖𝟐. Birkeland built a 'terrella', a small magnetised globe in a vacuum chamber, to recreate auroras in his lab

𝟖𝟑. Birkeland's face appeared on Norway's 200-kroner banknote

𝟖𝟒. Electric currents that run along magnetic field lines between space and the polar upper atmosphere are called Birkeland currents

🚀 SPACE AND OTHER WORLDS
𝟖𝟓. Astronauts on the International Space Station sometimes fly right through or above auroral displays

𝟖𝟔. From orbit, auroras look like glowing green rings wrapped around the poles

𝟖𝟕. Jupiter has the most powerful auroras in the Solar System, hundreds of times more energetic than Earth's

𝟖𝟖. Jupiter's volcanic moon Io feeds particles into the planet's auroras and leaves a glowing 'footprint' in them

𝟖𝟗. Saturn, Uranus and Neptune all have auroras too

𝟗𝟎. Mars has patchy auroras tied to magnetised rocks in its crust, and NASA's Perseverance rover photographed a visible Martian aurora in 2024

𝟗𝟏. Auroras on Jupiter's moon Ganymede helped scientists conclude it likely hides a saltwater ocean below its surface

𝟗𝟐. Auroras on other planets have been studied with Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope

🤔 ODD FACTS AND TIPS
𝟗𝟑. Some people report hearing crackling or hissing during strong auroras; Finnish researchers have proposed it comes from electric discharges near the ground

𝟗𝟒. Auroras are harmless to people on the ground; the atmosphere shields us

𝟗𝟓. Strong geomagnetic storms can still disrupt GPS, radio communications and satellites

𝟗𝟔. In February 2022 SpaceX lost about 38 of 49 newly launched Starlink satellites after a geomagnetic storm raised atmospheric drag

𝟗𝟕. Magnetic north slowly drifts, so the best aurora zones shift over centuries

𝟗𝟖. Japan sees red auroras only rarely, and old Japanese records describe them as 'red vapour'

𝟗𝟗. Auroras can be photographed with a phone on night mode and a steady hand or tripod

𝟏𝟎𝟎. A typical camera starting point is a wide lens, ISO 1600 to 3200 and a 5 to 15 second exposure

📸 The northern lights swirl over Flakstad in the Lofoten Islands, Norway. Photo: Johannes Groll, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

text:
I cannot begin to explain how much this woman touched my heart. I have spoken about her before because her visit meant more to me than I can ever adequately express.

This beautiful Muslim woman traveled 35 minutes just to ask me to pray for her. Think about that for a moment. She had heard about me through the villages in Pakistan, and somehow, word had reached her about this American woman who had come thousands of miles to pray for people and help make their lives a little better.

I am nobody special. I am simply a servant of the Lord my God, Jesus Christ. Yet this woman felt it was important enough to travel to where I was staying, at the home of Joshua Shamaun and his family, who are disciples of Christ.

She was a Muslim woman who came into the home of disciples of Jesus Christ because she wanted prayer. She wasn’t concerned about our differences in faith. She had a burden on her heart, and she came seeking help.

And what did she ask for? Not money. Not possessions. She wanted her husband to come home. She wanted her marriage restored. She wanted her family back together.

That absolutely touched my heart.

I prayed for her, her husband, and their entire family. I asked the Lord my God to bring peace, reconciliation, and restoration into their home, according to His will.

And now, to read Joshua’s testimony that her husband returned home and they reconciled brings me such tremendous joy! ALL GLORY TO GOD!

This is why I went to Pakistan. Not for recognition, not for praise, and certainly not for anything this world has to offer. I went because I wanted to serve the Lord my God and help people who needed someone to care, someone to listen, and someone willing to pray with them.

I think about the people I encountered in those villages every single day. Their faces, their struggles, their tears, their prayers. They are not forgotten.

And this woman will always hold a special place in my heart.

It is written in James 5:16 that the prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective.

And in John 14:13, Jesus tells us that whatever we ask in His name, He will do, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.

I want this woman to know that I have not forgotten her, and I continue to pray for her family. May the Lord my God bless their home, strengthen their marriage, and guide them into all truth.

Thank you, Joshua, for sharing this beautiful testimony. Thank you for opening your home and allowing me to serve alongside you and your family.

All glory, honor, and praise belong to the Lord my God, Jesus Christ!

What a privilege it was to travel halfway around the world and witness the lives of people I never would have met had I not gone to Pakistan. And what a blessing to know that this woman’s journey of 35 minutes brought her to a moment of prayer that neither of us will ever forget.

God is faithful!

text:
Why Do Helmets Still Fail to Stop Concussions? Scientists May Have Been Fighting the Wrong Force All Along. | Darren Orf, Popular Mechanics

An estimated 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur in the U.S. each year. They’re so common that you might assume they’re not as serious as other injuries—but in fact, these mild traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) can often be more dangerous. While tendons, muscle, and bone heal good as new, repeated and sustained concussions—a typical occurrence in many athletic endeavors—can lead to dementia and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), an aggressive degenerative brain disease.

Although helmets have grown safer over the years in certain sports, concussions are still commonplace. That’s especially true in football, even after the high-profile introduction of the Guardian Cap for NFL preseason practices in 2022 and then in regular-season games in 2024. This suggests that there’s something about concussions, specifically the relationship of linear and rotational acceleration and the brain, that scientists still don’t understand.

During World War II, Scottish physicist A.H.S. Holbourn argued that rotational acceleration (think of an uppercut to the jaw) was more dangerous than linear acceleration (a straight-on, direct hit whose force goes through the center of the head). His theory was that rotation was worse because it stretches and strains brain tissue by moving different parts at different speeds. Scientists have focused on protecting against rotation ever since.

However, a new Stanford Medicine-led study suggests that linear acceleration, not rotation, may be the better predictor of concussion. The research comes from the lab of bioengineer David Camarillo, who’s spent more than a decade studying concussions and helmet safety. By analyzing unprecedentedly accurate impact data from motion-sensing mouthguards worn by 203 athletes across seven different sports, Camarillo and his team discovered that Holbourn’s initial assumptions weren’t correct. The results of their study were published in the journal Annals of Biomedical Engineering.

“Holbourn’s reasoning was based just on mechanics; it wasn’t biology,” David Camarillo, senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “The question we started out with many years ago was, ‘What are the forces required to cause concussion?’ If we understand the nature of those forces and the limits of the human brain, then it might be possible to prevent concussions.”

Previous studies relied on helmet-mounted sensors, but the authors note that those sensors are often inaccurate because helmets tend to move around a lot. Across the mouthguard-enabled data set, the researchers analyzed 3,851 impacts, of which 47 were verified as concussions. In their mathematical models comparing the data, peak linear acceleration was the single most predictive factor in whether a hit eventually produced a concussion. Camarillo and his team haven’t pinned down a mechanism for this result, but they suspect one of two culprits: the brain striking the inside of the skull, or cavitation, in which sudden pressure changes form tiny bubbles that then collapse.

If these results hold up in future studies, they could have profound implications for helmet safety and design. The mouthguard data showed that a hit producing 100 g of linear acceleration (100 times the acceleration of gravity) carries a 50 percent risk of concussion. That’s far lower than the often-cited 192 g threshold from earlier helmet-sensor studies. At 150 g, a hit that older data would have considered below the danger line, concussion risk tops 99 percent.

“Why are there so many concussions even when people are wearing helmets?” Camarillo asked. “Part of the answer could be in this paper, which is that the linear accelerations that we previously thought were safe, we now see are much more dangerous.”

In a way, the new results offer a bit of hope that helmets do have room for improvement, and with a greater focus on addressing linear acceleration, concussions could significantly drop in the coming years and decades. One Stanford-developed technology is a helmet with liquid-filled pads that reduces peak linear acceleration and knocks nearly 20 percentage points off the chances of concussion on high-impact hits versus standard football helmets.

“If linear acceleration is its own distinct mechanism of concussion and it’s very common, then we’ve been missing a lot,” Camarillo said. “We haven’t tried as hard to optimize for this variable. It gives me some hope that there’s a new opportunity for preventing concussions.”

text:
a guy sold his company for $500 MILLION, 500 days after he started it.

a $1.5B investor who teaches the startup class at Stanford broke down how on a podcast this week.

his answer was one word. speed.

the guy hired his whole team in 72 hours. he brought signed job offers to the interviews.
he packed every investor meeting into a day or two and told them they were competing.

you're probably slower than you think. school trained you to move at the pace of a semester.

how to reset your speed bar this week:

1. pick a deadline instead of a goal. 8 days, then you ship whatever exists.
2. make version one ugly. it only has to be something you can measure.
3. test new ideas on a throwaway domain so a flop doesn't feel personal.
4. every ask you send gets a date. reply by friday or i move on.
5. spend time around people who move faster than you. their speed rubs off.
6. when the fear hits, give it 90 seconds. then do the thing anyway.

we launched Podex with no marketing plan. biggest mistake we made.
so now i post every single day.

what are you waiting on right now that could be done in 8 days?

MikshuAlpha pre-market analysis, Tuesday 17th November, 2026

1. Market Summary

• My bias remains defensive today, with the potential for a sharp recovery if volatility resets after this week’s AI events. Leadership still sits with defensives and selected financials. Yesterday, 77 of the 86 ETFs in my sheet fell, while equal-weight S&P declined 1.01% against the cap-weighted index’s 1.91% loss. Mega-cap weakness amplified an already broad sell-off.
• Yesterday delivered the downside scenario I discussed in Monday’s pre-market note, allowing us to bank substantial index profits. $SPY opened at 749.66, traded down to 738.07 and closed at 739.95, down 1.91%. SPX closed at 7,416.59, down 1.92%.
• $QQQ fell 2.67% to 661.75 as AI, semiconductors and mega caps led the liquidation. $IWM lost 1.66% to 272.94. Small caps offered relative resilience, but still participated in the selling.
• SPX remains below its 20-day near 7,600 and 50-day near 7,660, with the 200-day around 7,340 underneath. 7,400 is the immediate decision area while 7,490 to 7,500 is the more important reclaim for improving the weekly setup.

2. Macro analysis

• US: Retail sales and import/export prices arrive at 8:30 am ET, followed by industrial production at 9:15 am ET. The control-group sales reading and Treasury reaction matter for growth expectations and tech valuations. FOMC minutes follow Wednesday at 2:00 pm ET. 
• Nvidia: Earnings arrive after today’s close. My focus is guidance, margins, funding commitments and management’s response to export restrictions and leadership uncertainty. A headline beat alone may struggle to restore confidence. New US chip restrictions ahead of the Trump-Xi talks add another source of event risk.  
• Anthropic: IPO pricing is expected Wednesday, with trading Thursday. My working thesis remains that funding allocations could be contributing to liquidation elsewhere in AI. That is a possible flow explanation; the amount of selling still required is unknown.  
• China: October retail sales grew just 0.4% year on year, industrial production rose 4.8%, and January-to-October fixed-asset investment fell 8.1%. Domestic demand remains weak, limiting support for a broad cyclical recovery.  
• Eurozone: November ZEW expectations improved, with Germany rising to 35.6 from 28.1 and the eurozone to 26.5 from 18.5. That provides a constructive regional divergence, although German current conditions remain negative at -33.2. 
• Japan: Third-quarter GDP contracted 0.1% annualised, its first decline in four quarters. Business investment rose 1.6%, but household consumption weakened. The global growth backdrop remains uneven.  

3. Momentum and breadth

• Short-term breadth has deteriorated sharply: only 12% of S&P technology stocks sit above their five-day average, compared with 24.14% across the Nasdaq Composite. Tech is stretched, but oversold conditions still need a reversal trigger.
• Broader participation is weak: 39.01% of stocks are above their 20-day average and 42.22% above their 50-day. The recent breadth recovery has rolled over.
• Russell participation also remains soft: 37.10% above the 20-day, 40.64% above the 50-day and 44.59% above the 200-day. IWM’s smaller loss does not yet establish healthy risk appetite.
• The advance/decline momentum histogram has slipped back below zero. I want to see breadth improve alongside price before treating an index bounce as durable.
• There is a constructive volatility divergence: SPY is close to its early-November lows, while VIX remains below its earlier peak. That supports the possibility of a higher low, but price has yet to confirm it.

4. Volatility

• VIX opened at 20.00, reached 24.52 and closed at 22.91, up 18.70%. VVIX is around 114, while nine-day volatility near 23.15 sits slightly above VIX. Near-term event protection remains expensive.
• The second-to-first VIX futures ratio is around 1.015, indicating shallow contango. The curve offers little cushion, and Wednesday’s expiry will change which contracts sit at the front.
• Put/call ratios are 0.931 combined and 0.845 equity-only. Hedging demand is elevated without reaching the largest extremes visible on the charts.
• Dealer gamma remains deeply negative so expecting large intraday amplification of moves in either direction.

SPX levels I am watching:

• 7,400 to 7,425: immediate pivot. A sustained reclaim of 7,430 improves the bounce setup.
• 7,450 to 7,460: first meaningful overhead test.
• 7,475, then 7,505: major recovery hurdle. Holding above 7,500 would materially improve the flow backdrop.
• 7,550, then approximately 7,560 to 7,640: higher resistance and model-dependent gamma transition zones.
• Below 7,390 to 7,395: risk of acceleration through 7,380 to 7,350, with the 200-day near 7,340.
• 7,300 to 7,325: more substantial positioning support if the first downside zone fails.

I will assess defined-risk VIX or VXX put structures for a post-event volatility decline into next week's vol compression seasonality. A move towards VIX 18 next week is a scenario, with better confirmation coming from weaker volatility and stabilising equities after Nvidia. Elevated VIX alone is insufficient reason to sell early-session 0DTE gamma.

5. Credit and liquidity

• Credit remains a concern: high-yield bonds are near the lows of the displayed period, around 76.73. The high-yield/Treasury ratio has recovered from its early-November trough, but absolute high-yield prices have yet to confirm an equity recovery.
• Regional banks remain below their earlier highs, with the chart indicating pre-market weakness. Their relative resilience needs to translate into price strength.
• SOFR minus IORB is around zero, showing no persistent funding premium in this snapshot. That offers some reassurance on overnight funding, although it does not measure the whole liquidity backdrop.
• My read is equity de-risking with weak credit confirmation. A stronger recovery needs credit stabilisation alongside lower volatility.

6. ETF and Sector rotation

• Financials, staples, healthcare and insurance also satisfy the full ordering through the 200-day. Utilities pass the shorter stack but fail the full condition.
• Five names tied in the weakest RS group: technology -3.24%, semiconductors -5.11%, software -2.16%, global AI -3.22% and memory -7.38%. Every one fails the shorter bullish MA stack.
• Semiconductor weakness is broad: SOXX fell 5.41%, while equal-weight semiconductors lost 5.15%. The damage extends beyond Nvidia.
• Equal-weight technology fell 2.98% and momentum 3.34%, reinforcing the unwind across growth and crowded winners.
• Selective strength survives: healthcare services gained 0.79%, airlines 0.62% and transports 0.29%. Healthcare services retain both bullish MA stacks; airlines and transports do not.
• Staples remain a potential reversal trade if capital returns to growth, but their current strength argues for waiting for a failed breakout or loss of trend support before considering bearish spreads.

7. Summary
Defensive today. A post-event rebound is plausible, but needs confirmation.
• Bullish trigger: SPX holds 7,400 and sustains a reclaim of 7,430, followed by 7,455. Falling VIX and semiconductor leadership would favour a tactical Nasdaq bounce towards 7,475 and 7,500 on SPX.
• Bearish trigger: acceptance below 7,390 to 7,395 with firming volatility. That favours continuation towards 7,360 and potentially 7,325.
• Weekly view: 7,490 to 7,500. Until reclaimed, decay remains a headwind.
• My focus: protect yesterday’s gains, trade confirmed moves and assess the volatility fade around Nvidia’s reaction. Thanksgiving seasonality can help once price, breadth and volatility begin to align.

text:
Apple is playing favourites with customer privacy and security. It has introduced scary new warnings about the intrusive permissions that Meta's spyware agent Muse requests, while remaining silent when its close partner OpenAI built a ChatGPT integration specifically designed to access private iMessage conversations using the same permissions.

When OpenAI released its ChatGPT integration for Apple Messages, I published a technical investigation that exposed the privacy risks for everyone worldwide. Proton cited my findings, and Fortune interviewed me and questioned both companies. OpenAI responded with misdirection and obfuscation, but Apple refused to comment at all. Now that Meta has introduced a competing AI agent, Apple has suddenly decided those same permissions are dangerous.

With macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is introducing new controls over which files and applications AI agents and other software applications can access.

Apple's new warnings explicitly tell customers when applications and AI agents can read, change, delete and export private messages, emails, photographs, documents and other personal information, control other applications, monitor activity and potentially capture keystrokes.

Apple is splitting its Device Control and Data Access permission into two parts: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. Customers will be able to lock down specific apps or folders, make apps ask for permission every time, and see a clear alert whenever one app is about to control another.

While these changes give customers more control over their privacy, they also give Apple more control over which developers can access these capabilities and qualify for exceptions. The former benefits Apple customers, but the latter restricts their choice of third party developers.

Apple can now impose even greater restrictions on developers that compete with its own products or those of close partners like OpenAI. Instead of allowing every developer to operate under the same, transparent rules, Apple can decide which permissions competitors receive. That can determine if a product succeeds or never gets off the ground.

I call the ChatGPT integration for iMessage and agents like Muse spyware because people are giving tech companies extraordinary access to private conversations, emails, documents, photographs, financial information and other sensitive data without fully understanding the consequences.

Millions of people who install Muse or the ChatGPT integration for iMessage are exposing private information about everyone they communicate with, including people who never installed these AI products or consented to their information being accessed, analysed or potentially shared with governments, law enforcement and other third parties. This includes medical conditions, mental health, financial difficulties, sexual relationships, political beliefs, confidential business information and sensitive conversations protected by end-to-end encryption.

If 10 million people have installed Muse, that means hundreds of millions of others have already been exposed through their private conversations, contacts and personal relationships, and they will never know it happened. Meta's hidden prompts instruct Muse to create detailed dossiers about people, along with their relationships, personal histories, vulnerabilities, disagreements, and ways to influence their behaviour. Muse makes Cambridge Analytica look like a 2nd grade school science project.

Now imagine another 10 million people giving ChatGPT access to Apple Messages. That's potentially hundreds of millions more people who have their private conversations, phone numbers, email addresses, locations and relationships made accessible to OpenAI without their permission.

The FBI no longer needs to pressure Apple into creating a so-called safe backdoor for iMessage because investigators can request private conversations that people have already disclosed to OpenAI. Intelligence agencies can also use AI to interrogate massive datasets to identify conversations between specific people by name, phone number or email address, or groups. They can track relationships and locations over time. They can search for references to third parties, political opinions, personal vulnerabilities, keywords and sentiment. They can also identify patterns, infer relationships and build detailed dossiers of people who never even installed ChatGPT. 

All of this is like a dream come true for intelligence agencies like the NSA, CIA, MI6, Israel's Unit 8200.

iCloud makes it even easier for tech companies and governments to identify people because it synchronises contacts, phone numbers, email addresses, calendars and messages across Apple devices. When an AI agent is given access to this information, it can connect anonymous phone numbers and email addresses to real names, identify relationships between people and associate private conversations with their identities, appointments and locations. This makes their private data even more valuable to intelligence agencies that want to identify and monitor people who don't even know that someone else has invited a tech company into every conversation they have with them or about them.

End-to-end encryption becomes irrelevant once private conversations are accessible through a third party that can disclose them to the very tech companies, advertisers, brokers, authorities and bad actors that people are trying to protect themselves from. Governments have a long history of abusing surveillance technology, including mass surveillance programmes that courts have found unlawful. These capabilities extend way beyond investigating criminals and allow authorities to monitor people who haven't broken the law.

Combine all of this information with Palantir's predictive policing technology, and governments can potentially identify, monitor and investigate people based on what AI predicts they might do, instead of anything they've actually done. Private thoughts, conversations and hypothetical discussions can be interpreted as evidence of future criminal behaviour, even when someone has no intention of acting on them. AI gets things wrong all the time, and it will never be able to interpret sarcasm.

The concept of thought police becomes a technological reality when governments can use AI to identify and target people for crimes they haven't committed and have no intention of committing.

iMessage can no longer be considered suitable for journalists and their sources, whistleblowers, crypto investors, lawyers, activists or anyone who needs to keep their private conversations away from prying eyes. Most people don't realise how many people use iMessage for the protection offered by end-to-end encryption.

ChatGPT has effectively destroyed iMessage's value as a private messaging service. Muse has done the same to what little privacy WhatsApp offered, and even conversations on Proton's services can be exposed through Muse and other AI agents.

REMINDER: You will never be notified when someone else adds an AI spyware agent to your personal conversations.

OpenAI and Meta security teams don’t care about anyone’s safety.

Security and so-called “trust” teams at companies like OpenAI and Meta know full well that their AI agents collect highly sensitive personal information about people who never use their services or gave their consent. They provide a consent box for the person who installs their AI, but that person can't consent on behalf of everyone else they expose.

Building AI agents that integrate with workflows is one thing. Deliberately building agents to monitor and collect private conversations inside messaging services that are supposed to be protected by end-to-end encryption is completely irresponsible.

I found it highly suspicious that Apple refused to answer Fortune's questions about my technical analysis and privacy worries, given how it promotes iMessage as one of its most important protections for customer privacy and personal safety, especially when OpenAI had deliberately designed this consumer integration to access private iMessage conversations.

That alone made me suspect Apple was working hand in hand with OpenAI and potentially others who have a vested interest in accessing private conversations. There is less need for Israeli government-approved spyware when the friends, colleagues or family members of high-value targets invite an AI agent into their private lives and conversations.

The second Muse was “discovered” to have the same capabilities as ChatGPT, Apple suddenly acted as if it was appalled. Apparently so appalled that it has now introduced some of the most frightening privacy warnings imaginable when people install third-party software that requests these permissions. I suspect Apple and its close partners will receive more reassuring warnings for the same permissions, while competitors face messages designed to scare customers away.

Tim Sweeney, Epic Games' founder, warned me that Apple could use my technical analysis to justify anti-competitive restrictions that prevent third-party developers from competing with Apple's own services. Judging by Apple's latest decision, he may have been half right. Apple ignored my analysis and Fortune's reporting on ChatGPT, but suddenly acted when Meta launched Muse. Apple is now using the privacy risks “exposed by Muse” to introduce controls that could allow it to restrict specific competitors or entire categories of software that it considers unsuitable for customers.

I supported Apple's privacy-first principles for as long as anyone. Over the past year, I've watched the company apply those principles differently to its own services, commercial partners, competitors and, more worryingly, governments, based on who's making the request and who benefits.

Apple's new privacy warnings are necessary, but they probably won’t apply equally to every developer. Apple shouldn't be able to use privacy as a justification to restrict competitors while preserving privileged access for itself and its commercial partners.

---

For transparency: Johan Mackie, a former US Special Operator, diplomat and military communications expert, and I are building a new kind of messaging service. We only decided to build it a few months ago because we believe people need an alternative to Signal that offers more, and an easy way to encourage the people they care about to delete WhatsApp. It's important to read my criticism with this commercial interest in mind. I won't say any more about the service because this post isn't a product placement.

text:
Not all attractions must be like the tower in Paris or the Statue of Liberty in New York. Sometimes, it begins with a 13km road in the backwater of Abuja.

And it is a story that could cascade into something more lovely.  

To most people living along Jikwoyi-Kurudu-Karshi axis, the Karshi-Apo road is pure bliss, a possible end to decades of enduring the harrowing Nyanya-Kugbo-AYA road. If ever you knew that road, you'd understand the joy of people living in the aforementioned areas. 

I once lived in that axis when I returned from Lagos after a training spell in 2013. To get to work early, I needed to leave home at 5am due to traffic. To leave home at 5am, I needed to be awake at 4am to bath and prepare. Leaving home a minute after 5 would make me late to work. I suffered sleep deprivation, as did thousands of the others with whom we jostled for space on that road. It was bad. 

People arrived at work or business angry, frustrated, and confused. That road was breeding a ZOMBIE APOCALYPSE. 

Not forgetting the robberies at the Mararaba stretch of that murderous drive, reminiscent of what South African youth are doing on their highways with guns, traffic or no traffic; burst car windows, knife people, steal phones and other valuables, run away. 

Government after government, we were told not to worry, that a new road was being constructed to ease the pain. At night, the sound of explosives shook the very foundations of our houses, kilometres away from the site where that massive rock blocking the new road stood defiant, refusing to give way. 

I don't know who the contractor was, but they failed. The story going round was that the rock could not be moved. It became like the biblical 'Rock of Ages'. 

Along came this government, and an instruction to FIX it. Once there is purpose and a political will, anything can be done. 

Today, the road that changed everything is born and being celebrated because the giant rock that defied explosives has fallen to the will of the people and government. As it fell, it left behind a portion of itself that creates picturesque content in this social media era. 

Allow the people to bask in its glory and charm. 

What might have become zombie land has elevated into a small tourist attraction with possibilities of opening up one of Abuja's potentially viable destinations. Have you been to Karshi? Do you know they have a waterfall there that is undeveloped? People hike for hours to get there. This road, and the crowd it has brought with it, can lead to the development of that waterfall. People are happy, and it is not just because of the road. 

Have you seen the industrial estate in Karshi? Smooth roads, lots of land, but no industries. Because the major road into that town did not exist. Now, watch how the area explodes into its ordained destiny. 

Instead of cursing fellow Nigerians for taking harmless pictures and having well-deserved fun, you better go and buy land in that axis!! 

Karshi has some of the most undisturbed, original scenery in North Central Nigeria; undulating mountains, waterfalls, arable farmland, short-cut to Keffi, Nasarawa, Apo-FCT City center, etc. This 13km road was the only key holding it back, and now it has come. 

It is as attractive as the citizens decide it is. Let them enjoy it. The irony in these insults is, most of the people insulting others who chose to enjoy the road are nowhere near as globally travelled and educated as some of the people they are insulting. 

Have you seen some of the high-end cars going there? Have you seen some of the families making content on that road? They have physically visited the towers in Paris and the Statue of Liberty in New York. Yet, they chose to celebrate this 13km road that you insult. 

Many of them have farms and warehouse deep inside Karshi, and have, for years, suffered the logistical hell fire that the previous single road offered them. This 13km road has bought them..........

text:
1)As an IT specialist, here’s a clear technical explanation of the November 13, 2026, US airspace outage.**

On Friday, November 13, 2026, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop (halting departures) lasting roughly 4.5–5 hours after a network failure in the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) system. This was only the third such nationwide stop in the 21st century. It disrupted communications and some radar feeds across much of the National Airspace System, leading to thousands of cancellations (reports cite figures in the 8,000–12,000+ range for Friday alone, with more the next day).[](<https://t.co/kTtXmgp1Ay>)

### What Triggered It
Contractor L3Harris was doing routine maintenance at a remote radio communications site near El Dorado, Arkansas (with related activity at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas). They were upgrading an old copper telecommunications line—so outdated that the telecom provider was discontinuing it—to fiber-optic cable. This is part of a years-long shift from legacy copper/TDM (time-division multiplexing, older circuit-style transport) to modern IP-based services over fiber. About 70% of the planned copper-to-fiber conversion was already done; the rest is targeted for completion around 2027.[](<https://t.co/on2qvQEJOW>)

During the cutover, a new router was installed and activated (reporting identifies it as a Juniper Networks unit, replacing very old Cisco 600-series routers from roughly 2001–2006 that Cisco had long since end-of-life’d). That router (and the one in Texas) began flooding the FTI network with an extreme volume of connection attempts—on the order of 1,000 every 4–5 seconds.[](<https://t.co/9Jx6nIqCQY>)

### Why a Router Flood Grounded Flights
In networking terms, this is a control-plane or broadcast/discovery storm. Routers constantly exchange hellos, routing updates, neighbor relationships, and connection requests. A misconfiguration (wrong parameters, aggressive timers, improper broadcasting enabled, a loop, or incompatibility between the new IP gear and the old TDM/legacy environment), a hardware fault, or an installer error can cause a device to spam the network instead of joining cleanly.

The FTI backbone still depended on those ancient Cisco routers. They lacked modern rate-limiting, sufficient buffering, or isolation. The flood propagated and destabilized 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers (the facilities that handle high-altitude traffic). Controllers lost reliable voice links to aircraft and some radar data feeds. With safety at risk, the FAA grounded departures until the problem was contained.[](<https://t.co/ZunsNL43SN>)

Technicians isolated the El Dorado and Amarillo sites, disabled the problematic broadcasting function on roughly 60 similar new routers as a precaution, and the network stabilized. The ground stop was then lifted.

### Broader Context and Lessons
This is a classic tech-debt failure. The FAA’s telecom network has been flagged for years as aging and fragile (there was a similar 2009 outage during an earlier fiber cutover caused by a misconfigured temporary router). Copper-to-fiber is the right long-term move—fiber offers far higher bandwidth, lower latency, and immunity to electromagnetic interference—but mixed legacy TDM and new IP gear is unforgiving. A single poorly behaved edge device can cascade when the core is still running 20-year-old hardware.

Officials have ruled out a cyberattack or AI-related cause. The investigation continues into whether it was an L3Harris configuration/installer error, a faulty or poorly configured router, or an interaction with the old network. HPE (which owns Juniper) has stated the hardware functioned as configured.[](<https://t.co/eyB5J87Nhn>)

text:
Jimmy Carter (white trunks with black stripe) drops Paddy DeMarco in the 9th (pictured) and 15th rounds on November 17, 1954 and regains the World Lightweight Championship at The Cow Palace in Daly City, California.

DeMarco had dethroned Carter, at Madison Square Garden, on March 5th via 15-round unanimous decision.

(Note: Paddy DeMarco and Tony DeMarco were no relation. Tony was actually born Leonardo Liotta in Boston  while Pasquale "Paddy" DeMarco was born in Brooklyn, New York.)

This was the third of Carter's three reigns as Lightweight Champion and he'd lose the title for the final time in his first defense, in June of 1955, on a 15-round split decision to Wallace Bud Smith.

From Boxing Biographies dot com on three-time lightweight titlist Jimmy Carter:

James Walter Carter was born in Aiken,South Carolina, on December 15th 1923, but when he was aged nine the family moved to New York. Jimmy first learned how to use his fists on the tough streets of Harlem and, fortunately for him , was able to channel that aggression more positively when he joined the Catholic Boys Club at a local church. It was here that Carter took up boxing and he made his amateur debut at the age of 14.
The club made a lasting impression on the youngster and, when he returned to the church as world champion in 1952 Carter gave the parish priest a cheque for $1000 towards the cost of a community centre for the area. In 1943 carter joined the army and boxed in many Service contests while serving as a sapper in England, France and the Philippines. He was demobbed in 1945 and took a job as a grocery clerk before deciding to turn pro under the guidance of Willie Ketchum, a well known and long established manager in New York. The partnership was to continue to the end of Carter’s career.
Ketchum believed in keeping his boxers busy and Carter had 22 fights in his first 12 months as a pro, winning 18 and drawing one. It was a promising start and by the end he had fought his way out of the six rounder bracket and was topping the bill on shows at the small fight clubs which abounded in New York at that time. However it was success at a price as the New York managers were reluctant to risk their protégés against him and he was forced to go on the road to find work.
Carter’s first trip was more significant than either boxer realized at the time as he travelled down to New Orleans to fight local lightweight star Joe Brown, and lost a 10 round decision. Brown and Carter would each go on to become major figures in the division's history. At the time it was seen as a routine job for both men.
After two more wins Carter fought a tough 10 round draw with second ranked featherweight Sandy Sadler, but after three more wins his form slumped as he went four fights without a win, having three draws and losing on a cut eye to Cabey Lewis in November 1947. It was the first time in 34 fights that he had failed to go the distance, which would not happen again until September 1956.
Carter came through the bad spell and spent a busy 1948 criss crossing America for 14 fights, winning 11 and drawing one. A return visit to New Orleans did not bring him any luck as bobby McQuillar, a world ranked contender, outpointed him. However in those days the occasional defeat was not seen as the end of the world. Few fights were televised and losses in fights “on the road” could easily be dismissed as home town verdicts.
It was much the same story in 1949 with appearances In Detroit, New York and California, where carter scored an impressive eighth round win over Mario Trigo. He had finally edged into the world ratings, but with major fights still eluding him, Carter headed for Australia.
His first fight in Melbourne, in September, brought another defeat as Norman Gent outpointed him over 12 rounds, but a month later he knocked out Charlie Ashended in Sydney, and finished his three fight tour with a decision over Bernie Hall in Melbourne.
Back in the USA Carter opened 1950 with the first of his three meetings with Walter”Bud” Smith, the man who would in time end his championship career. They met in Smith’s home town of Cincinnati, and Carter proved a shade to experienced for the 21 year old. He won a ten round decision, but fights were hard to come by and Carter boxed only twice more that year. Beating Jesse Underwood and being held to a draw by Tommy Campbell.
A world title shot seemed far away when Carter lost his first outing in 1951 to Calvin Smith in Philadelpia – then, astonishingly came the call to fight the Ike Williams for the world lightweight championship. Williams was only 27 but a long, hard carrer was beginning to take its toll. He had been an outstanding champion but it was no secret that Williams was finding it hard to get down to the lightweight limit.Even so, the Williams camp were so confident they neglected to include the customary return bout clause in the contract. The national Boxing Association thought so little of Carter’s chances that they refused to recognize him as a contender.
Little more than 3,000 fans were in Madison Square Gardens in May 1951 to see the title change hands. What the crowd witnessed was a one sided contest as Carter, a comfortable two pounds inside the 9st 7lb (133 lb), dominated the weight drained champion, who came in exactly on the limit. Williams was down twice in the fifth round, once in the 10th and again in the 14th as the referee Petey Scalzo, former featherweight champion, signaled the end when the champion went sprawling for a fourth knockdown.
Williams said some years later that his manager, the notorious Blinky Palermo, had offered him $50,000 to lose, with a guarantee that in six months they would fight again with Williams winning. “I should have taken it, but I didn’t” he said. “That’s one of the reasons I’m broke now”. Such arrangements were not unusual at the time, but there is no evidence that Carter was aware of this. Carter had won the world title in style and the NBA had to make a humiliating climb down after the fight and acknowledge the new champion.
Although he was the new champion Carter was still a hungry fighter and keen to keep himself as busy as possible. His purse for winning the title was $1,270 and he used this to move his wife and 2 year old son out of Harlem. To keep cash coming in he took on a series of non title matches, beating such as Enrique Bolanos, Del Flanagan and Mario Trigo. However a split decision against Art Aragon in August 1951 earned the Californian golden boy a November rematch with Carter’s world title at stake.
Carter gained revenge for his earlier defeat with an emphatic points victory. It was an impressive close to the year for the lightweight champion, but he began 1952 with near disaster when he gave Mario Trigo another chance to test him over ten rounds in Philadelphia .
It was an appalling fight, so bad the referee had to warn both men that if they didn’t start trying they risked being disqualified. In the interval, between the 7th and 8th rounds, the Pennsylvania Boxing Commissioner, Ox De Gros, went to both men’s corners and told them that their purses would be withheld if they didn’t show some effort, and that was enough to spark Carter into life over the last few rounds to take the decision.
In February Carter outpointed Alan McFater over the unusual distance of nine rounds, and then, in March, he edged a split decision against the number two contender Luther Rawlings. It was anything but the ideal warm up for his title defense less than three weeks later in los Angeles against Lauro Salas.
Salas was an unranked, rugged Mexican brawler and he gave Carter an unexpected tough battle. The champion did not trouble him until the 15th and final round, when Salas was put down for a count of four. The judges were unanimous in Carter’s favor, but Salas had done well enough to earn a rematch which took place in May.
Carter was a 4-1 favorite for the return but after the 24 year old Salas won a split decision Carter accused his opponent of packing the hall with partisan supporters who cheered his every move and swayed the judges into believing that Salas was having more success than he actually was.
A third contest was arranged and the pair met in Chicago, in October. This time Carter took a comfortable verdict to regain the title, but he showed anything but championship form as he won only one of his next four fights, all being non title contests. This did little to encourage confidence in his chance of retaining the title against the hard hitting Tommy Collins whom he faced in the challenger’s hometown of Boston in April 1953
The fight which was screened live on TV was an appalling mismatch which did serious damage to boxing’s image. The challenger, too brave for his own good, was permitted to absorb one of the worst beatings in title history, while the referee, his own cornermen, commission officials and ringside doctor looked on. Collins was floored seven times in a brutal 3rd round, and the fight should have been stopped after the 3rd knockdown as Collins, his left eye closed, clearly had no idea what was going on.
Collins should never been allowed out for the 4th round, and Carter was obviously unhappy about it. He was reluctant to hit him again and kept looking at the referee Tommy Rawson in the hope that he would call a halt. When he did nothing he knocked the youngster down three more times.Even that was not enough for Rawson who was preparing to order them to box on when Collin’s manager and second at last jumped into the ring to signal their man’s surrender.
Carter’s next defense was against George Arujo in June 1953. Arujo had earned his title shot with wins over Sandy Saddler and Paddy De Marco, but had the misfortune of find the erratic Carter on top of his form and the champion stopped him in 13 rounds.
Ever unpredictable Carter lost his next fight, a ten round decision to Johnny Cunningham, a little known welterweight who boxed to supplement his wages as a garbage collector. It was a worrying result for Carter, but he got back in form with two quick non title wins before risking his title again, against Armand Savoie in November 1953.
Like Carter , the Canadian Savoie was a hot and cold fighter whose record was littered with surprising losses mixed in with brilliant victories. For three rounds of his championship challenge it seemed that Savoie was having one of his good nights as he speared carter with long jabs and stepped in with short hooks to the head. But Carter began to find his range in the fourth and ended the fight with a single, dramatic straight right to the chin in the fifth. Savoie crashed on his back and had only managed to make it to his hands and knees when he was counted out.
Carter opened 1954 with a trip to the Bahamas where he outpointed Billy Lauderdale, before defending in New York City against Paddy De Marco in March. Carter started as a 4-1 favorite, but De Marco chased him around the ring for 15 rounds and took a unanimous decision as the lethargic champion relied almost exclusively on his left jab.
Carter had a return bout clause in the pre fight contract, but after being originally scheduled for June the fight was twice postponed due to De Marco injuring an elbow in winning the title, The two men finally met in November 1954. De Marco built up a lead in the first five rounds but from the sixth Carter found his range and raised a swelling on the champs left eye. A left hook floored De Marco in the ninth, but he rallied to open a cut on Carter’s right eye in the 10th. De Marco was floored twice in the 14th and had nothing left when he came out for the 15th.
The final round lasted just 14 seconds as De Marco was battered across the ring and the fight was stopped. Carter was champion again for the third time. However the good times were almost over for Carter. He began his third reign with a 10 rounds points win over Bobby Woods, but was held to a draw by Tony De Marco (no relation to paddy) and beaten on a decision by the Cuban Orlando Zulueta. It was all poor preparation for his next defence against Wallace Bud Smith in Boston in June 1955.
Smith, a former USA amateur champion and 1948 Olympic Games semi finalist, was a much improved fighter from the youngster who had lost to Carter in 1950. Carter had the best of the early rounds, but Smith caught him repeatedly with short slashing left hooks in the latter stages to take a split decision. The return fight in Cincinnati ,in October, where 7,000 fans got full value for money, with the outcome in doubt all the way.Smith was just ahead after 12 rounds, having cut Carter’s right eyelid in the 3rd and closed his right eye in the 8th. However the challenger made his big effort in the 13th and pounded the weary Smith around the ring. Smith managed to stay on his feet, even though he had to use the ropes to keep him upright, and then boxed his way out of trouble in the last two rounds to take a unanimous decision.
Carter set about earning another championship chance, but his campaign took a knock when Cisco Andrade took a split decision in his first outing in 1956. Carter came back with a win over Phil Burton, and then had a series of three victories over Don Jordon, Art Aragon and Lauro Salas. When Carter faced 20 year old Larry Boardman in September he was virtually assured of a crack at new champion Joe Brown if he won.
Boardman had beaten Bud Smith and Sandy Sadler in the space of nine weeks, and also held wins over paddy de Marco and Frankie Ryff. The youngster proved too lively and ambitious for the veteran and Carter was floored three times before being stopped in the 8th.
He had been down only twice in his whole career, yet he refused to heed the warning signals that he was on the decline and boxed on for another four years. Defeats piled up – 8 in his last 12 fights – before he retired aged 36. He quit with a record of 81 wins and 9 draws in 120 fights. Carter died of a heart attack on September 21, 1994 aged 70.

text:
Chemists Weave Molecules Into a Powerful New Material That Traps Toxic Chemicals | University & Vincent L, SciTechDaily

A fabric woven at the molecular level could help factories separate chemicals with less energy, opening a new path toward more sustainable manufacturing.

Reducing the environmental impact of manufacturing requires more than finding cleaner materials. It also means finding ways to make industrial processes use less energy and produce fewer hazardous byproducts. One promising approach comes from an unexpected place: the ancient craft of weaving.

Researchers from the University of Texas at Austin and Zhejiang University have developed a molecularly woven fabric that can separate benzene from cyclohexane, two chemicals that are notoriously difficult to separate using conventional methods. The material could offer a more energy-efficient way to handle chemical separation, potentially reducing the energy demands of industries that manufacture nylon, paint, polyurethane, furniture foams, and detergents. The research was published in Nature.

Cyclohexane is an important industrial chemical used to manufacture a range of everyday products. It is commonly produced from benzene, a known carcinogen, which can also remain as an unwanted byproduct. Removing the benzene is essential, yet the two chemicals have nearly identical boiling points, making conventional separation difficult.

Chemical plants typically rely on distillation, a process that heats mixtures to separate substances according to their boiling points. Chemicals with sufficiently different boiling points can vaporize at different temperatures, allowing one to be collected separately. Benzene and cyclohexane, however, vaporize at nearly the same temperature and tend to separate poorly. The process often requires additional additives and considerable energy.

“Unbelievable amounts of energy go into chemical separation. It’s one of the top energy sinks in the modern world,” said UT chemist Jonathan Sessler, one of the corresponding authors of the study. “In a sense, we are addressing the challenge of improving efficiency using one of humanity’s oldest technologies: weaving. It’s remarkable that the same principle of interlacing works at the molecular level.”

A fabric woven from molecular networks

The researchers developed a material made from four molecular networks that weave over and under one another, forming an interconnected structure. Each layer can take one of two mirror-image arrangements. In one, the networks cross in a clockwise spiral, while the other follows a counterclockwise spiral. This property, known as chirality or handedness, allows the researchers to alternate between the two arrangements as they stack the layers.

The resulting material forms a springy, thick fabric that can capture benzene from a mixture. Its interlocking, multi-thread structure also makes it stronger than conventional fabrics made by weaving individual threads in a single layer.

Unlike materials that require complicated manufacturing processes, this molecular fabric is self-assembling. Its chemical structure naturally guides the networks into their woven arrangement.

“The whole thing converges by itself based on the underlying chemistry, which is especially cool because it allows the creation of these new materials in a facile way,” Sessler said.

Reusable filtering could reduce industrial energy demands

The fabric can also be reused. After absorbing benzene from a chemical mixture, researchers heat the material to vaporize the captured benzene, preparing it for another round of separation.

Sessler and the Zhejiang University team, led by professors Feihe Huang and Guangfeng Li, tested the material using a mixture containing equal amounts of benzene and cyclohexane. A single application absorbed 97.9% of the benzene. Multiple passes could provide additional separation for processes requiring greater purity.

The researchers also demonstrated that the material could separate several other compounds of commercial interest, suggesting that its potential applications extend beyond benzene and cyclohexane.

At Zhejiang University, the team has demonstrated how the fabric could be used on a larger, industrial scale. However, an economic analysis has not yet been completed, so its eventual cost and commercial practicality remain uncertain.

If the technology proves viable, it could offer manufacturers a way to reduce the energy required for separating industrial chemicals. Improving these processes could help limit the environmental footprint of manufacturing, particularly across industries that depend on cyclohexane and other commercially important compounds.

text:
Border & Cartel update 17 November 2026

THE PRESS
•Panama: a judge on Monday night upheld the arrest of taxi driver Luis Adriel Valiente Ortega, 50, and he will stay in provisional detention on an arson charge over Saturday's firebombing of La Prensa associate deputy editor Rolando Rodríguez's home. Prosecutors allege he drove the man who threw the device to the house and helped him get away, citing surveillance video of the two buying fuel at a gas station around 2:04 a.m. Prosecutor Leyda Sáenz says the investigation continues to identify others who may have taken part, and the court gave her six months.
•Acapulco follow-up: Guerrero prosecutors still had no arrests Monday in the strangling of reporter Eduardo Flores Salado. Breitbart Texas (Ortiz & Darby) noted that CPJ called on Mexico's government to investigate. Counts of this year's victims differ: AFP cites RSF at 10 journalists killed in Mexico in 2026, and CNN en Español cites the International Federation of Journalists at nine media workers.
•Mexican reporters can't cover the cartels the way U.S. outlets can, and many fear being killed for it. That's why we created Breitbart's Cartel Chronicles: Mexican journalists report under pseudonyms, and their work is published in English and Spanish. Much of what follows still rests on official statements.

THE BORDER
•Breitbart Texas (Randy Clark): Chief U.S. District Judge Alia Moses sentenced the last three defendants in a Western District of Texas gun-trafficking case to a combined 39.5 years. Edgar Josue Montelongo-Loera of Dallas got 15 years, Reymundo Hernandez-Nino, who is in the country illegally from Mexico, got 12.5 years, and his wife, Kenia Lizbeth Montelongo, got 12 years. Agents found 24 guns, more than 4,000 rounds and body armor at Hernandez-Nino's San Antonio home; ATF says the gear was bound for a Mexican cartel, and U.S. Attorney Justin Simmons says the 10-person ring smuggled more than 200 weapons into Mexico.
•DHS and CBP said Monday that October's nationwide encounters were the lowest ever recorded to open a fiscal year, and that October was the 18th straight month with zero releases at the border. DHS says daily Border Patrol apprehensions at the southwest border are down 95% from the previous administration.
•President Trump said Monday at the White House that the U.S. won't let the new caravan in, that Mexico will stop it, and that if it doesn't he will impose heavy tariffs on Mexico. He did not name a rate or a date. The "Dios con Nosotros" caravan, mostly Hondurans, reached Mapastepec, Chiapas, early Monday, about 140 km in 10 days; El País reports that immigration agents intercepted about 300 members Sunday night and about 1,300 remain together. Mexico's government says none of the 24 caravans formed in the south has reached the U.S. border, and Diario de Chiapas reports another group is starting to organize in Honduras.

MEXICO
•Sinaloa: Línea Directa's Monday tally lists a mechanic shot dead in Escuinapa, two men killed in Culiacán's El Mirador area, one person shot in Mazatlán's Casa Redonda neighborhood and another who died in a Mazatlán hospital after a shooting. Human remains were also found in a bucket outside a shopping plaza in Culiacán's La Campiña neighborhood. N+ identified one of the Culiacán victims as Irving Gerardo, 18; another 18-year-old was shot minutes earlier on the same avenue and is in serious condition.
•Ciudad Juárez: three shootings in less than 24 hours in the Rancho Anapra neighborhood, starting Sunday night, left four people dead and two wounded, local outlet xJuárez reports.
•Guanajuato: state prosecutors are investigating seven deaths and one wounded person in Irapuato, Pueblo Nuevo, Celaya, Huanímaro and Dolores Hidalgo. The causes of death have not been released.

GOVERNMENT & CARTELS
•Breitbart Texas (Ortiz & Darby): Querétaro police shut down corridos tumbados singer Gabito Ballesteros's show at the state's cattlemen's expo this weekend after organizers said he sang cartel-themed songs that weren't on his approved list, and he was arrested after barricading himself in his van. He says the songs weren't banned and that he doesn't promote violence. The FGR says a pistol, two magazines and 34 rounds were found in the vehicle, and it is investigating him and four members of his team for alleged possession of a military-only weapon and resisting authorities. He was released Saturday night after more than 15 hours at the FGR in Querétaro, Expansión reports.

WASHINGTON
•The State Department offered up to $10 million each for Guatemalans Axel Bladimir Montejo Sáenz, "Mosh," and Walfre Donaldo Calderón-Calderón, "El Teniente Jr.," whom it accuses of drug, weapons and human trafficking, extortion and murder along the Guatemala-Mexico border in association with CJNG. Federal prosecutors in San Diego say Montejo was arrested there by the Homeland Security Task Force and that the investigation seized more than 5,500 kg of cocaine and $3.7 million tied to him. Calderón, who prosecutors say runs an operation in northwestern Guatemala near the Mexican border, remains at large.
•ICE posted a reward of up to $5 million for José Salgueiro-Nevárez, "El Che," whom it calls a Sinaloa Cartel leader; Mexican outlet adn40 ties him to the Chapitos in Chihuahua. Mexico's Army and the then-PGR announced in 2012 that soldiers had arrested a José Salgueiro Nevárez, "El Che," in Hidalgo del Parral. ICE's notice does not address that arrest.
•A crew of Ecuadorian fishermen sued the U.S. government Monday in federal court in Pittsburgh, Courthouse News reports. They allege two U.S. drones struck and sank their boat on March 17, a day after Ecuador's navy inspected and cleared it, badly burning two crewmen, and that they were then held for days in El Salvador. Courthouse News says the government has not provided evidence tying the crew to drug trafficking.

LATIN AMERICA
•Guatemala: Congress is set to vote at 2 p.m. Tuesday on President Arévalo's 30-day state of siege in Zacapa and Izabal. Congress President Luis Contreras says there is consensus for the 81 votes needed. Rep. José Chic, who backs it, said there have been no significant arrests under the measure so far.
•Haiti: the European Union sanctioned four gangs, 5 Segond, Gran Ravine, 400 Mawozo and Krazé Baryè, citing killings, rape, child recruitment and attacks on health facilities, the Miami Herald reports. The listings freeze assets and bar travel to the EU.
•Ecuador: President Daniel Noboa met Italy's national anti-mafia prosecutor, Giovanni Melillo, in Italy to expand cooperation against organized crime and drug trafficking.

text:
how do most people keep themselves in the dark?

they usually don’t realize until it’s too late

it’s a shiny process

makes it easy to stay delusional

the call is at 10am. tomorrow. your first real sales call. feeling a tingling sensation on the side of your neck.

I got used to liking that feeling.

it means you’re nervous. but also means the reward is high.

tonight, you were going to prepare. write the questions. go over the offer.

it’s 11pm.

then your brain does something clever.

“one more YT video.”

all of a sudden it’s 4:12am.

you wake up foggy. skip the prep. wing it.

the call goes nowhere. the prospect asked you questions that made you stutter and question your reality.

“yeah I didn't close cuz I was running on 3 hours of sleep.”

feels better. doesn’t it?

and just like that... you’re off the hook.

you launch an offer in one hour. no edits. lazy structure. you did it while scrolling IG.

you tell yourself “it’s just a test.”

it flops. no one bought.

“well, I didn’t really try.”

you played the same trick on yourself again. it’s a never ending loop.

this is called self handicapping.

jon jones used to run it on himself.

he’d party a week before every fight he had. get blacked out drunk.

his logic: if he lost, he had a reason ready. it was the drinking.

he built in a safety net for himself. 

it’s a beautiful setup.

you can’t lose. that’s why it’s so comfortable.

but it’s costing you something you don’t see bro.

you never find out.

was the offer bad? was it the audience? was it you?

if the offer sold, why did it sell?

you’ll never know. the test was rigged before it started.

you took the bait and got no answer.

in a 1978 experiment a group of college students took a test. they scored great. but the questions couldn’t actually be solved.

they’d basically guessed and got told they “nailed it”.

then they heard round two of the test was coming.

before it started, they were offered a drug. one would make them sharper. the other would make them worse.

the guys who got lucky on the first test picked the pill that made them worse.

why?

the first win didn’t feel earned. felt lucky. so they picked the excuse before the test even started.

if they failed, the pill took the blame.

they picked looking lazy over looking stupid.

same reason you picked “one more YT video” over prepping for the call.

it’s not that you’re undisciplined.

you just couldn’t risk finding out it was you.

that’s how you stay in the dark.

next time...

prep the call. give the offer a full week. no excuse loaded.

if it fails, it hurts for a day.

but now you know exactly what to fix bro.

if it sells, you know it was you.

all in or nothing. 

you know what you did right and how you can use it again to print more $$

stay locked in

text:
However, I know this man. I know how he behaves when something is wrong, and I could tell that something had changed.

We eventually got home, went about our usual activities, and later went to bed.

I thought perhaps he was just having a bad day and that everything would be fine the following morning.

But something happened that night that left me even more confused.

I woke up in the middle of the night because I wanted to use the bathroom. As I got there, I found my husband sitting inside, crying.

Yes, crying.

I was shocked because, in all the time I've known this man, I've never seen him cry like that.

Immediately, I became worried.

I asked him what was wrong, whether something had happened, and why he was crying.

He told me he didn't even know how to explain what he was going through. He said he had a lot on his mind and had only come into the bathroom because he wanted some time alone to cry.

I was confused.

I asked him why he didn't wake me up so we could talk about whatever was bothering him.

I helped him get up, took him back to our bedroom, and tried to have a proper conversation with him.

I even offered to make him something, perhaps a cup of tea or coffee, if that would help him feel better.

But he insisted that he was fine now that he had let out his emotions.

Eventually, he went back to bed.

However, since that night, I haven't been able to get the incident out of my mind.

Something about the entire situation doesn't sit right with me.

You see, before we got married, I knew my husband had been in a very serious relationship with another woman.

They dated for eight years, but according to what he told me, the woman eventually ended the relationship because he wasn't making any moves towards marriage.

She wanted to settle down, but after eight years together, he still hadn't proposed or given her any assurance that marriage was in the picture.

Eventually, she felt he had wasted her time and decided to move on.

Now, there's something else I remember.

During the period my husband and I were preparing for our wedding, I came across some messages he had sent to his ex.

In those messages, he was apologising to her and telling her that he was finally getting married.

When I confronted him and asked why he was still sending messages to his ex, he explained that he felt he owed her an apology.

According to him, they had spent eight years together, and he felt terrible that he had allowed her to invest so much time in the relationship without giving her the marriage she wanted.

He said he didn't want her to hear about his wedding from other people. He simply wanted to apologise, give her closure, and say his final goodbye.

At the time, his explanation made sense to me, so I didn't think too much about it.

But now, after what happened at the supermarket, I'm beginning to question everything.

Think about it.

This is a woman he dated for eight years. A woman who left him because she wanted marriage and he wasn't ready to give it to her.

And now, less than a year after their relationship ended, he has married me and we're expecting a child.

So why did seeing her with another man, especially now that she's pregnant, affect him this much?

Why did his mood suddenly change?

Why did he become unusually quiet?

And why did I find him crying in the bathroom that same night?

I'm beginning to wonder whether my husband genuinely moved on from that relationship before marrying me.

What if he rushed into marrying me because he was trying to get over his ex?

What if he still has feelings for her but simply convinced himself that marrying someone else was the best way to move forward?

I know these are serious questions, but I can't help thinking about them.

The most painful part is that I'm currently five months pregnant. At this stage of my life, I want to feel secure in my marriage. I want to know that the man I'm carrying a child for genuinely loves me and chose me because he wants to spend the rest of his life with me.

But right now, I'm beginning to doubt everything.

I keep asking myself whether he ever truly loved me or whether I was simply the person who came along when he was trying to forget another woman.

And there's something else that bothers me.

My husband was the one who left our queue to approach his ex. He was the one who went over to greet her. He even offered to pay for her groceries.

If I hadn't walked up to him, I honestly don't know whether he would have introduced me to them.

I don't want to jump to conclusions, but the timing of everything is making me uncomfortable.

I haven't brought the issue up again because I don't want us to start arguing or create unnecessary tension in our marriage.

But I also don't think I can pretend that nothing happened.

So I'm bringing this here to hear what other people think.

Ladies, if you were in my position, what would you do?

Do you think my husband is still emotionally attached to his ex, or could seeing her pregnant and seemingly happy with another man have triggered emotions he wasn't expecting?

text:
video is having a purple cow moment on tech twitter

but standing out isn't the same as taking over a platform (X)

a face among walls of text gives you a different way to earn attention

i get why these videos are making people reconsider the format (i'm considering it myself)

what i'm less convinced about is everyone making the switch

the bottleneck isn't just showing your face, it's the cost of getting good

with text, you can change the opening, test another angle, post again

and good writing still takes work, but the production cost of another attempt is relatively low

now spend hours recording and editing a video that flops

was it the idea? the opening? your delivery? the pacing?

if you're new to the format, you might not even know what to change

the next attempt costs time before you know whether you've fixed anything

that's the part a viral example doesn't show you

"the cost of learning to do it consistently"

I've a bet on this actually

video will become a useful edge for people whose skills, audience and offer make those reps worthwhile

even though i'm less convinced it becomes the default on X (esp. money twitter)

there's an opportunity here but "i should try video" and "video is taking over X" are two very different conclusions
