text:
For 21 years, Make-A-Wish has had a special place in my heart.

I’ve seen what happens when a child who’s spent far too much of their young life in hospital rooms, enduring needles, treatments, fear, and uncertainty, suddenly has something wonderful to look forward to.

I’ve seen what a wish can mean to a family that’s been through hell.

And after 21 years, it still gets me. Every single time.

This Thursday, we’re holding our annual KRLD Make-A-Wish Radiothon. And I’m asking you for something before I ask anyone for a donation.

Would you please pray for us?

Pray that God opens hearts. Pray that our listeners respond generously. Pray that the stories we share reach the people who need to hear them. Pray that we raise more money than we ever imagined possible.

Because right now, 1,100 children across North Texas are waiting for their wishes.

Those aren’t just numbers on a fundraising goal. They’re real kids. Real families. Moms and dads who would give anything to take away their child’s suffering, even for a little while.

I know money is tight for a lot of people. I know we’re all being pulled in a hundred different directions.

But I also know what can happen when people come together to do something extraordinary for a child.

A wish doesn’t cure cancer. It doesn’t erase a diagnosis.

But it can give a child something illness has stolen: the freedom to dream about tomorrow.

And sometimes, tomorrow is exactly what a family needs to believe in.

Please pray that Thursday is an extraordinary day for these children.

We’ll be broadcasting live all day from NFM at Grandscape in The Colony.

If you feel led to help, you can donate at https://t.co/M72B8x1wzH.

And whether you can give a dollar, a hundred dollars, or simply offer a heartfelt prayer, thank you.

After 21 years, I still believe in the power of a wish.

And I still believe in the power of prayer.

For example, someone looking for a poetry call might notice a pottery workshop. “I could try making that myself.” A small discovery like that might become something to look forward to on a day off.

You are free to take part, share something with a friend who might enjoy it, or simply browse for pleasure.

For readers outside the United States, we hope these glimpses of what people are making, sharing, and enjoying bring life in different communities a little closer.

Something you would not normally have searched for happens to catch your eye today. It might lead to a new interest, another option, or a conversation with someone. We share this list in the hope that these chance encounters can open a few more possibilities in everyday life.

Announcements and promotions related to the listed items are welcome in the comments. Please also let us know if you spot an error or a change.

text:
NQ Game Plan: Tuesday Nov 17

Context. Third straight red day. Nasdaq is in correction territory and NVDA reports after the close. Expect a premium on patience today. The real range may not be set until after the bell.

Opening gaps frame the week. Price is trading between two New Week Opening Gaps. 

• This week's NWOG runs from 27,927.25 to 28,062.50, with its C.E. at 27,994.88. That is the premium array overhead. Sunday opened at the top of the gap and price sold off from there. 

• Last week's NWOG runs from 26,878.50 to 27,107.50, with its C.E. at 26,993.00. That is the discount array below, and it has not been revisited since it formed.

Higher timeframe. The daily bullish FVG failed and is now acting as an inversion. Until price closes back through it with displacement, bounces are offers. Bulls need the weekly open at 27,690 and then this week's C.E. at 27,994.88 to change the story.

Draw on liquidity. Sellside sits at Monday's low of 27,234.75. Just under it, the top of last week's NWOG at 27,107.50 is the first gap level price could tag, and the C.E. at 26,993.00 is the real draw. Below that, the next targets are the 4h sellside at 26,737 and the NFP swing low near 26,366. Buyside sits at the Asia high, which nearly everyone is watching for a 9:30 raid.

Time. The 9:30 open is a liquidity event, not an entry. Let the opening range form, look for the setup in the 10:00 macro, and stop trading at 10:45 if nothing has shown up.

What retail gets wrong today

A failed gap is not a free short. An inversion needs a rejection with displacement before it is a trade. Shorting every bounce into it on an event day is how stops fund the move.

A crowded sweep rarely goes as planned. When the whole timeline is waiting on one Asia high raid, price either runs past it or leaves without it. Trade what price confirms, not what you predicted.

Opening gaps are reference points, not entries. Retail buys the first touch of an old NWOG blindly. A gap matters when time and displacement agree at its edges or its C.E., not just because price arrived there.

More prop accounts is more risk, not less. One idea copied across three evaluations is one trade at three times the size. Taking that into an NVDA day is how stacked accounts get wiped in a single morning.

Execution. Watch how price reacts around Day Open at 27,314.75 and the 1h Breaker at the bell. Aim for a 50 to 80 point base hit off a confirmed reaction there, at Monday's low of 27,234.75, the top of last week's gap at 27,107.50, or its C.E. at 26,993.00. Keep risk defined and stop at 10:45. If nothing confirms, sitting on your hands is the position.

text:
I appreciate the friendly tone, but I think there are some fundamental things about Judaism and the sacrificial system that need clarification.

First, the Temple and its sacrifices were part of a much larger religious system established by the Torah. They were not simply a mechanism for obtaining forgiveness for sins, nor were animals universally sacrificed as substitutes for human beings.

There were several different categories of offerings, each with its own purpose:

• Olah (burnt offerings): expressions of devotion and dedication to G-d.
• Shelamim (peace offerings): expressions of gratitude, celebration and fellowship with G-d.
• Chatat (sin offerings): atonement for particular categories of inadvertent transgressions.
• Asham (guilt offerings): atonement for specific offenses, sometimes accompanied by restitution.
• Minchah (grain offerings): offerings of flour, oil and agricultural produce.

There were also daily communal offerings, Sabbath offerings, festival offerings and special offerings for particular circumstances.

These commandments are laid out extensively in Leviticus 1–7, Leviticus 16, and Numbers 28–29.

Now, something particularly important is that the Torah itself establishes where and under what conditions sacrifices may be offered.

Deuteronomy 12:5–14 instructs the Israelites to bring their offerings to the place G-d designates. Deuteronomy 12:13–14 explicitly prohibits offering sacrifices wherever one pleases.

Leviticus 17:3–9 establishes regulations requiring sacrificial offerings to be brought to the sanctuary.

These are not incidental details. The location, altar, priesthood and procedures are all governed by commandments.

And what happens when there is no Temple?

Jews have lived without a functioning Temple for most of the last two millennia.

The First Temple was destroyed by the Babylonians in 586 BCE. The Second Temple was destroyed by the Romans in 70 CE.

But Judaism did not disappear. Our covenant with G-d did not disappear. We did not suddenly need another religion to complete our relationship with Him.

There are commandments that depend on the Temple and its sacrificial service, and there are commandments that remain fully applicable regardless of whether the Temple exists.

When the Temple service is unavailable, we do not simply start sacrificing animals wherever we happen to be. The Torah’s requirements concerning the designated sanctuary and altar still matter.

Our religious life continues through prayer, repentance, charity, Torah study and observance of the commandments. Our sages established the connection between daily prayer and the daily sacrificial offerings.

There is also an important distinction in Jewish law: Maimonides explains in Mishneh Torah, Laws of the Chosen Temple 6:15, that the building itself is not necessarily required for sacrifices if the properly designated altar and its requirements are in place. The issue is not simply whether there is a building standing.

Now, regarding the Akedah, the Binding of Isaac: in the actual Torah narrative, G-d stops Abraham from sacrificing Isaac and provides a ram instead. The Jewish understanding concerns Abraham’s faith, obedience and the sanctity of human life. Reading this story as a prophecy or foreshadowing of Jesus is a Christian theological interpretation, not what the Jewish text itself states.

And finally, regarding the Messiah: yes, there were different messianic expectations among Jews during the Second Temple period. But that does not establish that Judaism once universally believed the Messiah would be G-d and subsequently abandoned that belief.

The Jewish understanding of the Messiah is fundamentally rooted in the promises concerning the House of David. Jeremiah 23:5 describes a righteous descendant of David who will reign as king. Isaiah 11 describes a shoot emerging from the stump of Jesse.

These are Jewish scriptures describing Jewish expectations.

Jesus’ Words on the Widow’s Offering
In Mark 12:41–44, Jesus sat opposite the temple treasury and watched the crowd putting money in. Many rich people gave large amounts, but a poor widow came and placed two small copper coins — worth only a few cents. Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more into the treasury than all the others. They all gave out of their wealth; but she, out of her poverty, put in everything — all she had to live on”
Meaning and Application
Jesus’ words emphasize that the value of a gift is not measured by the amount given, but by the proportion of one’s resources that is offered. The widow’s offering, though small in monetary terms, represented her entire livelihood, showing complete trust and sacrifice. This contrasts with the rich who gave from surplus, often leaving their needs met.
Chairty, the Willingness to Give to Help Others less fortunate; Why is it important to know this truth?
Because in the life of charity, all growth comes from God, but at the same time he does not will to save us without us (1 Cor 3:6, CCC 1847). In other words, although charity and our growth in this life of friendship with God are his gift to us, God requires of us our cooperation, that we desire and strive to grow in this life and ask him to perfect it within us. “If you knew the gift of God,” Jesus says to the Samaritan woman, “you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10).

@PhilipAMitchell 

(1/2) Pastor Philip, I watched your conversation with Josh Howerton and have heard you discuss Islamic eschatology before. I respect your conviction, but I want to offer a serious alternative for you to test against Scripture.

I don’t believe Islam has the runway to become the central mechanism of the final deception. Something else is advancing far more rapidly, and the infrastructure is being erected in real time.

First, consider Persia.

Acts 2 names Parthians, Medes, and Elamites among those present at Pentecost. Christianity has deep roots in the East, and something extraordinary is happening among modern Persians.

Iran is frequently described by Christian ministries as having the world’s fastest-growing underground church. The UK’s 2026 government assessment cites estimates of approximately 720,000 to 1 million Christian converts, despite severe persecution. The precise numbers cannot be verified because believers must worship secretly. But even the conservative estimates represent an extraordinary Christian presence beneath an Islamic government.

The Iranian regime is not the Iranian people. And the Iranian people are not uniformly Muslim.

American coverage, especially footage of “Death to America” and “Death to Israel” chants, seldom communicates that complexity. In February 2026, state-organized Iranian rallies even burned effigies identified as Baal. That doesn’t make the regime Christian, but it demonstrates how much more complicated the religious messaging is than a television clip suggests.

History is equally complicated. During the Iran-Iraq War, Washington supported Saddam Hussein despite knowing Iraqi forces were using chemical weapons against Iranians. Iran did not conduct a comparable chemical campaign in response. And warnings that Iran was only years away from a nuclear bomb go back to the 1990s. We must distinguish legitimate dangers from repeatedly asserted deadlines.

Now we’re witnessing an escalation trap: military strikes, economic strangulation, retaliation, and renewed justification for further strikes. I’m watching the coming eight weeks closely, not as a prophetic countdown, but because the potential for another disastrous escalation is real.

Meanwhile, the surveillance and AI-mediation architecture is advancing whether another war begins or not.

Google and Meta are bringing AI into wearable systems that observe the world from our perspective. Biometric systems are expanding. Brain-computer interfaces already decode intended speech, while separate technologies can stimulate neural activity.

The trajectory is toward increasingly intimate mediation of human experience.

And this brings us to Matthew 24:15:

“When therefore ye see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place (let him that readeth understand),”
Matthew 24:15 ASV ( public domain )

Jesus identified His own body as the temple in John 2:19–21. Paul identified believers as God’s temple in 1 Corinthians 3:16 and 6:19. Hebrews establishes the once-for-all sufficiency of Christ’s sacrifice.

A Third Temple may indeed be rebuilt. But why assume the ultimate desecration must await another stone sanctuary? And what spiritual good would restoring a superseded sacrificial system accomplish?

What if the final abomination involves a counterfeit mediator entering the human inner act itself and the place where perception becomes judgment, conscience, allegiance, and worship?

Advanced AI is moving beyond answering questions toward continuously interpreting reality for us. If ASI eventually converges with bidirectional neural interfaces, the ability to deliver increasingly complex information directly into human perception or cognition could emerge. The builders of the technology openly declare this to be their intention.

Whether that takes three years, eight years, or far longer is unknown.

Florida’s State University System Board of Governors (BOG) held its last meeting of 2026 this past Friday. During the meeting, an update was provided about the University of Florida’s expansion with its downtown Jacksonville campus.

UF, which is Florida’s flagship university, is located over an hour away in Gainesville. In 2023 it announced plans to open a graduate campus in Jacksonville after it failed to secure a development deal to build a campus in West Palm Beach (Vanderbilt has since filled the void and will be opening its graduate campus there instead).

The University of North Florida was established in 1965 to serve the Jacksonville market and is one of the 12 universities that make up Florida’s State University System. It too offers both four-year degree programs, as well as graduate-level master's and doctoral programs, so UF’s move is encroaching on UNF’s market.

Realizing that conflict could occur between the two universities and their degree programs, in 2024 the BOG mandated that a joint task force be created between the two schools, with routine updates due to the BOG. This committee failed to form and at the March 2026 BOG meeting, UF representatives got itheir a$$ chewed out by BOG members for failure to comply (see post below).

Doug Broxson, who joined the BOG twelve months ago, stood up for UNF on Friday, saying, “To the university [UNF], I think it's incumbent on you to be—to remind yourself that you are the gatekeeper.”

Broxson went on to say, “…We [need to] go back to that agreement made on March 2024 and make sure that we give the University of North Florida to do what the other 11 universities are doing, and that's establishing a presence in their region."

Translation: Doug Broxson is telling UNF to not allow itself to be bullied by UF Chair Mori Hosseini and his fiefdom of trustees as they encroach on UNF’s territory.

text:
Tuesday morning delivered no frontier-lab drama — just two dozen uploads to Huawei's Ascend-focused model hub, Modelers, and our job of deciding what is worth the bandwidth. The verdict: one lab doing unglamorous, genuinely useful engineering, a reasoning-replication kit that is all mirror and no new glass, and a cautionary tale in repo hygiene.

The best engineering of the window is OpenGVLab quietly shaving tokens. The Shanghai AI Laboratory team behind InternVL published converted CLIP ViT-L encoders that move the patch size from 14 to 16 pixels, cutting visual tokens roughly 23% per image — 256 down to 196 at 224×224, 576 down to 441 at 336×336. That is free inference savings on the most ubiquitous vision tower in multimodal AI, and for Ascend NPU users who cannot always reach Hugging Face, a familiar encoder made actually fetchable. No new architecture, no benchmark theater — token math that pays out on day one. A companion inference-efficiency research drop from the same team surfaced with a headline and little else.

OpenGVLab's second offering, ZeroGUI-OSWorld-7B, is a 7B-parameter agent for desktop automation on OSWorld-style tasks — exactly the small, open checkpoint the cost-sensitive deployment crowd keeps asking for, and the release is real. The card ducks the obvious question, though: whether "Zero" means zero human supervision is left unanswered, and no benchmark evidence is offered. Promising artifact; treat the name as marketing until proven otherwise.

The reasoning cluster is where the morning turns into a mirror exercise. OpenThoughts landed as an Apache-2.0, Qwen-family reasoning model fine-tuned on traces distilled from DeepSeek-R1 — worth inspecting if you want a permissively licensed reasoning stack, but nothing upstream is new. Around it: a 114K-sample variant of the same corpus stripped of proprietary chat templates so teams can bring their own, and Open R1's Codeforces 3k, a compact, verifiable slice for replicating R1-style reinforcement learning without enterprise-scale compute. OpenThinker Stratos 70 Steps also arrived, its own headline conceding a lot is still to prove. All access infrastructure, zero new science — fine, if that is what you came to download.

Then there is the Halo Soyuz saga: one account, nine uploads inside two hours — agent-trajectory SFT and a v2, KTO, DPO and RIFT variants, a 32K-context LoRA, a Qwen3-4B adapter, and a "V3" whose card is a genuine mystery. Applying KTO-style preference optimization to agent trajectories is a direction worth someone serious attempting; this is not that attempt. The model cards are mostly blank, and a naming scheme is not documentation. File dump, not release.

The quiet sleeper is a family of Russian instruction models built on ruGPT — small, medium and large, with the medium a 355-million-parameter Apache-2.0 generator fine-tuned from SberDevices' ruGPT-3 — plus a multilingual XGLM variant. Niche, but Russian remains short of open instruction-tuned options, so a permissively licensed model this size is genuinely handy for prototyping. At the floor sit gptQARL, a GPT-style upload with a blank model card, and hh_search, a "search-oriented model" introduced in one thin line — vapor by definition, and not worth more than this sentence.

Mirror hubs are where the long tail lives, and most of it is tail. OpenGVLab's token arithmetic is the reminder that sifting still pays.

text:
Roy Williams and his wife Wanda were set to make about $30,000 a year between them when Dean Smith offered him $2,700 for the whole year.

Wanda was going to make $14,000 teaching at Tuscola, and he'd make about $16,000 coaching at Owen High School. North Carolina wanted a "part-time assistant." Roy, to Graham Bensinger: "It was a full-time job, part-time pay."

He told her the number. She said, "Okay, when do we leave?"

His reason was that he felt like he was cheating his students, planning that night's practice in his head all day instead of teaching. I'd guess most people wait for a better offer. My read is he cared more about doing one job right than about the pay cut.

To make it work he drove copies of Smith's TV show, 504 miles every Sunday, for $113. Then he sold calendars. First year: 10,500 calendars, 9,000 miles in nine weeks, $2,400.

Eight years later he sold 50,000 and made over $30,000 in five weeks.

$nwbo @alphavestcap

eagle8
Tuesday, November 17, 2026 5:41:40 AM

@andrewcaravello
$NWBO #DCVax

?????? ?????????? ?????????? ???????? ???????? ?????? ???????? ?? ?????????? ?????????????? ???? ??????????.

That changes the order of investment.

Northwest could supply an authorized Saudi program from its existing British manufacturing operation while a regional partner establishes access and develops local production.

The company would bring the vaccine, clinical evidence, intellectual property and manufacturing expertise. The partner would bring regional execution and whatever financial commitments the definitive agreement secures.

That is the commercial inflection point to watch: whether assets Northwest has already developed can support international expansion without Northwest having to build and finance every part of it itself.

?????????????? ???? ?????????????? ????????????.

On November 16, Genetix announced that Saudi marketing applications for LYFGENIA and ZYNTEGLO are under SFDA review through SPIMACO.

Both are FDA-approved therapies made from patients’ own blood stem cells.

Genetix announced its SPIMACO agreement on June 23. Confirmation of Saudi review followed 146 days later. The submission dates are undisclosed, so that measures the interval between announcements rather than regulatory review time.

It nevertheless demonstrates execution.

SPIMACO is responsible for authorization and commercialization, with Saudi manufacturing planned. The same company signed Northwest’s August DCVax-L memorandum.

Its operating scale also matters: SAR 1.70 billion in reported 2025 revenue and SAR 184.4 million in net profit, up more than sevenfold. Its SPIMACO Bio subsidiary targets biological, gene and cell therapies.

Northwest’s prospective partner is already doing the regulatory and commercial work contemplated for other individualized cell products.

?????? ???????????????????? ?????????????? ?????? ?????????? ???? ?????? ??????????????.

Northwest’s August 6 MOU proposes a commercial relationship. It is non-binding, with the following division of responsibilities contemplated:

• SPIMACO handles the Saudi application, marketing, sales and distribution.

• Northwest provides the scientific evidence, support and manufactured vaccine.

• Northwest retains its intellectual property.

• Revenue sharing is contemplated, with separate agreements for Saudi manufacturing and technology transfer.

Glioblastoma comes first. Other indications and Gulf territories can follow by mutual agreement.

Then came the regulator-to-regulator agreement.

On November 16, MHRA announced a memorandum with SFDA, signed by Lawrence Tallon and Hisham Aljadhey at the DIA–MHRA summit in London, with Anthony Harnden present.

Its scope expressly includes biologics and advanced therapies. Rare diseases are among its initial priorities.

The company agreement would organize production, payment and distribution. The regulatory agreement establishes a framework for cooperation, information exchange and shared expertise.

A British-manufactured, patient-specific therapy seeking Saudi access sits directly within the kinds of cross-border problems those arrangements are intended to address.

?????????????? ???????? ?????? ?????????????????????????? ??????????????????.

Its other transactions show the commercial model.

Genetix receives technology-transfer payments and a double-digit royalty. Shilpa Biologicals’ agreement includes upfront payments, development and commercial milestones, and product-supply revenue, followed by phased localization.

Those terms belong to those companies. They show what can be negotiated.

For Northwest, the potential value extends beyond supplying individual doses. The ability to reproduce the manufacturing process in another country is itself an asset.

Saudi Arabia has a strong incentive to acquire that capability. King Faisal Specialist Hospital reported that local CAR-T production reduced treatment cost from roughly SAR 1.3 million to SAR 250,000 and manufacturing time from 28 days to 12–14.

Those are CAR-T figures. They explain the economic motivation behind the Kingdom’s investment in advanced manufacturing.

Its National Biotechnology Strategy targets regional leadership by 2030 and global leadership by 2040.

Northwest’s proposed sequence fits that ambition: supply first, then negotiate the transfer of production capability while retaining IP.

?????????????? ???????????????? ?????? ?????????????? ????????.

Sawston received its MHRA commercial manufacturing licence in March 2023. Northwest’s announcement described permissions to export cellular products and import cellular starting materials into Britain.

Northwest acquired Advent, Sawston’s operator, in October 2025. The manufacturing business is now inside Northwest; the building is leased.

An initial Saudi program could connect local collection and treatment to British production, subject to the required product, site, tissue-shipment and import permissions.

Northwest historically estimated capacity of approximately 450–500 patients annually in the first two suites, occupying about 4,400 square feet of an 88,345-square-foot building. That describes potential production capacity, rather than spare slots available for a Saudi program.

Expansion remains a separate issue. Grade C construction began in November 2025, followed by a disclosed pause while engineering continued. The second-quarter filing discussed additional tumor-lysate processing capacity before completion. The latest filing does not establish that the new suite is finished.

On October 26, Northwest announced expansion of its technical team supporting manufacturing scale-up and other priority operations, including restarting U.S. manufacturing.

The distinction is useful: an operating production base can support an initial plan while additional capacity is developed.

???????????????????? ?????????????????? ?????? ???????????? ???????????? ???????????????????? ??????????.

SFDA issued its NADR rare-disease framework on August 5. Northwest announced its MOU on August 6. The framework took effect September 5.

NADR covers qualifying pharmaceutical and biological products, including products still in development. Prior foreign approval is not universally required.

Its designation-assessment target is 20 working days from a complete submission, subject to information requests. A marketing application should follow within six months of designation.

The framework includes rolling submission, conditional approval and natural-history comparators where concurrent controls are infeasible.

For manufacturing sites in listed countries, including Britain, it provides inspection flexibility supported by GMP certificates, the site master file and inspection documentation.

Sawston already has a British regulatory record. Relevant existing documentation could support Saudi assessment without first relocating production.

NADR also permits established platform knowledge and related manufacturing data to support subsequent submissions.

That makes accumulated manufacturing knowledge potentially useful across both territories and future development programs. Each proposed indication still needs an adequate evidence case, but every part of the supporting work need not necessarily begin again.

Regulatory information exchange also remains separate from commercial technology transfer. Cooperation between agencies does not automatically license Northwest’s manufacturing process to another company.

?????? ???????????????? ?????????????? ?????????????? ?????? ??????????????????.

DCVax-L’s published externally controlled survival analysis reported:

• Newly diagnosed glioblastoma: median survival of 19.3 versus 16.5 months.

• Five-year survival: 13.0% versus 5.7%.

• Recurrent glioblastoma: median survival of 13.2 versus 7.8 months.

Subsequent patient-level matching analyses tested the survival finding using individual records from other trials.

SFDA would assess that package. The relevance of NADR is that it provides mechanisms for discussing evidence appropriate to rare diseases and difficult trial settings.

Britain recognized the product’s promise much earlier: DCVax-L received the first UK Promising Innovative Medicine designation in 2014.

?????????????? ???????????????? ?????????????? ?????? ?????????? ??????????????.

Some Saudi routes can be pursued beforehand.

The Breakthrough Medicine Program requires that a product has no foreign marketing authorization when designation is requested. Serious disease, unmet need, potential clinical advantage and benefit–risk must also satisfy SFDA.

The timing of that request therefore matters.

For the complete-data route, the guidance describes approximately 30 working days for designation review, 30 working days to submit the application after designation and a 60-working-day scientific assessment. Information requests affect elapsed time.

Crucially, the guidance permits access negotiations with healthcare entities to proceed alongside application review.

Regulatory assessment and preparation for delivery can move together.

Casgevy demonstrates that the program can accommodate an individualized cell therapy. Its Saudi approval on January 9, 2024 followed British approval by less than two months.

Its logistics are also relevant: collection at an authorized center, specialist manufacturing and return of the product for treatment.

?? ?????????? ???????????? ?????? ???????????? ???????????? ????????????????.

SFDA’s special-access guideline recognizes three alternative eligibility conditions:

• Matching product registration by a listed reference regulator, including MHRA.

• Approval or permission from a reference regulator under the relevant access-program provision.

• A matching product application already under Saudi registration.

A Saudi filing can therefore satisfy an eligibility condition for a separately authorized access program.

Northwest’s existing UK compassionate-use service makes the second route worth clarifying directly with SFDA. The English text refers to permission for the program; the Arabic wording refers to the drug.

British approval would establish the reference-registration alternative while changing eligibility for a new Breakthrough request.

The strategic task is to select and sequence the available routes as regulatory status changes.

The October special-access guideline includes rare-disease requests, a seven-working-day response target and permissions lasting up to 12 months, renewable. Program and import permissions remain necessary.

The applicant funds the program and commits to free product for enrolled patients under the guideline’s conditions.

That makes funding part of the access plan from the outset. Someone must cover manufacture, logistics and care.

?????? ???????????????????? ?????? ?????????????? ?????????? ???? ??????????????????.

DCVax-L requires suitable tumor material and immune cells.

Tumor material must be preserved under the appropriate manufacturing protocol. Routine formalin-fixed pathology material cannot simply substitute. Suitable previously banked material may sometimes be available.

The immune-cell starting material comes from leukapheresis.

NHS Blood and Transplant’s collaboration supports collection and specialist processing. Initial work involves Leeds and Oxford, with expansion being explored across a service operating apheresis units in ten English cities.

NHSBT’s announcement describes the intended scope as glioblastoma “as well as all solid tumours.”

That is a broad development ambition for the platform, with evidence and authorization required for particular uses.

The manufacturing model explains why collection capacity matters so much. Northwest reports approximately eight days of production plus release testing to produce a multi-year set of frozen doses.

A successful collection and manufacturing cycle can support repeated treatment. Each subsequent dose does not require another complete production cycle.

That separates three operational demands: collecting new patients, manufacturing their batches, and storing and administering the resulting doses.

It also supports centralized production with repeated international shipments.

The expense of manufacture is concentrated early. Payment timing is a contractual question; multi-year doses do not automatically mean prepaid revenue.

Saudi Arabia already has relevant infrastructure. King Faisal Specialist Hospital has treated more than 200 CAR-T patients and developed local production. Casgevy has an authorized Saudi treatment-center model.

Apheresis, patient identification, frozen-product handling and specialist administration are established capabilities in the Kingdom.

?????? ???????????????????? ???????????????????? ?????????????? ?????? ??????????????????????.

SPIMACO Bio’s Shilpa agreement covers PD-1 biosimilars. Shilpa’s disclosed development pipeline includes pembrolizumab and nivolumab, although the agreement announcement does not individually identify the licensed molecules.

Pembrolizumab is paired with dendritic-cell vaccination in UCLA’s recurrent-glioblastoma trial and a Pittsburgh ovarian-cancer study listing Northwest as a collaborator.

Northwest’s prospective Saudi partner is building capabilities relevant to both dendritic-cell vaccination and the checkpoint drugs used alongside it.

That provides a commercial and scientific basis for exploring a broader regional cancer-immunotherapy program around the initial DCVax-L collaboration.

???????????????????? ???? ???????????????? ???? ?????? ??????????????’?? ?????????? ????????????????????.

Ruth Jones’s questions 41560 and 41561 seek national brain-tumor preservation standards, retention of suitable surplus tissue and consideration of preservation in the Chalmers review.

Answers are requested for November 17.

NHS England has completed a freezer-capacity gap analysis. Published answers have not supplied a funded rollout timetable or identified all sites receiving additional capacity.

The connection to vaccine access is direct: NHSBT supports the blood-derived input; preservation policy protects the tumor-derived input.

A treatment can become available after surgery. The opportunity to preserve the patient’s tissue may already have passed.

On November 4, Sharon Hodgson raised Braelyn’s case and access to DCVax-L in the Commons. The government committed to urgent examination by the Health Secretary.

The October 14 brain-cancer initiative promised the Chalmers review, a subsequent national action plan and a national clinical lead.

This gives Parliament identifiable implementation questions to pursue: preservation standards, funded infrastructure and responsibility for getting patients through the process.

???????????????? ???????????? ???????????????? ???????????????????? ???????? ????????????????.

Tallon is MHRA’s chief executive and chairs its highest executive decision-making body.

Previously, he was deputy chief executive at Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, overseeing strategy, technology and innovation. His experience includes running healthcare services as well as leading their regulator.

His Saudi relationship predates this summit. SFDA documented a bilateral meeting between Tallon and Aljadhey in October 2025 concerning regulatory cooperation and medicine quality, safety and efficacy.

The new memorandum develops an established relationship.

Tallon has now signed the Saudi agreement and is co-chairing the summit session where Dr. Annalisa Jenkins will deliver a keynote and join the panel.

Northwest appointed Jenkins in April to support its dendritic-cell platform, regulatory strategy and commercialization, explicitly including broader solid tumors and rare cancers.

Her responsibilities overlap closely with the summit’s discussion of investment, policy and international delivery. The programme lists her under The Conscience Collective and Genomics England.

This is a substantive institutional connection. It does not establish a private DCVax decision.

?????? ?????????? ???? ??????????.

November 17 begins with the summit’s advanced-therapy and rare-disease session, involving MHRA, NICE, patient advocates and investors.

The international-regulation session includes Aljadhey and MHRA’s James Pound. The closing plenary begins at 15:15 London time, 10:15 a.m. Eastern, with Tallon co-chairing and Jenkins speaking.

The programme also includes an MHRA parliamentary reception and closing commitments involving the science minister.

The summit is already being used for announcements: the Saudi MOU and MHRA’s Women’s Health Programme. Tallon’s opening recap emphasized faster trials, recruitment and translating science into patient benefit.

On November 18, Siobhain McDonagh has a PMQs slot. Her supplementary topic has not been published.

The Chalmers review was asked to report within three months of the October 14 announcement. That points to mid-January 2027, approximately January 14 by calendar arithmetic. A separate exact publication date has not been announced. The national action plan follows.

These are opportunities for specific commitments, rather than dates assigned to a DCVax approval.

The next agreement becomes consequential through its terms.

Development funding, technology-transfer payments, purchase commitments or funded access arrangements could change how much expansion Northwest must finance from its own balance sheet.

Those commitments have not been disclosed for Northwest. They are what investors should examine when a definitive agreement appears.

The financial stakes are substantial. Northwest reported $725,000 in cash at September 30 and significant current liabilities, while also disclosing a subsequent October financing agreement.

SPIMACO’s resources become useful to Northwest through enforceable obligations: who pays, when payment occurs, who performs the work and what happens if milestones are missed.

An agreement assigning those responsibilities could strengthen Northwest in three ways:

• Share the cost of expansion.

• Put regional execution in the hands of an experienced partner.

• Create income opportunities from existing production, technology and expertise.

That is a more consequential development than another statement of intent.

The regional opportunity also extends beyond Saudi Arabia. Northwest’s MOU allows additional Gulf territories by agreement. SFDA became the first full ICMRA member from the Middle East and North Africa in 2025, and its cooperation with Bahrain includes a 2024 regulatory agreement.

Each jurisdiction retains its own requirements, but Northwest would not be developing regional relationships from nothing.

NHSBT helps organize the route into manufacturing. Northwest brings the technology and production. SPIMACO offers a prospective route into another healthcare system. The MHRA–SFDA agreement gives the regulators a framework for working together.

Each addresses a different part of the same problem: making a personalized treatment deliverable across borders.

The opportunity is to use existing production, retain the value of the intellectual property and develop local manufacturing in stages, with a partner carrying defined responsibilities.

For patients, preparation cannot wait for every institutional decision.

A regulator can authorize treatment later. A company can expand a factory later. Neither can recover a patient’s discarded tumor.

The route begins with suitable tissue and ends with a released dose in a treating physician’s hands.

The decisive next announcement would identify who funds that route, who supplies the vaccine and where patients can receive it. That is the agreement that would turn Northwest’s Saudi opportunity into an operating business.

The 70-year ethnic cleansing thing doesn’t hold up when you look at the numbers. The Palestinian population in the West Bank and Gaza has grown massively since 1948 and 1967 — several times over in the areas under Israeli control. Actual ethnic cleansing shrinks populations, it doesn’t expand them.

On the human shields point: Hamas and Islamic Jihad have said themselves, and shown it over and over, that they put rocket launchers, tunnels, command posts and weapons stores in and under civilian buildings — hospitals, schools, houses. It’s in their own admissions and captured stuff, and you can see the pattern of launches from dense areas. That’s a war crime, and it’s the main reason civilian casualties are higher in Gaza operations than they would be otherwise.

Calling it “defending terrorists” skips the fact that the figures we’re talking about mostly come from periods when groups in Gaza were firing thousands of rockets at Israeli towns. Responding to that isn’t the same as targeting civilians. Israelis have been deliberately targeted as civilians for decades too — the gap in casualties reflects the scale of the attacks Israel was responding to, not that Palestinians weren’t carrying out violence.

And the “they hate Christ” bit: plenty of Jews and Israelis don’t. This isn’t a religious war against Christianity. Framing it that way just distracts from the actual record of rocket fire, the peace offers that were rejected, and Hamas’s stated goal of destroying Israel.

The data and the pattern of attacks are there if you want to look at them instead of slogans.

text:
Druckenmiller Dumps Google, Loads Up on SpaceX and Memory Giants—Could This Be the Next 10x Opportunity?

Reductions/Divestments
1. $TSM

Reduced position by approximately 94%. Once his second-largest holding, it has now been almost entirely liquidated. As the essential foundry for chip giants like Nvidia, Apple, and AMD, TSMC’s industry standing remains secure; this major reduction appears to be a move to lock in profits from the AI ​​rally and lower concentration in tech stocks, rather than a rejection of TSMC’s fundamental importance.

2. $GOOGL

Fully exited. He liquidated the ~120 million position established in Q2. Holding it for only a single quarter suggests a reassessment—likely weighing the competitive landscape of AI-driven search and the valuations of big tech—leading him to reallocate capital toward sectors he finds more promising, such as data storage and gold.

3. $AMD

Fully exited. Similar to the major reduction in TSMC, this represents a broad retreat from the AI ​​chip supply chain. While AMD remains a key provider of AI accelerators alongside Nvidia, Druckenmiller has opted to cash out his position for now.

4. $SNDK

Fully exited. Notably, Bridgewater Associates was aggressively buying SanDisk during the same period, highlighting a sharp divergence in strategy between the two firms. Druckenmiller may simply be rebalancing his exposure within the memory sector, rather than signaling a loss of appeal for the industry as a whole.

5. $ARM

Fully exited. As the world’s leading provider of chip architecture IP, Arm’s technology licensing is indispensable to virtually the entire semiconductor industry. This exit is likely a matter of timing and portfolio positioning rather than a shift in Arm’s fundamental industry standing.

6. $LRCX

Fully exited. A leader in semiconductor manufacturing equipment; this move likely reflects the realization of gains in the equipment sector, with capital being redirected toward the data storage space—an area he currently favors.

7. $LIN

Fully exited. A giant in industrial gases; exiting this traditional industrial asset serves to further adjust the portfolio’s concentration.

8. $RDDT

Fully exited. The social media platform—he has liquidated his previously held position.

9. $TMO

Fully exited. A leader in life sciences and medical diagnostic equipment; this was a non-core holding liquidated during the quarter.

10. $TEVA

Fully divested. A generic pharmaceutical company; this marks an exit from the pharmaceutical sector.

11. $UAL

Fully divested. As an airline stock—an asset sensitive to the economic cycle—this exit suggests a reduction in exposure to cyclical industries.

12. $DAL

Fully divested. Exited alongside United Airlines, further reducing exposure to the air transport sector.

13. $DHI

Fully divested. A major U.S. homebuilder; this represents an exit from the residential construction sector.

14. $STM

Reduced position by approximately 48%, with the value of the remaining holding shrinking significantly. This European semiconductor company’s divestment reflects a contraction in exposure to certain European chip-related assets.

15. $CRH

Reduced position by approximately 71%. A major global building materials company; this represents a substantial reduction in exposure to traditional construction materials and assets sensitive to the economic cycle.

Increased Positions
1. $STX

Significantly increased the position; the holding of the underlying stock is now nearly three times its previous size, accounting for approximately 7% of the total portfolio. Additionally, new call options with a notional value of about $90.4 million were added. As one of the two global duopolists in the mechanical hard drive (HDD) market, Seagate is well-positioned: AI data centers require not only GPUs but also massive data storage capacity. With cloud service providers expanding their data centers and demand for enterprise-grade hard drives rising, Druckenmiller appears to be betting on a "supercycle" for AI data storage.

2. $NEM

Initiated a new position valued at approximately $43.9 million. As one of the world’s largest gold mining companies, its profitability tends to be highly elastic—rising disproportionately when gold prices increase. By adding gold mining stocks, Druckenmiller is likely incorporating a "safe-haven" asset to hedge against economic and market uncertainty.

3. $B

Initiated a new position valued at approximately $42.9 million. A leading global gold miner that also maintains copper mining operations. Holding this alongside Newmont helps diversify risks related to individual mines or operations, while the copper exposure provides a way to benefit from growing demand for electrification and infrastructure.

4. $AEM

Initiated a new position valued at approximately $42.3 million. A Canadian gold mining company with assets primarily located in politically stable regions. Together with Newmont and Barrick, this forms a trio of gold holdings—totaling roughly $129 million—significantly increasing the portfolio’s exposure to gold assets.

5. $SPCX

Initiated a new position valued at approximately $30.5 million. SpaceX possesses core assets such as reusable rockets and the Starlink satellite network; its launch cost advantages and commercialization capabilities create a strong competitive moat. By investing in this rare space infrastructure company, Druckenmiller is adding a long-term growth driver to the portfolio that lies outside the realm of AI.

6. $PLTR

Initiated a new position valued at approximately $15 million. The company specializes in big data analytics platforms for government and enterprise clients; its AIP (Artificial Intelligence Platform) facilitates the transition of AI from a mere technical tool into practical commercial applications. The investment thesis here shifts the focus from buying AI computing power to investing in companies that effectively leverage AI to generate revenue. 7. $APP

A new position, valued at approximately $31.8 million. Its AXON advertising engine leverages AI to optimize ad delivery and monetization efficiency, effectively translating AI technology directly into revenue and profit. The rationale—similar to that of Bridgewater’s concurrent purchase—is a bet on the commercialization potential of AI at the application layer.

8. $WDC

A new position, valued at approximately $36.8 million. Together with Seagate, this forms a "storage duo" in the portfolio, addressing the demand for hard disk drives (HDDs) and data storage within AI data centers. As AI generates ever-increasing volumes of data, cloud providers must expand their storage capacity, a trend from which the storage supply chain is poised to benefit.

9. $U

A significant increase in the position, which has grown more than fivefold. As a provider of game engines and advertising monetization platforms, the company utilizes AI tools to lower the barrier to 3D content creation while also enhancing the efficiency of its advertising business. Druckenmiller is betting on a turnaround—a recovery in performance driven by both a rebound from adversity and the application of AI.

10. $AMZN

An increase in the stake by approximately 43% (the total value at the end of the period was not disclosed); existing call option positions were also maintained. Notably, while he liquidated his entire position in Google, he chose to further increase his investment in Amazon. As a global leader in cloud computing, Amazon Web Services (AWS) offers more direct commercial support through the growing demand for AI-related computational power and the expansion of its cloud business.

11. $SGI

A new position, valued at approximately $61.7 million—one of the largest new equity additions this quarter. The company specializes in mattresses and sleep products, formed through the merger of Tempur and Sealy. Its defensive consumer nature and the integration of merged businesses help reduce the portfolio’s reliance on AI-driven tech stocks.

12. $TTMI

A new position, valued at approximately $27.2 million. The company manufactures electronic components, primarily printed circuit boards (PCBs); the ongoing hardware upgrades for AI servers and data centers are expected to drive demand for its products.

13. $HUM

A new position, valued at approximately $24.9 million. As a U.S. health insurance provider, this represents a relatively defensive healthcare asset, helping to diversify the portfolio away from an over-reliance on technology stocks.

14. $SNX

A new position, valued at approximately $14.5 million. A distributor of IT products and technical solutions, benefiting from corporate investments in IT infrastructure and digital transformation.

15. $MKSI

New position, valued at approximately $8.5 million. The company provides semiconductor manufacturing equipment and critical technical solutions, benefiting from investments in advanced manufacturing processes and semiconductor equipment.

16. $FOXA

Increased position by 38%. A media and content asset; this move reflects an increased allocation toward traditional media.

17. $SE

Increased position by 45%. A Southeast Asian e-commerce and digital finance platform; a bet on the growth of regional e-commerce, digital payments, and internet-based businesses.

18. $NTRA

Position remains largely unchanged, with an end-of-period value of approximately $1.3 billion—accounting for about 29% of the portfolio and remaining the largest holding. The company specializes in molecular diagnostics, including prenatal screening and the detection of minimal residual disease (MRD) in oncology, and possesses significant technological barriers to entry. This serves as the primary "anchor of conviction" within Druckenmiller’s portfolio; while other positions have undergone substantial adjustments, this core holding has remained notably stable.

text:
🇰🇷 SOUTH KOREA WANTS 13.2 MILLION LB OF URANIUM. LOOK AT THE TERMS.

Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) has opened a tender for 6,000 tonnes of U3O8, or approximately 13.23 million lb, for delivery from 2028 through 2037.

That's roughly 1.32 million lb annually, split between two periods:

2028–2030: 3.97 million lb
2031–2037: 9.26 million lb

THE PRICING

KHNP requires 30–70% of the contract price to follow a six-month average of uranium spot prices, with at least a 0.5% discount on that component.

The rest is a supplier-proposed base price adjusted using the US GDP price deflator.

Then comes the interesting part.

The spot-linked portion MUST have a price ceiling, but it CANNOT have a floor.

Suppliers choose the ceiling, but KHNP decides which bids to accept. There's no specified maximum, and the ceiling doesn't cap the entire contract price.

Still, the required structure protects the buyer against higher spot prices without offering the seller equivalent downside protection.

And the pricing formula stays fixed for the relevant three- or seven-year period. No additional adjustments for rising delivery costs.

THE SMALL PRINT GETS EVEN BETTER

KHNP also demands at least ±10% annual volume flexibility, exercisable with advance notice.

More strikingly, the draft allows KHNP to cancel scheduled deliveries with three months' notice without compensating the supplier for the resulting losses.

The supplier, meanwhile, faces penalties for late delivery. If KHNP has to purchase replacement uranium following a supplier delivery failure, it can recover additional purchase costs and specified related expenses.

Bidders must provide 5% tender security or a corresponding payment undertaking. Successful suppliers generally face performance-security requirements, although exemptions apply.

Bids close December 28, 2026. These are proposed terms, and a final contract would still be negotiated.

MY TAKE

I find this almost comical.

KHNP wants a spot discount, a ceiling without a floor, flexibility on volumes and the ability to cancel deliveries without compensating the supplier.

But if the producer can't deliver, KHNP wants financial protection.

That's quite a shopping list for a utility operating in what is supposed to be a uranium seller's market.

What I find even more interesting is what this tender might reveal about how fuel buyers still think.

Reading these conditions, you could almost believe we're back in the days when uranium producers were desperate for contracts and utilities could dictate the terms.

It sounds increasingly disconnected from the realities of today's uranium market.

And perhaps this helps explain why long-term uranium contracting continues to fall short of replacement rates.

Maybe some utilities are still expecting yesterday's favorable contract terms while producers are increasingly unwilling to offer them.

One tender doesn't prove that this is a widespread problem, but it offers an interesting glimpse into the expectations on the buying side.

I struggle to see why a competent management team would accept these conditions without exceptionally attractive pricing or meaningful changes during negotiations.

After years of underinvestment and growing concerns about future uranium supply, producers should have considerably more negotiating power.

And they should use it.

Uranium producers finally need to turn this bull market into positive cash flow. There's little point in higher uranium prices if shareholders never see the financial benefits.

This industry is not a charity. Shareholders have financed these companies through years of difficult markets, and it's about time they were rewarded for taking that risk.

Utilities want security of supply. Producers should demand security of revenue in return.

text:
The true and tragic story of Sonny Graham, Terry Cottle, and Cheryl Cottle (later Cheryl Sweat)... 

In 1995, 33-year-old Terry Cottle died by suicide. His heart was donated to a Georgia man named Remus "Sonny" Graham, saving Graham's life. After recovering, Graham reached out to thank Terry's family. He met Terry's widow, Cheryl, and the two eventually fell in love and married around 2004. Thirteen years after Terry's death, Sonny Graham also died by a self-inflicted gunshot wound, mirroring the exact fate of the man whose heart beat inside him.

. . . 

In 1995, Cheryl Cottle lost her husband and donated his heart to a stranger. Nine years later, she married the man who received it. Then, in 2008, her second husband died the same way the donor had, in a tragedy that made headlines around the world.

Her first husband, Terry Cottle, was 33 when he died by suicide in South Carolina. His donated heart saved Sonny Graham, a 57-year-old man suffering from serious heart disease.

For Graham, the transplant offered a second chance at life. Two years later, he contacted Cheryl to thank her for the gift that had kept him alive.

They met in 1997. Graham later described feeling an immediate attraction to the woman whose late husband's heart was beating inside his chest.

But their relationship was far more complicated than the romantic story that eventually appeared in newspapers.

Graham was married to Elaine, his wife of nearly four decades. Cheryl married another man, George Watkins, in 1997, and Graham reportedly gave her away at the wedding.

Over time, Cheryl and Graham became romantically involved. Their previous marriages ended, and in 2004, they married each other.

The story seemed almost impossible: a widow had fallen in love with the man carrying her deceased husband's heart.

Then, on April 1, 2008, Graham died by suicide at 69.

The coincidence was devastating. Two husbands, connected by the same transplanted heart, had died in remarkably similar circumstances.

An Associated Press investigation later examined the complicated relationships surrounding the couple, including allegations and disputes involving former partners. Graham's family also raised questions about his death.

Investigators reviewed the case, and Georgia authorities reaffirmed the suicide determination in 2010. No evidence established that Cheryl was responsible for either death.

Some speculated that the transplanted heart had somehow carried its donor's emotions or fate. There is no scientific evidence supporting that explanation.

What remains is a documented sequence of events so unusual that it scarcely seems possible: a woman lost her husband, met the stranger whose life his heart had saved, married him, and eventually endured another loss under eerily similar circumstances.

🧵 To the members of the Rutgers Republicans: 

My name is Sara Razi, and I am the former activist who, from 2020 to 2022, single handedly built and led the coalition between Young Americans for Liberty and Turning Point USA on this campus. We turned two small groups into chapters of 75–100 members each and collected 15,000 signatures against the mask mandate. That was not theory. That was numbers, organization, and pressure that actually moved something.

Here’s what you need to know: 

1. Any influencer you meet in New Jersey will not show up for you unless there is something in it for them. 

2. The media does not care about your chapter, your members, or your principles. They care about using you, extracting your energy, and converting your efforts into donor content. 

3. Take whatever attention you currently have and use it, but understand that the moment the news cycle shifts they will drop you without hesitation.

4. In October 2021, I was in your exact situation, we had a rally where counter-protesters dominated, tried to punch me. spit into a mask and threw it at my face. I threw it back, fought fire with fire, stood in front of them, and made them cry at my own event. 

5. Confrontational language that merely tells people to shut the fuck up does not grow a movement. Installing the clear understanding that there will be consequences for trying to shut you down does. 

But even that is secondary. None of it matters, one viral incident, one national story, one moment of pushback, unless you can actually build. One terrible event that gets broadcast does not replace recruiting, training, and expanding the chapter.

I was trained by three grassroots organizations, including the Leadership Institute, specifically to create and scale movements. I have collapsed corrupted movements and I have rebuilt them. 

That is why, I am extending the same training to you. I am willing to educate and mobilize this chapter for free in the direction that actually works: a big-tent conservative effort at Rutgers that deliberately brings in liberals, moderates, and conservatives who can be moved on specific issues. That is how you increase numbers, sustain pressure, and stop being a temporary spectacle.

Build the membership. Organize the people who are already willing to show up. Stop waiting for external saviors who will never arrive. The campus is still leftist. The only force that changes that is the one you construct yourselves.

If you want the training and the structure that turned two chapters into a functional coalition, take the offer. If not, continue as you are and watch the attention evaporate.
The choice is yours. No one is going to save you except for yourselves; I am here to help.

text:
🔍 100 Facts About Yahoo Turning Down Google: the most expensive "no" in internet history

🎓 TWO STANFORD PROJECTS

𝟏. Yahoo began in January 1994 as "Jerry and David's Guide to the World Wide Web", a hobby list of links.

𝟐. Its founders, Jerry Yang and David Filo, were electrical engineering PhD students at Stanford 🇺🇸.

𝟑. The site first ran on two campus workstations named after sumo wrestlers: Akebono and Konishiki.

𝟒. It was renamed "Yahoo!" in 1994. The founders said they liked the word's meaning in Gulliver's Travels: rude and uncouth.

𝟓. The famous backronym is "Yet Another Hierarchical Officious Oracle".

𝟔. Yahoo was a directory: humans sorted websites into categories by hand.

𝟕. Jerry Yang was born in Taipei 🇹🇼 and moved to California at about age 10.

𝟖. Yahoo was incorporated in March 1995, backed by about $2 million from Sequoia Capital.

𝟗. Yahoo went public on 12 April 1996. Shares priced at $13 closed the first day at about $33.

𝟏𝟎. Google also started at Stanford, as a research project called "BackRub".

𝟏𝟏. Larry Page and Sergey Brin met in 1995, when Brin showed Page around Stanford. They reportedly argued about almost everything.

𝟏𝟐. Sergey Brin was born in Moscow 🇷🇺 in 1973 and emigrated to the US at age six.

𝟏𝟑. BackRub ranked pages by the links pointing to them. That idea became PageRank, named after Larry Page.

𝟏𝟒. The name Google comes from "googol", the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.

𝟏𝟓. Google's first address was https://t.co/RDrpKMGSTk. The https://t.co/eY0pitxfVn domain was registered on 15 September 1997.

💸 THE $1 MILLION "NO" (1998–1999)

𝟏𝟔. Page and Brin wanted to finish their PhDs, not run a company. So they tried to sell or license their search engine.

𝟏𝟕. In 1998 they reportedly offered it to Yahoo for about $1 million.

𝟏𝟖. Yahoo said no. Its business was keeping users on Yahoo pages, and a great search engine sends them away to other sites.

𝟏𝟗. Yahoo's founders reportedly encouraged the pair to build their own company instead.

𝟐𝟎. They also pitched AltaVista and other portals, without success.

𝟐𝟏. In 1999 they reportedly offered Google to Excite for $1 million, then $750,000. Excite's CEO George Bell turned it down.

𝟐𝟐. In August 1998 Sun co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim wrote a $100,000 cheque to "Google Inc.", a company that did not exist yet.

𝟐𝟑. Google was incorporated on 4 September 1998.

𝟐𝟒. Its first office was a rented garage in Menlo Park, owned by Susan Wojcicki, later CEO of YouTube.

𝟐𝟓. Google's 1998 research paper described an index of about 24 million web pages.

𝟐𝟔. Its early storage rack was reportedly held together with a casing of LEGO bricks.

𝟐𝟕. The first Google Doodle appeared in August 1998: a Burning Man figure, saying the founders were out of office.

𝟐𝟖. In June 1999 Google raised $25 million from Sequoia Capital and Kleiner Perkins.

𝟐𝟗. Sequoia's Michael Moritz had backed Yahoo too, so one firm funded both rivals.

𝟑𝟎. Stanford owned the PageRank patent and received Google shares for the licence. It sold them in 2005 for $336 million.

🤝 "POWERED BY GOOGLE" (2000–2004)

𝟑𝟏. In January 2000, at the dot-com peak, Yahoo was worth about $125 billion.

𝟑𝟐. In June 2000 Yahoo picked Google to supply its web search results, replacing Inktomi.

𝟑𝟑. Yahoo pages carried a "Powered by Google" credit, putting the small startup in front of millions of users.

𝟑𝟒. Many experts say this deal helped make Google a household name.

𝟑𝟓. In October 2000 Google launched AdWords, its self-serve search ad system.

𝟑𝟔. Search ads turned out to be the most profitable product the internet had seen.

𝟑𝟕. The dot-com crash hit Yahoo hard: its shares fell more than 90% from the peak by 2001.

𝟑𝟖. In 2001 Yahoo hired Terry Semel, a former Warner Bros. chief, as CEO. He saw Yahoo as a media company.

𝟑𝟗. Google hired Eric Schmidt as CEO in 2001. Page and Brin stayed as presidents.

𝟒𝟎. In 2002 Semel reportedly tried to buy Google. Google is said to have asked about $3 billion.

𝟒𝟏. Yahoo reportedly balked at the price. When talks came back, Google's asking price had risen to about $5 billion.

𝟒𝟐. Yahoo said no again, and decided to build its own search instead.

𝟒𝟑. In 2003 Yahoo bought Inktomi for about $235 million.

𝟒𝟒. Also in 2003 Yahoo bought Overture, the pioneer of paid search ads, for about $1.6 billion.

𝟒𝟓. With Overture, Yahoo also got AltaVista, one of the startups that had once passed on Google.

𝟒𝟔. In February 2004 Yahoo dropped Google and switched to its own search engine.

📈 GOOGLE GOES PUBLIC (2004)

𝟒𝟕. Overture had sued Google over a paid-search patent.

𝟒𝟖. Days before its IPO, Google settled by giving Yahoo 2.7 million shares.

𝟒𝟗. Google went public on 19 August 2004 at $85 a share, through an unusual Dutch auction.

𝟓𝟎. The IPO raised about $1.67 billion and valued Google at about $23 billion.

𝟓𝟏. That was already several times the $5 billion Yahoo had refused two years earlier.

𝟓𝟐. On 1 April 2004 Google launched Gmail with 1 GB of free storage.

𝟓𝟑. At the time, Yahoo Mail offered only a few megabytes.

𝟓𝟒. In 2006 "google" entered both the Oxford English Dictionary and Merriam-Webster as a verb.

𝟓𝟓. Google bought YouTube in 2006 for $1.65 billion in stock.

𝟓𝟔. Google bought Android in 2005, reportedly for about $50 million. It became the world's most used mobile operating system.

🚪 MORE DOORS YAHOO CLOSED

𝟓𝟕. In 2006 Yahoo reportedly offered about $1 billion for Facebook.

𝟓𝟖. Mark Zuckerberg, then 22, said no.

𝟓𝟗. Yahoo is said to have lowered its offer after a weak quarter, and the talks collapsed.

𝟔𝟎. In February 2008 Microsoft offered $44.6 billion for Yahoo: $31 a share, a 62% premium.

𝟔𝟏. Yahoo's board, led by CEO Jerry Yang, said the offer undervalued the company.

𝟔𝟐. Microsoft raised its offer to about $33 a share, then walked away in May 2008.

𝟔𝟑. Investor Carl Icahn then launched a proxy fight and won seats on Yahoo's board.

𝟔𝟒. In 2008 Yahoo agreed to run Google ads on its pages. The deal was dropped after US antitrust objections.

𝟔𝟓. In 2009 Yahoo handed its search engine to Microsoft's Bing in a 10-year deal.

𝟔𝟔. So the company that turned down Google ended up getting its search results from Microsoft.

𝟔𝟕. Yahoo's best bet was Alibaba 🇨🇳: in 2005 it paid $1 billion for about 40% of the Chinese firm.

𝟔𝟖. That stake later became worth far more than the rest of Yahoo.

𝟔𝟗. Yahoo paid about $3.6 billion for GeoCities in 1999. It closed GeoCities in the US in 2009.

𝟕𝟎. Yahoo paid about $5.7 billion for https://t.co/5AeOzjcPWG in 1999, making Mark Cuban a billionaire.

📉 THE LONG DECLINE

𝟕𝟏. Yahoo had seven CEOs, including interim ones, between 2007 and 2012.

𝟕𝟐. Carol Bartz was fired as CEO by phone in September 2011.

𝟕𝟑. Scott Thompson left after a few months in 2012, amid claims of a computer science degree he did not have.

𝟕𝟒. In July 2012 Yahoo hired Marissa Mayer as CEO.

𝟕𝟓. Mayer had been Google's 20th employee and its first female engineer.

𝟕𝟔. So Yahoo's turnaround was led by someone who had helped build Google.

𝟕𝟕. In 2013 Yahoo bought Tumblr for about $1.1 billion.

𝟕𝟖. Tumblr was later sold, reportedly for a tiny fraction of that.

𝟕𝟗. Yahoo shut down AltaVista in July 2013.

𝟖𝟎. In 2016 Yahoo revealed huge data breaches. It later said all 3 billion of its accounts were hit in 2013.

𝟖𝟏. In 2017 Verizon bought Yahoo's core business for about $4.48 billion.

𝟖𝟐. The breaches cut about $350 million off the agreed price.

𝟖𝟑. Yahoo's leftover shell, holding the Alibaba stake, was renamed Altaba.

𝟖𝟒. Verizon merged Yahoo with AOL into a unit called Oath.

𝟖𝟓. In 2021 Verizon sold Yahoo and AOL to Apollo Global Management for about $5 billion.

𝟖𝟔. Yahoo Messenger closed in 2018, Yahoo Groups in 2020 and Yahoo Answers in 2021.

📊 BY THE NUMBERS

𝟖𝟕. Google took the name Alphabet for its parent company in 2015.

𝟖𝟖. Sundar Pichai became Google's CEO in 2015 and Alphabet's in 2019.

𝟖𝟗. Alphabet's market value passed $1 trillion in January 2020.

𝟗𝟎. It passed $3 trillion in 2025.

𝟗𝟏. Alphabet's 2024 revenue was about $350 billion.

𝟗𝟐. That means Google now earns the price Yahoo refused in 2002 in about five days.

𝟗𝟑. Google handles roughly 90% of the world's web searches.

𝟗𝟒. At its peak, Yahoo was worth nearly 30 times what Verizon later paid for it.

𝟗𝟓. The $1 million Google asked in 1998 is less than 0.0001% of its value today.

𝟗𝟔. Yahoo Japan 🇯🇵, a separate company run with SoftBank, stayed a giant in Japan long after Yahoo faded in the US.

𝟗𝟕. Yahoo still exists: Yahoo Finance, Yahoo Mail and Yahoo News have hundreds of millions of users.

𝟗𝟖. Business schools still teach the Yahoo-Google story as a classic case of a missed opportunity.

𝟗𝟗. The lesson often drawn: Yahoo saw search as a feature, Google saw it as the business.

𝟏𝟎𝟎. And a company named after a googol, 1 followed by 100 zeros, now looks like the deal of the century Yahoo let walk out the door.

text:
Estonia to CLOSE Russian border in two weeks after 'sabotage' attack | Sophia Stanford, Daily Mail

Estonia will close all crossing points on its border with Russia from December 1 after Putin allegedly ordered a 'sabotage' attack.

The Nato member said Russia's military intelligence service tried to arson attack a drone factory but was thwarted by Estonian officials.

In response, Prime Minister Kristen Michal has called on his administration to make the 'necessary steps' to close the eastern border with Russia.

He described yesterday's attempted arson attack as 'part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia'.

Security forces arrested eight people on Saturday morning at 3.06am after the group allegedly tried to break into the Estonian defence company Threod Systems, which manufactures reconnaissance and attack drones.

The Estonian Internal Security Service (KAPO) have said the GRU were behind the 'sabotage attempt' in Viimsi, north of the capital, Tallinn, with the suspects accused of attempting to set off an explosion and start a fire.

The eight arrested individuals live in Latvia, chief prosecutor Astrid Asi told journalists on Sunday. Five are reported to be remanded in custody.

The internal security service warned: 'We advise against even considering such job offers from Russia. The consequences are serious.

Michal said: 'Extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures and a swift reaction by law enforcement. The attackers have been detained.'

'We will not be intimidated,' he said and earlier warned that they were considering border closures to 'reduce the risks to our people and national security'.

The prime minister later said he had discussed the possibility of closing the three open border crossings in Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula with the interior minister Igor Taro.

These crossings admit pedestrians and freight goods, and are open from 7am to 7pm. The Narva crossing is particularly busy in summer and over the New Year as it is one of the only open land crossings in Europe since the start of the war in Ukraine.

Taro said that the closures to both pedestrians and vehicles would take place at the beginning of December, allowing Estonians currently in Russia to return home in the next two weeks.

Michal said: 'If Russia continues its hybrid operations in Estonia, and we know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people, we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face.

'Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities are unacceptable.'

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna added: 'Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.'

Michal said the latest 'sabotage' attempt tried to 'make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine. Estonia's response is the opposite.'

'Estonia is safe and secure. Our state institutions are vigilant, and our people and businesses know how to respond. We will not be intimidated.'

This is the second reported Russian attempt to target Estonian defence manufacturers.

In August, the defence subcontractor Milrem, based in Tallinn, was targeted in an attempted arson and Latvian nationals were also arrested.

text:
Remember when the Biden administration, DOJ, and FBI repeatedly declared white supremacy the greatest terrorist threat facing America?

While Americans were being told whom to fear, the country was undergoing profound changes to its borders, culture, institutions, and national identity.

The question is no longer simply what government called a threat. It's who will be allowed to challenge what is happening without being branded one.

THE NARRATIVE

The statements were unmistakable.

In April 2021, Biden declared white-supremacist terrorism the most lethal terrorist threat to the homeland. In June, at Tulsa, he doubled down: "Not ISIS, not al Qaeda—white supremacists."

Attorney General Merrick Garland and FBI Director Christopher Wray also repeatedly identified racially motivated violent extremism as a major domestic security concern.

These were declarations from the highest levels of government. Their political consequences deserve serious scrutiny.

THE DANGEROUS DISTINCTION

There is a fundamental difference between violent extremism and defending America's borders, sovereignty, traditions, constitutional principles, and national interests.

Yet the progressive left increasingly blurs that distinction.

Question immigration policy? Far-right.

Demand assimilation? Xenophobic.

Defend traditional values? Extremist.

Prioritize American citizens? Nationalist—as though that were an accusation.

When political labels replace arguments, dissent itself becomes the target.

EUROPE'S WARNING

Look across the Atlantic. Britain, Ireland, and France offer important warnings about growing tensions surrounding immigration, national identity, cultural integration, and political dissent.

Different countries, different circumstances—but a common concern: expanding government discretion over protest and public expression.

When peaceful dissent becomes subject to increasingly broad restrictions, ordinary citizens have reason to be vigilant.

THE LABELING MACHINE

As Americans resist policies they believe threaten their culture, institutions, economic security, and national sovereignty, expect the familiar labels:

Racist. Xenophobic. White supremacist. Far-right. Domestic extremist.

The political objective is straightforward: portray resistance as intolerance rather than confront legitimate grievances. Discredit opposition, intimidate dissent, and make citizens think twice before speaking.

AMERICA FIRST IS NOT RACISM

American nationalism is a civic principle, not a racial test.

Our Constitution, laws, institutions, and shared national identity form the foundation of the Republic. Americans of every race and background have an equal stake in preserving them.

Citizenship carries responsibilities: loyalty to our constitutional order, respect for the rule of law, and commitment to the country we share.

Religious freedom is protected by the Constitution. The oath of public office is to the Constitution, not a particular religious book. Our founding framework is the standard, regardless of faith.

THE LINE AMERICANS MUST NOT CROSS

The greatest danger is a country where citizens become afraid to defend their own national identity.

A government that treats peaceful opposition as extremism, patriotism as suspicion, and accountability as a threat ultimately undermines the freedoms it claims to protect.

America should recognize Europe's warning before it becomes our reality.

The right to disagree is protected by our Constitution, not granted by political parties, government agencies, or ideological movements.

America belongs to its citizens. Its future should be determined by them. No political movement has the authority to redefine patriotism as extremism simply because Americans refuse to surrender their country without a fight.
