text:
“I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God…” Paul does not begin with a demand. 

For eleven chapters he has been telling us what God has done. The sinner is justified because Christ’s righteousness is placed to his account. 

The Spirit comes to live within. God is known as Father. Glory waits at the end of the road. Even our desire for Christ rests upon a mercy that reached us before we ever reached for Him.

Then comes that enormous little word: therefore.

Paul is speaking to people already received in Christ. The sacrifice he asks for is no attempt to purchase love. It is what begins to make sense when a sinner realizes how completely he has already been loved.

“Present your bodies a living sacrifice.”

The Old Testament sacrifice was laid wholly upon the altar and nothing was saved for later. Paul takes that picture and places the Christian there. He calls it our reasonable service. After eleven chapters of mercy, surrender is the fitting answer of a redeemed life. Christ has laid claim to the whole person because He has redeemed the whole person.

John Stott would wake each morning and pretending his bed was an altar. Before anything had been accomplished or ruined, he would pray, “Lord, here I am. This is who I am. This is what I am. This is all I am, but it’s all for You.”

The Christian life starts in bed. Before your feet touch the floor, the day already belongs to Christ. Your hands are His. Your feet are His. Your voice, work, money, family life, body, plans, even your silences can be placed before Him. Here I am.

The unsettling thing is how easily an ordinary life can be lived with hardly any reference to God. We wake, eat, work, spend, plan, hurry, rest and sleep. We may never consciously shake our fist at heaven. We simply arrange an entire day without seriously asking, “Lord, what do You want?”

Paul calls us away from that life, “Be transformed by the renewing of your mind.”

The world is always teaching us what success looks like, what deserves envy, what should frighten us and what is worth chasing. Left to itself, the mind begins walking sideways. So we bring it again under the Word of God.

Lord, teach me to see this as You see it. Correct my ambitions. Reorder my loves. Show me where I have mistaken comfort for blessing or control for wisdom.

Then Paul says something beautiful. As the mind is renewed and the life is offered, we begin to “prove” the will of God. We discover by actually walking with Him that His way is good, acceptable and perfect.

I have found that discovery takes a lifetime. Every Christian will reach the far side of life carrying regrets. Words will remain that we wish we had never spoken. There will be choices we would gladly make differently and roads we wish we had never taken. Our deepest regrets will gather around the places where we wandered from God’s way.

We will never reach the end wishing we had trusted Christ less. That is what Paul wants us to prove while there is still time to live it. God’s will is good. His commands are the wisdom of a Father who knows precisely what His children were made for and that brings us back to mercy.

The One asking for your life is the One who gave His Son for you. The hands receiving your sacrifice are the hands that have carried you through every chapter of Romans. He justified you, placed His Spirit within you, taught your heart to call Him Father, promised to bring you home and loved you before you knew enough to ask for any of it.

Perhaps the prayer of Romans 12 does not need many words. Lord, You have done all this for me. Here I am. This is all I am. My remaining moments are Yours.

I used to only trade one asset in the past. That’s almost 10 years ago. 

My trading style, similar to a lot of you guys, was that I would wake up, I would look at the asset that I usually trade, if there was a trade present, I would take it. And if there is no trade present, I wouldn't take it. 

In simple terms, I would take whatever trade my asset is presenting me at the moment. If there's a trade, I'm taking it. 

My systems today offer me a much higher win-rate than what I’ve had before. What I do now is that I look at a massive amount of assets instead of focusing on one, now let's say that these different assets are presenting me with 10 trades at the moment, I don't take all of these 10 trades, I choose the one or the two that are the best, that are offering the cleanest setups, the cleanest fundamentals that exist in the clearest macroeconomic conditions, and then I'll only take these trades and ignore all of the others. 

So in the past, I used to take whatever trade my asset presented me with. But today, I don't take whatever trade is available, I choose the best trades. 

In the past, I use to search for a setup that is available. Today, I search for the best setup that is available amongst all available setups.

Now, because I’m only choosing the best of the best trades everyday, my win-rate has obviously skyrocketed.

It’s not just me by the way, I have this class I’m teaching right now of three students, these are starting traders, the lowest win-rate is 60%, with the highest being at 72.7%. 

Bigger watchlist with more optionality is better according to my experience and the experience of a lot others.

text:
Warning to Clergy

Tuesday 16th November 2010 @ 09:55

My daughter you were rejected yesterday as people tried to put doubts in your mind. You suffered for this. Do not despair, My Word will be heard. You will face obstacles that will make you feel disillusioned with the work.

My daughter I am guiding you. You must remember this and never forget My promise. I did as you requested, and allowed you to sleep peacefully last night. You are stronger now. Can’t you feel this?

Be careful who you communicate with. My followers, or those you think are My followers, are not always as they seem. You must do what your heart tells you.

The world may seem as it always has but there is change and it is happening now. This change is leading mankind into a darkness that will envelop them and which clouds their love for Me.

Why must My children keep questioning the truth? They do not follow My Teachings, yet they were given this gift from My apostles who, through love for Me and by the power of the Holy Spirit, gave the world a very special gift. The Gift of Truth was taught and spread to all My children throughout the world. Many children followed this guidance through the ages.

Others while knowing the truth, decided to twist it to suit their own means, desires, lust and quest for power. My followers then could not distinguish between the truth of the Word of God and the falsehoods spread by those who were misguided. This is how the deceiver works. He causes confusion, despair and a sense of hopelessness and has been doing this since My death on the Cross. But hear Me now. He will not win My daughter. The forces of Heavenly guidance will instill in the children their belief once more through the teachings of My prophets.

Ask My children to be alert to the changes they see in the world. Ask them to open their hearts, their eyes and minds to witness the lies spread by Satan. From him springs a web of promises designed to make My children feel attracted to external wonders. The wonders and false glory are empty.

They are not reflective of love nor do they offer any real comfort once the emptiness of them are revealed.

The forces of evil are getting stronger now My child. They are planned by Satan, through his army of wicked followers. These followers, through greed and love of self, follow in docile adoration and will be led into his flash paradise. His promised paradise is nothing but black darkness and by the time my children realise this, the time for redemption will have passed.

Prayer for Salvation.
All of My children must, even if it be for the love of their own families, wake up to this evil if they want to save each other. My Love will keep them guided if they turn to Me now. They must never be afraid to turn and say:

“O my Lord lead me to Your Kingdom and protect me from the darkness that has engulfed my soul. Hear me now O Sacred Heart and through Your Goodness let Your Light of Love and protection shine through.”

Those of My children who say this prayer will be heard. Their pleas for salvation, for they and those whom they love, will be answered. I have through My visionaries guided by My Blessed Mother, painstakingly tried to send warnings to the world. Many, many times My visionaries, though rejected in the beginning, were finally accepted. This time they will not be afforded the dignity of time for their messages to be heard by enough of My people.

Beware of false prophets.
But I must warn My children to be wary of false prophets. Many genuine visionaries have been misled. Visionaries who are genuine will be given the graces that will emit My Truth in such a way that they will be accompanied by supernatural occurrences and miracles that cannot and won’t be denied.

(Con’t)

“Adventurism.”

You know all the buzzwords to get the emotional response you hope will get you claps on the back from the “youth.”  It’s boring. 

When we decided, correctly, that Iran was threatening a NK strategy, I wrote that I’d support the war  *only if the goal was to win,* which involved the total removal of the Islamist government. 

That’s what needs to be done, but we as a country haven’t had the stomach to finish a war since WWII —largely because it’s so easy for people to accumulate virtue points by advocating for restraint or isolationist foreign policy, and because we’ve taken to using polls to determine our response to enemies. 

“Interventionist foreign policy” is the criticism offered by Father Charles Coughlin, Charles Lindbergh, Henry Ford, et al., as the reason the US should keep out of WWII. The war came for us anyway. 

All wars fought outside of the US fall under the rubric of “interventionist”; the real question is which interventions are necessary to protect Americans and America. 

Iran threatening to use a chemical or soft nuclear attack on American soil — given their longstanding willingness to target Americans, our allies, and our interests — is something I take seriously enough that I’d support an overwhelming response. 

Others have pointed you to the exact forms this could take — and no, it doesn’t need to be nuclear, though blowing open a mountain shouldn’t be off the table. 

Maybe one day you’ll wake up and realize who and what we’re dealing with. 

Maybe they’ll be a clear sign.  Like, say, airplanes full of our citizens flying into our skyscrapers and government buildings, or barracks full of Marines being bombed, or our embassy staff being held hostage for over a year, or an unprovoked attack targeting civilians on one of our important geopolitical allies. 

Meantime, hope is the best strategy!  Hope and change, even!

NABEEL RAJAB: THEY IMPRISONED THE MAN, BUT NEVER HIS CONSCIENCE
 A tribute by Arnold Tsunga

Today, I mourn a dear friend, a courageous leader and a fellow defender of human dignity, Nabeel Rajab of Bahrain. His passing leaves a painful absence in the global human rights movement. We have lost a man whose courage strengthened others, and whose humanity endured through years of persecution.

Nabeel paid dearly for speaking out. His peaceful human rights work brought repeated arrests, imprisonment, intimidation and restrictions on his freedom. He spent four years in prison between June 2016 and June 2020, with convictions arising from media interviews and social media posts addressing human rights abuses and the war in Yemen. 
 
Behind those years were days taken from his family, friendships interrupted, and the ordinary freedoms that no person should have to surrender for defending the rights of others.

What I will remember most is that he emerged unbroken.

The Nabeel I knew was never bitter. He had every reason to be angry at what had been done to him, yet he retained his warmth, his generosity and his belief in people. His refusal to hate did not soften his opposition to injustice. It gave that opposition an extraordinary moral force. He could confront cruelty without allowing it to govern his own character.

That was part of his greatness.

Prison is used against human rights defenders to punish the individual and frighten everyone watching. Its message is that speaking out will cost you your freedom, your family life and your future. Nabeel understood that threat. He bore its consequences. Yet he never allowed his persecutors to determine the worth of his convictions.

His life exposed the profound insecurity of power that fears a peaceful voice.

For the human rights fraternity, this loss must call us to renewed responsibility. We must stand beside imprisoned defenders while they are alive, support their families through the long years of separation, and sustain our solidarity after the headlines disappear. We must demand their unconditional release and accountability for abuses committed against them. No government should be allowed to make persecution so routine that the world learns to look away.

Our solidarity must also cross the boundaries that power uses to divide us. The dignity Nabeel defended in Bahrain belongs equally to people everywhere. Neither strategic alliances nor commercial interests can justify silence when peaceful defenders are punished for their work.

To his family, I offer my deepest condolences. You shared the burdens of his public courage and endured sacrifices that the world could never fully see. May you find comfort in knowing how deeply he was respected, how widely he was loved, and how many people drew strength from his example.

My dear friend, you leave us grieving, but you also leave us with work to do.

We will remember your warmth. We will remember your courage. And we will carry forward your insistence that every human being deserves freedom, dignity and justice.

They took years of your liberty. They never secured your surrender.

Rest in power, Nabeel. Our solidarity endures. The work continues.🕊️

Contemporary and later narratives, some of them from military and constitutional researchers who have reconstructed the episode, attribute the order to the incoming Roosevelt administration at the outset of the New Deal. The stated reasons, when any were offered, were that the material was “controversial.” The practical effect was that an entire generation of citizen-soldiers no longer received systematic instruction that the United States is a constitutional republic, that citizenship requires undivided loyalty and demonstrated capacity for self-government, and that immigration policy must be calibrated to the preservation of those conditions.
From that point the story of American civic education and immigration policy diverged from the manual’s premises. The New Deal expanded the administrative state and softened the older insistence on individual responsibility as the foundation of free institutions. Later decades dismantled national-origins selection, weakened enforcement of assimilation requirements, and treated the naturalization oath’s renunciation of foreign allegiance as largely ceremonial. Dual citizenship became commonplace even though the oath still requires the renunciation. Chain migration, refugee policies, and eventually the post-1965 system produced continuous high-volume inflows without the earlier expectation that newcomers would be selected and trained for rapid, full attachment to the republic’s habits. Border controls were repeatedly relaxed; interior enforcement became sporadic.
By the 2020s the practical results were visible to anyone who looked. Record numbers of encounters at the southern border, large populations living outside the legal system, parallel linguistic and cultural enclaves, and measurable strains on schools, hospitals, housing, and welfare systems in cities and border states. Crime statistics and fiscal analyses in high-impact jurisdictions showed the costs of admitting people who had not been screened for the capacity or intention to sustain ordered liberty. Public polling repeatedly showed majorities favoring reduced illegal immigration and stronger assimilation requirements, yet policy moved in the opposite direction under successive administrations, most dramatically under the Biden administration’s early decisions to pause border-wall construction, end Remain in Mexico, expand parole programs, and limit interior removals. The cumulative effect was an acceleration of the very pressures the 1928 manual had warned against: large numbers of people entering without the prior selection, the physical and moral screening, the language expectation, or the multi-year demonstration of attachment to constitutional principles that earlier law had treated as elementary.
Marcus closed the manual and thought about what its standards would look like if applied today. They would not be exotic. They would require applicants for permanent residence to demonstrate English proficiency, pass a meaningful civics examination on the Constitution and the republican form of government, show several years of self-supporting conduct without reliance on public assistance, and take an oath whose renunciation of foreign allegiance was treated as binding rather than symbolic. They would restore the right of the existing people to decide, through law, the volume and character of future admissions so that the institutions of self-government remained workable. They would treat assimilation, not perpetual hyphenation, as the successful outcome. None of these requirements is new; each appears, in substance, in the 1928 text and in the statutes it summarized.
The harm of their abandonment is not theoretical. A republic cannot indefinitely absorb large numbers of people who have not been selected or prepared for its requirements without eventually changing the character of the republic itself. The manual’s authors understood that. So did the Congress that wrote the 1924 Act.

Throughout the history of civilization, mankind has committed its highest conceptions of duty and divine order to the written word. Sacred texts have preserved the moral instruction of generations, giving enduring expression to those principles by which the individual may govern his passions, regulate his conduct, and discharge his obligations toward his fellow man.

Within Freemasonry, the Sacred Book offers a profound image of this governing principle. As the architect submits his designs to the laws of proportion and geometry, so must the moral builder submit his character to a standard higher than personal inclination. The passions of the moment, the demands of ambition, and the preferences of the individual must yield before the enduring requirements of conscience and duty.

Universal Co-Masonry upholds liberty of conscience, recognizing the dignity of sincere spiritual conviction and the individual's responsibility in approaching questions of ultimate truth. The sacred writings of humanity express distinct religious traditions, each deserving of consideration according to its own teachings. Freemasonry cultivates reverence for moral law while respecting these differences of belief.

The Sacred Book thus directs our contemplation toward one of the highest purposes of human existence: the deliberate government of the self according to principles worthy of obedience.

For the true Mason, liberty finds its noblest exercise in the willing discipline of conscience, and character acquires its strength through fidelity to the Good, the True, and the Just.

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT ANNOUNCES CHARGES INVOLVING 63 INDIVIDUALS FOR ELECTION-RELATED CRIMES

One-Sentence Summary: The Justice Department announced charges involving 63 people in cases alleging unlawful voting, fraudulent voter registration, or related offenses, with many of the allegations involving the 2024 election. United States Department of Justice

Key Takeaways:
• Most defendants described in the release were lawful permanent residents. Four were identified as being in the country unlawfully.
• The announcement covers several types of charges, so 63 is a count of people involved, rather than a count of ballots.
• Attorney General Todd Blanche called it the "largest surge of voter-fraud arrests since President Trump returned to office."

Article Summary: In a Nov. 2, 2026, release, the Justice Department announced charges involving 63 people across the country. Most of the defendants described were lawful permanent residents. The department said four were in the country unlawfully. The charges included voting in federal elections as a noncitizen and falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to register or vote.

Many allegations concerned the November 2024 election, while others went back years. In North Carolina, prosecutors alleged that one defendant voted in 18 general and primary elections from 2008 through 2026. In New Mexico, a Maryland resident was charged with submitting a voter registration application that allegedly misrepresented where he lived. In California, six defendants faced charges of making false statements on naturalization applications about their prior voter registration or claims of U.S. citizenship.

The department said it had charged 195 noncitizens in 25 states with voting or registration offenses over the preceding nine weeks and 239 people with voting fraud-related offenses since the start of the Trump administration. Those figures count people charged. The release reports no convictions in the announced cases and offers no assessment of whether the alleged conduct affected any election result. The defendants are presumed innocent.

"Justice Department Announces Charges Involving 63 Individuals for Election-Related Crimes." United States Department of Justice, 2 Nov. 2026, press release.

text:
Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Mom's Car: Nat Faxon

Overview
Nat Faxon's return to the show traces a throughline from adolescent risk to adult craft: boarding school at thirteen, early and heavy drinking, the pressure cooker of the Groundlings, and the improbable path from sketch comedy to an Oscar-winning screenplay. The core insight is that careers are rarely linear. Faxon and Shepard stumbled into writing out of frustration as actors, wrote their way into rooms they couldn't access otherwise, and learned that success often arrives through projects that felt like detours. Underneath the comedy is a candid account of how competition, loyalty, and luck shape creative lives.

Key Themes
- Early independence can accelerate maturity and exposure to risk at once; boarding school at thirteen delivered both autonomy and unsupervised drinking.
- Casual, pervasive substance use in youth was normalized across their social circles, and the escalation stories reveal how narrowly some outcomes were avoided.
- The Groundlings functioned as a meritocracy with finite slots, where failing to advance felt like leaving a cult and success arrived tangled with guilt over friends left behind.
- Writing became a strategic response to actors' frustration with limited roles, a way to generate material rather than wait for permission.
- Agents push multitracking because no single project is guaranteed; writers carry several at once even when it feels dishonest to collaborators.
- Studio odds are brutal: selling roughly seven features to make one signals persistence as a job requirement, not a virtue.
- Directing established actors is intimidating, and deferring hard notes to a partner is a real pressure valve rather than a strategy.
- Award momentum is built through intermediate wins, and even the Oscar moment can feel unreal years later.

Detailed Summary
Faxon and Shepard first crossed paths in the early levels of the Groundlings, likely in overlapping classes. Their shared history includes a recurring triplet sketch about Timmy, Tommy, and Todd, where the joke was that Todd didn't rhyme. They wore matching striped shirts and little boy shorts and pitched a Doublemint Twins-style commercial. Shepard's own monologue was a Boston-accented UPS character built around the words "hurt" and "lit."

Faxon moved to Los Angeles in fall 1997, right after college, and lived with a roommate named Tom, who later became successful at Amazon. Tom had one recurring complaint: Faxon and Shepard playing poker until three in the morning and making noise with quarters. The apartment was also where Shepard smoked Camel Lights indoors, a detail made sharper by the fact that Faxon's father was president of the Heart Association.

Smoking was pervasive and casual in their youth, indoors and at young ages. Faxon started at thirteen in junior high, and his mother let him smoke in the house during high school rather than in the garage in winter. A college prank involved preloading a bong with smoke and putting it to a sleeping roommate's lips before scaring him.

Faxon grew up in Manchester by the Sea, Massachusetts, attending Brookwood School, a day school, before Holderness School in Plymouth, New Hampshire, about two hours away. He started at thirteen, before puberty, and was called a "corner boy" for showering in the corner. The school was less preppy than expected and more granola and liberal, half an hour from a ski mountain with a strong racing team and good hockey. Shepard, now with a thirteen-year-old of his own, reflects that he couldn't imagine sending a child that age to boarding school.

The boarding school years were an education in independence and autonomy, and also rough given how young he was. Students could sign out for weekends and stay at a rented condo near a ski hill, where they drank heavily. His first drink came around eleven or twelve at an uncle's wedding, drinking champagne while his parents thought he was having ginger ale, then vomiting on the plane back to Boston. Another recurring story involves buying barrels of cider in Boston and having handles of Jim Beam drained into them at the cider mill. At eighteen, senior year, a friend who looked thirty-five bought three 64-ounce bottles of Colt 45 for opening day Tigers; they never got into the park and hung out in the parking lot, where a fight broke out with a large mustached man over a parking spot.

Recognition follows the work differently for each of them. One is stopped for Parenthood, Idiocracy, and the podcast; the other for Community and Super Troopers. A pizza delivery story captures the ethos of improvisation under pressure: someone took a bite, then the slice was put back and the cheese mushed together to hide it. The preference was a missing slice over a mangled pizza.

Sunday Company was more intense and stressful than the main company, with competition for finite spots forging stronger bonds among members. Not making the main company was experienced as devastating, described as leaving a cult. Faxon is praised as one of the best performers ever seen at the Groundlings, alongside Melissa, with no jealousy attached, just admiration and happiness when he got in. Performers with weirder sensibilities were often Wednesday night audience favorites, though the broader audience wasn't always savvy enough to embrace them. Pat Divine is cited as writing those weird sketches that scored well on Wednesday nights.

Competing for limited spots creates a tension: people root for themselves without wanting to succeed at others' expense, producing guilt and conflicted relief. When the call came, Faxon was living with Pat D, and calls arrived at the same apartment, possibly on a landline. Pat did not get in, complicating Faxon's elation. Faxon did the full year and a half in Sunday Company and was happy and excited to move up. Pixie shows were a fun last-night celebration where members wrote sketches about each other, though one such show involved taking too much GHB, becoming violently ill, and being revived in the alley behind the theater with cocaine. Another story involves staying up extremely late after a successful Letterman appearance, passing out, and being revived with meth to watch the broadcast.

The Oscar nomination was far outside their expectations. They entered sketch comedy aiming only at making a living and stopping side jobs like bartending and serving. Writing grew from frustration as actors not getting desirable parts; they wrote a pilot presentation at the Groundlings to create their own material. Fox loved it but was about to do Arrested Development, which had similar elements. They reworked a seed of it, sold to ABC, got a pilot made, and it was not picked up.

Writing The Way, Way Back opened doors even before it was made, leading to a meeting with Alexander Payne's production company. Payne's producing partner Jim Burke and the company loved the script and offered them a novel they had rights to. They were also offered a big Fox alien movie that agents called low hanging fruit, felt unsuited to it, and asked their agents to get them out so they could do The Descendants. Payne advised them not to be overly faithful to the source novel and to free themselves from the source material. The odds are stark: roughly seven features sold to studios, one made.

The Writers Guild strike caused about a three-month wait for notes on their first draft. Steven Frears was initially going to direct but dropped out, saying he didn't know Hawaii well enough. Payne became available at the same time and took the film after seven years without directing. They had done three or four drafts; Payne did his own pass, then Clooney got involved. Once Fox was excited, meetings about an Oscar push followed, which felt surreal.

A hockey injury story sits alongside the Hollywood material: hit, sliding headfirst into a goalpost, smashing a rusty cage into his forehead, concussed, taken to Brotman Medical Center in Culver City. There he heard but did not see an elderly patient being treated with a plastic tube, which he describes as terrifying. The alien project gets a joking fix: make the alien allergic to its reflection and in need of mirrors.

Awards season brought sudden attention, parties with major celebrities, excitement and surreality in equal measure. They did not win at the Critics' Choice Awards or the Golden Globes, where Moneyball was winning a lot. Wins at the Scripter Awards, a USC award given jointly to the novelist and screenplay writers, shared with author Kaui Hart Hemmings, and at the Writers Guild revived the sense that the Oscar was possible. At the Oscars, Angelina Jolie read the winner; one of them focused on her lips before hearing their name. Hearing it read was surreal and has never felt real, even years later.

Success gave them currency to return to The Way, Way Back. Directing famous actors is intimidating; one admits deflecting notes to Jim when nervous about giving notes to Julia Louis-Dreyfus. A story about Paul Thomas Anderson scrapping the first week of filming with Daniel Day-Lewis is cited as an example of directorial conviction. The Oscar is kept at home on a shelf and described as unglamorous; their kids are not impressed. One appeared in the Paw Patrol movie because their kids watched it. Bo Bridges appeared in Hit and Run, and directing him was intimidating because he had a thick Southern accent while the film was set in California. Julia Louis-Dreyfus is described as smart, funny, and unwilling to take nonsense, refreshing but a little scary. Fox Searchlight was developing a movie with her while another script gained momentum simultaneously, and their agents advised pursuing both.

Writers juggle multiple projects because they can't know which will get made; agents say to keep going even when it feels dishonest. One admits struggling with doing many things at once, believing he can't do a good job on nine things simultaneously. When one project was greenlit, they had to abandon Julia, a collaborator they'd been working with closely; Jim delivered the news, and she was understandably upset, saying good luck, Godspeed, and that they screwed her over. A chance encounter at a concert, with the speaker seated directly behind her and his father-in-law, a drummer, playing with James Taylor, led to an awkward attempt to apologize; she was gracious but still visibly upset, initially mistaking him for an annoying fan and not turning around until he shook her. The other movie ultimately fell through, forcing him to return to Julia, apologize in person in New York, and admit he screwed up. The cake challenge that bookends the conversation almost broke him, a fitting close: fun for about five minutes, and a real test of skill.

text:
In Chapter VII of The Prince, Machiavelli describes how Cesare Borgia tried to keep the benefits of a cruel policy while shifting responsibility for its cruelty. When Borgia took control of Romagna, he gave Remirro de Orco wide authority to restore order. Remirro succeeded, in Machiavelli’s account, but the severity of his rule bred resentment. Borgia then established a civil tribunal where each city had an advocate and had Remirro killed. One morning, Remirro’s body was displayed in the public square at Cesena. 

The sequence is what gives the episode its force. Borgia had chosen Remirro and given him the power he used. By publicly destroying him, Borgia invited the people of Romagna to assign the cruelty to the minister’s character and credit the duke with ending it. The new tribunal gave them a practical reason to accept that account. They had a different institution to turn to, and the man they associated with the old severity was gone. Borgia could now appear as the remedy for a condition he had helped create. 

Machiavelli says the people were left “satisfied and stupefied.” The two feelings belong together. The man they feared had been removed, and the manner of his removal showed what Borgia was capable of. The execution offered relief while renewing fear at a higher level. That is how the second act changes the meaning of the first. People could remember the same abuses and still come away with a different answer to the question of who had protected them from whom.

I led product for one of the largest aftermarket, OE, and tire marketplaces in the United States & Canada. Feel free to ask me any questions. Here's my take:

Car Dealership Guy drops his latest Tesla review after buying one.

Many of us already knew how this review would go down. He's impressed.

In the past year there has been a massive shift in FSD adoption. Go on TikTok, Instagram, etc. It's filled with videos of people saying "I don't drive...".

2026 is when the shift has finally happened. Some knew it has been a long time coming, but this year it really started to change.

The combination of EVs + Autonomy means a few things:

📈 tire sales: will keep going up until vehicle weight comes down and autonomy goes more mainstream. FSD will also normalize the number since it doesn't use the full power and acceleration that the EV has to offer saving your tires in return.

📉📈aftermarket parts: will keep going down, but some upside. The top sold items; disc brake pads, disc brake rotors, etc., are rarely changed out. Mechanical parts are completely out. Suspension still comes into play. Other than that.... windshield wipers, cabin air filters, and washer fluid will do just fine. Batteries will be a growing area. The ability to recycle and swap out a battery will be critical for the aftermarket to support EVs.

📉 collision parts: will keep going down. More miles driven on FSD means lower chances of collisions, it's in the data. Collision companies know this which is why they have all been scrambling to diversify their portfolio.

📉 insurance: mixed. EVs are more costly to repair, so there is a bump in prices, but overall this should trend down at some point as companies factor in FSD usage. Tesla already does this with their own insurance, but it's banned in states like California to prorate based on driving characteristics. At some point things will flip and you will be charged more for not having a vehicle equipped with and using FSD.

text:
The European Union has sanctioned an Irish journalist, frozen his bank accounts, and barred him from entering the EU, all without a trial or a single criminal charge.

Chay Bowes allegedly works for Russian state media, and some people in the West find his reporting on Ukraine to be the wrong side of the story they want to tell.

But here's the thing...You don't have to agree with a single word Bowes broadcasts to recognise the dangerous precedent being set here.

In a genuine democracy, the remedy for so-called bad journalism or state propaganda is better journalism and truth, an open argument, not stripping a citizen of his right to return home by executive decree.

Only days ago, Dublin hosted a grand summit under the slogan "Europe: strong, secure and connected." Nothing projects weakness quite like a continental bloc so terrified of an opposing narrative that it has to confiscate a reporter's livelihood to maintain consensus.

And don't hold your breath waiting for the British and Irish press corps to walk out in solidarity, waving placards declaring that "Truth Matters".

Much of our media establishment seems rather more comfortable defending free expression when the speaker follows the approved narrative. Challenge that narrative, particularly over Ukraine or Israel and suddenly the principles become negotiable.

Of course, governments have legitimate concerns about foreign interference. But those concerns cannot place allegations beyond scrutiny or make due   process an optional extra.

Once you accept that the state can financially erase a journalist for holding the wrong opinions on a foreign war, you have already surrendered the principle that protects everyone else...

Civil liberties mean very little if we defend them only for those whose opinions we share.

George Orwell understood this perfectly:

"If liberty means anything at all it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear."

And he offered another warning that seems particularly appropriate today:

"What is needed is the right to print what one believes to be true, without having to fear bullying or blackmail from any side."

Freedom of expression is worth precious little if it only protects the opinions those in power are prepared to tolerate.

text:
The European Union has sanctioned an Irish journalist, frozen his bank accounts, and barred him from entering the EU, all without a trial or a single criminal charge.

Chay Bowes allegedly works for Russian state media, and some people in the West find his reporting on Ukraine to be the wrong side of the story they want to tell. 

But here's the thing...You don't have to agree with a single word Bowes broadcasts to recognise the dangerous precedent being set here.

In a genuine democracy, the remedy for so-called bad journalism or state propaganda is better journalism and truth, an open argument, not stripping a citizen of his right to return home by executive decree.

Only days ago, Dublin hosted a grand summit under the slogan "Europe: strong, secure and connected." Nothing projects weakness quite like a continental bloc so terrified of an opposing narrative that it has to confiscate a reporter's livelihood to maintain consensus.

And don't hold your breath waiting for the British and Irish press corps to walk out in solidarity, waving placards declaring that "Truth Matters".

Much of our media establishment seems rather more comfortable defending free expression when the speaker follows the approved narrative. Challenge that narrative, particularly over Ukraine or Israel and suddenly the principles become negotiable.

Of course, governments have legitimate concerns about foreign interference. But those concerns cannot place allegations beyond scrutiny or make due   process an optional extra.

Once you accept that the state can financially erase a journalist for holding the wrong opinions on a foreign war, you have already surrendered the principle that protects everyone else... 

Civil liberties mean very little if we defend them only for those whose opinions we share.

George Orwell understood this perfectly:

"If liberty means anything at all it means the right to tell people what they do not want to hear."

And he offered another warning that seems particularly appropriate today:

"What is needed is the right to print what one believes to be true, without having to fear bullying or blackmail from any side."

Freedom of expression is worth precious little if it only protects the opinions those in power are prepared to tolerate.

17 November 1974 — 52 years ago

Erskine Hamilton Childers, Ireland’s 4th President, died suddenly while serving in office. He was TD for the Monaghan Constituency.

Born in London in 1905, he was the son of Robert Erskine Childers, the Irish nationalist and author of The Riddle of the Sands. Before becoming President in June 1973, Childers served as a TD, government minister & Tánaiste.

He died aged 68. Childers suffered a heart attack after addressing a dinner at the RCPI in Dublin - first President of Ireland to die in office.

His presidency lasted less than 17 months.

He is buried in a most beautiful setting near Roundwood,

Childers Presidency offered the hope of a new and open Presidency. We will never know his impact on the institution had he lived.

text:
🖌️ Jewish Artist Klára Geréb Was Deported to Auschwitz From This Home. Now It’s a Museum—and 1944 Files Reveal a Plan to Enlarge the City’s Museum With Looted Jewish Art

Before it became the Municipal Museum of Subotica, the Art Nouveau landmark at Trg Sinagoge 3 was a center of Jewish family life, art, and publishing. Inside Dömötör Palace, graphic artist and illustrator Klára Geréb lived with her husband, Lajos Fenyves, and their two children, Steven and Estera, above the family’s Minerva printing works.

In 1944, when the city was under Hungarian rule and known as Szabadka, the Fenyves family was deported to Auschwitz. Sixty-four years later, in 2008, the city’s museum moved into their former home. Yet a separate 1944 wartime file reveals that Hungarian officials had much earlier plans for Jewish-owned art in that same city: they wanted to use it to enlarge the local museum.

🕯️ The artist and her family

Klára Geréb (1897–1944) created portraits, prints, and book illustrations. The accompanying visual includes her work Notre-Dame, Paris, reproduced in a publication identifying it with the Municipal Museum of Subotica’s collection. It places an example of her art beside the photograph of the family whose life was destroyed by persecution.

Their dispossession began before deportation. After Hungary occupied the city in 1941, Lajos lost control of his publishing business, and Hungarian officers took over most of the family’s apartment. In 1944, Klára, her children, and her mother were forced into the ghetto and subsequently deported to Auschwitz. Klára and her mother did not survive. Steven and Estera survived; Lajos, who had been deported separately, returned but died a few months after the family’s reunion.

Some of Klára’s work survived because of Maris, a former family cook. While the apartment was being looted, she rescued a folder of Klára’s artwork and a handwritten family cookbook. She preserved them and later returned them to the surviving children.

A 1944 inventory from Subotica’s archives, published by historian Zoltán Dévavári, provides another record of the family’s belongings. Under Klára’s married name, Fenyves Lajosné—Mrs. Lajos Fenyves—it lists furnishings from their former apartment that were being kept in a warehouse. The contents of the study included “two crates of books” and “four pictures.” The entry gives no artists, titles, or dimensions for those pictures.

📜 The 1944 plan for the museum

The correspondence preserved in the @HolocaustMI/@WJRORestitution's Hungarian Documents Microfilm Collection concerns paintings and sculptures collected from Jews and held by the city. In July 1944, painter István Zombori Kiss offered unpaid assistance with their preservation, warning about their condition. By September, Dénes Csánky, the government commissioner overseeing the sequestration and safeguarding of Jewish-owned artworks, was organizing their administration through a local delegate, cultural councillor Dr. Aladár Vojnits.

Csánky’s instructions went beyond protecting the objects from damage. He wrote that works collected locally should, wherever possible, go to local museums, and described an “extraordinary opportunity” to enlarge the museum in Szabadka. His letter states, in translation: “The Szabadka museum would be collecting the material for itself.”

Csánky was proposing that the museum benefit from the dispossession of Jewish residents. He also ordered inventories and identifying labels for the works. Those records could be crucial to establishing whether, and how, the proposal was carried out.

🏛️ The museum today—and the history still to be traced

The Municipal Museum was re-established after the war, in 1948, and moved into Dömötör Palace in 2008. In 2014, it commemorated Klára with the exhibition Memento Geréb Klára, with contributions from her son Steven. Her former home thus became a place where her life and artistic work were publicly remembered.

The distinction between the surviving records matters. The wartime correspondence names no individual Jewish owner and does not connect Klára’s four pictures to the museum proposal or to works held by today’s museum. It establishes what officials intended for Jewish-owned art in the city; the history of particular objects still requires investigation.

The next records to locate and compare are the inventories Csánky ordered, warehouse records, postwar transfer papers, and museum accession registers. Together, they may identify former owners, establish where works went, and clarify whether restitution questions remain. Klára’s life and work deserve remembrance. The property taken from Jewish families deserves an equally specific accounting: who owned it, who received it, and what became of it.

Sources and image credits:

Municipal Museum of Subotica: institutional history and address, https://t.co/Mppqkm4QkH. Dömötör Palace and the Fenyves family’s connection to the building, https://t.co/ngey0k3QSO. Museum history and the 2008 move, https://t.co/UBjDsy0SSY.

United States Holocaust Memorial Museum: Steven Fenves’s biography, https://t.co/KUu9TYAApQ; Maris’s rescue of the family cookbook and artwork, https://t.co/SziIv43Og9. Family photograph: US Holocaust Memorial Museum, courtesy of Steven J. Fenves.

Zoltán Dévavári, Iratok a holokauszt szabadkai történetéhez (1941–1944), 2020, document 116, pp. 281–284; underlying archival reference: Istorijski arhiv Subotica, F:60:XX:34575/1944. See also Dévavári, Egy elmesélhetetlen történet, p. 210, note 838: https://t.co/z5t44yOq5o.

Csánky’s museum proposal appears on slides 860–861; the quoted sentence is on slide 861: “a szabadkai muzeum saját maga számára gyüjtené az anyagot.” Reel index: https://t.co/05StzArjr9.

text:
By my own count, if one includes these latest sanctions, the EU has now sanctioned 8 European citizens for speech:

- 3 German citizens: Alina Lipp, Thomas Röper and Hüseyin Doğru

- 3 French citizens: Xavier Moreau, Adrien Bocquet and Sylvain Afoua (aka Egountchi Behanzin)

- 1 Lithuanian citizen: Ernest Mackevičius

- 1 Irish citizen: Chay Bowes

The sanctions include freezing these people's assets and making it a crime for anyone in the EU to pay them, hire them or even lend them a single euro.

They also include a travel ban, which leads to some absurd situations: Doğru - based in Germany - was invited by some members of the EU parliament to Brussels to plead his case but he couldn't go due to the travel ban. As one of the MEPs who invited him - and made 40 phone calls to try, unsuccessfully, to get him cleared to come - put it: "It really was like something out of a Kafka novel" (https://t.co/lvF0WLFtCb).

And, probably worst of all, all of this was decided without any charge, trial or court ruling - simply as a unilateral decision of government ministers. Yesterday's sanctions, for instance, were decided at the Foreign Affairs Council meeting of EU Foreign Ministers and were simply signed by Kaja Kallas alone on behalf of the Council (https://t.co/XP7zeb9ueZ).

Put it all together, and this violates at least half a dozen of what the EU keeps saying are the fundamental values and principles it supposedly fights for:
1) Separation of powers: here we have government ministers - members of the executive branch of their countries - acting as prosecutor, judge and jury
2) Presumption of innocence (Article 48 of the EU’s own Charter of Fundamental Rights): they’re punished without guilt ever being established, and without being given a chance to plead their case before the decision
3) Right to a fair trial (Article 47): there was no trial at all, let alone a fair one
4) Freedom of expression and of the media (Article 11): they were sanctioned - explicitly so - for what they said and published. For instance, in these latest sanctions, Chay Bowes was sanctioned for, among other things, the speech crime of "participat[ing] in the spreading of anti-Western and anti-Ukraine disinformation at the UN Security Council" (https://t.co/XP7zeb9ueZ). Sanctioned in part for a speech at the UN, a forum that exists precisely so that clashing views on international matters can be heard, quite the message to send from the EU...
5) Freedom of movement (Article 45): they're under a travel ban
6) Right to work and to property (Articles 15 and 17): their assets are frozen and nobody may employ or pay them

You can think whatever you want about these 8 people. But ask yourself this: even if you are pro-Ukraine, pro-EU, anti-Russia and you view these people as malignant Russian operatives... what is the EU fighting for here, exactly?

This is more profound than you may think: we're speaking about the very foundation of modern European civilization, built on the very idea that political power alone cannot decide what is true.

I'm not exaggerating. What we’re witnessing is a return to the pre-Enlightenment playbook, when monarchic or religious authorities defined the truth, deviations from it were called heresy, and heretics were excommunicated - cut off from the community, so that no one could trade with them, employ them or help them. In Europe's darkest times, heretics were even famously burned at the stake - like Joan of Arc or Giordano Bruno.

It took literal centuries of religious wars and debates, and the likes of Voltaire, Kant and Mill, to replace it with a basic idea: that no single power, however legitimate, gets to be the final judge of what is true, and that you answer for your words only before a court, under laws written via a process separate from the power that does the accusation.

You can find countless works of European literature on this very matter. Take Spinoza, excommunicated in 1656 by the Portuguese-Jewish community of Amsterdam, with a decree ordering that "no one should communicate with him" nor "accord him any favor". He went on to write the Theological-Political Treatise, one of the founding texts of the Enlightenment, with an entire chapter arguing that "in a free state every man may think what he likes, and say what he thinks." Or Mill, two centuries later in On Liberty, Chapter 2: "All silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility." Or Kafka’s The Trial, the story of a man accused by an authority nobody can quite locate, of something nobody will explain.

How is what Europe is presently doing anything other than going back to that very system, under new appellations? The authority: government ministers. The heresy: "disinformation". The excommunication: assets frozen, banned from travelling and nobody may pay them, hire them or lend them a single euro. 

It’s basically Spinoza’s excommunication decree on EU letterhead, with a bit of Kafka sprinkled in given that the man invited to the European Parliament to contest his punishment couldn’t attend because of the very punishment he wanted to contest.

You don’t have to like these 8 people, or even care about them, to see the problem. Heck, this system was developed precisely for the people nobody likes: consensual ideas never needed protecting.

No, the real question here is this: do you want Europe to be the heir of Spinoza - or of Voltaire, or of Galileo, or of any of the countless Europeans who suffered or even died for thinking differently - or of their persecutors?

text:
In May 2011, two engineers from a Connecticut hedge fund entered a weekend hackathon in New York.

Last month, Salesforce agreed to pay $5.66B for what they built next.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐧

Bill Magnuson had worked at Google on App Inventor for Android, then joined Bridgewater.
Jon Hyman worked there too.
They won the TechCrunch Disrupt Hackathon in NYC with a plugin for flash-sale site Gilt.
Their inboxes filled with partnership offers.

One came from Mark Ghermezian, who had raised $3M from family and investors.
That summer, the three started Appboy.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐭

2011 was early mobile.
Brands had apps but no good way to talk to the people using them.
Appboy built the tools to message app users at the right moment.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐛

2017: renamed Braze.
2019: passed $100M in ARR.
2021: IPO at $65 a share, $520M raised.
2026: ~$910M in expected revenue and ~2,770 customers, including Canva, Instacart and Urban Outfitters.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐱𝐢𝐭

Salesforce is paying $47.50 a share in cash, a 58% premium to Braze's last close before the deal.
That's still below the $65 IPO price. But 2021 priced almost every software stock for perfection.
Magnuson stays as CEO, and Braze keeps its brand inside Salesforce.

It's Salesforce's 5th-largest deal ever. Its email business, Marketing Cloud, started as a $2.5B purchase of ExactTarget in 2013. Braze is the mobile-era version, at more than twice the price.

𝐋𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐬

→ Bet on the platform shift early. Mobile was "too early" in 2011.
→ A hackathon win is a relationship, not a company. The company came after.
→ Build the layer incumbents can't build fast, and they'll eventually pay for it.

Fifteen years from a weekend hack to a $5.66B deal.

What's the platform shift today that a hackathon team could build the next Braze on?

Views are my own and don't represent my employer.

I feel for you. 🙏❤️ Where do you think you & your mom would have moved to (assuming she were still alive today, considering all the global changes & instability)? That’s where I would target. Could you get your sister to relocate also?

I’m the youngest of 5 children (the Catholic oops-baby). Shortly after I left home at 17yo for college, one sister convinced our mom to sell the family home, use the proceeds for her own down payment, and live with her & her youngest family, forever. South central area of Southern California.

I no longer had a “home” (which was often tumultuous to begin with, but it was my home nonetheless). I couch-surfed among friends & family whenever I visited for holidays.

Two years later, my sister divorced her husband, followed by bankruptcy. Sister had had an affair with a young Marine stationed in San Diego, who was 19yo (my sister was 28yo at the time).

I’ve always felt out of place in my own family…the one who would recede into the background to avoid the chaos. Losing the only home that I knew was another dusruptive force, confirming my place as completely inconsequential within the family.

It’s been lonely!! I have become accustomed to the fact that any earthly home is impermanent. I try not to become too attached to belongings, as they’ll often get lost or broken in yet another move.

I focus on helping others now, offering compassion, sharing my talents where & when I can. But it’s a constant struggle. I pray throughout my day, focus on Christ, and try to do the best that I can & offer grace to others as I can. But I fail—daily!

I’m constantly recalibrating, more focused on moments of joy rather than pleasure. Centering myself on helping others as I attempt to help or heal myself.

You have a blessed artistic gift, Kylie. You are enough. You do enough. But you need to find that place of belonging, which is a struggle that you & I share.

Sit in a church, ask God for guidance. Confide in your guardian angel. And simply continue to be the amazing, talented woman that you already are! I’ll try to accept my own advice, too! 😇

text:
Guilty Without Question Requires Life in Prison

Post 4582
Posted on November 17, 2026 by Barry Zalma
Evidence Supports Murder ConvictionA .380 Smith & Wesson Used by Felon to Murder

In State Of Louisiana v. Curtis Joseph Thomas III, No. 25-KA-612, Court of Appeals of Louisiana, Fifth Circuit (November 4, 2026) the court noted that On Feb. 13, 2022, Thomas called 9-1-1 for an ambulance for a shooting victim at 645 Emile Avenue in Westwego. This was a known “trap house” where drugs were bought, sold and used.

Deputy Vasquez found Thomas walking away from the scene. He searched him and recovered a .380 Smith & Wesson pistol from his pocket. Charles McGehee was killed by two gunshot wounds.

Tyran Simpson was shot in the arm. Simpson identified Thomas as the shooter. The lights and TV went out, and he saw “flames from a gun” from the door where Thomas stood. Simpson admitted he was armed that night and had several prior convictions.

EXPERT TESTIMONY

The firearm examiner matched the casings and both projectiles from McGehee’s body to the pistol found on Thomas.

The DNA expert found McGehee’s blood on Thomas’s socks.

Thomas had a 2011 conviction for attempted second degree murder. The State introduced details of that shooting.

A jury convicted Thomas of second degree murder, attempted second degree murder and felon in possession of a firearm. He was sentenced to life, 50 years and 20 years, concurrently and at hard labor.
LAW

Courts view the evidence in the light most favorable to the prosecution. The Louisiana circumstantial-evidence rule is not a separate test. Credibility calls belong to the jury. One witness’s positive identification, if believed, is enough.
Courts view the evidence in the light most favorable to the prosecution. the circumstantial-evidence rule is not a separate test. Credibility calls belong to the jury. One witness’s positive identification, if believed, is enough.

The offenses were second degree murder (attempt) and felon in possession. Statutes limits jurors’ access to written evidence and bars repeating testimony. Access to physical evidence is within the court’s discretion and a statute bars reversal for errors that do not affect substantial rights and bars other-crimes evidence offered to show bad character. It allows such evidence for purposes such as intent, identity or modus operandi, subject to the art. 403 balancing of probative value against prejudice.

The harmless-error test asks whether the guilty verdict was “surely unattributable to the error.”

DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS

Sufficiency (identity).

Thomas argued Simpson was inconsistent and not credible. Simpson’s identification was corroborated by:

1.    possession of the murder weapon minutes after the shooting;
2.    the victim’s blood on his socks;
3.   his leaving the scene.

The court held the evidence sufficient.

ERRORS PATENT.
The trial judge failed to impose the mandatory fine of $1,000–$5,000 on count three. The court declined to remand because Thomas appears indigent and received a life sentence.
OTHER-CRIMES EVIDENCE.

The prior conviction itself was admissible as the predicate for the felon-in-possession count. The details of the 2011 shooting were more prejudicial than probative. The offense was too remote (2011 versus 2022) to show modus operandi, and intent was not at issue because the defense was identity. The trial court therefore erred in admitting the details. The error was harmless.

The eyewitness testimony, ballistics matching the weapon in his pocket, and the DNA on his socks mean the verdicts were surely unattributable to the prior conviction.

CONCLUSION

The Fifth Circuit affirmed all three convictions and the sentences. All three assignments of error failed. The court found trial error only in admitting the details of the prior offense and held it harmless.

The defendant received a life sentence for his conviction of second degree murder. For these reasons, there was no reason to remand the matter for imposition of the fine since he will not earn or have available the funds to pay the fine while incarcerated for life.

The defendant was advised by the opinion that no application for post-conviction relief the judgment of conviction and sentence has become final

ZALMA OPINION

Criminals, pistols and drugs are seldom healthy or peaceful. Mr. Thomas was not a nice man with a violent criminal history. One man died and one man was wounded with Thomas’ weapon and he was sentenced to life in prison and had the unmitigated gall to appeal. In a lengthy decision the Court of Appeals found the appeal to be without merit and made the judgments of conviction are final and should be. This type of appeal is wasteful and Thomas should have been punished for wasting the court’s time but he is already sentenced to life in prison.

    Somerville city council votes to divest from Israel

    The ordinance’s supporters say they won’t stand silent in the face of oppression

    By Gavi Klein, Jewish Chronicle, November 16, 2026:

    (JTA) — SOMERVILLE, Mass. — The City Council in this city north of Boston voted 10-1 Thursday night to ban the municipality from doing business with companies complicit in humanitarian violations, specifically naming those operating in “Israel and Palestine.”

    Councilor Kristen Strezo cast the only opposing vote on the 11-member board.

    Opponents of the ordinance fear that in execution it would be akin to a boycott of Israel, and as such would create a negative environment for the city’s Jewish and Israeli residents. The ban only involves companies that work with the municipality and does not impact companies that operate privately in Somerville. It also excludes sole proprietors (individuals operating as companies).

    Somerville Mayor Jake Wilson’s office said given that the ordinance passed with a veto-proof majority, the measure is now considered final.

    The ordinance was originally introduced in June by Councilors Ben Ewen-Campen and Ben Wheeler, after the City Council voted in November 2025 to implement ballot Question 3 on Israel divestment, which had been approved by 55.7% of voters earlier that month. Question 3 spoke of banning businesses that sustain “Israel’s apartheid, genocide, and illegal occupation of Palestine.”

    During his campaign in 2025, Wilson did not endorse Question 3.

    Nine councilors on Thursday night offered comments in advance of the vote.

    Ewen-Campen, who wrote and revised the ordinance along with Wheeler, spoke about the importance of a Massachusetts city passing an ordinance about a country across the world, especially at a time when the federal government has clamped down on pro-Palestinian student protesters, noting two incidents of protesters being detained by ICE allegedly for speaking against Israel.

    “I think the reason that people want us to be quiet about it is because when you do talk about it, there is just no way to justify it,” Ewen-Campen said.

    “I am not under any illusion that Somerville is going to have some enormous impact on the world [by passing this ordinance], but I do think that all of us collectively deciding to be silent about this does have an impact on the world,” he said. “That is why I think it is worth it to have taken this action, and that is why I have asked for all of your support tonight.”

    Strezo invoked the Holocaust to explain why she considered the ban antisemitic, referring to Kristallnacht, the Nov. 9-10, 1938, pogrom against Jews in Germany and Austria.

    “A few years before Kristallnacht, the Nazis worked to deter the public from shopping at Jewish businesses,” she said. “Their efforts started in moments like tonight.” On behalf of her Jewish community, Strezo emphasized that the ordinance “makes us feel targeted. It makes us feel unsafe. It makes us feel unwelcome.”

    As she spoke, members of the group Somerville for Palestine (S4P), who had gathered outside City Hall for a rally in advance of and throughout the meeting, could be heard through the window, the chanting getting increasingly louder until the words were clearly audible over Strezo’s speech: “Disclose, divest, we will not stop, we will not rest.”

    “This ordinance will do nothing to solve the real conflict in the Middle East,” Strezo said. “What it will do and has been doing is make Jewish people and Israelis feel less welcome in our city spaces.”

    One councilor pointed out that the ordinance, while worth passing, was not what she’d hoped. Councilor Emily Hardt said, “Supporting Palestinian human rights and standing firmly against antisemitism are not contradictory positions. I believe that both are essential to our commitment to human dignity.” She went on to say that she would have preferred an ordinance that was focused on the actions of the U.S. government, “our government,” but given that this was the ordinance up for the vote, she would support it. “I appreciate the attempts to align use of our resources with our commitments to the rights and dignity of all people, in Israel and Palestine and around the world,” she said.

    When the vote was finalized, members of the group Somerville for Palestine and other supporters of the ordinance, many wearing keffiyehs, stood up and cheered as they left the chamber. Shalom Somerville members and others opposing the ordinance, many of whom wore white shirts with blue square pins and had stickers with “I’m not welcome here” on their chests, stood silently as most of the room emptied.

🔴 PMP | AMERICA’S OUTAGE CRISIS 🇺🇸
THE FRAGILITY OF AMERICAN INFRASTRUCTURE
🧵 4/5

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
✈️ THE FAA’S WARNING SIGN
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

The FAA’s November 15 explanation provides unusually specific details about Friday’s nationwide ground stop.

According to the agency:

• Network instability affected 17 of 22 en-route air traffic control centers.

• Data flooded the telecommunications network at approximately 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.

• Investigators identified possible sources in Amarillo, Texas, and El Dorado, Arkansas.

• Approximately 3,500 aircraft already airborne landed safely.

• Air traffic resumed after the network stabilized.

The FAA says its legacy telecommunications equipment became unstable.

Its investigation into the precise cause continues.

The disruption demonstrates how a problem at a limited number of locations can affect an interconnected national system.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🏦 THE BANKING LESSON
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Monday’s banking disruption offers another example.

Associated Press reporting identified a software bug affecting JPMorgan Chase’s internal hardware systems.

Customers experienced transaction delays.

Some transfers involving other banks were affected.

But an important clarification:

Other banks were not necessarily experiencing independent system failures.

And Zelle’s network operator said its network remained operational.

The issue illustrates how a problem at one major institution can affect transactions involving others.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
💻 THE MICROSOFT LESSON
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Microsoft’s disruption similarly demonstrated how many organizations depend on the same technology platforms.

A failure affecting widely used services can interrupt work across numerous unrelated businesses and institutions.

The larger concern is concentration of operational dependencies.

When essential services rely on a limited number of critical systems, a localized failure can create widespread disruption.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🔵 WHAT THESE INCIDENTS SUGGEST
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

There is a common policy lesson even without a common technical cause.

America needs stronger resilience.

That includes:

🟢 Redundant communications systems.

🟢 Better testing before infrastructure changes.

🟢 Clearer incident-response procedures.

🟢 Independent technical reviews.

🟢 Modernization of aging equipment.

🟢 More transparent reporting after major disruptions.

The objective should be reducing the likelihood and consequences of failure, whether the cause is a software bug, human error, equipment malfunction, or malicious activity.
