text:
Chairman Ty Bommarito on the Results of the 2026 Midterms

Lansing, Michigan – 16 November, 2026
​
The Michigan College Republicans are devastated by the results of the 2026 midterms. Many, if not all, of our members are going through our first defeat as operatives within the party, as we were almost all in high school in 2022, and I am no exception. The task before me now is to set aside our disappointment  and deliver a sober-minded review of our involvement, a diagnosis of what went wrong, and a plan for what to fix in 2028. I will speak as both the trustee of the Michigan College Republicans, as they have placed their faith in me as their chairman, and as their direct representative to inform the Michigan GOP and Republican voters of the thoughts of their largest republican youth organization.
​
ON A REVIEW OF THE MCR’S EFFORTS
​
The Michigan College Republicans knocked approximately 160,000 combined doors for republican candidates across our 18 chapters. Our northern regional director single-handedly coordinated the knocking of 15 thousand doors in the north for the national Senate and Congress, helping to secure a win for General Jack Bergman in a national environment that would have claimed his seat as well if he followed the national result trend. Unfortunately, this is where our happy results end. We knocked for every candidate that reached out to us for help, but primarily for Mike Rogers and Congressman Tom Barrett. I am told by the Barrett campaign that CRs accounted for 90% of the doors knocked by the campaign, and by its campaign manager that he had never seen this level of involvement from the College Republicans in the 6 campaigns he's worked for.
​
Our work with campaigns was not limited to door knocking and phone banking. Michigan College Republicans participated in every facet of campaigning for various candidates. MCRs spoke to media for video interviews and articles dozens of times; they participated in opposition research, pouring through thousands of social media posts in an attempt to hold radical leftists accountable for their statements (most notably with the failed democrat senate candidate Mallory McMorrow). CRs were the go-to for volunteers to fill out parade rosters for candidates. The needs for campaigns are limitless, and CRs were plugged in everywhere and anywhere in 2026.
​
Outside of our impressive total door number, the other dramatic area of improvement for the MCR has been the professional development of our members. We have never had as many members serving in full-time roles for Republican offices, conservative 501c3/4s, the RNC itself, and republican campaigns as we did this cycle. I am more proud of this than anything else we did this cycle.
​
Finally, I would like to highlight the success of the structural and statistical improvements of the MCR. At 18 chapters and approximately 250 members, the MCR has reached its all-time high point in both total chapters and membership. Meanwhile, we have dramatically improved the communication and collaboration between chapters, and successfully rolled out our regional director program. Areas of improvement remain, namely through the generally underutilized committees and top-to-bottom communication, which sometimes tends to get lost between the statewide executive board and average members.
​
ON WHY WE LOST
​
With that review of our progress and achievements this year, I will now move towards what went wrong in 2026. Here I will be speaking as myself, not necessarily representing the views of every Michigan College Republican.
​
Michigan’s issue in 2026 was not one of candidate quality. Going from top to bottom, I will begin with John James. I openly opposed John James in the primary, preferring Mike Cox, but I am not so stubborn as to refuse to admit that John James was a good candidate, certainly one who was capable of beating Joeclyn Benson in an environment where it was possible. Undeniably, a moderate, African American combat veteran from Macomb was a strong candidate; minimally, he was not one who swung the electorate 12 points away from himself. Perhaps another candidate could’ve swung the final vote tally 1 or 2 points, but the national environment presented a brick ceiling. Mike Rogers was the perfect candidate to face Abdul El Sayed. While I consider Mike Rogers to be more moderate than myself, I can admit a moderate former FBI agent with a reputation as a professional and a statesman was the perfect candidate to oppose a radical DSA candidate. Anthony Forlini and Doug Lloyd were both highly qualified, highly electable candidates; it's hard to ask for improvement there. Congressmen Bouchard and Barrett were both veterans who ran mature and broadly appealing campaigns; I don’t think anyone claims they were weak candidates.
​
Without candidate quality as an explanation, we are left with three potential explanations for why we lost: lack of groundgame, poor messaging, or the national environment. I cannot find any verifiable or complete data on the ground game in Michigan to verify it as the culprit; the best way to approach the ground game after a loss is the same as we should approach it after a win: that it can always be better. We should never be satisfied with the total number of doors knocked, phones banked, signs put up, or (perhaps most importantly) ballots chased. Allow the ground game to be the number one reason we lost, just as it always should be the number one thing with room for improvement after a win. Unfortunately, the biggest cap on the ground game was and remains money; the number of people willing to do this work for free dwindles every year, and the motivation of volunteers was undoubtedly hurt by my next two points. Yes, we should foster an environment as a party that treasures our volunteers and makes sure they know how important they are, but to get the ground game to the level we need to dig out of this in 28, we will need to be able to pay foot soldiers, or minimally provide incentives for volunteering. I will not pretend to know the answer to fixing our fundraising problem, but I will say that we need leadership in our movement that understands the gravity of it.
​
I say, knowing full well that this is not the answer people want to hear, that the statewide races in Michigan were going to be lost regardless of the actions of anyone in our state due to the national environment. The final national environment number came down to +14 points for the democrats. Michigan’s final number was 4-6 points to the right of the national environment, which is simply unheard of. The last time Michigan finished 4 or more points to the right of the national environment was Nixon’s 520-point electoral victory. I’ll say that again, correcting for the national environment, this was Michigan’s best performance in more than 50 years. I do not say this to argue that all is well, but to highlight that the national environment was truly insurmountable. I’ll also say again that I know this is not what people want to hear right now, but it is true. This is not normal, and I do not expect it to become so, but there is a worrying trend of a nationalization of statewide races, particularly our Senate race. As a state, we need to do what we can to wrestle our statewide races away from nationalization in years when it will harm us; the only way to do that is through our messaging, and even so it may be an impossible task some years.

Finally our messaging as a party. I was not involved in the 2022 election as I was away at Basic Training, but I have always been told by mentors and politicians alike that the reason we lost was that we ran everything on how much we did not like Whitmer, not on a positive vision for what we would do with our state. It seems to me that we have made the same mistake two midterm cycles in a row. We did not run with our own solutions on how to fix the price of living, we ran a tabloid drama about how bad our opponents were. I’m not saying you can never attack your opponents, but you cannot attack your opponents more than you highlight yourself, your record, and your plan. I will also argue that the biggest gun our state party had was left on the table. If we would have campaigned on reasonable data center reform, much like Congressman Tom Barrett did, our attacks about Joeclyn Benson's ties would have landed. Unfortunately the issue was left on the backburner and I do not know why.
​
It leaves me a nasty feeling in my stomach to point out problems without offering solutions, but the task I am undertaking in this statement is to offer the perspective of the Michigan College Republicans. So, I will now move on to offering insights into what I know best: the Republican youth.
​
ON THE YOUTH
​
In 2026, the youth vote shifted 29 points to the left. That shift represents about 4% of the total votes in Michigan, meaning if we had held the youth where they were in 2024, we would have two more Republican Congressmen from Michigan (Huizenga, Barrett), six more Republican State Representatives (Kuhn, Martin, Thompson, Deboer, Tisdel, Linting) and one more Republican State Senator (Cole). To win again, our party needs to make adjustments to win back those youth who shifted to the left in 2026.
​
With the national environment that we as the youth organizers for our party were up against being what it was, we had to have a perfect ground game operation to buck the trend in Michigan. While we have the many organizational wins listed in the first part of this statement, my fear is that those wins are only due to a lingering effect from the 2024 election and the dramatic increase in youth involvement we saw after the tragic murder of Charlie Kirk. Without a course correction on national policy and the implementation of some of the MIGOP reforms I will recommend below, in two years we will not have these bright spots.
​
In our state party there are three top youth leaders at a time, each with similar but distinct tasks, goals, and constituencies. For the last two years they’ve been MIGOP Youth Chair Krish Mathrani, Michigan YR Chair Paul Stephens, and the Michigan College Republicans Chair, for 24-25 Zach Friedman, 25-26 Tyler Campbell, and May 26 on, myself, Ty Bommarito. Inarguably, each of the three youth leaders is severely underfunded, underequipped, and underutilized. If our party wishes to win the youth vote again, these leaders must be supported.
​
Politics is relational, and relationships are what enable one to be successful in politics. One acquires those relationships by spending more time in politics, meeting more people, and working with more people. Therefore, by the very nature of politics, young people have an automatic handicap. Fortunately, most people understand this, and the overwhelming majority of Republicans I’ve met in my time want to build up the youth, equipping them with the resources and relationships they need. Any party measures to support the youth would be popular and likely pass through the executive committee of MIGOP without a dissenting vote, but as it currently stands, there has not been a fighter for the youth within the party to get a single measure passed that would help equip young people.
​
There are various measures MIGOP could institute, many of which are already implemented by local county parties and by other state GOPs. Many county Lincoln Day Dinners offer free or reduced admission for students, but there is no similar program for state conventions. MIGOP does not offer credit-bearing internships to students. There is no formal mentorship program for young people in MIGOP. MIGOP has never had any youth-targeted events or programming at its Mackinac conference or, in my memory, anywhere else. Many other states offer voting roles to the chairs of an official auxiliary organization status to the Young and College Republicans; MIGOP does not. Though the MIGOP constitution outlines one, there is no youth committee in MIGOP. Instead, our outreach to the youth is limited to a Youth Chair on the executive committee, who is elected by precinct delegates with little to no youth representation, which clearly has not been a winning formula. In order to get these programs, which I believe would be popular, instituted, we need to recognize the importance of the youth for our party moving forward, and someone needs to be willing to be the fighter the youth needs in the party.
​
Winning back the youth is a complicated task. The above measures will serve the following purpose: to help promote youth involvement within the actual party, which serves two purposes: affecting its messaging as youth voices rise and youth concerns get heard, and because it will help to quell the ever-rising disillusionment young people feel with our political system. If I have one takeaway from the last 4 years (the time I became involved in politics), it's that the brick wall I thought kept young, unconnected, middle-class people out of politics is mostly fictional. Unfortunately, not everyone has had as charmed a walk through Michigan politics as I have, and most young people view politics the way I did four years ago, unaffectable. If our party takes the basic steps to uplift our youth, we can stop that worrying trend, win back the youth vote, and guarantee the long-term health of our party as we build our bench and supply ourselves with another generation of operatives.

I don’t believe young people are so naive as to expect a Republican party that aligns with them on every single issue, I certainly am not. What young people do expect is a party that at least hears them, understands that they will be needed to take it over one day, and treats them as a legitimate demographic that needs to be accounted for, just like any other. I don’t know if this disillusionment was the biggest reason why the youth turned away from the Republican party, but I do know that it was a reason why, and one that can easily be corrected. In 2024 our party was not just happy that we won, but happy because our future looked bright. If we want to feel that way again, we need to get serious about giving our youth institutional support.

text:
Trump – Xi and Putin at APEC: Nuclear Restraint and the Limits of Summit Diplomacy 
The most defensible positive outcome from Shenzhen is a mandate for sustained nuclear-risk negotiations; a comprehensive trilateral treaty would require substantial changes in publicly documented negotiating positions.

China has acknowledged the three-leader meeting, but its official account does not establish a detailed agreed agenda or negotiated deliverables. https://t.co/OAGgO7EP8d

New START expired on 5 February 2026. Its replacement requires a new agreement; its existing extension provision had already been exhausted. https://t.co/OvoUlyDV9h

Beijing reiterated in October that participation in trilateral nuclear-disarmament negotiations was unacceptable at the present stage. https://t.co/j0UuhSbnCW

Ukraine presents a separate implementation problem: three leaders cannot supply Ukrainian consent, European commitments or NATO accession by agreement among themselves.

European governments should assess any outcome against published mandates, verification provisions, participating authorities and implementation milestones.

The decisive uncertainty is whether political contact produces an authorised negotiating process with identifiable technical work and follow-up dates.

Shenzhen’s Real Test Is Whether Governments Can Deliver What Leaders Promise
The meeting involving US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin around the Shenzhen APEC summit should be judged by the commitments their governments can execute, not the breadth of their declarations. As of 17 November 2026, nuclear restraint, a Ukrainian settlement and European security guarantees depend on different authorities, resources and negotiating conditions. Treating them as one bargain risks exchanging immediate concessions for obligations that remain unfunded, legally unresolved or outside the negotiator’s control. Europe’s response should connect diplomatic participation to industrial delivery, national authorisation and sustained support for Ukraine. Otherwise, a summit announcement could reduce political pressure to act before it reduces the security risks that governments, manufacturers and public budgets must continue to carry.

A mandate would matter more than a promise of disarmament
New START’s expiration on 5 February 2026 removed a contractual framework for interpreting strategic forces as well as limiting them. Its ceilings depended on agreed definitions, declarations and verification procedures. Reintroducing a familiar number without its accounting rules would create the appearance of continuity while potentially regulating something different. Each deployed nuclear-capable heavy bomber counted as one warhead under New START, whereas deployed ballistic missiles were counted according to their actual warheads. That distinction makes counting rules a substantive negotiating issue, not technical housekeeping. The US Senate’s examination of New START shows why a political endorsement of restraint cannot substitute for an agreement about what restraint means.

China’s statement of 16 October 2026 rejected trilateral nuclear-disarmament negotiations at the present stage. Attendance at a leaders’ meeting would therefore not establish acceptance of arsenal reductions. A useful initial outcome would identify authorised delegations, defined subjects and subsequent meetings, allowing practical risk-reduction measures to develop without pretending that a comprehensive limitation framework already exists. The governing test is whether the process generates usable information or changes conduct. A meeting that merely schedules another meeting leaves the underlying planning uncertainty intact. China’s official negotiating position makes that distinction unavoidable.

The financial figures expose different obligations, not a common European war chest
France’s amended military programming provides a funding trajectory, while Germany’s parliamentary budget account describes proposed expenditure and Britain’s nuclear-enterprise figures cover a specialised national system. France’s updated mission Défense programming rises from €57.1 billion in 2026 to €75.7 billion in 2030, in current euros, excluding pensions and on a constant perimeter. Germany’s September first-reading account of the 2027 budget describes €109.7 billion in the regular defence budget and €29.9 billion from the Bundeswehr special fund, totalling €139.6 billion. These figures establish different financial decisions and stages; neither demonstrates completed capability. France’s amended programming law and the Bundestag’s budget account cannot be turned into a readiness ranking by placing their totals side by side.

Britain’s Defence Investment Plan provides £63.6 billion for the Defence Nuclear Enterprise over financial years 2026–27 to 2029–30. The enterprise reports more than 47,000 personnel and workforce demand expected to reach approximately 65,000 by 2030. At EU level, SAFE’s €150 billion loan envelope contained a €21.3 billion second call announced on 29 October 2026; almost €13.5 billion had been disbursed as prefinancing across 11 member states. The second call is part of the envelope, and prefinancing is not equipment delivery. These distinctions expose the real constraint: money must pass through national decisions, contracts, production, acceptance and sustainment before it can support an operational undertaking. The British investment answer and the Commission’s SAFE implementation record describe commitments whose practical effects arrive on different schedules.

Procurement decides whether European influence becomes usable power
The additional French SAMP/T NG order announced by OCCAR on 21 October 2026 illustrates the transmission mechanism. The programme links France and Italy through cooperative procurement, with EUROSAM responsible for the contracted systems. An order establishes demand and contractual responsibility; it does not establish the availability of the additional systems for an immediate security mission. Governments must still connect equipment to trained personnel, maintenance, interceptors and replenishment. If diplomatic commitments assume that these elements arrive together, procurement delay becomes a security exposure rather than merely a programme-management problem. OCCAR’s contract announcement supports an industrial commitment, not a claim of additional operational readiness.

Italy’s presidency of the Tallinn Mechanism offers a different contribution to the same problem of sustained implementation. The Rome declaration published on 30 October 2026 emphasised civilian cyber resilience, local infrastructure and cooperation with implementing partners. Such projects can preserve essential functions through negotiation and reconstruction, but installation without maintenance ownership creates another form of incomplete capability. Rome’s influence will depend on projects that remain effective after its rotating presidency ends, just as Berlin’s financial expansion must produce accepted equipment and London’s nuclear programmes must secure qualified personnel. The Tallinn Mechanism’s Rome declaration places continuity of delivery alongside the allocation of resources.

Consent prevents a three-leader bargain from becoming a European settlement
Ukraine’s Constitution makes territorial commitments more demanding than an exchange of presidential assurances. Article 73 assigns questions concerning changes to Ukrainian territory exclusively to an all-Ukrainian referendum, while Article 157 restricts constitutional amendments directed against territorial integrity and prohibits constitutional amendment under martial law or a state of emergency. These provisions do not make every operational ceasefire equivalent to a territorial transfer. They require the proposed instrument to distinguish where forces stop from what happens to sovereignty. A referendum provision is not a general licence for any concession, and a foreign government’s endorsement cannot resolve the constitutional requirements of the affected state. Ukraine’s referendum provision and its amendment restrictions therefore constrain the content and sequence of a settlement.

The Paris Declaration of 6 January 2026 also distinguishes ceasefire monitoring, continued support for Ukraine’s armed forces and a multinational contribution to regeneration and deterrence. These functions cannot be merged into a generic guarantee. Monitoring may document a breach without providing the authority or capability to stop it; a reassurance force may have a military task without adjudicating compliance. The declaration’s reference to national legal and constitutional arrangements reinforces the implementation constraint: collective language requires decisions by the governments expected to act. The Paris Declaration is consequently a framework for responsibilities that must be made executable, rather than proof that protection is already operational.

Europe’s leverage lies in decisions the summit participants cannot make for it
The European Council’s proposed negotiating team, outlined on 13 November 2026, comprises EU institutions alongside France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. Its importance lies in connecting negotiations to the authorities expected to provide resources and accept obligations. The proposal does not establish that every other negotiating participant has accepted that format, nor does a smaller European team eliminate the need for wider national decisions. Representation becomes consequential when it prevents promises being made about European contributions before their providers have agreed to them. The European Council’s account describes coordination intended to bridge that gap.

European sanctions demonstrate the same boundary of authority. The Council adopted additional listings on 16 November 2026 while diplomatic efforts continued; those measures did not disappear because another government might prefer a wider political exchange. Any proposed relief must identify the restrictions concerned, the competent decision-maker and the conduct expected in return. Linking sanctions, territorial terms and nuclear restraint can widen bargaining space, but it also increases the number of decisions that can fail to align. Europe should resist an arrangement in which it is expected to deliver a legal or financial concession against a reciprocal promise that remains outside the other negotiator’s control. The Council’s sanctions decision shows that economic pressure remains a separate policy instrument.

The next two years will reveal who has mistaken commitments for capacity
Over the 12–24 months following November 2026, the decisive evidence will come from implemented measures: working crisis procedures, accepted security responsibilities, sustained Ukrainian support and procurement milestones that produce maintainable capability. SAFE prefinancing, French military programming, Germany’s budget proposals and Britain’s Defence Nuclear Enterprise plans must each be assessed against their own intended outputs. A useful summit process would survive disagreement and produce corrections when implementation fails. An ineffective one would allow broad declarations to coexist with unresolved obligations while governments continue to credit themselves with progress.

The cost of inaction would fall first on Ukraine if protection and assistance remain conditional while its exposure persists. European armed forces would carry the operational cost where commitments exceed available capacity; public budgets would carry the cost of programmes that require correction, prolonged support or replenishment; manufacturers and specialist suppliers would face procurement schedules that do not match the political promises built upon them. For the Paris Declaration and Europe’s procurement instruments, the choice is whether to establish accountable, sustained implementation now or leave those costs to accumulate behind an announcement. Shenzhen can initiate a more predictable security relationship. It cannot supply Ukrainian consent, European authorisation or industrial delivery by declaration.

AN AMERICAN MINISTER'S 1830 ASSESSMENT OF MUHAMMAD WAS BRUTAL.

In 1830, Reverend George Bush published The Life of Mohammed: Founder of the Religion of Islam, and of the Empire of the Saracens.

He did not offer a flattering portrait.

Bush wrote:

“His whole history makes it evident, that fanaticism, ambition, and lust were his master-passions.”

He continued:

“An enthusiast by nature, he became a hypocrite by policy.”

And he accused Muhammad of gratifying his desires at the expense of:

“truth, justice, friendship, and humanity.”

These were the words of an American religious scholar writing in the nineteenth century, examining the life of Islam's founder.

This wasn't a modern political argument. It was a published American biography, printed by Harper & Brothers in New York.

You don't have to agree with Bush's conclusions to recognize the historical significance of his criticism.

Today, people sometimes act as though questioning Muhammad's character, conduct or teachings is a modern invention.

It isn't.

For centuries, Muhammad's life, his military campaigns, his marriages and the relationship between religious authority and political power have been subjects of intense criticism and debate.

No religious founder should be placed beyond historical examination. No religious doctrine should be immune from scrutiny.

If we can critically examine the founders of every other political and religious movement, we can examine Muhammad too.

Historical source: Reverend George Bush, The Life of Mohammed, 1830, page 161.

text:
TWO OPPOSITION FIGURES HELD IN ADJACENT ROOMS AT LUBOWA FACILITY YET BARRED FROM SPEAKING.

By Keefa Nuwahereza.
As Uganda marks two years since the dramatic seizure of Dr Kizza Besigye in Nairobi, the veteran opposition leader and his longtime lawyer, former Kampala Lord Mayor Erias Lukwago, find themselves in neighbouring rooms at the Joint Clinical Research Centre in Lubowa. Yet military and prison authorities insist the two men cannot communicate because they are formally held in separate prisons and face distinct though related charges.

Besigye, a retired army colonel, four-time presidential candidate and former personal physician to President Yoweri Museveni, was abducted on 16 November 2024 while in Kenya with his aide Hajji Obeid Lutale. The pair was driven overnight across the border and later charged with treason alongside UPDF Captain Denis Oola. After the Supreme Court ruled that civilians could not be tried in military courts, the case moved to the civilian High Court. On 29 July 2026 Besigye collapsed during proceedings in Kampala and was taken to Mulago National Referral Hospital’s intensive care unit. He was later returned to prison facilities before being transferred to JCRC in late August for ongoing care.

His wife, Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS, has described a man who can walk only short distances with crutches and assistance, whose right hand is largely non-functional for writing, and who has faced difficulties with speech. She has rejected official assurances that the transfer to JCRC has resolved his medical needs, stating that soldiers maintain a presence from the facility gate through to the ward and even inside his room. Byanyima has publicly warned that she does not want to be summoned to collect his body if he dies in detention, and she has demanded bail so that he can access specialised assessment and treatment, including possibly in Geneva where she works. She emphasises that bail would not end the criminal case.

Lukwago, president of the People’s Front for Freedom and one of Besigye’s defence lawyers, was arrested from his home in Wakaliga on or around 15 June 2026 by armed personnel. He was charged with misprision of treason—an offence of knowingly failing to report information about an alleged treasonable plot spanning 2021 to 2024. He has denied the charge. Bail applications have been repeatedly denied on grounds of the seriousness of the offence and ongoing investigations. Like Besigye, he has been moved between prison facilities and JCRC amid health concerns. Byanyima has reported finding him with very high blood pressure and pleading with guards for medical attention. There have been accounts of delayed responses to medical emergencies and of doctors recommending surgery abroad that has not been authorised.

The practical reality of their proximity at JCRC has drawn particular attention. According to statements circulating after Byanyima’s recent visit, the two men are in adjacent or neighbouring rooms yet are forbidden from speaking to each other. When the restriction was questioned, the explanation offered was that they remain classified as being in different prisons and face different charges, even though the matters are linked to the same broader case. Each is described as being held in conditions amounting to solitary confinement with tightly controlled access.

Prison authorities have at times stated that both men’s health is improving and that care is being coordinated with personal doctors. Family members, lawyers and opposition figures continue to dispute the adequacy of the treatment available under detention restrictions. Meanwhile, reports of quiet political engagement involving General Salim Saleh and Justice Minister Norbert Mao have emerged, aimed at exploring a possible political settlement. These efforts have been met with scepticism from Byanyima and from the People’s Front for Freedom, which has rejected the idea of dialogue or power-sharing proposals while its leaders remain detained. Besigye himself has been reported as rejecting closed-door deals and insisting that any genuine process must involve the public rather than private negotiations.

The cases continue in the High Court, with preliminary hearings concluded and assessors appointed, even as health concerns have periodically limited the accused’s full participation. Human rights groups and bar associations have previously raised alarms over the manner of the arrests, the prolonged detention, and the impact on the ability of the accused to prepare a defence. As of mid-November 2026 the two men remain at the Lubowa facility under guard, their physical conditions the subject of conflicting public statements, and their inability to speak to one another a stark illustration of the controls still surrounding them. The coming weeks will test whether medical realities, court rulings or political calculations ultimately shape the next phase of these long-running proceedings.

text:
JOHN QUINCY ADAMS DID NOT MINCE WORDS ABOUT MUHAMMAD.

In his 1829 writings on the Ottoman Empire and Islam, John Quincy Adams, America's sixth president and son of Founding Father John Adams, offered a scathing assessment of Muhammad and the religious system he established.

Adams criticized what he viewed as the connection between religious authority, warfare, polygamy and the treatment of women in Islamic societies.

He was particularly critical of the way Muhammad's teachings, in his view, combined religious authority with worldly power and physical conquest.

This is an important piece of American history because criticism of Islam did not suddenly appear in the modern political era.

Early American leaders and statesmen were already debating the relationship between Islamic religious doctrine, political power, individual liberty and the rights of non-Muslims.

And before anyone attempts to rewrite history, let's be clear:

You can defend an individual's right to practice Islam without declaring Islamic doctrines immune from criticism.

You can oppose discrimination against peaceful Muslims while openly questioning religious teachings that conflict with freedom, equality and constitutional government.

Freedom of religion includes the freedom to criticize religion.

America was not built on the principle that we must remain silent about ideas that deserve scrutiny.

Historical attribution: John Quincy Adams was the sixth U.S. president, not a Founding Father. His writings on the Ottoman Empire appeared in the American Annual Register for 1827–1829.

text:
#Iraq #Update: “We are on the verge of a crisis, a major crisis,” Kataib Hezbollah official Abu Talib al-Saidi warned during a press conference inside Jurf al-Sakhar, a.k.a. Jurf al-Nasr, on Tuesday, November 17. The group used the event to challenge the government’s oil-smuggling allegations and signal that it would avoid fighting Iraqi security forces. Al-Saidi accused unnamed political actors of seeking bloodshed and described the current prime minister’s approach as a political “adventure.”

Al-Saidi invoked the “shared blood” of Kataib Hezbollah, the Popular Mobilization Forces, Federal Police, Counter Terrorism Service and Iraqi Army during the battles against ISIS twelve years ago. He recalled fighters’ remains becoming indistinguishable after suicide bombings and said efforts to push these forces into fighting one another would be thwarted by “the wisdom of reasonable people.”

Addressing the government committee’s visit, al-Saidi said its members had been welcomed and offered lunch. “We held no ill will toward them. We did not know that they intended, unfortunately, to falsify the facts,” he said. He rejected government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi’s account of a provocation during the visit. “We did not restrict the committee,” he said, adding that journalists could inspect every location the investigators had visited.

Standing near a rudimentary processing facility, al-Saidi disputed its alleged connection to oil smuggling. He claimed it was approximately five kilometers from the three pipelines allegedly punctured to extract fuel and had been abandoned for months. He described it as an emergency facility used to process purchased heavy fuel oil, known locally as “black oil,” into what he called “gas” for generators and vehicles. 

“Certainly, this is a political issue. It is not a technical issue,” al-Saidi said. He argued that successive governments had failed to provide enough fuel for the group’s extensive operational sector, requiring it to buy supplies with its own funds.

Al-Saidi also portrayed Kataib Hezbollah as a fighting organization that had stayed outside government appointments, claiming it held no ministerial, deputy ministerial or municipal leadership posts. He recounted its opposition to Saddam Hussein, foreign occupation forces, al-Qaeda and ISIS. Al-Saidi closed by urging the assembled journalists to report what they saw and help calm public tensions.

text:
#Iraq #SITREP | Iraq’s government is moving to assert control over Jurf al-Sakhar, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, in Babil Governorate, following an investigation into alleged oil smuggling. The dispute is becoming a test of Baghdad’s authority over Kataib Hezbollah, which controls the area. Government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi said Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi ordered the armed forces to enter and set a deadline for the group to withdraw. A senior Iraqi official said that the deadline expires Friday.

On Tuesday, al-Aboudi said the government had prepared a plan to remove any party involved in exploiting the area’s oil resources. He said Interior Ministry surveillance cameras corroborated intelligence on smuggling and that further findings would be announced soon. A judicial committee, accompanied by a government committee, also visited Jurf al-Nasr to inspect suspected sites and establish the circumstances of the case.

The government has already announced measures against officials accused of failing to prevent the alleged smuggling. Following an emergency security meeting Saturday, al-Zaidi ordered suspects referred to the judiciary and removed nine security and administrative officials. They included Babil’s police chief, senior security and intelligence officials, the commander of the Sixth Energy Police Brigade, and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company. Subsequent military and security meetings focused on executing arrest warrants, strengthening checkpoints, and protecting oil infrastructure. Federal Police commander Mohammed Qasim al-Fahd also inspected the 16th Federal Police Brigade in Jurf al-Nasr.

Iranian media coverage is adding a political dimension to the dispute. Tasnim carried comments from State of Law Coalition media director Hisham al-Rikabi calling for dialogue, rejecting oil smuggling, and warning against an armed confrontation. His statement that “both sides are our brothers” reflects concern that the government’s planned entry could lead to fighting.

Tasnim also carried a competing account from Supreme Islamic Council political bureau member Furat al-Sharaa, who claimed that a government committee left the area without confirming oil smuggling. He questioned aspects of the investigation and linked the dispute to efforts to bring weapons under state control. His account conflicts with the government’s assertion that surveillance footage supported the intelligence findings.

The immediate issue is whether Kataib Hezbollah complies with the withdrawal deadline and allows government forces to enter. Baghdad is presenting the operation as an effort to protect public resources and enforce the law. Statements carried by Iranian media increasingly frame it as a sensitive dispute requiring negotiation to prevent bloodshed.

#Iraq #SITREP | A leaked 19-page Iraqi intelligence report prepared by the Federal Intelligence and Investigations Agency documents suspected oil theft, illegal refining, underground storage facilities, and petroleum smuggling networks operating in Jurf al-Sakhar, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, in Iraq’s Babil Governorate. 

The area is widely associated with the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia. The intelligence findings suggest that petroleum infrastructure has been illegally accessed and that organized tanker movements have supported the suspected operation over several years. Satellite imagery and geospatial analysis indicate that some facilities remained active into 2026. However, the available evidence does not independently establish the identities of those directing the operations or the total financial proceeds.

The investigation identifies at least six locations associated with suspected petroleum theft, storage, refining, and transportation activities. One suspected pipeline breach was identified near Bahbahani junction at MGRS coordinate 38SMB2883828797, with indications of activity during 2025 and 2026. Another possible breach was identified at 38SMB2914528645. At 38SMB2957629508, analysts documented excavations, oil staining, and tanker movements dating back to 2021. 

A separate location at 38SMB2415132129 was assessed as a possible underground petroleum storage and small-scale refining facility. Newly constructed petroleum-related infrastructure and tanker activity were also identified at 38SMB2407931433. The report’s use of satellite imagery and multiple observation periods suggests a sustained operation rather than isolated incidents of fuel diversion.

The intelligence assessment also documents tanker movements at suspected smuggling sites. At one location, analysts identified 21 tankers in imagery from 2022. Some vehicles were assessed to have capacities of approximately 36,000 liters. The report suggests that nighttime loading and transportation could conceal additional activity not captured in daytime satellite imagery. Although these observations support the possibility of organized petroleum transportation, the available reporting does not establish how many tankers were carrying illegally obtained fuel or the total volume transported.

The report identifies three possible transportation corridors connecting Jurf al-Sakhar with Baghdad and surrounding areas. These routes reportedly pass through Musayyib, Amiriyat al-Fallujah, Habbaniyah, Fallujah, and Abu Ghraib. The geographic distribution of the suspected facilities and transportation corridors suggests that the operation could involve multiple collection, storage, and distribution points.

Jurf al-Sakhar occupies a sensitive position south of Baghdad and has remained under the influence of Kataib Hezbollah and associated armed formations for years. The area’s restricted access and limited civilian oversight complicate independent verification of activities inside the district. The reported presence of suspected illegal petroleum infrastructure raises questions about whether armed groups operating in the area have benefited financially from unauthorized access to Iraq’s energy resources. Nevertheless, the published intelligence findings do not conclusively demonstrate that Kataib Hezbollah’s leadership organized, financed, or directly profited from the alleged smuggling network.

text:
In 1957, newspapers put Elvis Presley's income at close to $1 million. In March 1958, the U.S. Army started paying him $78 a month.

He could have had it much easier.

The military offered him Special Services. Six weeks of basic training, then he'd sing for the troops. No rifle, no barracks in Germany.

His manager, Colonel Tom Parker, said no. Those shows would have been filmed and recorded by the government, for free, and Elvis wouldn't own any of it. Parker's line was "Taking any of these deals will make millions of Americans angry."

So Elvis went in as a regular private. And the money kept coming anyway. RCA had a stack of unreleased songs ready, and he had ten top 40 hits while he was in uniform. Before he got home, Parker had already signed a $175,000 deal with Paramount for G.I. Blues and a $200,000 one with Fox.

Soldiers who served with him say he gave his Army pay to charity.

The case for Elvis: he could have taken the easy way out, and he didn't.

The case for Parker: he turned two years in the Army into the best publicity Elvis ever had.

So which was it, patriotism or the smartest business move Parker ever made?

Here's the AI's answer after analyzing all sorts of data:

Your claim that Ukraine used Starshield to strike civilian infrastructure (and that this allegedly made the United States complicit in war crimes) is not supported by either the facts or international humanitarian law (IHL).

1. What Starshield is and how it is used
Starshield is the military-grade version of the system (controlled by the U.S. government), not the commercial Starlink service. Ukraine primarily uses it for:

- controlling interceptor drones against Russian strike drones (Shahed and jet-powered variants) that attack Ukrainian cities, energy facilities, and civilian infrastructure;
- tactical operations on occupied territories.

Deep strikes into Russian territory (including against oil refineries) are mostly carried out by other means. The speed/functionality restrictions on the system in October–November 2026 primarily affected Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian drones attacking civilian objects, rather than any “targeting of civilian infrastructure.” Ukrainian officials and specialists have directly refuted Musk’s claims about violations of commercial Starlink terms of service.

2. Ukrainian strikes on objects in Russia are not strikes on “civilian infrastructure” under IHL
According to Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I (to which both Russia and Ukraine are parties), a military objective is an object which by its nature, location, purpose or use makes an effective contribution to military action and whose total or partial destruction, capture or neutralization, in the circumstances ruling at the time, offers a definite military advantage.

Oil refineries, fuel storage facilities, logistics hubs, and facilities supplying components for military drones and equipment fall under this definition: they supply the Russian army with fuel and material means. Independent legal analyses (Lieber Institute West Point, Just Security, and others) conclude that such facilities are lawful military objectives when used for military purposes. Ukraine has consistently stated that it targets military/military-logistics objects, not purely civilian ones.

This is fundamentally different from the systematic Russian strikes on Ukrainian power plants, residential buildings, hospitals, humanitarian points, and rescue workers — which the UN Commission of Inquiry, ACLED, HRW, and others have classified as war crimes and crimes against humanity.

3. Independent investigations
The UN Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine has documented systematic Russian strikes on civilian objects and people. Regarding Russian accusations against Ukraine (drone strikes on civilian targets), the Commission was unable to reach conclusions due to lack of access to the territory and Russia’s refusal to cooperate. The scale and nature of the violations are not comparable.

4. Regarding “U.S. complicity in war crimes”
Providing military assistance (including communications systems) within the framework of collective self-defense (Article 51 of the UN Charter) does not make the supplier complicit in the war crimes of the recipient if the recipient complies with IHL. There is no evidence that the United States transferred the system specifically for strikes on purely civilian objects, and no independent bodies have established facts of such strikes by Ukraine on a scale that could be called a systematic violation.

Conclusion: Ukraine is not conducting a campaign of strikes against civilian infrastructure in violation of IHL. Its strikes are directed at objects that have military significance for Russia’s military potential. Your thesis does not correspond to the documented practice of Starshield use, the rules of IHL, or the conclusions of independent investigations.

text:
Did a little thought experiment here for a 50 unit apartment complex I or near Lansing Michigan. At low rental prices it would take 185 years to recoup the cost..take a look. 

I’ve been looking at what it would take to privately develop a 50-unit apartment complex in the Lansing area, and the numbers raise some interesting questions about why more housing isn’t being built.

Consider this example:

A new 50-unit apartment complex consisting of:

35 one-bedroom apartments renting for $1,000 per month.
15 two-bedroom apartments renting for $1,300 per month.
Two full-time employees: a building manager and maintenance technician, each earning $75,000 annually.

This development would provide housing for 50 households, create two full-time jobs and represent approximately $21 million in private investment. At these rental rates in a low tax environment it would take 185 years to recoup the cost. 

The financial reality:

Estimated development cost: $17–24 million.
Annual potential rental income: $654,000.
Annual rental income after 5% vacancy: $621,300.
Employee salaries and associated costs: approximately $172,500.
Additional operating expenses: approximately $135,000.
Property taxes could add another $200,000–$640,000 annually, depending on the property’s assessment and tax district.

Under these assumptions, conventional property taxes could leave very little operating income, potentially making the investment financially unattractive before even considering mortgage payments.

So what could Lansing do differently?

Five opportunities to encourage private development:

Property Tax Incentives: Offer 15–18-year tax abatements or reduced-tax programs for qualifying developments that provide reasonably priced workforce housing.
Streamlined Permitting: Create a coordinated approval process with a 90-day target for qualifying apartment projects.
Reduce Construction Costs: Reevaluate parking requirements, zoning restrictions and unnecessary design requirements while maintaining safety standards.
Land and Infrastructure Assistance: Make city-owned land available at competitive prices and help with eligible water, sewer, road and stormwater improvements.
Development Incentives: Expand access to brownfield redevelopment programs, affordable housing tax credits, permit-fee assistance and other financing incentives.

Michigan already has programs such as Neighborhood Enterprise Zones, Residential Housing Exemption Certificates, PILOT arrangements and brownfield incentives. The opportunity is to make these programs more accessible and predictable for developers.

The Bigger Picture

This isn’t simply about giving developers tax breaks. It’s about making private investment possible while addressing Lansing’s housing needs.

Imagine attracting multiple $15–25 million apartment developments over the next several years. That means hundreds of additional apartments, construction jobs, permanent employment, more residents supporting local businesses and a stronger long-term tax base.

The city should be asking:

What combination of tax incentives, land assistance and building-code or permitting changes would make it financially attractive for private developers to build more housing without forcing rents higher?

If Lansing wants more housing, it needs to create an environment where building it actually makes financial sense.

You cannot expect private investment to happen if the economics of development don’t work.

text:
🔭 ASTRONOMY PICTURE OF THE DAY (APOD) 🌌

Discover the cosmos, one extraordinary image at a time. Every day, explore a different corner of our fascinating universe through a remarkable astronomical image, accompanied by insights that reveal the science, beauty, and mysteries behind the cosmos.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌌 NOVEMBER 17, 2026

✨ MILKY WAY VERSUS AURORA

Two enormous arches stretch across the Norwegian night sky, appearing almost to confront one another. One is a structure of stars that has existed for billions of years. The other is a glowing ribbon of light that may have formed only hours earlier.

Though they seem to share the same celestial stage, these magnificent formations belong to entirely different worlds.

📸 IMAGE CREDIT: Guillaume Scheib

📅 DATE: November 17, 2026

✨ THE COSMIC STORY

Are these two giant arches battling for control of the sky?

Not quite. But the resemblance is extraordinary.

The arch on the left is the luminous central band of our Milky Way Galaxy. It contains an immense concentration of stars, gas, and cosmic dust, forming part of the galaxy that has been our home for billions of years.

The arch on the right is an aurora, a brilliant display of light created high above Earth's surface. Unlike the distant Milky Way, this glowing ribbon belongs to our own atmosphere and may have developed only hours before the photograph was taken.

One structure is ancient and unimaginably distant. The other is temporary and comparatively close. Their apparent meeting is a remarkable coincidence of perspective.

But what creates an aurora?

The story begins with our Sun.

Our star constantly releases a stream of charged particles into space, known as the solar wind. When energetic particles interact with Earth's magnetic field, some are guided toward the upper atmosphere, where they collide with atoms and molecules.

These collisions transfer energy to atmospheric gases. As the energized particles return to lower energy states, they release light, producing the shimmering colors and shifting patterns we recognize as auroras.

The result can be spectacular: luminous curtains, ribbons, and arcs that ripple across the night sky.

And there is something wonderfully fitting about the two arches appearing together. The Milky Way contains our Sun, while the Sun supplies the energetic particles that help create the aurora. One is the vast stellar home of our solar system; the other is a nearby reminder that our star remains an active force shaping the environment around Earth.

Look beyond the two arches, and the photograph reveals even more.

Behind the middle of the auroral arch is the Big Dipper, the familiar star pattern within the constellation Ursa Major. Farther away still is the Andromeda Galaxy, visible as a bright spot near the top of the image, just left of center.

Andromeda is not simply another star. It is a separate galaxy, a vast collection of stars beyond the boundaries of our own Milky Way.

The featured photograph was captured about a month ago from Kvaløya, an island in northern Norway, where dark skies and favorable conditions can offer extraordinary views of the aurora and the stars beyond.

What makes this image so remarkable is not merely the beauty of either arch. It is the opportunity to see several vastly different scales of the universe in one frame: Earth's upper atmosphere, our home galaxy, and another galaxy far beyond it.

For a moment, the nearby and the distant appear almost side by side.

🌀 A COSMIC PERSPECTIVE

The night sky can make distant things appear close and neighboring worlds seem connected.

Yet the Milky Way and the aurora remind us how misleading perspective can be. One spans an enormous galaxy, containing hundreds of billions of stars. The other unfolds in the thin envelope of atmosphere surrounding our planet.

And still, they share a connection through the Sun.

That is part of astronomy's enduring wonder: seemingly separate phenomena often belong to a much larger story. The star that warms our planet also sends particles into space, helping paint the polar skies with light. And that same star is only one member of the galaxy whose distant glow stretches across the photograph.

Perhaps the greatest wonder is that we can stand beneath these arches, look upward, and recognize our place within them.

We are not merely observers of the universe. We are part of its story.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🔭 TOMORROW'S PICTURE

OPEN SPACE

🌠 Keep looking up. The universe never runs out of wonders.

text:
McDavid Chases History as the NHL Delivers an 11-Game Night

Connor McDavid is putting together a season that belongs in the history books. The Oilers superstar has points in all 22 games this season, piling up 53 (12 goals, 41 assists) and threatening to reach the 200-point mark. Only Wayne Gretzky has ever accomplished that.

Tonight, McDavid takes his streak into Sunrise against the defending champion Florida Panthers, looking to make it 23 straight games. That’s the headliner, but an 11-game slate has plenty more to offer.

Around the League: Edmonton (16-3-3) and Carolina are setting the pace, while Minnesota (15-3-4) continues to look like a defensive powerhouse. Ottawa has quietly emerged as a legitimate contender, Anaheim’s young guns are making noise, and Nashville is proving its early-season success is no fluke.

Keep an eye on Leon Draisaitl’s 20-goal start, Kirill Kaprizov’s production, and Nikita Kucherov, who celebrates his 900th NHL game tonight against Washington.

Weather for the Fans: Most arenas are looking at favorable conditions, with generally dry weather across much of the country. Florida is the exception. Heavy rain and gusty winds could make travel around Sunrise and Tampa unpleasant. Fans heading to either game should plan accordingly.

My Picks Tonight:

Edmonton gets past Florida, with McDavid extending his point streak.
Tampa Bay celebrates Kucherov’s milestone with a win over Washington.
Minnesota handles Nashville at home.
Boston takes care of business against Los Angeles.
Vegas edges Dallas in a heavyweight showdown.

This Day in NHL History — November 17

Hockey history runs deep tonight. In 1979, 51-year-old Gordie Howe and 18-year-old Wayne Gretzky shared the ice for the first time in an NHL game. Hartford won 4-0, with Howe recording an assist.

November 17, 1926, also marked the Chicago Black Hawks’ first NHL game, a 4-1 victory over Toronto. Nearly a century later, the modern-day Leafs visit Chicago.

Eleven games, a milestone celebration, and a superstar chasing history. McDavid is giving hockey fans another reason to stay glued to the ice. Don’t miss it!

text:
Of all the times and dates a baby could choose to arrive, J'Aime Brown seemed determined to make one number impossible to forget: 7-Eleven. 😂👶

The Missouri baby was born on July 11, 2019 — 7/11 — at exactly 7:11 p.m.

Then nurses put her on the scale.

She weighed 7 pounds, 11 ounces.

Her mother, Rachel Langford, told reporters that she had already noticed the numbers 7 and 11 repeatedly appearing during her pregnancy. She would sometimes look at the clock and see 7:11, but she never imagined the coincidence would continue all the way into the delivery room.

Once the story spread, it inevitably reached .

The company initially celebrated J'Aime's remarkably on-brand arrival with gifts for the family.

Then it took the coincidence one step further.

7-Eleven pledged $7,111 toward J'Aime's future college education. The company also provided diapers and other baby supplies, turning an already unforgettable birth story into something that could benefit her years later.

And there was another sweet detail: July 11 is already a special day for the convenience-store chain. In the United States, 7/11 is traditionally "7-Eleven Day," when participating stores celebrate the brand's birthday and have historically offered customers free Slurpees.

So J'Aime managed an almost absurd numerical hat trick:

Born on 7/11.
At 7:11 p.m.
Weighing 7 lbs., 11 oz.
Then receiving $7,111 for college. 🎉

Some babies arrive with a good story.

J'Aime arrived with what looks like a sponsorship deal written into the universe. 😂❤️

Sources: CNN; BBC News; USA Today; 7-Eleven; contemporary reporting from Missouri.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen

Subject: Building Diplomatic Relations and Strategic Partnerships with the Republic of Balochistan: An Invitation to International Recognition and Cooperation

Your Excellency,
Filipinos launched the 1896 revolution against Spanish rule, with figures like José Rizal and Andrés Bonifacio, and declared independence in 1898. They resisted American rule, endured Japanese occupation, and achieved full independence in 1946, then ended dictatorship through the 1986 People Power Revolution.
We admire the Philippines' People Power Revolution and the resilience of its people. Balochistan extends its warm friendship.
Southeast Asia’s great trading tradition and Balochistan’s Arabian Sea coast are natural partners on the Indian Ocean’s maritime routes.

The history of Balochistan
Balochistan is not a newcomer to sovereignty. The Khanate of Kalat held a distinct treaty relationship with the British Crown (1876) and was never part of British India’s princely states. On 4 August 1947, at a round-table meeting in Delhi attended by Lord Mountbatten, Mohammad Ali Jinnah and the Khan of Kalat, Mir Ahmad Yar Khan, it was agreed that Kalat (Balochistan) would become an independent sovereign state with a status different from that of the Indian princely states.
On 11 August 1947, three days before Pakistan came into being, Balochistan declared its independence from British rule. The announcement was published in the New York Times and broadcast by All India Radio on 12 August 1947. A standstill agreement with the new Dominion of Pakistan followed.
Kalat’s bicameral parliament, the Dar-ul-Awam (House of commons) and the Dar-ul-Umara (House of lords), unanimously rejected accession to Pakistan when it met in December 1947 and February 1948. On 27 March 1948 Pakistan illegally invaded and annexed Balochistan. The Baloch have never regarded this as a free act: the Khan and Jinnah were photographed together on other occasions, yet not a single photograph of the signing of the accession instrument has been published, which is consistent with our position that it was never a mutual agreement.

Since 1948 the Baloch people have continued to assert their right to independence and sovereignty, through political action, diplomatic manners and, at times, defensive armed resistance (1948, 1958, 1962, 1973–77 and since the early 2000s). Millions of Baloch, scattered across the globe but united in purpose, are raising one voice under the leadership of Hyrbyair Marri, President of the Free Balochistan Movement. They call on the nations of the world to recognize the Republic of Balochistan as an independent state, a recognition it has earned and rightfully deserves.
The Baloch nation has long suffered the plunder of its resources, enforced disappearances, ethnic cleansing, and relentless repression by Pakistan. Across the western part of Balochistan, the Baloch people face the same fate under Iranian rule: fabricated encounters, mass executions, expulsion from their own land, and the denial of birth certificates and legal identity, a deliberate effort to erase their existence.

The significance of Balochistan
Balochistan sits where South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East meet, on the Arabian Sea coast just outside the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil passes. It is a natural gateway for global trade. Two globally important deep-sea ports lie on the Baloch coast: Chabahar, which is under Iran’s illegal rule, and Gwadar, which is under Pakistan’s unlawful rule. Beneath the land lie Balochistan’s mineral resources include copper, gold, chromite, coal, natural gas, lead, zinc, barite, iron ore, limestone, gypsum, marble, granite, onyx, magnesite, sulphur, fluorite, antimony, manganese, bauxite, celestite, rock salt, silica sand, fuller’s earth, lapis lazuli, agate, and reported traces of uranium and rare earth elements of strategic value, including the Reko Diq and Saindak deposits and the Sui gas field.
Because the Republic of Balochistan declared independence on 11 August 1947, we, the Baloch, consider ourselves independent. A free, Secular, democratic and stable Balochistan is vital for regional and global peace and for connectivity between the Indian Ocean and the heartland of Eurasia.

Balochistan offers: Building Partnerships for Peace, Security, and Sustainable Development

The Philippines faces maritime pressure in the South China Sea, typhoons and floods, and insurgent and extremist groups in the south. A free, stable Balochistan, as an Indian Ocean coastal state committed to freedom of navigation and the rule of law at sea, proposes cooperation in maritime security and coast-guard training, disaster-response and early-warning experience, and the sharing of lessons in counter-extremism and community reconciliation. We hope in this way to contribute to peace, security and connectivity in the region.

The Republic of Balochistan offers your country:
•Maritime security: training and information-sharing between two archipelagic and coastal peoples, and Mindanao–Balochistan peace-building exchange.
•Maritime security: cooperation on anti-piracy, anti-smuggling and coast-guard training along the Arabian Sea and the wider Indian Ocean.
•Climate resilience: cooperation on drought, flood and water management, and on renewable energy.
•Countering extremism: as a Secular state with deep Secular and tribal traditions of tolerance, Balochistan offers intelligence-sharing, joint training and a model for countering radicalisation. 

Our request
On behalf of the Republic of Balochistan, we respectfully ask your Government to:
1.Recognize the Republic of Balochistan as an independent state and establish diplomatic relations;
https://t.co/HiRWcoQDnP appropriate observer-level engagement for Balochistan at the United Nations and, in line with each Organization’s own procedures, at the European Union, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and the African Union.
3.Stand with the Baloch in nation-building: education, health, infrastructure, technology, defense and security.
The commitments in this letter are those of the Republic of Balochistan as it takes up the effective exercise of sovereignty over its territory and resources; we make them in good faith so that your Government can plan with us from the outset.
Partnership with Balochistan is of real benefit to your country and to the world. We would welcome the opportunity to meet your representatives at the earliest convenience.

With our highest consideration,
THE REPUBLIC OF BALOCHISTAN

Mir Yar Baloch

text:
🚨🇸🇦 🇾🇪 Beyond the Coast: Yemen’s Strategic Reset

The threat to Yemen’s coastal positions came from inland. The redeployment towards Aden addresses that strategic imbalance.

On Nov 15, government-aligned forces withdrew from positions around Bab al-Mandab to reinforce Aden. Reports described a Houthi flanking move threatening their supply lines. By Nov 17, reinforcements were reaching Tur al-Baha, about 85 kilometres from Aden.

Defending the coast served Yemen and international shipping. But October’s gains around Dhubab remained vulnerable as the Houthis advanced inland. A force holding the shoreline could still be cut off from the territory sustaining it.

Reinforcing Aden and the approaches to Taiz can preserve troops, secure the government’s base and rebuild the depth needed to recover territory. Correcting an exposed deployment is necessary; restoring the initiative will require results.

Securing Aden and relieving Taiz should preserve the capacity to restore the legitimate Yemeni government’s authority beyond both cities.

The correction concerns what those forces were built to achieve.

After Sanaa fell in 2014, rebuilding from 2015 too often gave political and regional factions military titles without replacing their loyalties. A common national objective did not follow.

The UAE-backed separatist project represented by al-Zubaidi exposed this contradiction. In 2019, separatists seized Aden’s presidential palace and Emirati aircraft struck government troops. In Dec 2025, Riyadh backed Yemen’s demand for Emirati forces to leave within 24 hours, accusing Abu Dhabi of encouraging operations threatening Saudi security.

🔴 These actions underpin the charge of betrayal: support for armed partners had undermined the government the coalition existed to restore. A southern project cannot secure its future by weakening that government while the Houthis threaten Aden.

Saudi Arabia’s Nov 16 assignment of Chief of General Staff Fayyad al-Ruwaili to joint forces command should serve this correction: military support tied to state institutions and operations directed towards restoring the legitimate Yemeni government’s authority.

Yet rebuilding that authority can’t make Saudi Arabia solely responsible for a global shipping artery.

On Nov 12, the Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2837, renewing targeted sanctions until Nov 2027. It envisaged agreement by Jan 11, 2027 on specified dual-use items sustaining Houthi weapons production.

Security Council Report described Russian objections to restoring the terrorist label and strengthening maritime provisions. China opposed immediate controls based on a provisional components list references to precursor chemicals were softened.

Iran arms the Houthis. Chinese-origin components and Russian-Chinese support for Tehran can indirectly sustain Houthi power in a contest for regional influence. Such channels can reinforce each other without a formal alliance.

One strategic reading is that Moscow and Beijing resist U.S. dominance of regional security even where they share an interest in safe shipping. That divergence can give Tehran more room to advance its regional agenda through the Houthis. China’s commercial exposure doesn’t guarantee support for U.S.-preferred enforcement.

🔴 Saudi civilians and international shipping face the consequences. A U.S.-Saudi-led international military coalition should integrate air defence, maritime protection & arms embargo enforcement into a sustained strategy.

Its purpose should extend beyond intercepting attacks to preventing the Houthis from rebuilding the capabilities behind them. Restoring the legitimate Yemeni government’s authority and cutting weapons supplies are essential to making that protection last.

Redeployment offers a chance to correct past mistakes. Success means stronger inland defences, civilian relief, recovered territory and an end to the transcontinental Houthi terror threat.

RESTORE THE STATE. SECURE THE RED SEA.

A moron saying shitty does not make the retort any less moronic. The Atlantic trade took about 12.5 million people over 350 years with roughly 1.8 million deaths on the crossing mostly from disease. That is not a downplaying of anything. It is the scale that the records support. African kingdoms and coastal traders raided captured and sold captives to the ships. The buyers paid for what the sellers offered. Pointing that out is not an excuse. It is the basic commercial fact of the market. Every slave system in history had sellers and buyers. Pretending one side invented the other does not change who supplied the cargo.
The Arab trades across the Sahara Red Sea and Indian Ocean ran for more than a thousand years and took comparable or larger numbers by the estimates historians use on the thin records. They preferred females for households and castrated boys for eunuchs with mortality often reported between 60 and 90 percent. The desert marches killed half or more before any buyer saw them. Noting that longer eastern traffic existed is not finger pointing. It is the comparison that shows the Atlantic version was not the unique peak of cruelty or duration. Forced labor and brutality were the point of every slave system for thousands of years before and after. The Atlantic form was race based chattel in the Americas and that shapes American history. It does not turn one episode into the single worst event humans produced.
Calling the observation mentally ill or traitorous does not answer the numbers or the agency. Selective memory that erases the sellers and the longer eastern trades does not make the Atlantic trade the unique summit of human evil. Other events killed far more people in shorter time. The record is what it is.

🧭 HAMNØY | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
📍 Getting There

Hamnøy lies along the E10 road near Reine in western Lofoten. Fly to Leknes Airport and continue by rental car or bus, or take the Bodø–Moskenes ferry (approximately 3.5 hours) before travelling onward. Check Reis Nordland for local bus connections.

🗺️ What to Explore

Start with the famous view of red fishermen’s cabins from Hamnøy Bridge. Continue to neighbouring Sakrisøy and Reine for contrasting coastal scenery. Guided kayaking on Reinefjord offers a different perspective when conditions permit.

⏱️ Time Needed & Where to Stay

Allow half a day to explore the nearby fishing villages. For a more relaxed visit, stay overnight in a restored rorbu cabin. Reine is another convenient base.

🌤️ When to Visit

Summer brings extended daylight and greater flexibility for outdoor exploration. From late August to mid-April, darker skies offer opportunities to see the Northern Lights, although sightings are never guaranteed.

💰 Costs & Booking

Accommodation and activity prices vary by season. Reserve cabins early for popular travel periods, and confirm ferry schedules, transport connections and current rates before departure.

text:
Some Veterans know they had a disappointing service history, and that doesn’t reflect their willingness to fight for America. Many were not allocated to Black Hawk Down, Generation Kill, Saving Private Ryan, Navy Seal combat situations. 

Ridiculing them for chain of command decisions is just kicking them while they are down. Nearly every soldier I knew wanted to get into “the shit”, but it was always too little too late for them. American military is 100% volunteer, and every person wanted to fight but ended up somewhere they didn’t want to be stationed, you don’t get a choice where you go, you just say yes sir/ma’am. 

What needs to be admired is the willingness to fight and the sacrifice of that person’s youth. 

Many days I spent questioning why when I was on patrol or sitting in a guard tower why no one cared about me. I’d scroll through Facebook for a few minutes when I was allowed to use a computer and see people popping bottles, partying, spending time with their family, asking myself why would I do this when no one cares. 

What got me through was knowing that me doing this (serving) means my mother doesn’t have to do this when on our own land, even if people think I’m “killing for the Jews”, I believed that if anyone was going to do it, it would be me and not my mother. Disparage and grumble all you want but there is a real sacrifice for veterans, and you can’t say no to leaders without reprimand. 

@soldiersangels was the only tender hearted support I’d received on deployment. You have to have an APO address to sign up (forward deployment mailing address). I got matched with someone and they sent correspondence by mail to me, it was one of the only things I looked forward to, it was lonely. 

Also, they could purchase things I couldn’t and I’d offer to send them money for their trouble (which they refused). God Bless Soldiers Angels they really do have a selfless and loving team. Without it, I would have made a mistake outside the wire (on purpose).

If you’re deployed right now and you feel lonely or under appreciated, there are people who care, and people who admire your sacrifice. Your service is not for nothing, and those that have the ultimate sacrifice, your soul will be prayed and remembered, especially venerated by @dodpaa. God Bless America. 

Foot note, for those who may have apathy for the veterans who present as malingerers, let’s focus on fraud that has the largest impact first, then work our way down. America is young and while we’re not perfect, there are many good willed people who want what’s best for the sake of America. Stay safe, and put down the phone if you get too worked up, call a friend, or do something to take your mind off things. Rome was not built in one day.
