text:
We've spent the last 11 years building Cardinal Senior Living. We've made plenty of mistakes, learned some expensive lessons, and changed how we think about growth along the way.

I wrote a little about what we've learned, why we believe long-term ownership matters, and the kind of company we're trying to build.

Chuck and I started Cardinal Senior Living in 2015 with a pretty simple idea. We wanted to build a great senior living company.

Not just acquire real estate. Not build something to sell in five years. Build a company that owns great communities, employs great people, and takes care of residents for a long time.

We've learned a lot along the way. Some lessons were expensive. Others took me longer to figure out than I'd like to admit.

Today, Cardinal owns and operates senior living communities across Michigan, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. We're still family-owned, and we intend to stay that way.

The longer I'm in this business, the more convinced I become that our ownership structure is one of our greatest advantages.

Senior Living Communities Aren't Pokémon Cards

There's a tendency in our industry to treat senior living communities like Pokémon cards.

Buy one. Improve it. Trade it. Sell it. Move on to the next one.

I understand why that model exists. There's a lot of capital invested in senior housing, and investors expect returns.

I'm not against making money. We're a business, and profitability matters.

But I think there's a fundamental problem when your exit strategy starts determining your operating strategy.

A senior living community isn't just a piece of real estate. It's someone's home. It's where people work, build relationships, and spend some of the most important years of their lives.

When ownership changes every few years, it creates uncertainty. New systems, new expectations, new leadership, and sometimes an entirely different operating philosophy.

That's a lot to ask of residents and employees.

One of our greatest competitive advantages might simply be that we don't have to sell.

We can make decisions based on what's best for the community over the next 10 or 20 years, not what makes the financial statements look best before an exit.

Stability Equals Profitability

This is something I've come to believe more strongly every year.

The best-performing senior living communities aren't necessarily the newest buildings or the ones with the nicest finishes.

They're often the communities with the strongest, most stable teams.

An Executive Director who has been there for years knows the residents, their families, and the employees. They understand the local market. They know what works and what doesn't.

That stability leads to better employee retention.

Better retention leads to better care and stronger relationships.

Those relationships lead to referrals, higher occupancy, and ultimately better financial performance.

It's not particularly complicated, but it is difficult to execute.

We've made our share of mistakes at Cardinal. We've had leadership turnover, made bad hires, and taken on communities that were harder to operate than we expected.

But those experiences have reinforced something important for me.

You can't build a great senior living company without building great teams.

And you can't build great teams if you're constantly changing direction.

Growth Isn't the Goal. Building a Better Company Is.

We've grown significantly over the last several years, but my perspective on growth has changed.

Earlier in my career, I probably placed too much importance on the number of communities we owned.

More buildings meant a bigger company. A bigger company meant we were doing something right.

I've learned that isn't necessarily true.

Growth creates complexity. Every acquisition brings new employees, residents, families, systems, and challenges.

If you're not careful, you can grow your way into a worse business.

Today, we're much more disciplined about the communities we acquire.

We like good buildings with strong reputations in markets we understand. We look for opportunities where we can make meaningful improvements without having to reinvent the entire operation.

We're not interested in being heroes who turn around every struggling community in America.

We want to buy good communities and make them better.

Growth is only impressive when the business gets better because of it.

The Opportunity Ahead Is Enormous

One of the reasons I'm so excited about senior living is the opportunity in front of us.

Occupancy across the industry has been recovering, and new construction has been limited.

Meanwhile, the population of older Americans who will need senior housing is growing rapidly.

I believe we're heading into a period when demand for quality senior living will significantly outpace available supply.

That's exciting from a business perspective.

But it also creates an enormous responsibility.

We need more people entering this industry. More talented Executive Directors, nurses, sales leaders, caregivers, and young professionals who see senior living as a place to build a meaningful career.

I worry that we spend too much time talking about real estate, interest rates, and valuations and not nearly enough time talking about the people who actually make these communities work.

The buildings matter. The capital matters.

But none of it works without great people.

We Need to Make Senior Living a Career People Want

I think our industry does a poor job of selling itself to young people.

We offer the opportunity to run multimillion-dollar businesses, lead large teams, develop meaningful relationships, and make a genuine difference in people's lives.

That's a pretty compelling career.

Yet I rarely hear young professionals talk about wanting to work in senior living.

We need to change that.

At Cardinal, I want people who are ambitious, entrepreneurial, and interested in taking ownership of their work.

I want our Executive Directors to feel like they're running their own businesses, with the support of a larger organization behind them.

I want people to see a future with us, not just their next job.

And I want to build a company where talented people can stay for 10, 15, or 20 years and continue growing.

That requires us to be better employers, invest in leadership development, and give people a reason to stick around.

It also requires stability from ownership.

It's hard to ask employees to think long term when the owners are thinking about their next exit.

We're Building for the Next Generation

I don't think there's one perfect ownership model for senior living.

There are great operators backed by private equity, publicly traded companies, nonprofits, and family-owned businesses.

But I know which model I want to build.

I like knowing that when we acquire a community, we can make decisions with a long-term perspective.

We can invest in the building, develop the leadership team, and build relationships in the community without worrying about when we're going to sell.

We can make mistakes, learn from them, and keep improving.

And hopefully, 20 years from now, we'll still own many of the same communities, with employees who have spent much of their careers growing alongside us.

That's the kind of company I want to build.

We're not building Cardinal for the next transaction. We're building it for the next generation.

Life is short. Old people are cool.

text:
Greta Thunberg is a Parasitic Fraud: The Corporate-Backed Demagogue Who Sold Out Science for Marxist Sabotage

Greta Thunberg is a parasitic fraud, a manufactured messiah of the climate cult, a sour-faced Swedish puppet assembled in a laboratory by globalist handlers and shipped to the world stage to guilt-trip working people into accepting economic suicide. Strip away the PR machine, the staged photo ops, the plaintive stare designed to melt the hearts of weak men, and what remains is a hollow vessel of borrowed talking points, empty slogans, and chilling anti-capitalist rage. She is not a scientist, not an engineer, not an economist, not a policymaker. She is a scowling fool with a ponytail, and the West has spent a decade groveling at her feet while her prescriptions gut our industries and drive up the price of everything we cannot live without.

Look at the theatrical mechanics of the original performance. The trembling child routine was pure psychological manipulation, a deliberate device to disarm dissent. You cannot question a weeping teenager without the mob tearing you apart. She spoke in performed bursts of rage, scripted platitudes about stolen futures and dead planets, and the world applauded as if she had invented them. The self-diagnosed condition was baked into the brand, the monoculture of grievance, the sense of a prophet too pure for this fallen world. Then the fad curdled. The school strikes, that absurd weekly truancy presented as moral superiority, lost their novelty. So the caravan of fraud rolled on. Maritime photo stunts, Atlantic crossings by racing yacht while the chase planes burned fuel overhead, endless geopolitical grandstanding in front of any camera willing to point in her direction, and finally the mask sliding off entirely into unmasked, snarling anti-capitalist agitation. Every time one grievance exhausts itself, she pivots to the next, preserving the same grim, prickly, permanently offended exterior while her handlers manage the optics.

Her hypocrisy has become caricature. She preaches sacrifice while flying first class, lectures on carbon while dragging camera crews across continents, and lashes out at private jets while sitting inside one. She tells the world to give up meat while her handlers arrange the itinerary. She speaks of planetary emergency while attending glittering galas in borrowed gowns paid for by the very corporate-media complex she pretends to oppose. Blue-eyed Scandinavian wealth, insulated from consequence, scolding the shop clerk in Ohio and the miner in Poland about their carbon footprints. She has never fixed a boiler, never paid a mortgage, never worried about heating prices in winter, and yet she demands the forced deindustrialization of the West with all the confidence of a woman who has never made payroll.

Then came the political unmasking. The climate banner fell to the floor and she raised the Palestinian flag instead, which told us everything we needed to know about the real project. Climate was never the destination; it was the vehicle. The climate was the gateway drug, and the destination was the whole Marxist package: anti-capitalism, anti-Westernism, anti-sovereignty, the great collective grievance dressed up as planetary science. She attacks the one system that actually works, the market engine that lifted over a billion people out of abject poverty in three decades, the same engine that funded the innovation now driving real emission reductions. She offers no engineering, no scalable energy blueprint, no cost curves, no intellectual rigor. She offers a tantrum, a mood, and a demand for sacrifice from people who never caused the problem she claims to be fighting.

Her disciples are the most pathetic element of the circus, a legion of restless, rudderless adults who attach themselves to a moral crusade because they lack the competence to build anything of their own. They swallow her bitter rhetoric because it flatters their ignorance and licenses their envy. They wear the T-shirts, sign the petitions, retweet the scowls, and feel righteous for doing absolutely nothing. They treat the utterances of a schoolgirl as scripture and dismiss the working engineer as a corporate shill. It is a cargo cult of competence envy, worshipping a child who claims to speak for science while flunking the actual discipline of it.

And what has she actually achieved? A mood, a decade of protest, and a slower transition than the market would have delivered on its own. She has not built, financed, or engineered a single gigawatt of anything. She has not solved a supply chain, not designed a reactor, not modelled an electricity grid. She has only complained, loudly, profitably, and continuously, while insulated by wealth and protected by media that refuse to press her. Her demands would plunge humanity back into cold rooms and brownouts, and her followers would applaud the darkness as authenticity.

History will record her not as a prophet but as a callous, cynical prop, a product of adolescent angst monetized into global influence and pointed at the foundations of Western prosperity. Cheap to manufacture, impossible to question, and useful for exactly as long as the guilt holds out. She is the mascot of managed decline, and her entire career is a monument to the proposition that a scowling face and a borrowed script can outperform a working economy every single time.

text:
The passengers of an American airliner, Delta Flight 15, tried to pay the small Canadian town that fed and sheltered them after 9/11. The town refused every dollar.

So on the flight home they passed pledge sheets through the cabin, and by the time the jet landed in Atlanta they had promised about $15,000 to the town's children.

Flight 15 left Frankfurt, Germany, for Atlanta on September 11, 2001, with 218 passengers. When the United States closed its airspace, the jet became one of 38 airliners sent down to Gander, Newfoundland.

Nobody could get off at first. The passengers sat inside the parked plane for about 27 hours.

Then buses carried them 45 kilometers north to Lewisporte, a town of about 4,000 people that suddenly had 773 stranded strangers to look after.

The travelers had no rooms, so the town opened its schools, churches and community halls. One passenger, Shirley Brooks-Jones of Columbus, Ohio, slept on an army cot at the Lions Club.

Some had left their medicine on the plane. Residents delivered prescriptions and drove the sick to local doctors.

The town bakery worked overtime to keep up with the bread. People handed out laundry tokens, donated towels, blankets, baby food and toys, and local fishermen offered boat rides.

When the passengers tried to pay, nobody would take the money. "They wouldn't take anything in payment," Brooks-Jones said.

The answer came in the air. A doctor on board suggested a scholarship for the town's young people.

Brooks-Jones, a longtime fundraiser at Ohio State University, drew up makeshift pledge sheets. Capt. Michael Sweeney let her make the pitch over the plane's PA system, and then he made the first donation himself.

In 2002 she set up the fund at The Columbus Foundation in Ohio. It has since passed $1 million, and by 2021 it had paid scholarships to 341 students of Lewisporte Collegiate.

She kept flying back to hand out the awards, 27 trips by 2017.

In 2005 the high school made her its first honorary graduate.

text:
The pilot passed out, the plane started diving toward the ocean, and the passenger who grabbed the controls sold flooring for a living. He had never flown a plane before—and after landing it, he offered to clear the runway for other aircraft.

Darren Harrison was 39 when a fishing trip to the Bahamas ended with him having to land a Cessna. On May 10, 2022, he was flying back to Florida, relaxing in the rear of the aircraft with his shoes off. Up front were the pilot and another passenger. At home, Harrison’s wife was seven months pregnant with their first child.

Then the pilot said he didn’t feel good. He complained of a headache and feeling fuzzy. Harrison asked what they needed to do, but the pilot stopped responding. By the time Harrison reached the front, the aircraft was diving and turning. He could see the ocean through the window and knew it was getting closer fast.

He reached over the unconscious pilot and grabbed the controls. Before speaking to a single air traffic controller, Harrison had to get the aircraft out of the dive himself. He gradually pulled back and brought it under control. Asked how he knew what to do, he called it common sense: he believed a sudden, violent movement could stall the aircraft or tear it apart.

Getting into the pilot’s seat brought another problem. Harrison tried to put on the pilot’s headset and discovered frayed wires and a missing plug. His way of asking for help was broken. He borrowed the other passenger’s headset and reached air traffic control with a message nobody in a control tower wants to hear: “My pilot has gone incoherent. I have no idea how to fly the airplane.”

Controllers in Fort Pierce and Palm Beach coordinated the emergency. Robert Morgan, an air traffic controller who was also a flight instructor, was called back from his break to help. A colleague brought him printed cockpit layouts. From the ground, Morgan talked Harrison toward Palm Beach International Airport, explaining how to descend, approach the runway and use the brakes once he reached it.

At around 200 feet, Harrison recalled being told he was still coming in too fast. He asked the other passenger to pull the throttle back, then brought the aircraft onto the runway. He eased onto the brakes with his bare feet. And once he felt the plane slowing under his control, he radioed another request: “Do you guys want me to turn off the runway to clear this thing out?”

text:
In October 2012 the Thunder offered James Harden about $54 million over four years. He wanted the max, $60 million. Sam Presti gave him 60 minutes to say yes. He didn't, and that night he was traded to Houston.

In the video below, Kevin Durant and Harden look back on it for Netflix's Starting 5. Durant's verdict: "It wasn't about no real money. It was a couple million dollars."

When Oklahoma City reached the 2012 Finals, Durant, Russell Westbrook and Harden were all 23 or younger. Harden was the Sixth Man of the Year. That August the Thunder had already given Serge Ibaka four years and $49 million. Presti's explanation after the trade: the value was greater "based on the fact that the Rockets could offer him the contract he was seeking."

Houston gave Harden five years and $78.8 million. He won MVP in 2018. Durant left in 2016 without a ring. The Thunder waited until 2025 for their first title, with none of the three on the roster.

I think the gap came to about $1.5 million a year to keep a 23-year-old who became an MVP. The Thunder saved it and spent the next decade trying to rebuild what they already had.

Thunder fans, was Presti right not to blink over a couple million a year, or did that one hour cost you a dynasty?

text:
SCP-443: SOMEBODY ELSE'S THOUGHTS, IN CRAYON

SCP-443 is a worn set of crayons that lets you record other people's thoughts. That could easily turn into a story about espionage or some hidden catastrophe. Instead, the file gives us a small network of ordinary people around Portland, Oregon, going about their lives without knowing anyone is listening.

Each color corresponds to a particular person. Red is a medical secretary with a daughter. Yellow is the doctor she works for. White is a waitress at a nearby diner. Other colors connect to friends, relatives, classmates, and people who regularly cross paths.

When you draw with one, your hand produces that person's stream of thought rather than whatever you intended to draw. You can't see that this is happening while you're doing it, even if you already know how the crayons work. Stop, and you can finally recognize what's on the page.

Most of it is writing, sometimes interrupted by small pictures. The language adapts to the person holding the crayon. Names appear as unreadable symbols, so the Foundation has relationships and personal details without confirmed identities.

The details are messy in very ordinary ways. Someone is cheating on a partner. Someone is preoccupied with their weight. Two children hate each other for reasons the researchers haven't worked out. A diner regular keeps inserting himself into conversations.

I like that scale. There doesn't need to be a secret world-ending plan behind every anomaly. A handful of lives can be interesting because people are complicated, and because hearing what they think would not necessarily make understanding them easy.

It would also be a serious invasion. An unspoken thought isn't the same thing as a decision, a confession, or a settled belief. People think things when they're angry or frightened that they would reconsider five minutes later. Collect enough of those moments without context and you could construct a very unfair version of someone.

The physical limitation adds another layer. These are ordinary-sized crayons, and using them wears them down. The most frequently used color is already little more than a stub. Somebody is effectively deciding whose private life is interesting enough to consume the remaining access.

I keep wondering about the two missing colors. The file doesn't identify who they belong to. They could provide important context, or they could simply be two more people with lives of their own. Either way, the surviving set offers a partial picture, and that seems worth remembering before treating it as the whole story.

text:
Michael Jordan made about $94 million in salary across his entire NBA career. Six titles, five MVPs, 15 seasons. In 2023 alone, Nike paid him an estimated $330 million.

It goes back to 1984. Jordan was a rookie out of North Carolina, and he didn't want Nike. He wore Converse in college and loved Adidas. Nike was mostly a running company back then, and he didn't even want to get on the plane for the meeting. His mom, Deloris, made him go.

Nike offered him something no basketball player had: his own signature shoe line and a cut of the sales. That royalty, reportedly around 5%, is still paying him 40 years later. Jordan hasn't played an NBA game since 2003, and Jordan Brand is now a multibillion-dollar business selling sneakers to kids who never saw him play.

The best decision of Michael Jordan's career might not have been his. It was his mom's. Every athlete now asks for equity, a piece of the company, a cut of the back end. Jordan proved why, and his mom is the reason he was in the room.

Hung Cao: Senator Sheehy, I began my questioning concerning the frigate program and so I appreciate you circling back to the importance of that type of vessel also.

Wicker: And I believe, Senator Rosen, you are next.

Rosen: Well, thank you. Thank you, Chairman Wicker, Ranking Member Reed, for holding this hearing. I'd like to thank Secretary Cao for testifying today for your service to our country and for meeting with me, I guess, a month ago, maybe a month and a half ago now. Of course, I want to talk about continuing to implement Fallon modernization as we discussed in my office. And so I do want to thank you for sending Assistant Secretary Rogers to Fallon last month to meet with me and Churchill County and the impacted ranchers so that we can finally work together to implement the FY23 NDAA in line with congressional intent and make things right for my constituents. It was a very productive meeting, I'm sure that you heard. However, as you and I discussed and we met a few months ago, we're nearly four years into the modernization effort of the Fallon Range Training Complex, and in that time, the divide between the Navy and local community has only grown larger. I've made it clear each time that Navy leadership has come before this committee that as part of the deal struck in 2022, the Navy must fully and completely compensate the grazing permit holders for their lifetime loss of ranching operations due to the necessary range expansion. Yet the payments offered to the ranchers in the B-16 range completely missed the mark. The Navy is not utilizing existing USDA metrics and formulas to evaluate the ranching operations, which would be the appropriate way to do this. And so we've had two years with no progress addressing the gap between the Navy's offers and what existing U.S. government data says they should be. That's why our teams, this committee, other committees in Congress working on that language to include an FY27 NDAA to address these issues, clarify our congressional intent of the 2020, excuse me, 2022 agreement under which multigenerational ranchers agreed to give up their livelihood in service to this country. If you heard a readout of the meeting, they are patriots. They love living next to Fallon. They are out there on their ranch every morning. They hear that national anthem in the morning. They hear the taps at night and they said there is nothing that feels more American to them. And so it is really important. So if confirmed, when you make those fair valuations and standardized payment offers, would you commit to utilizing existing data from the Department of Agriculture from qualified USDA appraisers who understand ranching operations, as was the congressional intent to ensure that every single permit is made whole?

Hung Cao: Senator, thank you for that question.

Rosen: Thank you again for the time in your office where we're able to discuss this. And thank you also for receiving Secretary Rogers. He's one of the brilliant men that have been able to negotiate so many things for us and as well as to help get the good, clean, safe, comfortable housing for our sailors and Marines. But right now, to be able to finally come to, I think we're almost at the finish line on this, where we're able to work with the ranchers. Because one of the issues we had was we didn't know how they got to that. Well, their estimate is like 10 times off of ours. I don't want to pay them too low. But then we're seeing-- I think that's where we had agreement using the USDA, those standard metrics. I know we can meet with this offline. I have a couple other things.

Hung Cao: Absolutely, Senator. It was a terrific meeting, but we do-- time is of the essence in order to get this in this year's NDAA. And so I want to just bring up the other portion, which are the roads, moving the roads. The Navy's agreed to take on maintenance and liability requirements on the relocated Sand Canyon Road. Churchill and Pershing Counties are still concerned about underlying maintenance and liability requirements falling to them for Sand Canyon and Pole Line Roads in particular. During the meeting last month with Assistant Secretary Rogers, all parties were happy with the Navy's commitments related to maintenance and liability for the relocated Sand Canyon Road, working collaboratively to address ongoing certainty related to Pole Line Road. The Navy offered to coordinate with Department of Interior to see if there's that opportunity to seek a waiver for maintenance and liability requirements when granting a Bureau of Land Management right of way.

Rosen: So will you commit to working with my office? I think we're about there, but to meaningfully address the issue of the roads as we move them and take care of them with the Department of Interior and get their authority to grant this important waiver.

Hung Cao: Absolutely, Senator. I mean, we've discussed in your office where, you know, I want to make sure we're not closing off roads with our gates and stuff like that. And where does our-- where do we end? You know, does it start where-- This is more the maintenance and liability of these types of roads. Absolutely, Senator. Counties have never had to do before and in Pershing County I think it's 4 million acres and 8,000 people. We'll absolutely continue working with your office, Senator.

Rosen: Thank you, appreciate it. Thank you, Mr. Chair.

Wicker: Thank you very much, Senator Rosen.

Moody: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Good to see you. Thank you for being here. Congratulations on your nomination. I want to raise Naval Support Activity Orlando. It's an installation that matters to Florida and to the entire Joint Force. Naval Support Activity Orlando anchors the Central Florida Research Park and that's the nation's premier hub for modeling, simulation, and training, an ecosystem worth over 7 billion a year to Central Florida. Every soldier, sailor, airman, marine, and guardian trains on systems touched by this ecosystem. Its security detachment provides the armed response that classified facilities across the park need to keep their skiffs within the five to 15 minute window intelligence community standards require and it's not just a Navy issue. The Navy may be able to protect its own spaces but the partners cannot. Army, Air Force, and Marine Corps commands in the park have told us they would lose their skiffs without this detachment. So with the Navy Space Force and UCF Warming Gaming Center set to stand up in fiscal year 2027, Florida has invested over 150 million to build space for these missions. text:
of resurrection in Psalm 16, yet Peter explained that David was buried and his sepulchre remained with them; therefore David, “being a prophet,” spoke of the resurrection of Christ. David called his descendant “my Lord” in Psalm 110, creating a difficulty the Pharisees could not answer without acknowledging that Messiah was more than an ordinary son of David. The Holy Ghost could use David’s throne, troubles, victories, prayers, and praise as a framework through which the greater King was revealed. David held the pen; God controlled the prophecy; Christ fulfilled the words.

3. Sacrifice and Offering Could Not Finish the Work

Psalm 40:6 begins, “Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire.” That cannot mean God never commanded sacrifices, for the same God gave Israel exact instructions concerning burnt offerings, meat offerings, peace offerings, sin offerings, trespass offerings, priests, altars, blood, and appointed days. The problem was not that the sacrifices were unauthorized. The problem was that they were provisional. They belonged to an arrangement that instructed Israel concerning holiness, guilt, substitution, blood, priesthood, and access to God, but they could not remove sin permanently. Hebrews 10:4 states the matter without issuing a theological apology: “For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.” If a man cannot understand “not possible,” a stack of diplomas will not rescue him.

The sacrifices taught by repetition that the work remained unfinished. Another morning brought another sacrifice. Another evening required another offering. Another year brought another day of atonement. Another sin sent another Israelite toward the altar. The blood flowed, the smoke rose, the priest ministered, and the worshipper went home, but the system continued because no animal possessed the moral value required to redeem a human soul. A bull had not broken God’s law, and a goat could not consciously obey it. Those creatures could serve as appointed shadows, but a shadow cannot perform the work of the substance. The sacrificial system was a divine classroom, not the final graduation. It pointed forward while demonstrating its own inability to finish the problem.

Hebrews 10 contrasts those repeated offerings with the obedience and sacrifice of Christ. The old sacrifices said, “Sin remains and another victim must come.” Christ’s offering said, “The work is accomplished.” Hebrews 10:11 describes every priest standing “daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.” The next verse turns the entire scene: “But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God.” The old priests stood because their work never reached finality. Christ sat down because His sacrifice required no successor, repetition, repair, or supplement. Religion keeps rebuilding altars because religion cannot tolerate a finished work that leaves human pride with nothing to contribute.

4. “Mine Ears Hast Thou Opened”

Psalm 40:6 continues, “mine ears hast thou opened.” The language presents an obedient servant ready to hear and perform the will of his master. Scripture repeatedly connects hearing with obedience because genuine hearing is more than sound waves reaching a man’s head. Israel often possessed ears physically while remaining deaf spiritually. God spoke, but they would not hear. He commanded, but they hardened their hearts. He sent prophets, but they persecuted the messengers. An opened ear describes receptivity to the voice of God and submission to what that voice commands. The Messiah would not arrive with the deafness, rebellion, excuses, and delays that marked fallen men. He would hear perfectly because He came to obey perfectly.

text:
The land was never a sovereign Palestinian Arab state. For centuries it was Ottoman territory (an empire that collapsed in World War I). The 1922 League of Nations Mandate for Palestine explicitly recognized the historical connection of the Jewish people to the territory and provided for a Jewish national home while protecting the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities. 

At the time of the Mandate, the area contained a Jewish population with continuous presence dating back millennia (kingdoms of Israel and Judah, Second Temple period, and ongoing communities) alongside an Arab majority that had grown under Ottoman rule through natural increase and migration. Neither group held exclusive title in the modern sense of a nation-state.

In 1947 the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 181 partitioning the Mandate into a Jewish state and an Arab state. The Jewish leadership accepted it; the Arab leadership and neighboring Arab states rejected it and launched war. Israel declared independence in 1948, was recognized by the United States and others, and was admitted to the UN in 1949. That is the same legal pathway used by many post-imperial states. 

The subsequent Arab-Israeli wars, refugee flows in both directions (roughly 700,000 Arabs left or were expelled; roughly 800,000 Jews were expelled from Arab countries), and armistice lines did not erase the original partition decision or the prior Jewish legal claim under the Mandate.

Claims that Israel is uniquely illegitimate because it sits on “Palestinian land” usually rely on one of two assertions that do not hold under scrutiny: (1) that demographic majority at a particular moment in the early 20th century confers exclusive permanent title, or (2) that Jewish return and statehood after the Holocaust and centuries of diaspora is somehow more illegitimate than other post-imperial partitions and population movements. Both standards, if applied consistently, would dissolve the legitimacy of numerous existing states. 

Palestinians have a legitimate national claim that can be addressed through negotiated borders, security arrangements, and self-determination; that claim does not require or justify denying the parallel Jewish claim or Israel’s existence as a recognized state.

The practical outcome of the “no right to exist” position has been repeated rejection of partition offers (1947, 2000, 2008) in favor of maximalist demands. That is a political choice, not a historical necessity.

“If you voted for ___” you’re not a Christian.” On *both* sides of the isle. Like the grace of Christ is constrained to a single political vote.

text:
I despise the politics that exists in Christendom. I’m no one special, but my company does coach a lot of people across Christendom. I get texts and emails quite often questioning why I’m friends with so and so. 

Guys, I run a health company. I want Christians to be healthy and fit for service. Do you really want me to say, “eh, you’re a Baptist so it’s a no go? Or, ehh you questioned the post war consensus so it’s a no.” The only people I can help have to align with your camp? 

The worst is when I have influential people say I so many words, “We can help your business, but not if you help so and so.” 

I am friends with many in the SBC. I have many friends in Moscow. I have friends in Ogden. I have friends in the conservative wing of the Methodist church. I have friends in sovereign grace, I have friends in the IFB. 

As my mom lay dying of cancer Mark Dever was a constant prayer companion, texting me daily. He still does and we’ve had very cordial debates about Christian nationalism. 

I can find stuff in each of these camps I don’t agree with, but I don’t want to see any of them fail. They would all find things in me they don’t like and agree with, but we serve the same Christ. 

If you disagree then wash your hands of them and go serve the Lord in your place, but quit running them all down. 

We’ve got to stop eating our own. 

What I won’t do is play the performative denouncement game in order to get business clout. If that costs me money then so be it.

text:
The land was never a sovereign Palestinian Arab state. For centuries it was Ottoman territory (an empire that collapsed in World War I). The 1922 League of Nations Mandate for Palestine explicitly recognized the historical connection of the Jewish people to the territory and provided for a Jewish national home while protecting the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities. 

At the time of the Mandate, the area contained a Jewish population with continuous presence dating back millennia (kingdoms of Israel and Judah, Second Temple period, and ongoing communities) alongside an Arab majority that had grown under Ottoman rule through natural increase and migration. Neither group held exclusive title in the modern sense of a nation-state.

In 1947 the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 181 partitioning the Mandate into a Jewish state and an Arab state. The Jewish leadership accepted it; the Arab leadership and neighboring Arab states rejected it and launched war. Israel declared independence in 1948, was recognized by the United States and others, and was admitted to the UN in 1949. That is the same legal pathway used by many post-imperial states. 

The subsequent Arab-Israeli wars, refugee flows in both directions (roughly 700,000 Arabs left or were expelled; roughly 800,000 Jews were expelled from Arab countries), and armistice lines did not erase the original partition decision or the prior Jewish legal claim under the Mandate.

Claims that Israel is uniquely illegitimate because it sits on “Palestinian land” usually rely on one of two assertions that do not hold under scrutiny: (1) that demographic majority at a particular moment in the early 20th century confers exclusive permanent title, or (2) that Jewish return and statehood after the Holocaust and centuries of diaspora is somehow more illegitimate than other post-imperial partitions and population movements. Both standards, if applied consistently, would dissolve the legitimacy of numerous existing states. 

Palestinians have a legitimate national claim that can be addressed through negotiated borders, security arrangements, and self-determination; that claim does not require or justify denying the parallel Jewish claim or Israel’s existence as a recognized state.

The practical outcome of the “no right to exist” position has been repeated rejection of partition offers (1947, 2000, 2008) in favor of maximalist demands. That is a political choice, not a historical necessity.

I booked a call girl from a call girl agency, and my own younger sister showed up at my hotel room.

I had absolutely no idea who I was dealing with until she removed her wig.

I'm still struggling to explain how that night changed my entire family.

I was 34 years old, divorced, financially comfortable, and living in Atlanta, Georgia.

I had travelled to Miami, Florida, for a business conference and decided to extend my stay over the weekend. After a particularly stressful week, I wanted some adult company.

One of my friends recommended an exclusive companionship agency. He told me they were discreet, professional, and offered private bookings.

Out of curiosity, I contacted them.

They sent me a catalogue of women, each with a different profile, photographs, and rates.

One particular woman caught my attention. She called herself Vanessa.

Her profile described her as a 27-year-old brunette with a beautiful figure and a pleasant personality.

Her pictures were professionally edited, and most showed her wearing makeup, wigs, and different outfits.

I didn't think much about it.

I selected her, paid the required $800, and arranged for her to visit my hotel room at 9 p.m.

That evening, I ordered dinner through room service, opened a bottle of champagne, took a shower, and waited.

At 9:12 p.m., someone knocked...

text:
Culture Wars: Is Wikipedia’s Leo Frank Article Occupied Territory Guarded by Fanatical Hasbara Sentinels?

In my view, the Leo Frank article on Wikipedia is under occupation by Frankites.

What's a Frankite?

By “Frankites,” I mean those multigenerational devotees, who defend Leo Frank's innocence with what I regard as an almost religious fanaticism. I believe some will say or do anything to convince people Leo Frank was innocent or, failing that, to cast doubt on his guilt. Frankites will even openly commit academic fraud, knowing that 99% of their readers will never fact verify their unsupported claims and unsubstantiated assertions.

Over the years, I have challenged what I consider academic fraud in accounts of the case, including stories of antisemitic death threats shouted inside the courtroom that I regard as historical hoaxes. I examine these disputes in my 2025 revised second edition of The Murder of Little Mary Phagan. CP Connolly and Arthur Burton Rascoe have both promoted these hoaxes in print.

My criticism is not that every historian who believes Frank was innocent has engaged in fraud. It is that historians must separate what the original records establish from what they believe those records mean. When an allegation first appears decades after an event, I want to know where it originated and whether anybody checked it against the surviving evidence.

Some problems in Wikipedia's article involve interpretation. Others concern dates, figures, and historical assertions that can be checked against the original records.

The Mary Phagan Bite-Wound Hoax

One of the most questionable stories repeated in pro-Frank books defending Leo Frank concerns alleged bite marks on Mary Phagan's body and photographs supposedly showing that Frank's teeth did not match them.

The legend can be traced to Pierre van Paassen's 1964 autobiography, To Number Our Days. Van Paassen claimed that in 1922, while researching the case at the Fulton County Courthouse, he discovered photographs showing bite marks on Mary's neck and shoulder. He also claimed to have found X-ray photographs of Frank's teeth supposedly demonstrating that Frank could not have inflicted the injuries (van Paassen, 14).

I have spent more than half a century examining the trial record, contemporary newspapers, medical testimony, appeals, and Governor Slaton's commutation proceedings. I have not found a contemporaneous medical report identifying those bite marks, a dental comparison excluding Frank, or the photographs van Paassen claimed to have discovered.

Dr. H. F. Harris, who examined Mary's body on May 5, 1913, testified about the head injury, strangulation, and other findings. His surviving testimony does not identify the bite marks later described by van Paassen (Harris, 13).

Yet Wikipedia states that an analysis of a bite mark on Mary's shoulder helped cast doubt on Conley's testimony (Wiki Con, 4).

What analysis? Conducted by whom? Where are the original photographs, medical reports, and findings?

Van Paassen published his account in 1964, fifty-one years after the murder and forty-two years after he supposedly discovered the photographs. Furthermore, an X-ray of someone's teeth is not the same as a dental impression suitable for comparison with an injury. Modern forensic research has also raised serious questions about the reliability of human bite-mark identification.

Wikipedia does not expressly repeat the supposed dental X-ray story from 1964, but it presents the alleged bite-mark analysis without explaining its uncertain documentary foundation.

Until the original evidence is produced and examined, this should be treated as an unverified allegation, not established forensic proof of innocence.

The Knights of Mary Phagan Hoax

Another disputed claim involves the name “Knights of Mary Phagan.”

The men who abducted and lynched Leo Frank on August 16 and 17, 1915, were identified in contemporary accounts as a vigilance committee. I have not found a contemporary statement from the actual lynching party identifying itself as the Knights of Mary Phagan.

On Saturday, June 26, 1915, approximately seven weeks before Frank's lynching, The New York Times published an article titled “Violence Feared in Atlanta Today.”

The report claimed that approximately 150 citizens had gathered near Mary Phagan's grave in Marietta and formed an oath-bound organization to be called the Knights of Mary Phagan (NYT, 10).

But this was published before the lynching. The newspaper did not establish that the alleged organization's members were the same men who later abducted Frank. 

The reported gathering of 150 people was not a membership list for the approximately twenty-five to thirty men involved in the lynching. Nor have I found evidence that those men publicly identified themselves as Knights of Mary Phagan.

Wikipedia acknowledges the name Vigilance Committee but introduces the Knights of Mary Phagan in its discussion of the Ku Klux Klan's revival as though the organizational connection had been established (Wiki Con, 4).

A newspaper reports the possible formation of an organization in June. Later writers associate that organization with the August lynching. Eventually, the association is repeated so often that readers assume it has been proved.

Where is the contemporary document establishing the connection?

Show me a membership list, a statement from an identified participant, or an organizational declaration.

My family condemns Frank's lynching. We believe in law and order, not vigilantism. But condemning an unlawful killing does not justify attaching an unverified organizational identity to its perpetrators.

The June 1915 report establishes that the name was circulating before the lynching. It does not prove that the lynching party belonged to that organization.

Wikipedia Gets the Ku Klux Klan Revival Timeline Wrong

Wikipedia also states that the Ku Klux Klan's revival occurred one month after Frank was lynched.

That is incorrect.

Frank was lynched on Tuesday, August 17, 1915. William J. Simmons conducted the ceremonial revival of the second Ku Klux Klan at Stone Mountain on Thanksgiving evening, Thursday, November 25, 1915.

That was exactly 100 days later, not one month (Stewart, 11).

The New Georgia Encyclopedia identifies Simmons and his followers as the organizers and discusses the influence of D. W. Griffith's film The Birth of a Nation.

Historians have connected the atmosphere surrounding Frank's trial and lynching to the Klan's revival. That connection deserves examination, but the actual founding date should not be confused with an earlier organization whose connection to the lynchers remains disputed.

This is not a disagreement over a witness's memory. It is a straightforward calendar error.

The Supposed Jewish Exodus From Georgia

Wikipedia claims that following Frank's lynching, approximately half of Georgia's 3,000 Jewish residents left the state (Wiki Con, 4).

Half of 3,000 is 1,500 people.

Where are the population records showing that 1,500 Jewish residents left Georgia because of the lynching?

The Goldring/Woldenberg Institute of Southern Jewish Life reports that Atlanta alone had approximately 4,000 Jewish residents in 1910. Its historical account also reports that Atlanta's Jewish population grew to approximately 12,000 by 1937 (ISJL, 12).

Wikipedia's implied statewide population of 3,000 in 1915 is therefore lower than the independently reported population of Atlanta alone five years earlier.

That discrepancy does not prove nobody left Georgia. Population estimates differ, and people move in both directions. But it requires an explanation.

Steven Hertzberg, in his 1978 study Strangers Within the Gate City, also challenged exaggerated accounts of a general Jewish panic and exodus following the lynching.

I do not dispute that Jewish residents experienced fear or that individual families may have left Georgia. But a claim that half the Jewish population of an entire state departed is measurable. How many left? During which months? Where did they relocate?

If the figure cannot be documented, Wikipedia should correct or qualify it.

The Evidence Against Leo Frank

My strongest objection to Wikipedia's treatment of the criminal case is how frequently it introduces evidence against Frank only to follow it with the defense's preferred explanation.

The article presents the modern historical consensus that Frank was innocent and Jim Conley was probably the murderer as though the central question has been settled. Among its sources are Leonard Dinnerstein, Steve Oney, Jeffrey Melnick, and other authors sympathetic to Frank's innocence.

Their research deserves examination, but modern historical consensus does not establish that Conley committed the murder. Conley was never convicted of killing Mary Phagan.

Frank was convicted by twelve jurors on August 25, 1913. His appeals failed. The Georgia Supreme Court upheld his conviction, and the United States Supreme Court denied federal habeas corpus relief by a vote of seven to two on April 19, 1915.

Those judicial decisions do not eliminate the possibility of a wrongful conviction. Courts can make mistakes. But historians should not confuse their retrospective conclusions with a judicial determination that Conley was the murderer.

I reject the suggestion that Frank was convicted without evidence. The prosecution presented witness testimony, circumstantial evidence, a timeline, and Conley's account of events. The defense disputed much of this material, and the jury evaluated the competing accounts.

Readers should examine the original trial brief of evidence rather than rely entirely on summaries written decades later.

Monteen Stover and the Word “Irrelevant”

Consider Monteen Stover, the young factory worker who testified in July that she waited in Frank's office from 12:05 to 12:10 p.m. on April 26, 1913, and did not see him.

Frank told police that Mary Phagan had entered his office between 12:05 and 12:10 p.m., perhaps around 12:07. That statement appears in State's Exhibit B (State of Georgia, 7).

Stover's testimony therefore raised an obvious question about Frank's whereabouts during those five minutes.

Wikipedia acknowledges the conflicting accounts but calls Stover's testimony and its implications “irrelevant,” relying on a reconstruction of Mary's streetcar journey and estimated arrival time (Wiki Con, 4).

Irrelevant according to whom?

The streetcar witnesses did not all give identical times. The reconstruction depends on estimates of walking time and the time needed to enter the building and reach Frank's office.

Why should one defense interpretation of the trolley evidence automatically eliminate the conflict between Stover's testimony and Frank's original statement?

Newt Lee and the Murder Notes

Newt Lee, the Black night watchman who discovered Mary's body, became an early suspect. Three items raised questions about him: the murder notes found near Mary's body that implicate Lee, the manufactured gaps in his time card, and the blood-smeared shirt discovered at his residence.

The prosecution contended that Frank had attempted to direct suspicion toward Lee. The defense maintained that Conley independently wrote the murder notes and that Lee knew more about the murder than what he was telling.

Conley admitted writing them but testified that Frank dictated their contents to frame Newt Lee.

These were central questions at trial. Yet Wikipedia's narrative encourages the conclusion that Conley was the murderer.

Readers should examine Conley's original testimony, the detectives' accounts, and the defense's objections. They should also investigate how Frank's explanation of Lee's time card changed during the investigation.

The original questions and answers deserve more attention than the conclusions later pro-Frank authors drew from them.

The 1986 Pardon Was Not an Exoneration

On March 11, 1986, the Georgia State Board of Pardons and Paroles granted Frank a posthumous pardon.

The board expressly declined to determine guilt or innocence. Its decision recognized Georgia's failure to protect Frank from lynching and to bring his killers to justice. The board had rejected an earlier pardon application in 1983 because it could not conclusively determine guilt or innocence (Georgia Board, 8).

Wikipedia acknowledges these limitations later in the article, but its introduction describes Frank as wrongly convicted. The Wikipedia article presents a lopsided defense team version of the case, the prosecution gets little hearing. The evidence against Frank gets little hearing.

These are different conclusions. One reflects the prevailing interpretation among modern historians. The other concerns the actual legal scope of the pardon.

The pardon did not establish that Conley was the murderer or that Frank was innocent. The pardon did not vacate Frank's conviction. 

Readers should understand that from the beginning.

Wikipedia Founding Father Larry Sanger and Decentralization

Larry Sanger deserves credit for helping establish an encyclopedia that anybody could contribute to.

Jimmy Wales and Sanger launched Wikipedia on Monday, January 15, 2001. Ordinary people could share knowledge, correct mistakes, and make information freely available worldwide.

My understanding of that mission was decentralization, not control by small groups of politically committed editors.

On July 8, 2026, Sanger wrote that Wikipedia was ruled by “a few hundred anonymous demagogues who dominate the rest.” He argued that powerful editors could use vague rules and administrative authority to exclude views they opposed (Sanger, 1).

I believe the Leo Frank article illustrates some of his concerns.

There have also been actual classes teaching people how to influence Wikipedia.

In August 2010, My Israel, working with the Yesha Council, conducted a seminar in Jerusalem called “Zionist Editing for Wikipedia.” Experienced editors taught volunteers how to contribute to articles in ways intended to improve Israel's public image (Baruch, 2).

On August 18, 2010, Israel National News, also called Arutz Sheva, published a video report documenting the event (Arutz Sheva, 6).

Ayelet Shaked of My Israel explained that even the terminology describing Ariel in the West Bank could become an editorial contest. Naftali Bennett, then director of the Yesha Council, said the organizers wanted to present their side (Shabi, 3).

I have not established that anyone involved in those workshops edited the Leo Frank article, and such a connection should not be asserted without evidence.

But the workshops demonstrate that political organizations have deliberately trained volunteers to influence Wikipedia's wording.

That is why readers should examine an article's edit history rather than assume that every statement appearing under Wikipedia's name is impartial.

Read What Wikipedia's Editors Said About My Work

The public discussion page attached to the Leo Frank article is worth reading.

On July 8, 2026, an editor wrote, “Phagan-Kean is not an expert.” Other participants questioned whether my book qualified as a reliable historical source. On July 14, another editor asked critics to identify qualified modern historians who considered Frank guilty (Wiki Con, 5).

Well, I began visiting public libraries in Georgia with my mother and father in the late 1960s and early 1970s.

I read books on the case and compared their accounts with original newspaper reports and legal records. When an author told me what a witness said, I wanted to know whether that was what the witness actually said.

Sometimes the very next question changed how I understood the answer.

I have spent more than half a century studying the Mary Phagan case, especially Leo Frank's trial and appeals. To my knowledge, few authors have spent more years examining the surviving records.

Yet an anonymous Wikipedia editor can dismiss my work without identifying a single factual error in the passage being challenged.

If I have quoted a witness incorrectly, tell me the witness, date, page number, and what the source actually says. I will examine it.

My book and my understanding of the case remain works in progress, even after fifty years of research.

I made numerous changes to my 2025 revised second edition compared with the 1987 publication. I invite readers to compare them. The original edition is available online for free, without registration, at https://t.co/J3I52F2XEP

I am not asking anybody to accept my conclusions because of the number of years I have studied the case. I am asking that claims be judged against the original evidence.

That applies to my research just as much as it applies to Dinnerstein, Oney, Melnick, Frey, or anybody else.

The Leo Frank Wikipedia Challenge

An anonymous writer once recommended what I call the Leo Frank Wikipedia Challenge. Every year I invite people who believe the article gives the prosecution a fair hearing to try it.

Open a Wikipedia account under an ordinary username. Spend two years contributing to articles on subjects you know. Learn the rules, study the policies concerning reliable sources, make several hundred legitimate contributions, and recognize when another editor raises a fair objection.

Then study the 1913 trial evidence, newspaper reports, appellate decisions, and modern historical works. Go to the Leo Frank article and propose a carefully documented correction that challenges its prevailing interpretation.

Start with “irrelevant” in the discussion of Monteen Stover. Or ask the editors to explain the evidence behind the alleged bite-mark analysis, the Knights of Mary Phagan identification, or the Jewish population exodus.

The Klan-revival timeline offers an especially straightforward test. Replace the claim that the revival occurred one month after the lynching with the documented date, November 25, 1915.

Put your correction on the Talk page with the source and page number. If rejected, examine the editor's explanation and the evidence used to justify it.

Keep a record of the exchange. Wikipedia's revision histories and discussions are public.

I believe you may discover why I describe the article as occupied territory.

But do not take my word for it. See for yourself.

An Invitation to Future Historians

I would also like to invite university students, especially those who already hold bachelor's degrees and are considering graduate study, to consider pursuing a Ph.D. in history.

The Mary Phagan case offers serious research opportunities in legal history, Southern history, journalism, antigentilism, public memory, and the development of historical narratives over generations.

I invite students to help examine the original evidence, publish articles, and write books that challenge inaccurate accounts of the past.

Do not simply repeat my conclusions. Question everybody's conclusions, including mine. Examine the prosecution and defense with equal care.

If a source contradicts something I have written, bring it forward.

I want a new generation of historians who understand how to read trial transcripts, trace claims to their earliest appearance, compare newspaper accounts, and distinguish evidence from interpretation.

Consider what ten or twenty trained historians could accomplish over the next thirty years with access to an organized archive containing the surviving records.

We need independent research, books grounded in primary sources, and opportunities for readers to examine the evidence without depending on one encyclopedia or one group of authors.

We must take back our history through scholarship, not by replacing one unquestionable narrative with another.

The Mary Phagan-Kean Legacy Project

My family has been fighting for more than a century to set the record straight about what happened to little Mary Phagan.

Today, the Mary Phagan-Kean Legacy Project is bringing that work to a worldwide audience.

My team and I have transcribed more than 2,200 newspaper articles published between 1913 and 1915, principally from the Atlanta press, together with thousands of pages of legal records and historical documents.

These records cover the investigation, coroner's inquest, grand jury proceedings, murder trial, appeals, commutation, and aftermath of Frank's lynching.

They are the same kinds of records I began searching for with my mother and father in Georgia libraries during the late 1960s and early 1970s.

Back then, much of the material existed only in bound newspaper volumes, on microfilm, or in difficult-to-obtain legal collections. Researching one question might require several library visits and hours of searching.

Now we can distribute the records electronically.

Over the coming years, I intend to make these transcriptions available through X and other online platforms so present and future generations can examine the original material themselves.

We are also producing thousands of audio recordings, historical newspaper-clipping videos, and lip-sync presentations recreating the words preserved in contemporary sources.

People throughout the world can now read the same newspaper reports, examine the same trial testimony, and compare the original records with books published decades later.

We no longer need to depend entirely on a small number of authors to understand what was reported during the original investigation and trial.

I want students to build dissertations from these records. I want historians to challenge established interpretations. I want readers to identify errors in my work if they can document them.

And I want those defending Frank's innocence to examine the entire prosecution record rather than dismiss it through a few familiar quotations.

Our family does not condone violence, lynching, or vigilantism. We believe in law and order.

The reckoning I am calling for is historical and scholarly. It belongs in archives, books, journal articles, classrooms, public debates, and documented corrections to the historical record.

For more than a century, arguments over Leo Frank have often overshadowed the life and murder of Mary Phagan herself.

I intend to keep her at the center of this work.

The original sources belong to history, not to any political organization, institution, author, or Wikipedia editor.

Our family's struggle to preserve this history has lasted more than a century. I want the work we are doing today to continue for generations.

We will take back our history, one original document at a time.

text:
a coding agent's first source edit was already the right fix in up to 82% of its solved runs

then it kept going.

Penn State researchers saved the agent's patch after every step on SWE-bench, and checked each one against the benchmark's tests, which the agent never sees.

the steps between the first passing patch and the moment the agent stops on its own, they call termination lag.

median share of the run that came after the fix was already in:
> Qwen3-Coder: 35-37%
> Laguna-XS.2: 54-60%
> Claude Haiku 5.5: 54%
> GPT-6 Luna: 36%

most of those extra steps are verifying and exploring, not editing.

and they aren't always harmless: in 1-8% of runs the agent broke a working patch and ended unsolved.

the paper doesn't offer a stopping rule. "stop at the first correct patch" needs the hidden tests, which the agent doesn't have.

so before switching models to save steps, I'd log where your own tests first pass in each agent run.
if a third of the run comes after that point, that's the part to cut first.

text:
In 45 days, US payers running Medicare Advantage and Medicaid must offer prior authorization through a FHIR API, and OpenAI just shipped agents that click through the same authorization in a web portal.

On November 16 OpenAI added computer use agents to ChatGPT for Healthcare. The model reads the screen, clicks and types inside EHRs and payer portals, because those systems often have no API you can actually work with. CVS Health and Cigna already run them in production, and more than 20 new plugins came with the update, Availity and Redox among them. The same day August AI showed the patient side: an agent that calls clinics and appeals insurance denials, and that spent 366 minutes on hold for a single user. Hold music finally has a listener who never complains.

Now the math. OpenAI says GPT-6 Luna scores 91.8% of rubric points on HealthAdminBench at 8.5 cents per task. Stanford’s benchmark has 135 tasks and 1,698 checkpoints, so about 12.6 steps per task, and a task only passes if every step is right. With independent errors, 0.918 to the power of 12.6 comes out to roughly 34% of tasks fully completed, close to the best end to end score in Stanford’s April paper (36.3%). OpenAI didn’t publish an end to end number.

If you build prior auth automation, the portal clicking agent pays off where no API is coming: commercial employer plans, which CMS-0057-F doesn’t cover, and legacy EHRs. For Medicare Advantage payers the same path moves to FHIR in January, with no CAPTCHAs or session timeouts, which Stanford simplified away in its test anyway. Put the human approval at the “attach and submit” step, because that’s where the agents in the benchmark failed most often.

The RTTL case is extremely strong. Imposing membership requirements on a private association would be extremely difficult considering RTTL doesn't own any land or housing, it's very selective on many factors regarding membership, it doesn't operate public facilities, and doesn't function commercially. The government generally cannot force it to accept particular members or dictate its membership requirements and there is very strong case law to support this.

The Arkansas community has a strong case as well, it owns the property but doesn't sell land or real estate, or offer housing, it doesn't do business with the public, or advertise, nobody can apply to live there, it doesn't even have a website. Multiple agencies have been investigating for nearly a year and haven't been able to find anything. 

It's more of a weaponization case where the government wants to drag the investigations out indefinitely to bankrupt us instead, which is why we're suing these agencies to force them to close their investigations and decide if what we're doing is legal.

Added: 1959 aerial photo coverage for Anderson County, South Carolina!

See Anderson, famously known as “The Electric City,” and explore its historic textile mills, downtown neighborhoods, and industrial landscape as they appeared in the late 1950s.

But there's another fascinating piece of history captured in 1959. Lake Hartwell had not yet been filled! Construction of Hartwell Dam began in 1955, but the reservoir didn't begin filling until 1961, reaching full pool in 1962.

These photographs offer a rare opportunity to explore portions of the original river valleys and surrounding countryside before the creation of one of the Southeast's largest reservoirs.

Take a look back and discover how Anderson County has changed over more than six decades!

text:
Origins of Totalitarianism, Hannah Arendt, 1957

Propaganda is indeed part and parcel of "psychological warfare"; but terror is more. Terror continues to be used by totalitarian regimes even when its psychological aims are achieved: its real horror is that it reigns over a completely subdued population. Where the rule of terror is brought to perfection, as in concentration camps, propaganda disappears entirely; it was even expressly prohibited in Nazi Germany.'^ Propaganda, in other words, is one, and possibly the most important, instrument of totalitarianism for dealing with the nontotalitarian world; terror, on the contrary, is the very essence of its form of government. Its existence depends as little on psychological or other subjective factors as the existence of laws in a constitutionally governed country depends upon the number of people who transgress them.

Terror as the counterpart of propaganda played a greater role in Nazism than in Communism. The Nazis did not strike at prominent figures as had been done in the earlier wave of political crimes in Germany (the murder of Rathenau and Erzberger); instead, by killing small socialist functionaries or influential members of opposing parties, they attempted to prove to the population the dangers involved in mere membership. This kind of mass terror, which still operated on a comparatively small scale, increased steadily because neither the police nor the courts seriously prosecuted political offenders on the so-called Right. It was valuable as what a Nazi publicist has aptly called "power propaganda": [1] it made clear to the population at large that the power of the Nazis was greater than that of the authorities and that it was safer to be a member of a Nazi paramilitary organization than a loyal Republican. This impression was greatly strengthened by the specific use the Nazis made of their political crimes. They always admitted them publicly, never apologized for "excesses of the lower ranks"—such apologies were used only by Nazi sympathizers—and impressed the population as being very different from the "idle talkers" of other parties.

[1] Eugen Hadamovsky, op. cit., is outstanding in the literature on totalitarian propaganda. Without explicitly stating it, Hadamovsky offers an intelligent and revealing pro-Nazi interpretation of Hitler's own exposition on the subject in "Propaganda and Organization." in Book II, chapter xi of Mein Kampf (2 vols., 1st German edition, IV.5 and 1927 respectively. Unexpurgated translation, New York, 1939).

text:
Matthew McConaughey said no to $8 million. Then $10 million. Then $12 million. Then $14.5 million.

He was out of work at the time, with his first child on the way.

In the video below, he explains why he kept turning down the money and what it cost him.

By the late 2000s McConaughey was Hollywood's go-to romantic comedy guy. He'd taken the baton from Hugh Grant. The roles were easy and the checks were huge.

Then his partner Camila got pregnant, and he decided he wanted dramas. Hollywood wouldn't offer him one, no matter how big a pay cut he offered to take.

So he told his agent: no more romcoms. He moved to his ranch in Texas and waited.

Nothing came for months. He says he started thinking about becoming a teacher, or going back to law school.

Then an action comedy offer arrived. $8 million. He said no.

The studio came back with $10 million. No.

$12 million. No.

$14.5 million. He admits he read the script again, and it was funnier this time. He still said no.

His own brothers asked him: "What is your major malfunction, little brother?"

The case for taking it: $14.5 million for one movie, a baby coming, and zero other offers on the table.

The case for walking away: once you say yes to that money, you're the romcom guy forever.

20 months after he stepped out, the offers changed. The Lincoln Lawyer. Mud. Magic Mike. Dallas Buyers Club. True Detective.

Dallas Buyers Club was shot in 25 days on a $4.9 million budget. It won him the Oscar for Best Actor.

He says those roles would never have come if he hadn't turned down the money.

Would you have walked away from $14.5 million with no backup plan, or taken the check and figured it out later?

text:
There’s no traction on this cause where is it gonna be built and who’s paying for all that. 

Unplugged Performance is pitching a CyberSUV (and continued Cybertruck production) as Tesla winds down the truck line.
Tesla plans to phase out Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas around mid-2027 (roughly June/July) to free space, focus, and battery cells for Cybercab (its Robotaxi). Elon Musk has described the opportunity cost of the Cybertruck platform as too high compared with scaling Cybercab.
In response, Unplugged Performance (a long-time Tesla aftermarket specialist known for performance upgrades and Cybertruck packages) has made a public “open offer” to take over the line. Key elements of their proposal (updated around November 15 as “Phase 3”):
•Form a new company funded by outside investors (they’ve referenced nine-figure scale potential).
•Build the Cybertruck plus a three-row CyberSUV as the main product (and potentially an unmanned CyberCargo hauler).
•Tesla retains the IP, gets a free equity stake, collects a license fee per vehicle, earns from parts/FSD/Robotaxi network revenue, has approval rights over leadership/specs/brand, a quality veto, and the option to reclaim the line later.
•No added cost or risk to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus; Cybercab keeps priority on cells. The line would leave Giga Texas on Tesla’s schedule.
•Concept images (not official Tesla designs) show a Cybertruck-like stainless-steel body with an enclosed rear for family seating. A poll of 892 responses showed ~82% preferring a three-row SUV. Versions with and without driving controls are discussed for private ownership vs. Robotaxi use.
This remains a proposal only—Tesla has not announced any agreement, and investor commitments are described as preliminary. Unplugged has never run a high-volume production line, so execution, certification, warranties, and capital are open questions.
Background context includes Tesla design chief Franz von Holzhausen saying “wait and see” in 2025 about Cybertruck-platform variants (including SUV ideas), plus earlier clay models spotted in Tesla videos.

Recent coverage is concentrated on Tesla-focused sites (Teslarati, TeslaNorth, etc.) from the past few days. No official Tesla response has appeared yet.

text:
Imagine entering this room and attempting small talk. Dostoevsky has turned a simple question into a confession, Nietzsche is questioning the morality behind it, and Camus is wondering whether the conversation needs a purpose at all. Kafka suspects the invitation was a summons. Somewhere in the middle of this, Oscar Wilde delivers one devastating sentence, and suddenly everyone needs a moment.

The appeal of this imaginary gathering is the collision of minds that approached existence so differently. Think of Virginia Woolf's attention to the movements of consciousness beside Tolstoy's searching moral questions, or Sylvia Plath's fierce poetic imagery beside the unsettling worlds of Kafka. These are writers whose works make private fears feel recognisable, even when their answers offer very little comfort. Reading them can feel like finding someone who has already visited the darkest room in your mind.

Of course, this would probably be an exhausting evening.
There would be disagreements about faith, art, suffering, freedom, and whether anyone should have been invited in the first place. But I would stay for the uncomfortable questions, the unexpected humour, and the possibility of hearing something I would spend the rest of my life thinking about. My only contribution would be pouring the coffee.
