Twenty-Fifth Sunday after Pentecost (taken from the Sixth Sunday after Epiphany) ON THE DEATH OF THE JUST by St Alphonsus Liguori.
.
“The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal until the whole was leavened.” MATT. xiii. 33.
.
IN this days gospel we find that a woman, after putting leaven in the dough, waits till the entire is fermented. Here the Lord gives us to understand that the kingdom of heaven that is, the attainment of eternal beatitude is like the leaven. By the leaven is understood the divine grace, which makes the soul acquire merits for eternal life. But this eternal life is obtained only when”the whole is leavened ;” that is, when the soul has arrived at the end of the present life and the completion of her merits. We shall, then, speak Today of the death of the just, which we should not fear, but should desire with our whole souls. For, says St. Bonaventure, “Triplex in morte congratulatio, hominem ab omni labore, peccato, et periculo liberari.” Man should rejoice at death, for three reasons First, because death delivers him from labour that is, from suffering the miseries of this life and the assault of his enemies. Secondly, because it delivers him from actual sins. Thirdly, because it delivers him from the danger of falling into hell, and opens Paradise to him.
.
First Point. Death delivers us from the miseries of this life, and from the assaults of our enemies.
.
 1  What is death? St. Eucherius answers, that “death is the end of miseries.” Job said that our life, however short it may be, is full of miseries, of infirmities, of crosses, of persecutions, and fears. “Man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries.” (Job xiv. 1.) What, says St. Augustine, do men who wish for a prolongation of life on this earth desire but a prolongation of suffering ?” “Quid est diu vivere nisi diu tor queri.” (Serm. xviL de Serb. Dom.) Yes; for, as St. Ambrose remarks, the present life was given to us not for repose or enjoyment, but for labour and suffering, that by toils and pains we may merit Paradise. ”Hæc vita homini non ad quitem data est, sed ad laborem.” (Serm. xliii.) Hence the same holy doctor says, that, though death is the punishment of sin, still the miseries of this life are so great, that death appears to be a relief rather than a chastisement: ”Ut mors remediuni videatur esse, non pœna. ”
.
2   To those who love God, the severest of all the crosses of this life are the assaults of hell to rob them of the divine grace. Hence St. Denis the Areopagite says, that they joyfully meet death, as the end of their combats, and embrace it with gladness, because they hope to die a good death, and to be thus freed from all fear of ever again falling into sin. ”Divino gaudio et mortis terminum tanquam ad finem certaminum tendunt, non amplius metuentus pervertii.” (De Hier. Eccl., cap. vii.) The greatest consolation which a soul that loves God experiences at the approach of death, arises from the thought of being delivered from so many temptations, from so many remorses of conscience, and from so many dangers of offending God. Ah! says St. Ambrose, as long as we live, “we walk among snares.” We walk continually in the midst of the snares of our enemies, who lie in wait to deprive us of the life of grace. It was the fear of falling into sin that made St. Peter of Alcantara, in his last moments, say to a lay brother who, in attending the saint, accidently touched him: ”Brother, remove, remove from me, for I am still alive and in danger of being lost.” The thought of being freed from the danger of sin by death consoled St. Teresa, and made her rejoice as often as she heard the clock strike, that an hour of the combat was past. Hence she used to say: ”In each moment of life we may sin and lose God.” Hence the news of approaching death filled the saints not with sorrow or regret, but with sentiments of joy; because they knew that their struggles and the dangers of losing the divine grace were soon to have an end.
.
3  ”But the just man, if he be prevented with death, shall be in rest.” (Wis. iv. 7.) He who is prepared to die, regards death as a relief. If, says St. Cyprian, you lived in a house whose roof and walls were tottering and threatening destruction, would you not fly from, it as soon as possible? In this life everything menaces ruin to the poor soul the world, the devils, the flesh, the passions, all draw her to sin and to eternal death. It was this that made St. Paul exclaim: ”Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. vii. 24.) Who shall deliver me from this body of mine, which lives continually in a dying state, on account of the assaults of my enemies? Hence he esteemed death as a great gain, because it brought to him the possession of Jesus Christ, his true life. Happy then are they who die in the Lord: because they escape from pains and toils, and go to rest. ”Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From henceforth now, saith the spirit, that they may rest from their labours.” (Apoc. xiv. 13.) It is related in the lives of the ancient fathers, that one of them who was very old, when dying, smiled, while the others wept. Being asked why he smiled, he said: “Why do you weep at seeing me go to rest? Ex labore ad requiem vado, et vos ploratis ?” At the hour of death, St. Catherine of Sienna said to her sisters in religion: Rejoice with me: for I leave this land of suffering, and am going to the kingdom of peace. The death of the saints is called a sleep that is, the repose which God gives to his servants as the reward of their toil”When he shall give sleep to his beloved, behold the inheritance of the Lord.” (Ps. cxxvi. 2.) Hence the soul that loves God neither weeps nor is troubled at the approach of death, but, embracing the crucifix, and burning with love, she says: ”In peace in the self same I will sleep and I will rest.” (Ps. iv. 9.)
.
4  That “Proficiscere de hoc mundo,” (” Depart, Christian soul, from this world,”) which is so appalling to sinners at the hour of death, does not alarm the saints. ”But the souls of the just are in the hands of God, and the torment of death shall not touch them.” (Wis. iii. 1.) The saint is not afflicted, like worldlings, at the thought of being obliged to leave the goods of this earth, because he has kept the soul detached from them. During life, he always regarded God as the Lord of his heart and as the sole riches which he desired: ”What have I in heaven? and, besides thee, what do I desire upon earth? Thou art the God of my heart and the God that is my portion for ever.” (Ps. Ixxxii. 25, 26.) He is not afflicted at leaving honours, because the only honour which he sought was, to love and to be loved by God. All the honours of this world he has justly esteemed as smoke and vanity. He is not afflicted at leaving his relatives, because he loved them only in God. In his last moments he recommends them to his heavenly Father, who loves them more than he does. And having a secure confidence of salvation, he hopes to be better able to assist his relatives from Paradise, than on this earth. In a word, what he frequently said during life, he continues to repeat with greater fervour at the hour of death”My God and my all.”
.
5 Besides, his peace is not disturbed by the pains of death; but, seeing that he is now at the end of his life, and that he has no more time to suffer for God, or to offer him other proofs of love, he accepts those pains with joy, and offers them to God as the last remains of life; and uniting his death with the death of Jesus Christ, he offers it to the Divine Majesty.
.
6 And although the remembrance of the sins which he has committed will afflict, it will not disturb him; for, since he is convinced that the Lord will forget the sins of all true penitents, the very sorrow which he feels for his sins, gives him an assurance of pardon. ”If the wicked do penance. … I will not remember all his iniquities that he hath done.” (Ezec. xviii. 21 and 22.) “How,” asks St. Basil, “can anyone be certain that God has pardoned his sins? He may be certain of pardon if he say: I have hated and abhorred iniquity.” (In Reg. inter. 12.) He who detests his sins, and offers to God his death in atonement for them, may rest secure that God has pardoned them. ”Mors,” says St. Augustine, ”quæ in lege naturæ erat poona peccati in lege gratiæ est hostia pro peccato.” (Lib. iv. de Trin. c. xxii.) Death, which was a chastisement of sin under the law of nature, has become, in the law of grace, a victim of penance, by which the pardon of sin is obtained.
.
7 The very love which a soul bears to God, assures her of his grace, and delivers her from the fear of being lost. ”Charity casteth out fear.” (1 John iv. 18.) If, at the hour of death, you are unwilling to pardon an enemy, or to restore what is not your own, or if you wish to keep up an improper friendship, then tremble for your eternal salvation; for you have great reason to be afraid of death; but if you seek to avoid sin, and to preserve in your heart a testimony that you love God, be assured that he is with you: and if the Lord is with you, what do you fear? And if you wish to be assured that you have within you the divine love, embrace death with peace, and offer it from your heart to God. He that offers to God his death, makes an act of love the most perfect that is possible for him to perform; because, by cheerfully embracing death to please God, at the time and in the manner which God ordains, he becomes like the martyrs, the entire merit of whose martyrdom consisted in suffering and dying to please God.
.
Second Point. Death frees us from actual sins.
.
8 It is impossible to live in this world without committing at least some slight faults. ”A just man shall fall seven times: ” (Prov. xxiv. 16.) He who ceases to live, ceases to offend God. Hence St. Ambrose called death the burial of vices: by death they are buried, and never appear again. ”Quid est mors nisi sepultura vitorum?” (De Bono Mort. cap. iv.) The venerable Vincent Caraffa consoled himself at the hour of death by saying: now that I cease to live, I cease for ever to offend my God. He who dies in the grace of God, goes into that happy state in which he shall love God for ever, and shall never more offend him. ”Mortuus,” says the same holy doctor, ”nescit peccare. Quid tanto pere vita mistam desideramus, in qua quanto diutius quis fuerit, tanto majori oneratur sarcina peccatorum.” How can we desire this life, in which the longer we live, the greater shall be the load of our sins?
.
9 Hence the Lord praises the dead more than any man living: ”I praised the dead rather than the living.” (Eccl. iv. 2.) Because no man on this earth, however holy he may be, is exempt from sins. A spiritual soul gave directions that the person who should bring to her the news of death, should say: ”Console yourself, for the time has arrived when you shall no longer offend God.”
.
10 St. Ambrose adds, that God permitted death to enter into the world, that, by dying, men should cease to sin: “Passus est Dominus subintrare mortem ut culpa cessaret.” (Loco cit.) It is, then, a great error to imagine that death is a chastisement for those who love God. It is a mark of the love which God bears to them , because he shortens their life to put an end to sin, from which they cannot be exempt as long as they remain on this earth. ”For his soul pleased God: therefore he hastened to bring him out of the midst of iniquities.” (Wis. iv. 14.)
.
Third Point. Death delivers us from the danger of falling into hell, and opens Paradise to us.
.
11 ”Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of the saints.” (Ps. cxv. 16.) Considered according to the senses, death excites fear and terror; but, viewed with the eye of faith, it is consoling and desirable. To the saints it is as amiable and as precious, as it appears terrible to sinners. ”It is precious,” says St. Bernard, ”as the end of labours, the consummation of victory, the gate of life.” The joy of the cup-bearer of Pharaoh, at hearing from Joseph that he should soon be released from prison, bears no comparison to that which a soul that loves God feels on hearing that she is to be liberated from the exile of this earth, and to be transported to the enjoyment of God in her true country. The Apostle says, that, as long as we remain in the body, we wander at a distance from our country in a strange land, and far removed from the life of God: ”While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord.” (2 Cor. v. 6.) Hence, St. Bruno teaches, that our death should not be called death, but the beginning of life. ”Mors dicenda non est, sed vitæ principium.” And St. Athanasius says: ”Non est justis mors sed translatio.” To the just, death is but a passage from the miseries of this earth to the eternal delights of Paradise. O desirable death! exclaimed St. Augustine; who is there that does not desire thee? For thou art the term of evils, the end of toils, and the beginning of everlasting repose!”O mors desirabilis, malorum finis, laboris clausula, quietis principium.”
.
12 No one can enter into heaven to see God without passing through the gate of death. ”This is the gate of the Lord the just shall enter into it.” (Ps. cxvii. 20.) Hence, addressing death, St. Jerome said: ”Aperi mini soror mea.” Death, my sister, if you do not open the gate to me, I cannot enter to enjoy my God. And St. Charles Borromeo, seeing in his house a picture of death with a knife in the hand, sent for a painter to cancel the knife, and substitute for it a key of gold; because, said the saint, it is death that opens Paradise. Were a queen confined in a dark prison, how great would be her joy at hearing that the gates of the prison are open, and that she is to return from the dungeon to her palace! It was to be liberated by death from the prison of this life that David asked, when he said: ”Bring my soul out of prison.” (Ps. cxli. 8.) This, too, was the favour which the venerable Simeon asked of the infant Jesus, when he held him in his arms: ”Now thou dost dismiss thy servant.” (Luke ii. 29.)”As if detained by force,” says St. Ambrose, ”he asked to be dismissed.” Simeon sought to be delivered by death, as if he had been compelled by force to live on this earth.
.
13 St. Cyprian says, that the sinner who shall pass from temporal to eternal death, has just reason to be afraid of death. “Mori timeat, qui ad secundum mortem de hac morte transibit.” But he who is in the state of grace and hopes to pass from death to eternal life which is the true life tears not death. It is related that a certain rich man gave to St. John the Almoner a large sum of money to be dispensed in alms, for the purpose of obtaining from God a long life for his only son. The son died in a short time. The father complained of the death of his son; but, to console him, the Lord sent an angel to say to him: “You have sought a long life for your son, and the Lord has heard your prayer; for your son is in heaven, where he enjoys eternal life.” This is the grace which, according to the promise of the prophet Osee, the Redeemer obtained for us. ”death, I will be thy death.” (xiii. 14.) By His redemption, Jesus Christ destroyed death, and changed it into a source of life to us. When St. Pionius, martyr, was asked how he could go to death with so much joy, he answered: ”You err; I do not go to death but to life.”“Erratis non ad mortem, sed ad vitam contendo.” (Apud Eusub., lib. iv. cap. xiv ) Thus also St. Symphorosa exhorted her son, St. Symphorian, to martyrdom: ”My son,” said she, ”life is not taken away from you; it is only changed for a better one.”
.
14 St. Augustine says, that they who love God desire to see him speedily, and that, therefore, to them life is a cause of suffering, and death an occasion of joy. “Patienter vivit, delectabiliter moritur.” (Trac. ix. in Ep. Joan.) St. Teresa used to say, that to her life was death. Hence she composed the celebrated hymn, ”I die because I do not die.” To that great servant of God D. Sancia Carriglio a penitent of Father M. Avila it was one day revealed, that she had but a year to live; she answered: ”Alas! must I remain another year at a distance from God? O sorrowful year, which will appear to me longer than an age.” Such is the language of souls who love God from their heart. It is a mark of little love of God not to desire to see him speedily.
.
15 Some of you will say: I desire to go to God, but I fear death. I am afraid of the assaults which I shall then experience from hell. I find that the saints have trembled at the hour of death; how much more ought I to tremble! I answer: It is true that hell does not cease to assail even the saints at death, but it is also true that God does not cease to assist his servants at that moment; and when the dangers are increased, he multiplies his helps. ”Ibi plus auxilii,” says St. Ambrose, ”ubi plus periculi.” (ad Jos. cap. v.) The servant of Eliseus was struck with terror when he saw the city surrounded by enemies; but the saint inspired him with courage by showing to him a multitude of angels sent by God to defend it. Hence the prophet afterwards said: ”Fear not, for there are more with us than with them.” (4 Kings vi. 16.) The powers of hell will assail the dying Christian; but his angel guardian will come to console him. His patrons, and St. Michael, who has been appointed by God to defend his faithful servants in their last combat with the devils, will come to his aid. The mother of God will come to assist those who have been devoted to her. Jesus Christ shall come to defend from the assaults of hell the souls for which he died on a cross: he will give them confidence and strength to resist every attack. Hence, filled with courage, they will say: “The Lord is my light and my salvation: whom shall I fear?” (Isa. xxvi. I.) Truly has Origen said, that the Lord is more desirous of our salvation than the devil is of our perdition, because God’s love for us far surpasses the devil’s hatred of our souls. ”Major ilia cura est, ut nos ad veram pertrahat salutem, quam diabolo, ut nos ad æternam damnationem impellat.” (Hom, xx.)
.
16 God is faithful, he will never permit us to be tempted above our strength: ”Fidelis Deus non patietur vos tentari supra id quod potestis.” (1 Cor. x. 13.) It is true that some saints have suffered great fear at the hour of death; but they have been few. The Lord, as Belluacensis says, has permitted this fear to cleanse them at death from some defect. ”Justi quandoque dure moriendo purgantur in hoc mundo.” But we know that, generally speaking, the saints have died with a joyful countenance. Father Joseph Scamacca, a man of a holy life, being asked if, in dying, he felt confidence in God, answered: Have I served Mahomet, that I should now doubt of the goodness of my God, or of his wish to save me? Ah! the Lord knows well how to console his servants in their last moments. Even in the midst of the agony of death, he infuses into their souls a certain sweetness and a certain foretaste of that happiness which he will soon bestow upon them. As they who die in sin begin to experience from the bed of death a certain foretaste of hell certain extraordinary terrors, remorses, and fits of despair; so, on the other hand, the saints, by the fervent acts of divine love which they then make, and by the confidence and the desire which they feel of soon seeing God, taste, before death, that peace which they shall afterwards fully enjoy in heaven.
.
17 Father Suarez died with so much peace, that in his last moments he said: ”I could not have imagined that death was so sweet.” Being advised by his physician not to fix his thoughts so constantly on death, Cardinal Baronius said: Is it lest the fear of death should shorten my life? I fear not; on the contrary, I love and desire death. Of the Cardinal Bishop of Rochester, Saunders relates, that, in preparing to die for the faith, he put on his best clothes, saying that ho was going to a nuptial feast. When he came within view of the place of execution, he threw away his staff, and said: O my feet, walk fast; for we are not far from Paradise. ”Ite pedes, parum a paradiso distamus.” Before death, he wished to recite the TE DEUM, in thanksgiving to God for permitting him to die for the holy faith; and, full of joy, he laid his head on the block. St. Francis of Assisium began to sing at the hour of death. Brother Elias said to him: Father, at the hour of death, we ought rather to weep than to sing. But, replied the saint, I cannot abstain from singing at the thought of soon going to enjoy God. A nun of the order of St. Teresa, in her last moments, said to her sisters in religion, who were in tears: O God! why do you weep? I am going to possess my Jesus; if you love me, weep not, but rejoice with me. (Dis. Parol. i. 6.)
.
18 Father Granada relates, that a certain sportsman found in a wood a solitary singing in his last agony. How, said the sportsman, can you sing in such a state? The hermit replied: Brother, between me and God there is nothing but the wall of this body. I now see that since my flesh is falling in pieces, the prison shall be destroyed, and I shall soon go to see God. It is for this reason I rejoice and sing. Through the desire of seeing God, St. Ignatius, martyr, said, that if the wild beasts should spare him, he would provoke them to devour him. “Ego vim faciam, ut devorer.” St. Catherine of Genoa was astonished that some persons regarded death as a misfortune, and said: ”O beloved death, in what a mistaken light do men view you! Why do you not come to me? I call on you day and night”(Vita, c. 7.)
.
19 Oh! how peculiarly happy is the death of the servants of Mary! Father Binetti relates, that a person whom he assisted in his last moments, and who was devoted to the Blessed Virgin, said to him: ”Father, you cannot conceive the consolation which arises at death from the remembrance of having served Mary. Ah! my father, if you knew what happiness I feel on account of having served this good mother! I cannot express it.” What joy shall the lovers of Jesus Christ experience at his coming to them in the most holy viaticum! Happy the soul that can then address her Saviour in the words which St. Philip Neri used when the viaticum was brought to him: ”Behold my love! behold my love! give me my love!” But, to entertain these sentiments at death, we must have ardently loved Jesus Christ during life.

text:
SURAH AL-HAJJ
Number of verses: 78 | Period: Mecca (six verses, 19-24, are Medinan) | Pedagogical order: 82
Subject: Global Equality — The Transition from Eschatology to Law
Reference Frame: Qur'an Tafsir Reference Protocol v27 | Foundational Axiom: an-Nisa 136 | Epistemic Limit: Allah knows best.
INTRODUCTION: THE SURAH'S PLACE, ITS PROCESS OF REVELATION, AND THE FOUNDATIONAL AXIOM
The surah was sent down in Mecca except for six verses (19-24); these six verses are Medinan. But this classification does not mean that the surah was sent down in a single sitting: it was revealed at different times and in different contexts. In this respect the surah belongs to the category of “Composite (Compound) Surahs.” Its process of revelation extends from the last years of Mecca to the first years of Medina.
Socio-political context: in the last years of Mecca the pressure of the polytheists had intensified, the believers were placed under social and economic boycott, and tortures had increased. The migrations to Abyssinia had begun, yet the believers were still confronted with severe oppression in Mecca. The verses revealed in this period aim to give the believers spiritual resilience, to remind them through the consciousness of the Resurrection of the transience of worldly hardships, and to prepare them for arduous processes such as hijra and jihad. The verses revealed in the Medinan period, for their part, recall to the believers — now entered upon the process of building a society — the original nature of the hajj, the law of war, and the promise of divine aid.
FIRST GROUP: THE CONSCIOUSNESS OF THE RESURRECTION AND THE FOUNDATIONS OF TAWHID (VERSES 1-24)
1.1. Siyaq-Sibak and Context Analysis (0a, 0b)
This group of verses forms the opening of the surah and confronts its addressees with two basic realities: the shattering reality of the Resurrection and the rational foundations of tawhid. The verses were revealed toward the end of the Meccan period, in a time when the pressure of the polytheists was intensifying. The themes of tawhid and the hereafter treated in the previous surahs (for example al-Mu'minun, al-Anbiya, adh-Dhariyat) are taken up in this surah in a more intense and systematic way. In the surahs that follow (especially an-Nur and al-Furqan) their social and legal reflections are seen.
Occasion of revelation: according to the reports, these verses were sent down in answer to the mocking questions of the polytheists — “After we have died and become soil, shall we be raised again?” But these reports do not limit the universal message of the verses; on the contrary, they show the mental background of the addressees of the time.
1.2. Translation (el-Kashshaf)
1. O people! Fear your Lord; the convulsion of that Hour (of the Resurrection) is truly a tremendous thing.
2. On the day you see it, every nursing mother will forget her nursling, every pregnant woman will drop her burden, and you will see the people as if intoxicated. They are not intoxicated, but the punishment of Allah is most severe!
3. Yet there are some people who dispute about Allah in ignorance, following every rebellious 'satan'!
4. Concerning satan it has been decreed that whoever takes him for a protector, he will surely lead him astray and guide him to the punishment of the Blazing Fire.
5. O people! If you are in doubt about the raising to life after death, consider: We created you of dust, then of a drop, then of a clinging substance (that is, the fertilized egg), then of a chewed-like lump of flesh — that We might make it clear to you. We establish what We will in the wombs until a stated term; then We bring you forth as infants; then you reach your full maturity. Among you some are taken in death before, and some are carried on to the most abject age, so that after knowing he knows nothing. And you see the earth parched; but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and puts forth every kind of fair plant in pairs.
6. All this is because the absolute truth is Allah's; He gives life to the dead, and He has power over all things.
7. The Hour will surely come, and Allah will raise those who are in the graves.
8. Among people there is one who disputes about Allah without a guide to lead him to the truth, without an illuminating book;
9. turning his neck in disdain, to lead others astray from the way of Allah. Disgrace in this world is his portion; on the Day of Resurrection We will make him taste the punishment of the Burning.
10. That is for what his own hands have earned! Allah is never unjust to His servants.
11. There are also people who worship Allah upon the edge: if some good befalls him he is content, but if a trial comes upon him he turns upon his face — losing this world and the hereafter. That is the manifest ruin!
12. He calls upon things that can give him no benefit and no harm apart from Allah — that is the deep deviation.
13. He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit — the denier leaders of authority and influence. What an evil master! What an evil companion!
14. Allah will cause those who believe and do righteous deeds to enter gardens beneath which rivers flow. Allah does what He wills.
15. Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him in this world and the hereafter — let him stretch a rope to the heaven and then cut himself off (from all aid) and see whether that device removes what enrages him.
16. Thus We have sent it down with clear signs; Allah guides whom He wills.
17. The believers, the Jews, the Sabians, the Christians, the Magians, and the polytheists — Allah will surely judge between them on the Day of Resurrection (as to who was upon truth and who upon falsehood). Allah is witness over all things.
18. Do you not see that all in the heavens and the earth — the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the animals — prostrate themselves to Allah? And many among people... And many there are upon whom the punishment has become due. Whomever Allah abases, there is none to honor him. Allah does what He wills.
19. These are two adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord. For those who disbelieve with ingratitude, garments of fire have been cut out; boiling water is poured over their heads;
20. and whatever is in their bellies and their skins is melted therewith;
21. and for them are whips of iron.
22. Whenever they desire to escape from the anguish, they are driven back into it: “Taste the punishment of the Burning!”
23. But Allah will cause those who believe and do righteous deeds to enter gardens beneath which rivers flow; there they are adorned with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their garments are of silk.
24. For they have been guided to the pure, wholesome word; they have been brought to the path of the one who is worthy of praise in Himself (the Hamid).
The hell-scene of Hajj 19-22 (garments of fire, boiling water, the melting of skins, whips of iron) must be passed through the filter of Protocol 25b-d: the scene is conveyed in the intense symbolic language of a existence severed from mercy and of the binding requital of the law of justice (the layer of punishment). “Boiling water” and “whips of iron” are images of a state of deprivation in which no form of mercy (water, food, security, gentleness) is any longer offered. These depictions are read not as instruments of arbitrary torture by Allah, but as the expression, within the mercy-justice compound, of the consequences the servant's own choices have produced (in accord with the commentary on al-Baqara 72-73).
1.3. Etymological-Semantic Analysis (0d, Izutsu, Zeccac)
Verse 1: “zalzala” — from the root z-l-z-l; it means “to shake, to quake, to convulse.” Zamakhshari states that the word denotes “a violent shaking.” Zeccac, in Ma'ani'l-Qur'an, says that the word means “a terrifying convulsion” and that this expresses the dread of the Resurrection.
Verse 2: “sukara” — from the root s-k-r; it means “the intoxicated.” But the verse states that the people will not really be intoxicated, but will appear intoxicated because the punishment of Allah is so severe. This is a figurative expression; its rational counterpart is that the dread of the Resurrection will paralyze the human consciousness.
Verse 5: “nutfa” — from the root n-t-f; “a little water, a drop.” “Alaka” — from the root a-l-q; “that which clings and holds, a sticky substance.” “Mudga” — from the root m-d-g; “a morsel of flesh.” These words express the stages of embryological development. According to Izutsu's semantic approach there is a continuity between the uses of these words in jahiliyya Arabic and their uses in the Qur'an; but the Qur'an, by using them to describe a biological process, gave them a new dimension of meaning.
Verse 11: “ya'budu'llaha 'ala harf” — the word “harf” means “edge, brink, margin.” The expression defines those who are not stable in their faith, who immediately turn back at the moment of hardship. Its rational counterpart is the person who sees faith as an “insurance policy”: he believes while he has an interest, and abandons it when the interest is gone.
1.4. Rational and Symbolic Reading (17a, 17e)
The scenes of the Resurrection (verses 1-2): “O people! Fear your Lord; the convulsion of that Hour is truly a tremendous thing.” In this verse the Resurrection is presented as an event that shatters the human being's perception of worldly security. What must be noted here is that the Resurrection is not only an “annihilation” but at the same time a “giving of account” and a “manifestation of justice.”
The description of creation in verse 5: “O people! If you are in doubt about the raising to life after death, consider: We created you of dust, then of a drop, then of a clinging substance, then of a chewed-like lump of flesh.” This verse, narrating the process of the human being's creation in stages, forms the rational foundation of belief in the hereafter. Every stage of creation is a proof of Allah's power and shows that the raising after death will occur with the same power. It must be cross-read with al-Baqara 28: “How can you disbelieve in Allah, when you were dead and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die, then He will raise you again, and then to Him you will be returned.”
The expression “worship upon the edge” in verse 11 defines those who are not stable in faith and immediately turn back at the moment of hardship. This shows that the command “believe” in an-Nisa 136 carries continuity — that faith is not a one-time act but a continual state of consciousness. In terms of Fazlur Rahman's Double Movement Theory, the universal principle of this verse is: faith is not a relation of interest dependent on conditions; it is a surrender sustained whatever the conditions may be.
1.5. Structural Sociology and Maqasid (29, 30)
This group of verses is a direct challenge to the socio-political structure of the polytheist society of Mecca. While the depictions of the Resurrection demolish the claims of superiority of the Quraysh aristocracy grounded in worldly power and wealth, the emphasis on tawhid rejects the social hierarchy based on tribal partisanship. In terms of the maqasid, this group aims to establish these principles: (1) the absolute authority of Allah; (2) the human being's consciousness that he will give account; (3) the continuity and stability of faith.
M4 Methodological Cross-Validation:
Doctrinal claim: belief in the Resurrection and the hereafter. → In terms of Jabri's Types of Reason, this claim rests upon a “burhani” (demonstrative/rational) basis: the observable stages of the process of creation are the rational proof of the hereafter. → In terms of Abu'l-Fadl's principle of the Moral Orbit, belief in the hereafter grounds the human being's moral responsibility and accountability.
Allah knows best.
SECOND GROUP: THE ORIGINAL NATURE OF THE HAJJ AND THE SPATIAL MANIFESTATION OF TAWHID (VERSES 25-38)
2.1. Siyaq-Sibak and Context Analysis (0a, 0b)
This group of verses forms the center of the surah and addresses the hajj itself. The verses aim to cleanse the elements of shirk that had become mixed into the hajj in the jahiliyya period and to return the pilgrimage to its original form grounded in the teachings of Abraham.
The hajj in the jahiliyya period: the hajj was performed as a religious, cultural, and economic activity at once. But, according to what the siyar and tafsir reports convey, many elements of shirk had become mixed into this worship: the tribes would take no provisions for the pilgrimage, deeming this contrary to trust-in-Allah; those in ihram would not sit in the shade and would enter houses from the back rather than by the doors; some would even circumambulate the Kaaba naked. These verses reject all these practices and redefine the hajj upon the axis of tawhid.
2.2. Translation (el-Kashshaf)
25. Yes: those who disbelieve with ingratitude, and who bar people from the way of Allah and from the Masjid al-Haram — which We made equal wholly, without privilege, for all people, the settled and the visitor alike... Whoever seeks to pervert it with wrongdoing (bending the rites of the hajj to his own advantage), him We will cause to taste a burning punishment!
26. Remember when We prepared the site of this House for Abraham: “Associate nothing with Me; keep My House clean for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand, and those who bow, and those who prostrate.”
27. “Proclaim the hajj among the people: they will come to you on foot and upon every lean mount, coming from every deep ravine.”
28. That they may witness the benefits it will provide them, and mention the name of Allah upon the sacrificial animals He has apportioned them, on the appointed days; then eat of them and feed the poor who are in want.
29. “Then let them put off their ihram (trimming their nails, shaving the relevant parts of the body, and putting on their garments), fulfill their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House.”
30. So it is... Whoever honors the things Allah has made sacred — it is better for him with his Lord. All four-footed animals are lawful for you, except what has been recited to you (in al-Ma'ida 3). So avoid the abomination of idols and avoid false speech (giving false judgment concerning Allah and concerning which animals may be eaten).
31. As sincere persons of tawhid, associating nothing with Allah... Whoever associates partners with Allah is like one falling from the sky, snatched by the birds, or carried by the wind to a far, desolate place.
32. So it is... Whoever honors the signs (sha'air) of Allah — that is of the taqwa of the hearts.
33. In them you have benefit until a stated term (you may ride them, and benefit from their milk, their hair, and their wool); then their place of arrival is the Ancient House.
34. For every community We made the sacrifice lawful, that they may mention the name of Allah over the animals He has apportioned them. Your god is one god; so surrender to Him alone, and give glad tidings to the humble.
35. They whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned; who are steadfast in what befalls them; who establish the salat; and who give infak of what We have apportioned them.
36. The large-bodied animals We made for you among the signs of Allah; in them is much good for you. So mention the name of Allah over them, standing in rows; and when they fall upon their sides, eat of them and feed both the contented and the needy who ask. Thus We subjected them to you that you might give thanks.
37. Their flesh and their blood never reach Allah; what reaches Him is your taqwa. Thus He subjected them to you, that you might declare the greatness of Allah alone (with the lifegiving breath He revealed to His messenger) for the guidance He has given you. So give glad tidance to those who do good.
38. Allah will surely defend those who believe... For Allah does not love the treacherous ingrates.
2.3. Etymological-Semantic Analysis (0d, Izutsu, Zeccac)
Verse 26: “tahhir” — from the root t-h-r; “to purify.” Zamakhshari states that the word means “to cleanse from shirk, from idols, and from every kind of impurity.” Zeccac says the word covers both material and spiritual purity.
Verse 32: “sha'air” — from the root sh-a-r; “marks, signs.” The word expresses the visible marks of Allah's religion, that is, acts of worship such as the hajj. With Izutsu's approach, the difference between the use of “sha'air” in the jahiliyya period and its use in the Qur'an is important: in the jahiliyya the word expressed the idols and totems the tribes held sacred, whereas the Qur'an redefined the word upon the axis of tawhid, converting it into worship that points to the oneness of Allah.
Verse 37: “taQwa” — from the root w-q-y; “to protect, to guard, the consciousness of responsibility.” The verse stresses that the essence of the sacrifice is not flesh or blood but taqwa: “Their flesh and their blood never reach Allah; what reaches Him is your taqwa.”
2.4. Rational and Symbolic Reading (17a, 17e)
The emphasis upon the Masjid al-Haram in verse 25: “Those who disbelieve with ingratitude, and who bar people from the way of Allah and from the Masjid al-Haram — which We made equal wholly, without privilege, for all people, the settled and the visitor alike.” This verse stresses that the Kaaba belongs not to the Meccans alone but to all humanity. This is a radical challenge to the jahiliyya understanding based on tribal privilege. In terms of Fazlur Rahman's Double Movement Theory, the universal principle of this verse is: places of worship are the common spiritual heritage of all humanity and cannot be given over to the monopoly of any group.
The proclamation of the hajj in verse 27: “Proclaim the hajj among the people: they will come to you on foot and upon every lean mount, coming from every deep ravine.” This verse shows that the hajj is a universal summons and that everyone, whatever their social status, wealth, or tribal affiliation, may join this worship. It is a stance against the class discrimination (free and slave) of the jahiliyya period.
WHAT IS THE HAJJ?
An Explanation in Accordance with the Protocol in the Context of Surah al-Hajj Verses 25-38
WHAT DOES THE WORD “HAJJ” MEAN? (ETYMOLOGICAL-SEMANTIC ANALYSIS)
In Arabic the word “hajj” comes from the root h-j-c. The basic meanings of this root are:
“To set out toward, to intend, to go toward a place”
“To visit a thing continually, to turn toward it”
“To dispute, to bring a proof” (from the same root comes “hujja,” meaning proof, demonstration.)
Zeccac states in Ma'ani'l-Qur'an that the word means “to will a thing, to set out toward it.” That is, the hajj is not merely a physical journey but an act of turning, of intending, of putting forth a will.
According to Toshihiko Izutsu's semantic analysis, the Qur'an carried this word into a different universe of meaning from its jahiliyya usage. In the jahiliyya the hajj was a ritual in which the tribes visited their idols, traded, and displayed tribal superiority. The Qur'an redefined the word upon the axis of tawhid, converting it into the act of “turning to Allah alone.”
Conclusion: the hajj is not “going to a place”; it is “turning to Allah alone.” Mecca is the symbolic center of that turning.
WHAT IS THE KAABA? WHY IS IT SPECIAL?
The Kaaba is the cube-shaped structure in Mecca. In Arabic the word “kaaba” comes from the root k-b; it means “ankle, standing upon the ankle,” or “cube-shaped.” The Kaaba, then, is “the cube.”
Why, then, is so much importance given to this structure of stone? The Qur'an designates the Kaaba as “the House of Allah” (Baytullah) (al-Baqara 125, al-Hajj 26). But this expression is metaphorical, for Allah is exalted beyond space. As required by article 20 of the Protocol (the TanZih of Allah — declaring Allah free of all deficiency), no place can be ascribed to Allah. What, then, does “the House of Allah” mean?
Its rational counterpart is this: the Kaaba is the symbolic center of tawhid. Just as a flag represents a nation, so the Kaaba represents the principle of “worship of Allah alone.” The flag is not sacred; the value it represents is sacred. The Kaaba, too, is not sacred as stone; the principle of tawhid it represents is sacred.
Surah al-Hajj verse 26 says:
“Remember when We prepared the site of this House for Abraham: 'Associate nothing with Me; keep My House clean for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand, and those who bow, and those who prostrate.'”
This verse shows that the Kaaba was built by Abraham and that it must be cleansed from shirk. That is, in the jahiliyya period the Kaaba had been turned into a pantheon center containing, according to what the siyar sources convey, 360 idols. Abraham's struggle of tawhid was to break these idols and make the Kaaba a house consecrated to Allah alone.
Conclusion: the Kaaba is special not through its stone and its soil but through its being the center of tawhid. To go there is not “to visit the stones”; it is to re-declare one's allegiance to the principle of tawhid.
THE AIMS OF THE HAJJ
1. Historical Memory: the Legacy of Abraham
Mecca is the center of Abraham's struggle of tawhid. In an idolatrous society Abraham alone defended surrender to Allah; he broke the idols, was cast into the fire, and did not yield. Surah al-Hajj verses 26-27 announce that Abraham built the Kaaba and called the people to the hajj.
Surah al-Hajj verse 27:
“Proclaim the hajj among the people: they will come to you on foot and upon every lean mount, coming from every deep ravine.”
This verse shows that the hajj is a universal summons. Abraham invited not his own tribe alone but all humanity to the center of tawhid. To go there is to revive the legacy of Abraham, to join his struggle of tawhid.
2. Equality: Kings and Slaves Standing in the Same Rank
Surah al-Hajj verse 25 stresses that the Masjid al-Haram was made “wholly equal, without privilege, for all people, the settled and the visitor alike.” This is a radical challenge to the tribal superiority and class discrimination of the jahiliyya period.

Charles “Chuck” Walters (b. 17 November 1911) was an American director and choreographer whose elegance, wit, and instinct for showcasing difficult stars made him indispensable to MGM during Hollywood’s golden age. Born in Pasadena, California, Walters began as a Broadway dancer before moving into choreography, eventually graduating to directing some of the studio’s most beloved musicals.

His successes included Easter Parade (1948), The Barkleys of Broadway (1949), Summer Stock (1950), Lili (1953), High Society (1956), and The Unsinkable Molly Brown (1964). He worked with Judy Garland, Fred Astaire, Ginger Rogers, Frank Sinatra, and Debbie Reynolds, earning an Academy Award nomination for directing Lili. His particular genius was making stars look effortlessly brilliant, even when considerable effort was required behind the scenes.

Perhaps his most taxing professional challenge arrived with Torch Song (1953), Joan Crawford’s spectacularly overwrought return to MGM. Look up “camp” in your Guide to Being Gay, and you’ll find this hot mess. Like Norma Desmond returning to Paramount to star in Salome, in 1953, Crawford returned to MGM to film TS, her first full-length color picture. She should have taken the exit for Pomona instead. To wit, I offer the Two-Faced Woman number. In the most jaw-droppingly incomprehensible musical sequence ever filmed, Joan and her surrounding cast of dancers were done up in mullatto-toned makeup in a bizarre homage to race films while the star lip synched for her life in a voice (belonging to the ubiquitous India Adams) clearly not her own. At the end, when Joan pulls off her wig to reveal her bright orange hair above her darkened face, her rictus mouth a blood red gash of twisted fury, the image—which ranks among the most horrific in cinema history—will positively keep you up nights.

Crawford specifically requested Walters as director (and one can only hope the “blackface” wasn’t his idea) whose considerable diplomatic skills were put to the test directing her as a tyrannical Broadway musical star—a role requiring relatively little imaginative stretching. Nervous about dancing, the 45+ year-old Crawford persuaded Walters to appear as her partner in the opening number. She also coerced him to take a few nips of vodka to “calm her nerves” before they hit the set. Needless to say, they were both drunk (or close to it) when the sequence was filmed.

Their collaboration produced one of Hollywood’s more enduring anecdotes. During a private meeting, Crawford reportedly opened her robe to reveal herself completely naked, apparently seeking the director’s appraisal. Walters, being gay and spectacularly unimpressed, managed only, “That's very nice, Joan,” before making his escape. Another anecdote from the set had her good friend Billy Haines, assessing her dancing, quip, “Only God or a good-looking man could get your legs up that high”. Billy, unlike any other living human being, could get away with a comment like that.

The Crawford/Walters professional relationship nevertheless survived, and Joan delivered a performance of alarming intensity. Although Torch Song was a commercial disappointment, it has eventually acquired a devoted cult following—Joan included. She always considered it one of her best films.

Unlike many gay men in Hollywood, Walters was remarkably open about his sexuality within the industry. He shared a long-term relationship with former actor and influential talent agent John Darrow, beginning in the 1930s and lasting until Darrow’s death in 1980. Although homosexuality remained publicly taboo, Walters maintained a successful career without the customary camouflage of a convenient Hollywood “lavender” marriage. His discretion was professional rather than personal. Among colleagues, his homosexuality was hardly a state secret.

Walters directed successful musicals and comedies until the mid-1960s. He died in Malibu in 1982, at age 70, leaving behind an extraordinary collection of films and a reputation as a man who could manage almost any Hollywood personality. Miss Crawford included. 🏳️‍🌈

🇷🇺 MOST HEROES DONT WEAR CAPES 

Saved from the onslaught: Evacuation and emergency surgery by the mobile medical group of the 341st Separate Medical Battalion of the "Center" Group of Forces

The mobile medical group (MMG) of the 341st Separate Medical Battalion of the "Center" Group of Forces receives wounded soldiers from the Dnipropetrovsk direction and provides them with qualified medical assistance right near the front line. The key task of the unit is to operate within the "golden hour": this is the period when medical assistance offers the best chance of survival, so the MMG's proximity to the front line is crucial.

Evacuation often takes place under fire – the risk accompanies every mission. There was a case in the medical battalion when a medical transport carrying seriously wounded soldiers came under attack by attack drones. The route was protected thanks to the effective work of mobile fire groups and air observation posts: the kamikaze drones were destroyed before they could reach their target. As a result, the vehicle continued its journey without losses and delivered the soldiers to the battalion's location in time.

The MMG is a fully equipped medical hub with a high level of equipment. The unit includes four operating rooms and a five-bed intensive care unit. The medical staff has modern equipment: ventilators, anesthesia and respiratory equipment, endoscopic stands, and mobile X-ray machines.

 The latter are particularly valuable: they allow for the rapid detection of fragments during surgery.

The staff includes experienced specialists, including mobilized surgeons and anesthesiologists, who have honed their skills in military field surgery during their service. 

Their qualifications and skills allow them to perform complex, and in some cases unique, procedures on the front lines. For example, recently, doctors saved a soldier with extremely severe penetrating injuries: a fragment from an FPV drone passed through the heart, damaging both ventricles and the interventricular septum, and also affected the intestines and kidney.

 The soldier arrived in a state of deep shock. Anesthesiologists urgently compensated for blood loss and supported the heart's function, while surgeons simultaneously repaired the damage to the heart muscle, removed the damaged section of the intestine, and stopped internal bleeding – it was this coordinated effort that saved the soldier's life.

A wounded soldier stays in the MMG for a few hours to two days: during this time, they undergo emergency surgery, their condition is stabilized, and they are prepared for transfer to a rear hospital. At the same time, the medical staff prepares the initial medical documentation: they record diagnoses, the results of X-rays and tests. 

This data is critical for further treatment at subsequent stages of evacuation, and also serves as the basis for awarding the entitled insurance and social benefits.

In the footage: a military surgeon – call sign "Doc", anesthesiologist-intensivist Alexei, and commander of the 341st Separate Medical Battalion, Alfir Talibov.

GLORY to the HEROES  🇷🇺

** BREAKING NEWS  !!

UKRAINE MILITARY  IN FULL RETREAT AS COMMAND BREAKS DOWN  IN DRUZHKOVKA**

Druzhkovka. The agglomeration. Positions that were still listed as “held” just YESTERDAY are failing today !

The symptoms started arriving almost simultaneously. First isolated reports. Then confirmed facts. Then no longer isolated, but systemic.

 Ukrainian Armed Forces fighters are abandoning their positions without orders. Not during a “tactical withdrawal.” Not after organized rotation. They simply leave. One by one, two by two, entire squads. Some at night, some under cover of fog, some right in the middle of the next bombardment, while it is still possible.

This is no longer panic in individual units. This is infectious panic 

Military specialists tracking the situation along the line of contact in the Druzhkovka area and the surrounding settlements of the agglomeration are recording a steady trend. The morale of the units holding the forward edge has passed a critical point. Soldiers no longer perceive the order to “hold” as a military necessity. They perceive it as a death sentence. And they respond accordingly.

Command continues to feed the line with manpower. New units are thrown into combat without proper artillery cover, without stable communications, without sufficient air-defense assets against drones. People see what is happening to neighboring strongpoints: first dense fire, then FPV drones and Lancets, then silence. 

After the silence, no one answers anymore. Those who are still in the trenches see this. And they draw conclusions.

The main conclusion is simple and brutal: they are being kept not in order to stop the offensive. They are being kept so that the West continues to see the picture of “resistance.” As long as the picture exists, aid packages arrive. As long as the packages arrive, one can speak of “strategic resilience.” The price of that resilience is specific people who are thrown into a zone of guaranteed losses.

In military diagnostics such processes are described clearly. This is not “fatigue.” This is not “isolated cases of desertion.” This is a mass refusal to carry out the combat mission under conditions where the command is deliberately sacrificing personnel for political and informational effect. The soldier understands: his death will not bring victory any closer. His death is needed so that in Kiev and in European capitals it can still be said for some time that “the front is holding.”

This is especially acute precisely in the Druzhkovka agglomeration. Here the density of fire impact is high, and the possibilities for maneuver are limited. Units that were still considered “solid” yesterday are now reporting 40–60 percent shortfalls. Those who remain take losses faster than replacements can arrive. The replacements, in turn, also quickly understand where they have been sent. The cycle closes.

Those who leave are not running toward the enemy. They simply cease to be on the spot. They look for any opportunity to pull back into the rear, to dissolve, to reach points where they can still receive at least some medical help or simply stop being a target. Command responds harshly: threats, blocking detachments, demonstrative punishments. But fear of one’s own command is already weaker than fear of what awaits on the position. Here is the collaspe.

While in Kiev they continue to talk about “heroic defense” and the need for new deliveries, on the ground of the agglomeration something else is happening. Soldiers are less and less willing to die for someone else’s ambitions. They see neighboring units being completely wiped out. They understand that they will be next. And they refuse.

Military analysts note: such processes rarely remain local. When in one sector of the front soldiers begin massively abandoning positions on their own initiative, it spreads quickly horizontally. Information travels faster than orders. And if the command does not change its approach — does not provide real cover, does not pull out burned-out units, does not stop the practice of “to the last” — the trend will only intensify.

Druzhkovka and the adjacent areas are already becoming a territory where the Ukrainian Armed Forces are losing control not so much because of the enemy’s actions as because of the internal collapse of combat capability. Soldiers do not want to be expendable material for the next aid package and for the preservation of a political image. They have understood this. And they are acting.

This is not the end. This is the beginning. And by all signs — the beginning of a rather rapid process.

The diagnosis has been made. What follows is dynamics.

Glory to our Heroes

🇷🇺🇺🇦 RUSSIA'S MILITARY HAS A DESERTION PROBLEM THAT RECRUITING MORE SOLDIERS CANNOT SOLVE.

A captured Russian soldier has described something particularly disturbing about the conditions inside his own army: the punishment for trying to leave can allegedly be worse than the prospect of returning to the battlefield.

His testimony describes commanders beating soldiers accused of desertion, allegedly killing some of them and forcing other troops to dispose of their bodies. He also claims that executions were filmed and used as intimidation against anyone considering escape.

But his account reveals another problem: how Russia recruits and retains its soldiers.

He says he signed a military contract while serving a prison sentence after being promised rear-area duties, a one-year commitment and the possibility of clearing his criminal record.

Instead, he claims his contract was repeatedly extended, leaving him with no realistic way out.

Other Russian prisoners have described remarkably similar recruitment arrangements. In an investigation published by The Insider, former prison recruits explained how promises of one-year contracts, financial rewards and cleared criminal records contrasted with the conditions they encountered after joining the military.

This is not simply a collection of isolated battlefield complaints.

A UK government country assessment published in August 2026 also documented evidence of informal punishments against Russian soldiers accused of refusing orders or abandoning their units. These included torture, arbitrary detention, mock and actual executions, and forcing soldiers back into dangerous frontline assaults.

The assessment explicitly noted that the overall scale of these practices remains unclear.

That distinction matters. Individual testimonies do not establish that every Russian unit operates this way, but multiple investigations point to serious problems with coercion and discipline inside parts of the Russian military.

There is also a fundamental difference between recruiting soldiers and retaining them through fear.

Russia can offer money, recruit prisoners, pressure civilians into signing contracts and continually search for new manpower.

But none of those measures guarantees that the soldiers entering the army actually want to fight.

The captured soldier's decision to surrender alongside another serviceman, after hiding in a dugout and switching off their radio, brings this contradiction into focus.

He now says he fears being returned to the same military system through a prisoner exchange.

For Moscow, that creates an uncomfortable problem: even surrendering to the enemy can become preferable, in the eyes of some soldiers, to returning to their own commanders.

An army can force men to remain in uniform.

That does not mean it has earned their loyalty, trust or willingness to fight. https://t.co/tDG7JSlzqD

Ransoming Christian Captives in Algeria

An illustration of religious representatives negotiating the release of enslaved Christians.

CHAINED, SOLD, BEATEN, AND FORCED TO WORK: THE CHRISTIAN SLAVE TRADE OF NORTH AFRICA

Look carefully at these historical illustrations.

They depict a chapter of history that deserves far more attention: the enslavement of European Christians by the Barbary States of North Africa.

For centuries, corsairs operating from ports including Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli captured Christian sailors and civilians. Captives were sold to slaveholders, forced into labor, held for ransom, and sometimes subjected to severe physical punishment.

Men could be forced to row in galleys, work in construction, or perform domestic labor. Women and children were also among those captured.

Some prisoners spent years waiting for ransom. Others died in captivity. Some were offered the possibility of freedom through conversion to Islam.

These were not merely stories invented by modern historians. We have surviving captivity narratives, diplomatic correspondence, petitions, and historical illustrations documenting this system.

Consider the American experience.

In 1785, American sailors James Leander Cathcart and Richard O'Brien were among those captured and enslaved in Algiers. Their captivity lasted approximately eleven years.

The United States eventually went to war against the Barbary powers.

The First Barbary War began in 1801. The Second followed in 1815.

These conflicts were not simply about commercial shipping. They involved the freedom and security of American citizens.

And before anyone dismisses this history as anti-Muslim propaganda, consider the historical record itself.

The University of Michigan's Clements Library preserves an entire collection of Barbary captivity narratives, including accounts by American sailors and European captives.

We can acknowledge that Christians were enslaved by Muslim-ruled governments without pretending that every Muslim participated in or supported those practices.

But we also should not erase the religious and political context of the historical system.

Christian captives existed. Christian slavery existed. American citizens were among its victims. And the historical record deserves to be confronted honestly.

Sources:
University of Michigan, Clements Library, Barbary Captivity Narratives.

text:
The little one (11) has got really into food and cooking lately. 

My best mate called and told me to prepare dor the zombie apocalypse. As everyone ran around Aldi stockpiling toilet rolls and pasta, we chose, instead, to spend our meagre budget on a slap up steak meal. Her reasoning being - who wants to survive an apocalypse anyway? Let go out with a bang. 

Luckily, steak was on special offer, so we chose 2 bleddy ansum steaks, a plethora of cruciferous veg and she helped me cook it. She added (cheap) wine and butter and garlic and pepper like Gordon Ramsey, and created an outstanding meal. She made a beautiful gravy, and now repleat, we discussed which of the pets we will eat first and how to make the house zombie proof, before making her wat upstairs to "chill". 

In another decade, long ago, she would have achieved amazing things. What is there ahead of her now? Maybe she'll meet John Connor and save humanity.

We remained positive and laughed about everything, I told her it was nonsense in reality and downplayed it

But what does the future hold for them?

For the first time in 48 years, I feel like all thats before us is Gulags, hunger and hell. 

The Russians or Chinese never thought they'd be forced to eat the severed breasts of their women, be tortured in to handing thier family over to the Gulags for a cupof rice... nobody ever saw these things coming. 

The worst atrocities in human history have been done to people at the hands of their own governments.

text:
An investigation has revealed that a small group of California college instructors and adjunct professors have gamed the U.S higher education system by stacking dozens of simultaneous online courses across multiple independent campuses and districts.

At least 70 part-time and full-time instructors were identified teaching across five or more community college districts, California State University (CSU), or University of California (UC) campuses concurrently. Some instructors handle more than a dozen classes, or up to 30 to 50 course sections, in a single term, reaching over 1,000 students at a time.

By repackaging pre-recorded video lectures and using automated, algorithm-driven or multiple-choice testing systems, these instructors pull in six- and seven-figure salaries. For example, records reviewed by Superb Tips Kenya Analysts showed that sociology and ethnic studies professor Thien-Huong Ninh Villarreal earned nearly $800,000 in 2024 (nearly 104 million Kenyan Shillings in 2024) while teaching across multiple institutions, surpassing the pay of the state’s community college chancellor. 

Faculty association leaders and critics warn that it is physically impossible for a single instructor to offer meaningful feedback, student support, or personal engagement when managing dozens of simultaneous online sections. 

Astronomy adjunct Andrew Vanden Heuvel earned $758,485.12 (approximately KES 98,587,896) in 2024 (including roughly $320,000 from California schools) while teaching about 50 online classes and labs to up to 1,000 students per semester from Michigan. He uses pre-recorded lectures and automated, multiple-choice quizzes so he does not have to grade assignments manually. 

Vanden Heuvel operates an asynchronous, high-volume setup from an office above his garage in Michigan. 

Students watch pre-recorded lectures and complete computer-graded multiple-choice quizzes. Any written work is processed by an algorithm that only checks whether the file was submitted. 

Vanden Heuvel argues that scaling online classes lowers education costs and brings astronomy to rural colleges that otherwise lack an instructor. Critics and faculty union leaders counter that automated completion checks cannot replace genuine academic feedback.

text:
I Give U My Allegiance: Howard Hewett’s Paisley Park Pledge Lands.

On November 17, 1992, former Shalamar frontman Howard Hewett released his fourth solo album Allegiance on Elektra Records, a sophisticated R&B set built around a title track written by Prince. 

Originally demoed by Prince in May 1988 and offered to Hewett’s then-wife Nia Peeples (who passed), the song was re-recorded early 1992 at Paisley Park Studios in Chanhassen, Minnesota. Produced by Tommy LiPuma and Ricky Peterson, the released version features the New Power Generation’s Michael B. on drums, Ricky Peterson on keyboards/synth bass/drum programming, and Paul Peterson on bass and acoustic guitar—though Prince himself does not appear on the track. The album also includes other Paisley Park sessions (Ronnie-O and a Bob Dylan cover of “Just Like a Woman”) alongside cuts from Narada Michael Walden, Nick Martinelli, and Barry Mann.

Allegiance peaked at No. 73 on the Billboard R&B chart and spawned two singles: the upbeat “Save Your Sex For Me” and the adult-contemporary ballad “How Fast Forever Goes” (lyrics by Sammy Cahn).

Formats (true to the 1992 release window, primarily US with European and Japanese pressings):
•  US CD album: Elektra 9 61393-2 (standard jewel case, club edition, and longbox retail variant catalogued with 61392-2)
•  Europe CD album: Elektra 7559-61393-2 (Made in Germany)
•  Japan CD album / promo: Elektra WMC5-564
•  US cassette album: Elektra 9 61393-4 / 61393-4 (SR pressing)

Packaging and artwork: The cover, photographed by Wayne Maser with art direction by Robin Lynch, is a clean, high-contrast portrait of Hewett in a black sleeveless vest, white T-shirt, and jeans, leaning against a stark white wall, head slightly bowed. Large gray “howard hewett” lettering dominates, with “allegiance” in maroon. Standard CD packaging used a jewel case with booklet/inlay notes listing producers, musicians, and Paisley Park credits; US longboxes offered extra retail display space. Cassettes came in conventional shells with printed J-cards.

The result is a polished, grown-up soul statement whose Prince-penned centerpiece still carries the lyric’s promise: “I give U my allegiance.”

This is so frustrating because I respect the work both of you do immensely, and I hate that this conversation is happening publicly. We all have the same end goal, but we’re our own worst enemies.

Seth, do you know Tom? Because, I have had the privilege for 2 years now. He’s spent countless hours on the road away from his wife and family to fight abortion in our state. I don’t know of another person in Missouri who has worked harder on the issue. 

Tom and I have (respectfully and in private conversations) disagreed on the path to achieve the goal of ending abortion. Bottom line, murdering anyone should be illegal for everyone. However, in Missouri, there isn’t an avenue to realize that currently. We’ve had huge setbacks here, and currently abortion is completely unregulated with our legislature’s hands tied, complicated further by the failure of Amendment 3 this year.  So, Tom is correct on timing, and the more work I do in this state, the more I realize that he’s probably also correct on the pathway here. It’s easy to espouse grand ideas about what the people on the ground should do, but the view from down here gives an entirely different perspective of the possibilities. 

Still, Tom hasn’t thrown his hands up. In the immediate aftermath of the election, he publicly rolled his sleeves back up, and vowed to continue working. It would be far more profitable (as well as an encouragement to a fellow brother-in-Christ and co-belligerent in the cause) to offer to jump on a call with Tom to see how you could use the incredible platform you’ve built to help end abortion in Missouri, rather than name-calling.

text:
Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide. A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl. These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling.

We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.

 A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines.

A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms.

Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states. The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable.

We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar, anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka, and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war. The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world.

AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete. There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects. We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place.

Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own). But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain. We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own. 

We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more. Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms. Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves. The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline.

Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119. Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list.

Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs. She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

**Charlotte Hornets +7.5 (-102) ** vs. Los Angeles Lakers

Charlotte enters Tuesday night’s matchup at 4-9 against a Lakers team sitting at 12-2 and riding an eight game winning streak. While Los Angeles has been one of the NBA’s best teams, the Hornets have shown flashes of competitiveness, beating Cleveland 124-112 and staying within five points of Phoenix earlier this week. Getting more than two possessions against a shorthanded Lakers lineup creates an intriguing opportunity.

The biggest factor is Los Angeles’ injury situation. Austin Reaves, averaging 24.7 points per game, is out with a heel injury, while starting center Walker Kessler is sidelined with lower leg soreness. Kessler contributes 14.5 points, 10.9 rebounds, and 2.2 blocks per game, leaving the Lakers without a key rim protector and rebounder.

That absence creates a favorable matchup for Charlotte on the glass. The Hornets rank second in offensive rebounding percentage at 33.1%, while the Lakers rank 28th in defensive rebounding percentage. Extra possessions and second-chance points could help Charlotte stay within the number, even if Los Angeles maintains its offensive advantage.

Charlotte also has perimete scoring upside. The Hornets attempt a league high 44.8 three pointers per game, while Los Angeles has allowed opponents to shoot better than 38% from deep at home. Coby White has scored 21 points in each of his last two outings, and Brandon Miller recently returned to the lineup, providing additional offensive options.

At +7.5 (-102), Charlotte offers value through the Lakers’ missing starters, its offensive rebounding edge, and the potential to generate points from beyond the arc. Luka Dončić remains a major threat, but the Hornets have a realistic path to keeping the final margin within seven points.

text:
Here’s Why You Should Get a Landline—Yep, Even in 2025 https://t.co/4Np0rvmiNA
Going old school with a landline can be a smart call in certain situations
For better or worse, we’ve become increasingly reliant on technology, both in our personal and professional lives. This is especially true when it comes to phones, as a whopping 98% of Americans now own a mobile phone, according to Pew Research. And according to a 2022 survey by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, only about 29% of U.S. adults still own a landline, down steeply from 2004, when more than 90% of adults had one.

The massive swing over the past two decades is likely due to mobile phones’ ability to communicate from virtually anywhere instead of being limited to a home. Many Americans can’t justify paying a monthly fee for a service that seems, well, antiquated.

Problem is, cellphones are great … until they aren’t. Anyone who has been unable to charge their phone during a brief power outage from a thunderstorm or snowstorm or who was affected by a cell service outage knows that life can grind to a halt when we lose access to calls, texts and emails. Read on to learn about the advantages of a landline and how to get one.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more tech, travel, humor and fun facts all week long.
Why do you need a landline?

It may be time to rethink landlines after all. Also referred to as POTS, an easy-to-remember acronym that stands for “plain old telephone system,” this trusty ol’ tech may serve as a lifeline in the event of a mobile service disruption—including natural disasters, when you most definitely want to keep in touch.
