“Actually, I still own a landline,” concedes Tony Anscombe, chief security evangelist for ESET, a leading cybersecurity company. “It’s mostly because I live in a house that’s remote, and so we still use copper for internet and phone service here.”

A landline can be a lifesaving backup if your mobile phone service goes down, which happens from time to time on all the major carriers, whether because of a random service outage or one caused by inclement weather.

AT&T customers, for example, experienced a wireless outage for several hours in February 2024, due to what was billed as a coding error during network expansion. In September 2024, Verizon suffered a major outage, and two months later, so did T-Mobile.

Hurricane Milton, a Category 4 hurricane that hit the United States in October 2024, caused 12.3% of cell sites to be down in areas of Florida impacted by the storm, according to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Disaster Information Reporting System report. AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon were all affected, as were other carriers.
How could a landline help in an emergency?

Landlines work better during power outages because they receive power directly through the phone line itself, which is separate from the household electricity grid. Therefore, the phone company’s backup generators can power the lines even when your home power is out.

Another advantage in an emergency situation: Landlines allow emergency services to locate a 911 caller‘s origin more easily than an enhanced 911 (also called “e911”) call on a cellphone or smartphone. That’s because mobile phones aren’t associated with one fixed location or address.

That said, enhanced 911 calls have improved over the years, thanks to advancements in carrier services, GPS tracking and dispatching equipment, which help emergency service pinpoint your location. “While it’s getting better, an e911 call [on a smartphone] doesn’t provide your location as accurately as a 911 call on a landline, when you’re right at the handset and they know your exact address, even if you can’t talk,” says Anscombe.
What is a landline?

Before we discuss why you might want a landline, it’s helpful to understand the technology.

POTS
A POTS phone system (aka traditional landline) was the standard form of telephone service from the 1880s to the fairly recent past. If you’re over 40 years old, you likely grew up with one of these in your home.

This technology (almost always) uses copper wires to transmit your voice, which is converted into analog electrical signals and then converted back into audible sound waves when it reaches its destination, allowing the person you’re calling to hear your voice.

While telephone users may think they’re calling someone else directly, behind the scenes, there is an extensive network of interconnected telephone lines, switches and infrastructure to enable communication between POTS lines. (As you may have seen in old movies, switchboard operators, usually female, played an important role in routing calls until the 1960s.)

Over the past couple of decades, digital and internet-based communication technologies took over, though landlines were still used in business environments until fairly recently.

The benefit of POTS
While POTS lines have declined in popularity since the rise of cellphones and smartphones, they are still common in regions with unreliable or limited internet access. They’re also ideal for critical services like emergency lines and home or business alarm systems that demand high reliability.

“In case of a power or cellular outage, I can see the appeal of a landline, as it should still work, unless you only have a cordless phone at home, which would also rely on power,” says Carolina Milanesi, president and principal analyst at Creative Strategies, a Silicon Valley–based market research firm. “Also, good luck in trying to remember anyone’s phone number if you lose power on your smartphone,” she adds with a laugh. “We’ve grown reliant on everything being stored on our smartphones.”

Landlines are also essential for connecting devices like fax machines, which are still heavily used in the health care and finance industries today, as they’re considered secure and dependable means of transmitting crucial and sensitive information.

Plus, compared with mobile phones, landlines are less likely to drop calls or have poor reception, often have better sound quality and are generally easier to operate for aging adults, especially among those with dexterity challenges. (An exception to the sound-quality benefit is the cordless phone, “which may sound worse than a mobile phone, especially older models that could have static and such,” Milanesi says.)

Anscombe says another consideration is that some fall detectors, like the Lifeline products—often worn on a lanyard or wrist of someone at risk of falling—may require a landline for the device to call someone in the event of a fall. This is something to keep in mind before considering the cancellation of landline service.

“I also think there’s a perceived security around owning a landline, especially for older folks,” adds Anscombe. “They could get rid of their landline, but many won’t, as they know they can pick up the handset, and it just works.” He adds that his mom falls into that category, “but if I asked her when the last time she actually used her landline was, it would probably be years ago.”

The disadvantages of POTS
Landlines can be difficult to find these days, as some telecommunications companies have ceased (or limited) their offerings. Because demand has subsided, the costs for a POTS line could be higher than a few years ago, even upwards of $50 per month. Additional charges may apply for features like long-distance calling, caller ID, voicemail and other add-ons.

“This isn’t always the case, though,” counters Milanesi, who says the only reason she still has a landline is because she gets the service for free from her mobile and internet company. “I don’t think I’ve ever used it, to be honest.”

Other downsides: You’re limited to using the landline at home. And it’s not a given that you’ll get service. Because fewer people now own a landline, the FCC is phasing out requirements for phone companies to provide landline services. In many new homes, builders aren’t even installing phone jacks.

With his cybersecurity expertise, Anscombe provides one more advantage to a smartphone compared with a landline: “Cordless phones are also less secure than smartphones, [as they’re] more susceptible to eavesdropping and open to other vulnerabilities.”

What’s the best alternative to a landline?

If your internet service provider or TV company doesn’t offer a landline service, you can research the companies in your area that can still provide one. A quick Google search may do the trick, or you can ask neighbors which service they use.
Still striking out? The following are alternatives to a traditional landline.

Consider a VoIP line

If you’re having trouble finding a POTS provider, an alternative would be a VoIP phone, which uses the internet to make phone calls. VoIP services are often more cost effective than landlines (especially for long-distance calls), and you often get free features and add-ons, such as voicemail, three-way calling, call forwarding and caller ID.
Use messaging apps, websites and smart speakers

Another option is to leverage messaging apps and websites to make free phone calls to others. But the caveat is the person you’re calling must be on the same service as you. Popular options include WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, Skype, FaceTime, Zoom, Google Meet, Signal and Microsoft Teams. These services support video calls and file transfers, and they offer other benefits.
If you have power and internet connectivity, remember that you can place free audio calls using a smart speaker, such as an Amazon Echo or Google Nest device. Simply say the wake word, like “Alexa” (on Amazon devices) or “Hey Google” or “OK Google” (on Google Nest speakers), followed by “dial [10-digit number].” No smartphone is required.

Consider backup power

Both a VoIP phone and messaging apps require power and internet access. While there’s little you can do if your Wi-Fi or wired (Ethernet) connection fails, such as if your internet service provider experiences an outage, you can invest in a backup solution for your devices should you be without power.
Similar to small and portable chargers (“power banks”) that juice up a smartphone and other gear, larger battery-based power generators can keep appliances, computers, medical devices and other equipment running for days. (A rechargeable battery-based generator may be better than a gas one since it can be used indoors, is quieter and doesn’t produce carbon monoxide.)

SOS satellite services

If your mobile phone can’t access cellular towers because your carrier’s network is down or you find yourself “off the grid” (such as in the woods), both Apple and Samsung support emergency satellite SOS services on the latest iPhones and Samsung Galaxy phones, respectively. Free for now, this feature first connects you to satellites via on-screen instructions. From there, you can type text-based messages to emergency services. You can also share location info and a description of what’s going on.
Mobile phone carriers, including AT&T and Verizon, are also offering emergency satellite support on certain devices.

Some satellite-based internet services, like Starlink, also support calls in emergencies. But be aware that the dish, router and other equipment will require power.

On the topic of satellite connectivity, Anscombe says the school his partner teaches at has satellite phones for use in case of earthquakes or other natural disasters that can knock out power or cellular service. When pressed about these phones still requiring power to use, Anscombe says they’re always charged up and ready to use in should an emergency occur.

🎤 FEATURED SEMINAR & SPECIAL GUEST SPEAKER

🧬 DR. JONATHAN M. FIELDS
THE FUTURE OF WELLNESS:
INTEGRATING FUNCTIONAL MEDICINE, FITNESS & WELLNESS REAL ESTATE

What if the future of better health isn't simply about treating illness, but about transforming how we live, move, recover, and design the environments around us?
Join Dr. Jonathan M. Fields for a fascinating exploration of the emerging world of longevity, functional medicine, human performance, and wellness-centered living.
This thought-provoking presentation will introduce exciting ideas about how modern science, ancient wellness practices, advanced technologies, and healthier living environments are shaping the future of human health.

🔬 1. THE EVOLUTION OF LONGEVITY

Discover the growing movement from reactive healthcare toward proactive functional and longevity medicine.

Explore the roles of gut health, hormone optimization, and preventative approaches in supporting healthier aging.

🧬 2. THE BIOCHEMICAL FUTURE
Learn about emerging approaches attracting attention in longevity medicine, including:

• Peptides and their potential applications in tissue repair and metabolic health
• NAD+ and its relationship to cellular energy and mitochondrial function
• The science and questions surrounding biological aging
• How researchers and clinicians are exploring new approaches to long-term wellness

💪 3. MOVEMENT AS MEDICINE

Why are muscle mass, cardiovascular fitness, and VO2 max so important to healthy aging?

Explore the connection between strength, endurance, mobility, recovery, and long-term physical performance.

Dr. Fields will also discuss:

• High-intensity training and mindful movement
• Somatic practices and mind-body wellness
• Recovery technologies such as red light therapy, PEMF, and hydrogen/oxygen therapies
• Building a lifestyle that supports physical resilience

🏡 4. WELLNESS REAL ESTATE: DESIGNING A HEALING HOME

Can your home become an important part of your wellness strategy?

Explore the emerging concept of wellness real estate and how healthier residential environments may support everyday well-being.
Topics include:
• Indoor air quality and whole-home filtration
• Water quality and filtration systems
• Circadian lighting and healthier sleep environments
• Home recovery spaces and infrared saunas
• Building materials and reducing unwanted environmental exposures
• Integrating wellness technology into modern homes
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

👨‍⚕️ MEET DR. JONATHAN M. FIELDS

Dr. Jonathan M. Fields is an integrative specialist, author, keynote speaker, and martial arts instructor known for bridging ancient wisdom with modern science.

Founder of multiple longevity clinics in South Florida, his specialties include:

🧬 Longevity & Functional Medicine
🌿 Herbal Medicine
📍 Acupuncture
💪 Regenerative Medicine
🧠 Mental-Emotional Resilience

His professional experience includes working with Fortune 500 executives, elite athletes, universities, and transformational retreats.
With more than 35 years of martial arts training and 20 years of teaching martial arts and qi gong, his journey has included living among Shaolin monks, clinical work in Beijing hospitals, and decades of cross-cultural study.
His approach combines modern anatomical understanding with traditional Eastern wellness philosophies.
🎯 WHO SHOULD ATTEND THIS SEMINAR?

✅ Anyone seeking more energy and improved performance
✅ Adults interested in healthy aging and longevity
✅ People exploring additional approaches to persistent health concerns
✅ Fitness and wellness enthusiasts
✅ Healthcare and medical professionals
✅ Anyone interested in emerging medical technologies
✅ Homeowners interested in healthier living environments
✅ Business owners exploring opportunities in the growing wellness economy

This is an educational presentation, not a substitute for individualized medical advice. Emerging therapies may have varying levels of clinical evidence.

text:
Tiger Woods cheated on his wife and lost up to $35 million a year in sponsorship deals. Accenture, AT&T and Gatorade dropped him one by one.

On February 19, 2010, Woods delivered a prepared statement at TPC Sawgrass in Florida. About 40 people were there, including his mother. Television networks interrupted their programming to carry it.

He had not spoken publicly since his November 27 car crash, which was followed by weeks of reports about multiple affairs. In December, he admitted infidelity and announced an indefinite break from professional golf.

Accenture ended its six-year sponsorship on December 13. AT&T followed on December 31. Two major sponsors had ended their relationships with him before this televised apology.

In the video below, he begins by apologizing to the people who supported him. He says Elin had made clear that repairing the damage would depend on his behavior over time. Their conversations, he says, would stay private.

Then he addresses the people whose livelihoods and reputations were tied to his: employees, business partners and the staff and sponsors of his foundation. He acknowledges the “considerable worry” his behavior had caused.

Later in the statement, he admits the affairs directly: “I had affairs. I cheated.”

He says he knew his actions were wrong but had persuaded himself that ordinary rules didn’t apply. He describes believing that years of hard work entitled him to the temptations his fame made available.

“I felt I was entitled.”

Woods says he had spent 45 days in inpatient therapy and would return for more treatment. He offers no date for a return to golf.

The companies around him made different decisions. Nike and Electronic Arts stood by him. On February 26, Gatorade confirmed that its endorsement relationship was over, while continuing its support for his foundation.

Woods returned to competitive golf in April. On August 23, he and Elin Nordegren announced their divorce.

text:
There are many policy manifestations that provide irrefutable proof of Plato's assessment, particularly in America over the past half-century, but one grim bit of anecdotal evidence presently at hand is the accelerating collapse of even the most basic structures providing law and order. 

Traffic laws and civic codes governing public behavior are Exhibit A. 

Beginning in the summer of 2020, when a certain urban miscreant perished by his own bad decisions and the nation was plunged into a pre-loaded InstaRiot that produced the desired looting and arson on a staggering scale, law enforcement agencies and governments at the state, county and municipal levels across the country immediately suspended virtually all forms of traffic law enforcement, civic codes regulating public behavior (i.e. quality of life strictures such as prohibiting loud noise at certain hours, loitering, illegal parking, etc.) and anything else that could be seen as benchmark of a well-preserved high trust Western society. 

The rationale for the near-instantaneous jettisoning of civic standards and the demolition of the social pillars (few seemed to notice or question that the base charges had been carefully and methodically planted well before the alleged triggering event) was declared to be a reckoning with a social order that oppressed racial minorities as evidenced by 'disparate impacts.' 

Simply put, if more black drivers than white drivers were cited for reckless driving, then reckless driving prohibitions must be inherently oppressive and designed to target black drivers versus coercively prohibit dangerous driving. 

In Southern California — the birthplace and car culture capital of America — the California Highway Patrol disappeared from the regions freeways almost overnight and local police agencies suspended traffic law enforcement (including license, insurance and vehicle registration requirements) en masse. 

Now, more than six years down the road, all across Southern California and indeed throughout many other locales around the nation, wild-eyed savages terrorizing drivers and pedestrians alike can be seen everyday. In Los Angeles, so-called 'street takeovers' are a near nightly occurrence that see hundreds and sometimes thousands of bipedal primates packing metro intersections as muscle cars shriek and scream in smoking circles of burning rubber on the asphalt as the savage primates jump up and down, grabbing their crotches with one hand and holding their iPhones with the other as they livestream the chaos. 

LAPD units usually remain at a distance in observance of the policy that, on paper anyway, prioritizes concepts of deescalation and non-intrusive policing posture that is said to restore confidence in the community. 

In actual fact, the policy is clearly designed to facilitate, accelerate and propagate total social collapse into a permanent state of Third World chaos. Police protocols today are the real-world application of a governance committed to destroying the American construct and the Western world's imprint on the American homeland. 

Throughout the suburbs now, a dysfunctional rite that was forged in the tribal lands of Baltimore decades ago in what became known as the 12 O'clock Boys movement where hundreds of 'teens' (always the 'teens') raced through streets on dirt bikes and ATVs, taking over city blocks and riding like mad circus monkeys that were making a mass escape from the big top and their cruel captors at Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey garish exhibitions. A documentary that captured a granular look at the madness of the 12 O'clock Boys revealed that while most of them were descendants of people who have been in America for several centuries, their language skills were so limited that captions had to be used in an effort to interpret what they were apparently trying to say. Little understandable or coherent English was on offer from the 'teens' despite being born in the U.S. and having a bloodline that reached back to the 1700s in some cases. 

What was once confined to the urban jungles dotting eastern seaboard is now a feature of Southern California's streets (as well as Dallas and Miami, where I have witnessed it firsthand as well), as roving packs of savages fill the streets on E-bikes, motorcycles and bicycles where they intentionally harass and threaten other drivers and pedestrians alike for obvious sport. 

This past weekend, as many as 40 or so 'teens' took their circus monkey show into a large and somewhat upscale mall in the bedroom community of Montclair, about 40 miles east of LA. Inside the mall, the primates took to popping wheelies and peddling furiously at all manner of shoppers. Gas-powered minibikes also raced through the mall. 

If you are wondering what this very specific display of chaotic lunacy in a shopping mall has to do with Plato's observation that Chad has rightly highlighted, well, to bring it all back home: the rise of inferior cultures driven by the mass importation of foreign peoples — both historically and currently — from Third World tribal lands rooted in nihilistic and subsistence lifestyles is not a misunderstood or unanticipated byproduct of bad policy. 

It is the policy. 

The chaos unfolding on the streets in real time, right now even as you read this, is the desired result produced by a strange coalition of agents and operatives (sounds very cloak and dagger, but mostly its not) that seek to establish a new rule following the wholesale, top-to-bottom annihilation of America and its heritage population. 

In Montclair, a nice shopping mall that was already struggling in this economic climate may well have just received its death blow at the hands of the savage primates who raced across its polished floors. Word of that sort of experience spreads rapidly and consumers retreat, which triggers a hand off of sorts to the bipedal primates who consider such violent dysfunction to be something akin to a half-time show. They like it. Feels like home to them, or school when manage to attend. They call it 'Wildin' Out!' 

But it can be fatal for the businesses. 

So these are the stakes. Either we resolve to excise the tumors that are spreading or, and very soon, the cancer will be too far along and what remained left to us will be overwhelmed. 

A parting suggestion: Savages are as savages do. Never forget that. And never be afraid to call a savage a savage, a primate a primate, a spade a spade.

text:
🧭 VAIEA VILLAGE | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
✈️ Getting There

Fly from Auckland to Niue with Air New Zealand. Flights are limited, so plan around the return schedule. Vaiea is approximately 14 km (20 minutes) by road from Alofi. With no public transport, renting a car is the practical choice; a local driving licence is required.

🗺️ What to Explore

Discover the village's peaceful rural setting and consider Fatiau Tuai Vaiea, the former settlement where old graves and church foundations remain. Its overgrown access road is unsuitable for ordinary rental cars, so confirm access locally. Nearby Avatele Beach offers a coastal alternative.

⏱️ Time Needed & Where to Stay

Allow a short village stop, or half a day when combining Vaiea with nearby attractions. Alofi or Avatele provides a convenient accommodation base.

🌤️ When to Visit

May–October generally brings drier weather. November–April is warmer and wetter, with tropical cyclone risks.

💡 Local Insight

Vaiea is a living community rather than a developed tourist attraction. Its historical sites require more careful planning than a conventional sightseeing stop.

So what did Trump say in Manila when asked if he was worried? “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.” His own White House Rapid Response account posted this disaster of an answer proudly.

Even Fox isn’t buying it. Brian Kilmeade said “I think we are being probed.” Jesse Watters said his family has 90 days of weapons, water, and peanut butter. Hannity told viewers about his emergency stockpile. Sen. Josh Hawley said if it’s all a coincidence, it’s “the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Former Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said she’s checking her bank account with some worry and the White House needs transparency.

Mullin’s Very Bad Morning

On CNBC’s Squawk Box, Mullin blamed companies for “pushing new technology on top of really old computer systems.” He said they should schedule upgrades between 1 and 4 a.m. The reporter pointed out that the FAA did its own upgrade on a busy Friday afternoon. Then the Wall Street Journal reported that the NSA outage was a software patch in the middle of the day.

Mullin also had to answer for a New York Post scoop from Emily Goodin. Yes, Murdoch’s New York Post. Mullin flew his government plane to the LSU–Texas game while thousands of travelers were still dealing with the fallout of the ground stop. He watched from the private box of Ben Bordelon, CEO of Bollinger Shipping, which has billions in DHS contracts, including a recent $2.2 billion deal for six icebreakers. His defense to Joe Kernen was that airspace was open and that Steve Scalise helped him get tickets. He also offered this: “We have a president that doesn’t sleep, so nobody in the cabinet gets to sleep.” Enough already with the Trump praise!!! Be serious!!

NSA Updates

The NSA outage lands on top of a Bloomberg report of at least 11 suicides among NSA and Cyber Command personnel in roughly the past year, including five between early June and early July. The White House and Congress have reportedly been looking into it behind closed doors.

Remember how this agency got here. You know we keep receipts here. In April 2025, Trump fired Gen. Timothy Haugh, head of both the NSA and Cyber Command, and his deputy Wendy Noble, a day after Laura Loomer lobbied him in the Oval Office. Neither was given a reason. Loomer said publicly that they were “disloyal.” This regime purged our cyber defense leadership on “loyalty” grounds and now acts surprised that everything is breaking.

On a related note, at Navy Secretary nominee Hung Cao’s confirmation hearing, Sen. Mark Kelly raised eight suicide attempts on the USS Abraham Lincoln during one deployment. Cao called them “8 suicide mitigations.” Kelly answered that sailors shouldn’t be in conditions where they want to end their lives.

text:
Volusia's tallies have several layers of protection. Even a hacked transmission couldn't change the official count, because the official count never comes from the transmission.
What happens on election night
• The results are printed before anything is sent. When the polls close, each tabulator prints a tape of its totals, and the sworn poll workers there check it. Only after that are the results encrypted and sent to DeLand over a cellular modem. Those totals are preliminary and unofficial. This comes from the Florida Department of State's safeguards summary (https://t.co/irLkM5jzSq).
• The modem is only on briefly. The tabulators aren't connected to the internet during voting. The transmitting equipment is turned on after the polls close and turned off once the results are sent.
• Only encrypted results with the right key get in. The state document says the main office accepts only results it recognizes and can decrypt, and it compares them against the printed tapes before posting. Supervisor Lisa Lewis told the News-Journal in 2018 (https://t.co/PGdnFuhqep) that the results land on "our single server that doesn't touch the internet or any other computer whatsoever." She added that the encrypted key has to match the county's server.
• The machine is built to resist tampering. ES&S says (https://t.co/t27UtJnuOo) the DS200 accepts only approved memory sticks with a signed key, digitally signs its data, and encrypts results twice.
• The memory stick sets the official count. The ES&S results-transmission FAQ (https://t.co/oRjkYTShlp) says official results are loaded from the memory sticks at headquarters. A tampered transmission would show up as a mismatch with the stick, the tape, and the paper ballots.
Safeguards behind that
Volusia's fact sheet (https://t.co/u5a8aGmg7C) lists these:
• Every voter marks a paper ballot.
• The voter rolls and the vote-counting database sit on separate servers.
• The office patches its software monthly, and an outside firm tests and monitors the network.
• The county tests its equipment in public before every election.
• After the election, the county checks results against the paper ballots. In 2024 it used an automated check of at least 20% of precincts, and the state reported 99.99% accuracy (https://t.co/7GUaHbrlKY).
How robust it is
The design is strong where it matters most. Paper ballots, printed tapes, and stick-based official results mean a hack of the transmission could at worst mess up the election-night numbers for a while. The official count would still be safe.
The modem step is the weakest link. Election-security critics argue that any wireless connection, even a brief encrypted one, is a possible way in. That's why some Florida counties, such as Marion, hand-deliver results instead (https://t.co/xRju2I01TS). ES&S offers a private cellular network that keeps transmissions off the public internet. I couldn't find anything public saying whether Volusia uses it.
The records also leave some gaps. The county's fact sheet still describes the after-election check as a hand count of one race in one precinct, which is very small. That doesn't match the 2024 state report, which shows the larger automated check. I also didn't find any public report of a breach or of results being changed in Volusia. The one attack Lewis described was a 2016 phishing email that nobody in her office opened. Volusia's results-transmission problems in 2000 and 2004 were caused by bad memory cards on the old Diebold equipment, not hackers.
If you want the details that aren't public, you could send the Supervisor of Elections a public-records request. It would ask whether Volusia uses the private cellular network, which modem carrier it uses, and for the most recent outside security-test summary. I can draft that request for you.

text:
Gina DeJesus was 14 and Amanda Berry was 16 when a man chained them inside his house and r*p*d them for 10 years, sometimes up to 5 times a day. Amanda kept count in her diary with little X's: 3X, 4X, 5X. He ab*sed them in front of each other and laughed when they cried, so they learned to stop crying. When Amanda got pregnant, he made her give birth in a plastic kiddie pool on her bedroom floor. He was the father of Gina's school friend.

It was 2003 and 2004 in Cleveland, Ohio. Amanda was walking home from her shift at Burger King when a van pulled up and the driver offered her a ride. A year later, 14-year-old Gina was walking home from school with her friend Arlene. They split up, and minutes later Arlene's father, Ariel Castro, a local school bus driver, pulled over and asked Gina to help him find his daughter. She got in.

Inside his house on Seymour Avenue they found another girl, Michelle Knight, who had been locked there since 2002.

In the video below, Amanda and Gina tell the BBC what happened inside that house: the chains, the r*p*s, the diary of X's, and how Castro fed on their pain.

For 10 years they lived in dark rooms with boarded windows, chained by the ankles, half-starved and beaten. Castro once rode his motorcycle up to Gina's mother while she was handing out "missing" flyers, took one, and asked if there was any news about her daughter. Then he brought the flyer home and showed it to Gina.

On Christmas Day 2006, Amanda gave birth to his daughter Jocelyn. Castro wanted no baby crying in that house, so Amanda raised her in a locked room and played "school" with her every morning, walking her around the room and pretending to cross streets.

Amanda's mother never stopped searching. She died in 2006, without ever knowing her daughter was alive less than 4 miles away.

On May 6, 2013, Castro left the front door unlocked. Amanda pushed her arm through a gap in the screen door and screamed until neighbors kicked it open. Her 911 call is still one of the most famous ever recorded: "I've been missing for 10 years and I'm here."

Castro was sentenced to life plus 1,000 years. He served one month, then hanged himself in his cell. The house was torn down.

Three girls, 10 years, one house in the middle of a city. How did nobody see anything?

text:
Steve Oney, Wikipedia, and the Evidence Against Leo Frank

Argument: Steve Oney's Selective Presentation of the Evidence is Biased on Behalf of Leo Frank and His Defense

One of my strongest criticisms of Wikipedia's article on Leo Frank is its reliance on Steve Oney's 2003 book, And the Dead Shall Rise: The Murder of Mary Phagan and the Lynching of Leo Frank.

In my view, Oney's book is a deeply biased, pro-Frank account of the Mary Phagan case. He repeatedly favors the defense's interpretation of the evidence while diminishing the significance of testimony that supported Frank's conviction.

I have spent more than half a century studying the Mary Phagan case. My team and I have transcribed thousands of pages of legal records and more than 2,200 newspaper articles published in the Atlanta press between 1913 and 1915.

I began examining those records with my mother and father in Georgia public libraries during the late 1960s and early 1970s. I learned early that the way an author describes a witness's testimony can be quite different from what the original record actually says.

Oney spent seventeen years researching his book, and I give him credit for that work. But seventeen years of research does not guarantee impartiality. And that goes for any author studying the case. Time doesn't make someone necessarily impartial. 

In a review published May 5, 2004, University of Georgia law professor Donald Wilkes quoted Oney as saying he was “95 percent certain Conley did it” (Wilkes, 15).

Oney is entitled to believe Frank was innocent. He is entitled to believe Conley murdered Mary Phagan. But his belief is not evidence, and Wikipedia should not treat his interpretation as the final word on a disputed murder conviction. Oney's book cherry picks the evidence to convince the reader Leo Frank was supposedly innocent. 

Monteen Stover: Five Minutes That Oney Never Brings Together

One of the most damaging problems with Oney's presentation concerns Monteen Stover, the fourteen-year-old factory worker who went to the National Pencil Company on Saturday, April 26, 1913, to collect her pay.

The issue turns on five minutes.

On Monday morning, April 28, 1913, Leo Frank gave Chief of Detectives Newport Lanford an account of his activities on the day of Mary's murder. The statement was recorded and subsequently introduced at trial as State's Exhibit B.

Frank said Mary Phagan entered his office between 12:05 and 12:10 p.m., perhaps around 12:07.

His original words were:

“She came in between 12:05 and 12:10, maybe 12:07” (State of Georgia, 21).

Now compare that with Monteen Stover.

Stover testified at trial in July, 1913, that she entered Frank's office at 12:05 p.m. and waited until 12:10 p.m. She looked in both the outer and inner offices but did not see Frank.

She also did not see Mary Phagan.

The Atlanta Constitution, reporting her testimony on August 1, 1913, quoted her description of the office clock:

“It showed that it was 12:05” (AC, 23).

She said the clock showed 12:10 when she left.

Look at those times. They are identical.

Frank told police that Mary Phagan was in his office during the very five minutes Stover said the office was empty.

Oney reports both accounts, but he separates them.

On page 50 of And the Dead Shall Rise, he actually quotes Frank's precise arrival time from State's Exhibit B.

On pages 100–101, he describes Stover's discovery that the office was empty.

On pages 227–228, he recounts her trial testimony.

Then, on pages 299–305, he examines Frank's August 18 statement to the jury (Oney, 17).

The individual facts appear in the book. What I find missing is a direct examination of their combined significance. 

Why not put Frank's April 28 statement beside Stover's testimony and ask what happened during those five minutes?

Oney spends considerable space describing Frank's business activities, financial calculations, and defense explanations. Yet he does not give comparable attention to the specific contradiction between the two accounts.

A reader should not have to search through hundreds of pages to discover why Stover's testimony was so damaging to Frank's account of his movements.

Frank's Explanation: He Might Have Gone to the Men's Toilet in the Machine Department Where Blood was Found on the Floor and Hair on a Lathe

There is another part of Frank's statement that I believe Oney should have examined more closely.

On Monday, August 18, 1913, Frank addressed the jury in an unsworn statement. He maintained that, to the best of his recollection, he had remained in his office from noon until he went upstairs to speak with Arthur White and Harry Denham.

But he acknowledged a possible exception:

“It is possible that in order to answer a call of nature or to urinate I may have gone to the toilet” (Frank, 9).

He also explained that such actions could be performed unconsciously and that he could not remember how often or when he might have done so.

Frank did not positively testify that he visited the toilet at 12:05 p.m. He suggested it as a possibility.

That is a significant qualification.

The toilet he referred to was in the second-floor metal department, the area where the prosecution maintained that Mary Phagan had been assaulted. Conley testified to finding Mary Phagan dead in that machine department, known as the metal room, adjacent to the entryway of the men's toilet. 

Frank also argued that the open 4.5 foot tall office-safe door could have obstructed the 5'1" Stover's view of him.

These were alternative explanations. He might have been sitting behind the safe door, or he might have briefly left his office.

But what does either explanation do to his original statement that Mary Phagan entered his office between 12:05 and 12:10?

If he remained behind the safe door, why did Stover report that she could find nobody when she looked into his office?

If he went to the toilet, when did he leave, how long was he gone, and how did that journey fit the time he originally assigned to Mary's visit?

These are questions the jury could consider.

Frank's statement about the possible toilet visit also appears in the surviving trial record. Although the language is conditional, its relationship to Stover's testimony deserves examination.

Oney devotes pages to Frank's lengthy explanations of invoices and financial calculations. Yet I have not found Frank's specific toilet explanation reproduced in that discussion.

In my judgment, that omission weakens Oney's account of one of the most consequential conflicts in the prosecution's timeline.

Why These Five Minutes Matter

The importance of Stover's testimony is not that she witnessed a murder.

She did not.

Its importance is that she gave investigators a narrow interval during which Frank was not where he had previously placed himself. And he had placed himself with Mary at that exact time. 

The prosecution argued that Frank had taken Mary toward the metal department, where the murder occurred. The defense argued that Mary arrived later than Frank originally estimated and that Stover therefore missed both of them. Conley stated Mary went upstairs before Monteen Stover. 

Those are competing explanations.

The streetcar timetable was disputed, and different witnesses offered different arrival estimates. At the end of the trial witness remember seeing Mary enter the factory at about noon. 

But an author should not simply accept a reconstructed streetcar schedule as though it automatically cancels the time Frank himself gave police.

The correct historical question is whether the original accounts can be reconciled and, if so, how.

Oney's @steveoneywriter  treatment leaves the reader without the direct comparison I believe the evidence demands.

The Grand Jury: Oney's Unsupported Reconstruction

Another serious problem appears on pages 115–117 of Oney's book.

On May 23 and 24, 1913, the Fulton County grand jury considered the evidence against Leo Frank, after several days.

The grand jury returned a murder indictment. Unanimously, 21 to 0, at least four of its members were Jews.

Oney describes the prosecution as presenting a limited amount of evidence and suggests that the grand jurors accepted Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey's assurances that additional evidence would be revealed later, but that's not how a grand jury works. Grand juries don't indict on promises to later provide evidence. 

On page 116, he writes that the jurors were:

“evidently taking on faith Dorsey's assurances” (Oney, 17).

That is a serious historical assertion.

What evidence establishes that Dorsey made such assurances inside the grand-jury room?

Where is the contemporary report quoting the alleged promise?

Where is the statement from a grand juror saying he agreed to indict because Dorsey promised to produce more evidence later?

The proceedings were secret, and no verbatim transcript of the grand jury's testimony or deliberations survives.

That makes Oney's reconstruction especially questionable.

His use of the word “evidently” signals an inference, but readers are entitled to know that it is an inference rather than a documented account of the jurors' reasoning.

Oney does not claim the indictment vote itself was unanimous. On page 117, he acknowledges that the individual votes were unknown and that only twelve were required. To admit that it was unanimous would be dis-favorable to Leo Frank. 

The contemporary evidence does, however, establish that twenty-one grand jurors signed the indictment. I publish the legal records and newspaper accounts on my website https://t.co/MNvBytB3CS 

That fact deserves to be considered alongside what the witnesses reportedly told the grand jury.

What the Atlanta Journal Reported on May 25, 1913

On Sunday, May 25, 1913, The Atlanta Journal published a detailed report titled:

“State Didn't Show Its Case to Secure Indictment Against Superintendent Leo M. Frank.”

The headline acknowledged that Dorsey had not presented his entire case.

But the article also identified substantial witness testimony presented before the grand jury (AJ, 24).

According to the newspaper, the witnesses included Dr. J. W. Hurt, Police Sergeant L. S. Dobbs, Detective J. N. Starnes, machinist R. P. Barrett, former policeman W. W. Rogers, Grace Hicks, day watchman E. F. Holloway, factory foreman M. B. Darley, Pinkerton detective Harry Scott, Detective B. B. Haslett, Monteen Stover, J. M. Gantt, and undertaker William Gheesling.

We have their later trial testimony through the Leo Frank trial brief of evidence. 

These witnesses addressed different parts of the investigation.

Dr. Hurt described medical findings concerning Mary's body.

Sergeant Dobbs discussed the discovery of the body and the original basement investigation.

Barrett addressed the suspected blood and hair evidence discovered in the metal department.

Rogers described Frank's conduct during the early investigation.

Holloway discussed the condition and position of the factory elevator.

Scott reported his investigation and Frank's encounter with Newt Lee.

Haslett testified concerning Frank's demeanor when arrested.

Stover addressed the critical noon-hour interval during which she found Frank's office empty.

Gantt described Frank's behavior when he returned to the factory on the evening of April 26.

That is not a grand jury that heard no evidence was presented to, so the Oney idea that the grand jury would indict on no or little evidence, only on Dorsey's promise to later provide evidence, is a totally bogus assertion.

It was a grand jury that heard multiple witnesses presenting medical observations, physical evidence, investigative findings, and circumstantial evidence concerning the accused.

The Journal also reported that Dorsey had not introduced the murder notes, Frank's police statement, or the complete results of various tests. Conley did not testify at the grand jury, meaning that Frank was unanimously indicted without Jim Conley's oral testimony. 

Those omissions by Oney are significant. But the absence of some evidence does not mean the jurors relied on a promise of evidence later to convict later.

The grand jury's responsibility was to determine whether probable cause existed to issue an indictment, not whether the prosecution had already established guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

The May 25 newspaper report stated that twenty-one of the twenty-three grand jurors signed the indictment, the other two being absent. The jurors deliberated for approximately five minutes (AJ, 24). 21 jurors present voted to indict Leo Frank.

A short deliberation does not prove the jurors were deceived, nor does it establish that their decision was correct. They heard the testimony of people who had testified at the Coroner's inquest which was published in the press and they also testified at the trial which was also published in the press and legal records published on my website. 

What it establishes is that the grand jury acted after hearing witness testimony.

Oney's suggestion that the jurors relied on assurances about evidence to be produced later requires proof beyond the fact that Dorsey did not present every item then available.

The Indictment Did Not Depend on Jim Conley's Later Murder Accusation

There is another point worth emphasizing.

Conley had not yet given the full account of the murder that he subsequently presented at Frank's trial.

The May 25 Journal reported that Conley was not examined before the grand jury and that Dorsey had not introduced his statement about writing the murder notes. That's worth contemplating. 

Consequently, the indictment against Frank did not depend upon Conley's later account of helping Frank move Mary's body.

That fact challenges the suggestion that the entire prosecution case consisted of Conley's word against Frank's.

The grand jury had already found grounds to indict Frank before hearing Conley's eventual trial account.

The indictment was not a conviction. It did not establish Frank's guilt. But it was a genuine legal proceeding supported by real testimony from real witness. I encourage you to read what they swore to under oath at the Mary Phagan Coroner's inquest and later at the Mary Phagan murder trial where Leo Frank was defendant. 

Oney's account should not diminish that distinction by suggesting that the grand jurors relied principally upon a promise of future proof.

The Elevator Pit: Evidence That Deserves More Attention

A similar question arises concerning Oney's treatment of the factory elevator.

One of the defense's strongest arguments concerned human waste found in the elevator pit.

Conley testified that he had relieved himself near the elevator pit on Saturday morning, April 26, and later helped Frank transport Mary's body into the basement using the freight elevator.

When police operated the elevator on Sunday morning, the descending car crushed the waste.

The defense argued that if the elevator had carried Mary's body down on Saturday afternoon, it would have crushed the waste then.

Governor John M. Slaton considered that argument when he commuted Frank's sentence on June 21, 1915 (Slaton, 22). Slaton looked at the elevator shaft 2 years after the murder after it had been cleared out and the elevator could descend plum to the ground, but that elevator shaft 2 years earlier was filled with debris from stem to stern. Steve Oney’s And the Dead Shall Rise is biased in favor of Leo Frank from stem to stern. His book is advocacy, not dispassionate history. In my 1987 book the Murder of Little Mary Phagan, I gave both the prosecution and defense a fair hearing. In my 2025 book, I expose many of the frauds and hoaxes promoted by pro-Frank activist authors. 

And with regard to the "shit in the shaft theory" the original police testimony establishes that the bottom of the elevator pit was not an unobstructed surface. And the police went through that trash looking for evidence.

At the coroner's inquest, policeman R. M. Lassiter described finding Mary's parasol, a ball of wrapping twine, and substantial debris in the elevator pit. Think about how much trash would be required in an elevator pit to make it so that the bottom couldnt be seen. 

Asked about the material forming the floor, he explained that he could not see it because the pit was full of trash (AG, 18).

The trial brief also records Lassiter's description of the debris.

“There is a whole lot of trash at the bottom.” (BOE, 19).

That detail mattered in 1913 because it was observed on April 27.

Before declaring that the elevator's descent must have crushed every object beneath it, investigators needed to establish the depth and distribution of the debris, the precise position of the human waste, and the elevator's clearance above the underlying floor.

The surviving testimony does not establish all those measurements.

Lassiter also testified that officers found and removed objects from the pit during the initial investigation. The removal of objects might have enabled the elevator to go down further. 

That raises questions about whether the original position of the loose debris was preserved before later elevator movements.

Oney mentions the trash, parasol, twine, and waste on pages 30–31. My criticism is not that he excluded every reference to these objects.

It is that he does not reproduce Lassiter's specific testimony that the debris prevented him from seeing the floor, a detail directly relevant to the elevator reconstruction.

The physical evidence should be examined before accepting a mechanical explanation as conclusive.

Counterargument: Oney Reports Much of the Evidence

Defenders of Oney can fairly point out that his book contains substantial material concerning the prosecution's case.

Oney quotes Frank's April 28 statement, reproduces Monteen Stover's account, describes the grand-jury proceedings (in my opinion ridiculously), and discusses the elevator evidence. But he scatters these facts throughout his book, making it difficult for readers to connect the dots. More troubling, he omits or minimizes critical details that would allow readers to understand how the evidence fits together.

Oney's supporters may argue that his book contains enough information for readers to compare the competing explanations. They may also argue that a historian cannot reproduce every question, answer, and document in a single volume. I agree. But that is precisely why an author's choices are so important. What he includes, what he leaves out, and how he arranges the evidence can fundamentally change the reader's understanding of the case.

My criticism is that Oney repeatedly makes those choices in Frank's favor. He provides enough information to appear thorough but too often fails to bring together the very facts that challenge the defense's narrative. Readers should not have to reconstruct the prosecution's case from fragments scattered across hundreds of pages. In my view, Oney's book is biased in favor of Leo Frank.

The Reader Should Not Have to Reconstruct the Case for the Author

My response is straightforward.

A historian does not have to reproduce every page of a trial transcript. But when several pieces of evidence bear directly on the same question, the author has a responsibility to explain how those facts fit together. 

Most readers do not have the time to examine 3,000 pages of legal records and 10,000 pages of newspaper reports in this case between 1913 and 1915. That is precisely why historians are expected to sift through the evidence, separate fact from speculation, provide historical context, and explain how the pieces fit together. Their job is to help readers understand the evidence, not scatter critical facts throughout a book or leave out details that might challenge the author's preferred conclusions.

Frank gave police a specific time for Mary's arrival in an unsworn deposition.

Stover testified that Frank's office was empty during those exact minutes.

Frank later acknowledged that he might have left his office to use the men's toilet. 

Conley testified he found the dead body of Mary Phagan near the corridor entry way to men's toilet. 

Those are four facts should be examined together.

Oney presents the first two in different portions of his book, but I have not found a direct discussion of all four in which the toilet explanation receives the attention it deserves. Yet the prosecution brought these points up. So why does Oney diminish the prosecution's key points, and scatter them, omit them, or seemingly hide them? 

Likewise, the grand jury heard numerous witnesses before indicting Frank. It did not need to hear the entire prosecution case, nor did it need Conley's eventual trial testimony. Why does Oney hide the names of people who testified and what they said at the Coroner's inquest and later at the trial to suggest what they might have testified at the grandjury? Instead he tells us the indictment was sort of based on a promise that evidence would be revealed later after they indict. Loosely: "Just indict now with no evidence, I promise to later deliver evidence after you indict at the trial"

Oney's suggestion that the jurors accepted a promise of additional evidence goes beyond what the surviving newspaper record establishes.

I do not regard that as a fair substitute for documentary proof of a sealed hearing.

The same problem appears in the elevator discussion. Oney recounts some of the physical findings but gives insufficient attention, in my judgment, to testimony that complicates the defense's explanation.

And his handling of Pierre van Paassen's alleged bite-mark evidence helps preserve a story for which the original photographs and authenticated forensic findings have not been established.

These are just some examples of why I consider And the Dead Shall Rise a defense-oriented account rather than an impartial history. His book is filled with these kinds of biases from beginning to end.

I am not asking readers to accept my conclusions without examination.

I am asking them to compare Oney's presentation with the original sources. The trial brief of evidence and newspaper accounts of the case are now all available online. They are public domain. When he published his book they were not on the Internet so he could get away with saying whatever he wanted. Now his book can be fact checked and its filled with bias on behalf of Leo Frank. 

If my interpretation is wrong, show me the relevant page, testimony, or document. My belief is in open debate, and I have debated a number of people here on X. I believe the truth is a process, not a destination. I have made mistakes in my 1987 book that I corrected in my 2025 book.

But if an author makes a claim about what twenty-one grand jurors supposedly believed inside a closed proceeding, the author should be expected to identify the evidence supporting that claim.

And if a defendant gives police a precise time for his encounter with a murder victim, then a witness says his office was empty during those same five minutes, the contradiction deserves direct examination.

My team and I have spent years transcribing the original evidence so that readers can conduct those comparisons themselves.

Wikipedia should apply the same scrutiny to Oney that it applies to writers who challenge Frank's innocence.

The original records should control our understanding of the case, not the personal convictions of authors writing ninety or a hundred years later.

text:
Michael Jordan won his first three rings on $2.5 million, $3.25 million and $4 million a year.
For 12 seasons the best player alive was paid like a good starter.
Then he collected the back pay in two seasons flat.

Receipts: $28.7 million for his first 12 NBA seasons, per Basketball-Reference. Then $30.14 million in 1996-97 and $33.14 million in 1997-98.
That's $63.3 million in two years. About two-thirds of everything the NBA ever paid him.

In the video below, Jordan at his Hall of Fame speech. Back from a broken foot in 1986, he wanted more minutes. He says owner Jerry Reinsdorf told him he had to protect the "long term of investment."
The investment was making $630,000 that season.
Then the contract flex: a "love of the game clause." Any time, any place.

How did that happen? He locked in early. Then TV money flooded the league, the salary cap more than tripled, and his paycheck stayed parked.
The Layaway GOAT.

In 1993 he quit to play minor league baseball. Reinsdorf kept paying his basketball salary anyway.
The only Double-A outfielder in America on an NBA contract.

1996, after ring No. 4. By Reinsdorf's own telling, he offered $20 million. Agent David Falk came back with two options: $30 million for one year, or $55 million for two.
Reinsdorf took the one year to keep it short.

A year later the price went up. $33 million.
He paid $63 million to avoid paying $55. Saving money cost him eight MILLION.

That $30.14 million alone was bigger than the entire 1996-97 salary cap, $24.36 million for a whole team.
One man, over the cap by himself.

"Someone has to generate the revenue to pay them," Reinsdorf says at his own Hall of Fame speech.
For 12 seasons, that someone was Jordan.

Hypothetical: you own the Bulls in 1996. $30 million for one year of Jordan, or $55 million for two. Which one do you sign?

text:
In 1998, Warren Buffett gave a 1-hour masterclass on how to never lose money investing.

Here are the 22 most valuable lessons from his lecture:

1. You only have to get rich once. If you have $100 million and can make 10% unleveraged or 20% leveraged, the difference between $110 million and $120 million at year-end means nothing to your life, your family, or anything. But the downside, especially with other people's money, is disgrace, humiliation, and facing the friends whose money you lost. The equation never makes sense.

2. To make money they did not need, they risked money they did have and needed. That is just plain foolish, Buffett says, regardless of your IQ. If you hand him a gun with a million chambers and one bullet and offer him any sum to put it to his temple and pull once, he will not do it. There is nothing on the upside that justifies the downside. People do this financially all the time without thinking.

3. The smartest people in finance went broke, and that is the most fascinating story Buffett knows. Long-term Capital Management had 16 people with possibly the highest average IQ of any business in the country, 350 to 400 combined years of experience, and most of their own net worth in the firm. They still went bankrupt. Buffett says if he ever wrote a book, it would be called why smart people do dumb things.

4. Beta and sigmas tell you nothing about the real risk of going broke. The LTCM team relied heavily on mathematics and believed a six- or seven-sigma event could not touch them. They were wrong. History does not tell you the probabilities of future financial events. The real risk is not volatility. It is a permanent, irreversible blind spot in something crucial, often caused by knowing a great deal about something else.

5. Invest only in businesses you can understand. That one rule narrows the field by about 90%, and that is fine. Buffett can understand Coca-Cola. he cannot value an internet company, and he says if a student handed him a valuation of one on a final exam, he would flunk them. People thought Enron was incredible because it had a good track record, but almost nobody understood how it made money. That was the signal to avoid it.

6. You want a business that is a castle with a wide moat around it. Inside the castle, you want an honest, able, hard-working duke. The moat can be low cost, like Geico in auto insurance, or brand, or patents, or location. But a wonderful castle will always be attacked, so the job of every manager Buffett owns is one thing: widen the moat. Throw crocodiles and sharks into it to keep competitors out.

7. Moats change slowly and invisibly, but they change. Thirty years ago, Kodak's moat was as wide as Coca-Cola's. They had share of mind; the little yellow box meant best in everyone's head. Then they let Fuji into the Olympics and narrowed their own moat. Coca-Cola's moat, by contrast, is wider now than 30 years ago. Every time infrastructure gets built in a country that is not yet profitable, the moat widens a little. You cannot see it day by day, but in 10 years, the difference is enormous.

8. Share of mind beats share of market. When you say Disney, every person in the room has something in their head. Say Universal Pictures or 20th Century Fox, and you have nothing. A mother with two kids will pick the $17.95 Disney video over the $16.95 alternative because she knows it will be fine and does not want to preview ten videos to decide. That little bit of certainty in the customer's mind is worth a fortune.

9. The best businesses have pricing power and require little capital. see's candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 when Buffett bought it for $25 million. The entire thesis was whether the price could go to $2.25 without hurting sales. It could, because nobody wants to hand their valentine a box of candy and say, "This year I took the low bid." Today, See's makes $60 million on the same formulas and still takes almost no capital. Compare that to GM, which had to reinvest every dollar into better factories and whose stock barely moved over 50 years.

10. The best businesses earn a royalty on other people's capital. Coca-Cola sells a formula and collects a royalty on every drink. American Express takes a few percent of every dollar you spend. You put up the capital, they take a cut. Low capital intensity is one of the most underrated qualities in a business and one of the surest paths to durable wealth.

11. Define your circle of competence and stay inside it. The size of the circle does not matter. Staying inside, it does. If you know which 30 companies out of thousands you actually understand, you are fine. Buffett understood H.H. brown shoes and Frank Rooney, so he closed that deal in five minutes. If you do not know enough to understand a business instantly, you will not understand it in a month either.

12. Ignore the macro entirely. Buffett has never bought or skipped a business because of a feeling about interest rates, the economy, or any macro forecast. If Alan Greenspan and Bob Rubin both whispered exactly what they would do for the next 12 months, it would not change what he pays for anything. You want to focus on what is important and knowable. The macro is important but not knowable, so you ignore it.

13. Inactivity is the strategy, not a flaw. Wall Street makes money on activity. You make money on inactivity. A broker is like a doctor paid by how often he changes your pills. If everyone in a room trades their portfolio with everyone else every day, they all end up broke, and the intermediary keeps the money. Buffett looks for one good idea a year and rides it to its full potential. He measures Berkshire by how little turnover there is, like a church where the same people fill the seats every Sunday.

14. If you understand businesses, diversification is a mistake. For the 99% who will not evaluate businesses, Buffett recommends a low-cost index fund and extreme diversification. But if you bring real intensity to evaluating companies, owning more than six is a terrible idea. Very few people got rich on their seventh best idea. A lot of people got rich on their best one. Buffett keeps about half his money in what he likes best.

15. Buffett's biggest mistakes are mistakes of omission, not commission. The times he understood a business well enough to act and instead sat there sucking his thumb. He passed on healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan and on Fannie Mae in the mid-eighties, each a multi-billion-dollar miss. Accounting never captures these. The $2,000 he put into a Sinclair service station as a young man, money he lost, has an opportunity cost of about $6 billion today.

16. Focus on what will happen, not when. Coca-Cola went public in 1919 at $40 a share and dropped to $19 within a year. There was always a reason not to buy: the great depression, world war, sugar rationing, thermonuclear weapons. But one share bought then and reinvested would be worth about $5 million. If you are right about the business, you will make a lot of money. The timing is the tricky part, so do not focus on it.

17. When hiring, look for integrity, intelligence, and energy. But if the person lacks the first one, you actually want them dumb and lazy. Because a person with intelligence and energy but no integrity will destroy you. Buffett borrowed this from Pete Kiewit. The trait everyone screens for last is the one that matters most.

18. Here is a thought experiment Buffett gives students. Imagine you could own 10% of one classmate for the rest of their life. You would not pick the highest IQ or the best grades. You would pick the person you respond to best, the one who is generous, honest, gives credit to others, and has leadership qualities. Now imagine you also had to short one classmate. You would pick the egotistical, greedy, slightly dishonest one. The qualities that decide both are not talent. They are character.

19. Every quality on the admirable side is achievable, and every quality on the repellent side is removable. The things that make you want to own 10% of someone are not the ability to throw a football or run fast; they are behavior, temperament, and character, all of which anyone can choose. Buffett's point: you already own 100% of yourself, so you might as well become the person worth betting on.

20. The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken. Buffett sees people in their forties and fifties trapped by self-destructive patterns they can no longer change. At a young age, you can choose any habits you want. Ben Franklin and Ben Graham both did exactly this, looking at people they admired and simply deciding to behave like them. There was nothing impossible about it.

21. Take a job you would take if you were already independently wealthy. Buffett told a 28-year-old at Harvard who wanted a consulting job "to look good on his resume" that it was like saving up sex for your old age. There comes a time to just start doing what you love. Buffett offered to work for Ben Graham for free, was told he was overpriced, and kept pestering him for years. Take the job you would jump out of bed for. You cannot miss.

22. You won the ovarian lottery, and that should shape how you think. Buffett imagines a genie 24 hours before your birth letting you design the world's rules, with one catch: you do not know which of 5.8 billion balls you will draw. Born here or in Afghanistan, with an IQ of 130 or 70, male or female, able-bodied or not. If you could put your ball back and draw one of 100 random others, most people would not, because they are already in the luckiest 1%. Buffett knows he is perfectly wired for a market economy that pays him like crazy, while an equally good citizen leading scout troops and teaching Sunday school is not, purely by luck.

text:
🏛️ ROMAN MYTHOLOGY IN 100 FACTS

⚡ THE GREAT GODS
𝟏. Jupiter was king of the gods, ruler of the sky and thunder, the Roman counterpart of Zeus

𝟐. His Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill was Rome's most important temple, traditionally dedicated in 509 BC

𝟑. Jupiter, Juno and Minerva were worshipped together as the Capitoline Triad

𝟒. Juno, queen of the gods, protected women and marriage, and the month of June is often said to be named after her

𝟓. Rome's mint stood by the temple of Juno Moneta, which is where the words "money" and "mint" come from

𝟔. Minerva, goddess of wisdom, crafts and strategy, was the Roman equivalent of Athena

𝟕. Mars, god of war and father of Romulus and Remus, was second only to Jupiter in importance, and March is named after him

𝟖. The Campus Martius, the "Field of Mars", was where Rome's armies once trained and assembled

𝟗. Venus, goddess of love, was honoured as the ancestress of the Roman people through her son Aeneas

𝟏𝟎. Julius Caesar's family claimed descent from Venus, and he built her a temple as Venus Genetrix, "Venus the Mother"

𝟏𝟏. Neptune, god of the sea, is thought to have originally been a god of fresh water

𝟏𝟐. Pluto, also called Dis Pater, ruled the underworld, like the Greek Hades

𝟏𝟑. Apollo was one of the few gods Rome took over from Greece without changing his name

𝟏𝟒. Diana, goddess of the hunt and the moon, had a famous sanctuary in the woods by Lake Nemi

𝟏𝟓. Mercury, messenger of the gods and patron of trade, was linked by ancient writers to "merx", the Latin word for goods

𝟏𝟔. Vulcan, god of fire and the forge, gave his name to the word "volcano"

𝟏𝟕. Vesta, goddess of the hearth, had no statue in her round temple in the Forum, only an eternal sacred flame

𝟏𝟖. Ceres, goddess of grain and harvests, gave English the word "cereal"

𝟏𝟗. Bacchus, god of wine, was so feared for his secret night rites that the Senate cracked down on the Bacchanalia in 186 BC

𝟐𝟎. Saturn, god of sowing, was said to have ruled Italy during a lost Golden Age, and Saturday still carries his name

𝟐𝟏. Janus, the two-faced god of doors and beginnings, had no Greek equivalent and gave his name to January

𝟐𝟐. The doors of the Temple of Janus stood open in wartime and were closed in peace, which reportedly happened only a handful of times

𝟐𝟑. Gilded statues of the twelve Dii Consentes, the great gods of Rome, stood in a portico in the Roman Forum

𝟐𝟒. Five planets visible to the naked eye carry Roman god names: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn

𝟐𝟓. Cupid, the winged son of Venus, was the Roman version of the Greek Eros

🐺 THE FOUNDING OF ROME
𝟐𝟔. Aeneas, a Trojan prince, fled burning Troy carrying his father Anchises and leading his son Ascanius

𝟐𝟕. Virgil's Aeneid, written in the time of Augustus, tells of his long journey to Italy

𝟐𝟖. In Carthage, Aeneas fell in love with Queen Dido, and her dying curse was said to explain Rome's wars with Carthage

𝟐𝟗. Aeneas visited the underworld, guided by the Sibyl of Cumae

𝟑𝟎. In Italy he fought and killed Turnus, king of the Rutuli

𝟑𝟏. His son Ascanius, also called Iulus, founded Alba Longa, and the Julian family claimed descent from him

𝟑𝟐. Rhea Silvia, a Vestal priestess, bore the twins Romulus and Remus, fathered by the god Mars

𝟑𝟑. Her uncle, King Amulius, ordered the babies drowned in the Tiber

𝟑𝟒. A she-wolf found and nursed the twins, and a woodpecker, a bird sacred to Mars, is said to have brought them food

𝟑𝟓. The shepherd Faustulus and his wife Acca Larentia raised the boys

𝟑𝟔. The Lupercal, a cave below the Palatine Hill, was honoured as the place where the wolf nursed them

𝟑𝟕. Romulus killed Remus in a quarrel over the new city's walls

𝟑𝟖. Rome's traditional founding date is 21 April 753 BC, still celebrated as the city's birthday

𝟑𝟗. Romulus was said to have vanished in a storm and to have been worshipped afterwards as the god Quirinus

𝟒𝟎. Short of wives, the first Romans abducted women of the neighbouring Sabines

𝟒𝟏. The Sabine women later threw themselves between their fathers and husbands to stop the war

𝟒𝟐. Numa Pompilius, Rome's second king, is said to have set up many religious rites on the advice of the nymph Egeria

𝟒𝟑. The twins under the famous bronze Capitoline Wolf were added in the Renaissance, and some tests suggest the wolf itself is medieval

🔥 PRIESTS & SACRED RITES
𝟒𝟒. The Vestal Virgins, six priestesses of Vesta, served for at least 30 years

𝟒𝟓. A Vestal who broke her vow of chastity was buried alive

𝟒𝟔. If Vesta's sacred fire ever went out, it was taken as a terrible omen for Rome

𝟒𝟕. The chief priest of Rome was the Pontifex Maximus, a title later used by the popes

𝟒𝟖. Augurs read the will of the gods from the flight of birds, which gave English the word "auspices"

𝟒𝟗. Haruspices, following an Etruscan tradition, read the gods' messages in the entrails of sacrificed animals

𝟓𝟎. The Sibylline Books, a collection of prophecies, were consulted only in times of crisis

𝟓𝟏. The Salii, leaping priests of Mars, danced through Rome with sacred shields, one of which was said to have fallen from heaven

𝟓𝟐. The Flamen Dialis, Jupiter's priest, lived under many taboos, among them a ban on riding a horse

𝟓𝟑. Julius Caesar became the first Roman officially made a god, helped by a comet that appeared after his murder in 44 BC

𝟓𝟒. The Pantheon, a temple to all the gods rebuilt under Hadrian, still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome

🏠 SPIRITS & LESSER GODS
𝟓𝟓. The Lares were guardian spirits of the home, honoured at a small household shrine called a lararium

𝟓𝟔. The Penates watched over the family's pantry and food stores

𝟓𝟕. Every man was believed to have a guardian spirit called his Genius, and every woman her Juno

𝟓𝟖. The Manes were the spirits of the dead, honoured by their families

𝟓𝟗. At the Lemuria festival in May, the father of the house threw black beans to drive restless ghosts away

𝟔𝟎. Terminus, god of boundary stones, was said to have refused to move when Jupiter's temple was built on his spot

𝟔𝟏. Fortuna, goddess of luck, was often shown with a ship's rudder, a wheel or a horn of plenty

𝟔𝟐. Faunus, the god of forests and herds, was linked with the Greek Pan

𝟔𝟑. Pomona, goddess of fruit trees, was won over by Vertumnus, the god of the changing seasons, in Ovid's tale

𝟔𝟒. Flora, goddess of flowers and spring, gave her name to the word "flora"

𝟔𝟓. Robigus was the god of crop disease, and a dog was sacrificed at his festival to protect the wheat

𝟔𝟔. Portunus was the god of keys, doors and harbours

𝟔𝟕. Bellona, goddess of war, had a temple where the Senate met to discuss wars and receive returning generals

𝟔𝟖. Victoria, goddess of victory, had an altar in the Senate House whose removal in AD 382 caused a famous dispute

𝟔𝟗. Aurora, goddess of the dawn, lends her name to the northern and southern lights

𝟕𝟎. Emperor Aurelian made Sol Invictus, the "Unconquered Sun", an official cult in AD 274

𝟕𝟏. Somnus was the god of sleep and his brother Mors the god of death

🎉 FESTIVALS
𝟕𝟐. Saturnalia began on 17 December with feasting, gift-giving, the cry "Io Saturnalia!" and masters sometimes serving their slaves

𝟕𝟑. At the Lupercalia on 15 February, young priests ran around the Palatine striking women with goat-skin straps, believed to bring fertility

𝟕𝟒. During the Lupercalia of 44 BC, Mark Antony publicly offered Julius Caesar a crown, which Caesar refused

𝟕𝟓. The Parilia on 21 April purified shepherds and their flocks and doubled as Rome's birthday

𝟕𝟔. The Floralia, held from late April into May, was known for its lively games and theatre

𝟕𝟕. At the Vestalia in June, Rome's matrons walked barefoot to the temple of Vesta with offerings

𝟕𝟖. The Ludi Romani, the oldest regular games of Rome, were held each September in honour of Jupiter

𝟕𝟗. In the October Horse rite on 15 October, a winning chariot horse was sacrificed to Mars

𝟖𝟎. The early Roman year began in March, which is why September, from "septem", once meant the seventh month

📜 MYTHS & LEGENDS
𝟖𝟏. Ovid's Metamorphoses, finished around AD 8, retells more than 250 myths and shaped how later Europe saw the gods

𝟖𝟐. Ovid's tale of Pyramus and Thisbe, two lovers kept apart by their parents, influenced Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet

𝟖𝟑. Baucis and Philemon, a poor old couple, welcomed Jupiter and Mercury in disguise and were rewarded when everyone else turned them away

𝟖𝟒. Apuleius's novel The Golden Ass, from the 2nd century AD, contains the love story of Cupid and Psyche

𝟖𝟓. Horatius Cocles is said to have held a bridge over the Tiber alone against an Etruscan army

𝟖𝟔. Mucius Scaevola put his right hand into a fire to show the Etruscan king Lars Porsena that Romans did not fear pain

𝟖𝟕. The story of Lucretia is tied to the fall of Rome's kings and the birth of the Republic in 509 BC

𝟖𝟖. Tarpeia betrayed Rome's citadel to the Sabines and was crushed under their shields, giving her name to the Tarpeian Rock

𝟖𝟗. Marcus Curtius is said to have ridden his horse into a chasm in the Forum to save the city

𝟗𝟎. The sacred geese of Juno are said to have woken the defenders when the Gauls tried to take the Capitol around 390 BC

𝟗𝟏. The twins Castor and Pollux were said to have fought for Rome at the Battle of Lake Regillus and had a temple in the Forum

𝟗𝟐. Hercules was said to have killed Cacus, a fire-breathing giant who stole his cattle, near the future site of Rome

🌍 LEGACY
𝟗𝟑. Spanish weekdays still honour the gods: martes (Mars), miércoles (Mercury), jueves (Jupiter) and viernes (Venus)

𝟗𝟒. English words like "jovial", "martial" and "mercurial" come from Jove, Mars and Mercury

𝟗𝟓. January, March, May and June are all linked to Roman deities: Janus, Mars, Maia and Juno

𝟗𝟔. Shakespeare, Titian and Rubens were among the many artists who retold the Roman myths found in Ovid

𝟗𝟕. The central figure of Rome's Trevi Fountain is often called Neptune but actually represents Oceanus

𝟗𝟖. NASA's Mercury, Gemini and Apollo programmes all drew their names from Roman and Greek mythology

𝟗𝟗. Rome adopted foreign gods too, bringing the mother goddess Cybele, the Magna Mater, from Asia Minor in 204 BC

𝟏𝟎𝟎. Under Emperor Theodosius in the late 4th century, pagan sacrifices were banned, and the Vestal fire was reportedly put out around AD 394

📸 The Capitoline Wolf nursing Romulus and Remus, Capitoline Museums, Rome. Photo: Merulana, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
