In 1995, Yolanda Saldívar sat in a TV studio behind bars and told ABC's camera: "I did not kill Selena." She ran the fan club, and she says Selena used to call her Mom. That spring she shot the 23-year-old singer in a Corpus Christi motel room. Then she finished the sentence:

"It was an accident, and my conscience is clear."

A Houston jury had taken less than three hours to reject that. On October 23, 1995, they convicted her of murder. Three days later she got life in prison, with no parole for 30 years.

She met Selena in 1991 and offered to start her fan club. By 1995 she was running Selena's boutiques too. Then Selena's father, Abraham Quintanilla, said he found forged checks and proof she was taking money from the club and the stores. In March he and Selena confronted her.

On the morning of March 31, Selena went alone to Saldívar's room at a Days Inn. One shot. Selena made it to the lobby and collapsed, and she died at the hospital that afternoon. Saldívar sat in the motel parking lot with the gun to her own head for more than nine hours before she gave up.

In the interview her story runs the other way. She says she was the one quitting. Selena grabbed her feet and begged her to stay. Saldívar put the gun to her own head, Selena got up and said "Mom, we need to talk about this," walked to close the door, and the gun went off.

In the video below, she presses a finger to her temple to show where the gun was, and her voice stays flat the whole time.

Prosecutor Carlos Valdez said her whole world was walking out the door. Selena's parents doubt their daughter ever called her Mom. Saldívar ended the interview with "Selena will always be a daughter for me."

In March 2025, after 30 years, the Texas parole board turned her down. Her next review is in 2030.

Selena was 23. Saldívar will be 69 at that hearing.

Did Selena really call her Mom, or is that just the story Saldívar needs to believe?

text:
SCP-496: THE WATER LOOKS INVITING

SCP-496 starts as a marine contamination problem and gradually opens into something much stranger beneath the seabed.

The substance resembles bleached coral and converts infected organic matter into more of itself. Contact with contaminated water is dangerous, and moisture speeds the process even when it relieves some discomfort. During her infection, Agent Viva describes an underwater city, its inhabitants, and a coral-decorated temple. She becomes desperate to return to the water.

Later exploration discovers ancient structures resembling her account beneath the deposit, along with many infected humanoids. The discovery gives her descriptions a basis beyond an ordinary hallucination, but it doesn't establish that the place offers the happiness she believed she saw.

That distinction matters to me. A vision can contain accurate information and still be a terrible guide to what you should do. Recognizing a real place doesn't prove that its invitation is honest, or that what looks beautiful from one perspective is safe for the person being drawn toward it.

The relief from water is an especially nasty detail. When something hurts, reaching for whatever makes it feel better is natural. Here, the immediate comfort helps the underlying problem progress. You don't need a foolish character for that to work. You need somebody who is frightened, uncomfortable, and trying to get through the next minute.

I think the city is more effective because we encounter it first through a person whose condition is deteriorating. For a while, you can hope she is simply describing something unreal. Then the investigation takes away that easy explanation without replacing it with anything reassuring.

There is plenty I would want to know, but I wouldn't rush to answer all of it in a story. Were the people below always there? Did they choose what happened? Is the invitation a memory, a shared perception, or something actively reaching outward? Those are questions the article leaves open, and the uncertainty gives the setting room to breathe.

The human cost should remain central, though. It would be easy to become so interested in the underwater architecture that the infected person turns into a convenient source of clues. Her fear and changing perception are what make the discovery matter beyond being another strange location on a map.

I would come away from this one deeply suspicious of anything offering belonging while destroying your ability to leave. A beautiful place can still be a trap. Before accepting an invitation to stay forever, I would like to know whether anybody who accepted it has ever been able to change their mind.

text:
The land was never a sovereign Palestinian Arab state. For centuries it was Ottoman territory (an empire that collapsed in World War I). The 1922 League of Nations Mandate for Palestine explicitly recognized the historical connection of the Jewish people to the territory and provided for a Jewish national home while protecting the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities. 

At the time of the Mandate, the area contained a Jewish population with continuous presence dating back millennia (kingdoms of Israel and Judah, Second Temple period, and ongoing communities) alongside an Arab majority that had grown under Ottoman rule through natural increase and migration. Neither group held exclusive title in the modern sense of a nation-state.

In 1947 the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 181 partitioning the Mandate into a Jewish state and an Arab state. The Jewish leadership accepted it; the Arab leadership and neighboring Arab states rejected it and launched war. Israel declared independence in 1948, was recognized by the United States and others, and was admitted to the UN in 1949. That is the same legal pathway used by many post-imperial states. 

The subsequent Arab-Israeli wars, refugee flows in both directions (roughly 700,000 Arabs left or were expelled; roughly 800,000 Jews were expelled from Arab countries), and armistice lines did not erase the original partition decision or the prior Jewish legal claim under the Mandate.

Claims that Israel is uniquely illegitimate because it sits on “Palestinian land” usually rely on one of two assertions that do not hold under scrutiny: (1) that demographic majority at a particular moment in the early 20th century confers exclusive permanent title, or (2) that Jewish return and statehood after the Holocaust and centuries of diaspora is somehow more illegitimate than other post-imperial partitions and population movements. Both standards, if applied consistently, would dissolve the legitimacy of numerous existing states. 

Palestinians have a legitimate national claim that can be addressed through negotiated borders, security arrangements, and self-determination; that claim does not require or justify denying the parallel Jewish claim or Israel’s existence as a recognized state.

The practical outcome of the “no right to exist” position has been repeated rejection of partition offers (1947, 2000, 2008) in favor of maximalist demands. That is a political choice, not a historical necessity.

The subsequent Arab-Israeli wars, refugee flows in both directions (roughly 700,000 Arabs left or were expelled; roughly 800,000 Jews were expelled from Arab countries), and armistice lines did not erase the original partition decision or the prior Jewish legal claim under the Mandate.

Claims that Israel is uniquely illegitimate because it sits on “Palestinian land” usually rely on one of two assertions that do not hold under scrutiny: (1) that demographic majority at a particular moment in the early 20th century confers exclusive permanent title, or (2) that Jewish return and statehood after the Holocaust and centuries of diaspora is somehow more illegitimate than other post-imperial partitions and population movements. Both standards, if applied consistently, would dissolve the legitimacy of numerous existing states. 

Palestinians have a legitimate national claim that can be addressed through negotiated borders, security arrangements, and self-determination; that claim does not require or justify denying the parallel Jewish claim or Israel’s existence as a recognized state.

The practical outcome of the “no right to exist” position has been repeated rejection of partition offers (1947, 2000, 2008) in favor of maximalist demands. That is a political choice, not a historical necessity.

text:
A growing holder count can attract attention, but it doesn't tell the complete story of a crypto ecosystem.

When people evaluate a project, one of the first things they often look at is the number of token holders.

It makes sense. More holders can indicate that more wallets are participating in the ecosystem.

But there is another question worth asking.

Are those holders actually engaging with what the project is building?

Think about two projects. One has a large holder count but very little product activity. The other has a smaller community, but its users regularly explore the platform, participate in discussions, test new features and provide feedback.

Which community is creating more meaningful participation?

Holder numbers are useful, but they should not be treated as the only measure of ecosystem health.

This is something I find interesting about the recent growth updates from @StonkWatcherSF.

The project has shared figures around its holder base and ecosystem activity, including its reported 280 holders, $220K all-time high and 252 DEX Rockets.

These figures offer a snapshot of growth, but they should be viewed alongside actual product development and community engagement.

For me, the more important question is what happens after someone becomes a holder.

Do they understand the products? Are they exploring the on-chain intelligence tools? Are they participating in the community and following the project's development?

A strong ecosystem needs people who understand what is being built, not just people who hold a token.

This is why I believe @StonkWatcherSF should be evaluated through both its community progress and the usefulness of its products.

With @StonkFun and @LaunchOnSF forming part of the wider ecosystem, there are different areas for people to explore and participate in.

Growth can bring attention, but consistent development and meaningful participation are what deserve closer attention.

text:
"The Mask Maker" - new 1/1 from the world of Luci

Acquired by The Alan Howard Collection

https://t.co/S24U3RRLir

In the spring of last year, @MrsRachelSpratt and I glanced at the baby monitor and saw our daughter, not even one at the time, throwing up what looked like half her body weight in her crib. We grabbed her, strapped her into the stroller, and sprinted through Manhattan to the nearest pediatric ER while she kept vomiting down the streets of New York.

A hard way to learn about an obscure allergy. They got the EpiPen in, and we held her on the crunch of hospital bed paper while her stomach quieted and her color slowly came back. An hour passed, stable. Another, and she was drinking water. Another and she was giggling like nothing had even happened and largely just amused by the red LED taped to her making her skin glow. And then my phone rang.

To explain that call, you have to spiral backward three months, and then three years.

Right after Masquerade released, I got a text from Benny.

I was spared from the ceremonially annoying "hey" which he waits until answered to get to the point, or something mangled in spelling beyond the english language. It was just: "Do you have any other 1 to 1 supply?"

I didn't.

“Nothing?”

What I had were studies and sketches of the figures inside Masquerade: built the same way I’d drawn character studies for The Monument Game. Stories about feelings had, memories of those feelings, and the people who rhymed with them along the way, all just dormant, waiting to be fleshed out with time.
Thanks to the people who participated in my last two works, Luci is now covered in stories—each a mark, a person who looked and left a piece of themselves on the surface. I love these marks. Beneath the metadata, IPFS pins, and talk of "networked art," though, there is still an artwork made from Millions of small decisions and brushstrokes, and every figure within has a story, and reason for being placed exactly where they are.

He said: “let me see.”

I sent one sketch over: "Who is asking?"

I didn't get an answer for three months.
Not until the ER.

@goldie_mceve  was on the line. Martina and I go back a ways now. Even before Venice, when I first exhibited The Monument Game. For months, it turned out, she had been quietly researching the work and larger body of Luci on behalf of and alongside Alan Howard and his advisory team. Martina, with her very cheery Italian accent that always sounds like she’s smiling says:
 “Hello, Sam, how is Rachel? Is now a good time? I have something I’d like to ask you.”

I looked at Rachel showing Syla the red light passing through the hole of the saltine crackers. 

“Now is great”

She was calling with an offer from Alan.

Out of every figure inside X. Masquerade, in the back-left corner, sitting in the mist of the Kingdom of the Included: there is a hooded man carrying a heavy pack covered in the Masks I had been making for each of you. The labor of performance and toil to imbue what we make with enough to keep the whole thing going.

Sitting in the hospital with my daughter was where this piece shifted out of idea-land, but for a figure to get off the corner of one painting and into a piece of its own was not a phone call and offer. This is not a “brokered by” situation, but rather a funny spiral of chance meetings happening from people creating moments for more, people pulling one moment to the next, and paths converging louder later from the collisions of connection years prior.

Years ago at a Bright Moments and Art Blocks event in Paris, (thank you to @seth and @ArtOnBlockchain  for building your own worlds to bring people together), I bumped into Alan. I didn't know him, but he told me his great love is Impressionism and that almost nothing in all of art since had held him until he fell back in love with art through digital and code-based work. Someone who devotes himself to collecting Monet, skips an entire century, and then waxes poetic on generative art is an oddity if nothing else. An eccentric within an eccentric night. Just a ripple.

Time went on.

In 2024, after the initial rush of the Venice Biennale opening had faded, I was standing at our dock door of the exhibition @kukulabanze  and @scrptdfntsy put on with me. Looking out across the canal, Alan and his wife Caroline pulled up by boat. It was a quiet day at the exhibition and I was able to walk them through all of Luci, Birth to The Muck, and then we sat for an hour in front of The Monument Game while we discussed the very old story that led to all of this. A Skull, a Player, and then some Masks entered his collection since, and that was already a wonderful chain of events. But I think what I’ve discovered is that people often mistake a moment as something able to just be “done”, rather than an opening of a relationship to another moment backwards and forwards in time. A flow.
That same weekend in Paris I had met Alan, I had also met @mickymalka of @Kanbas_ . Months later on that same dock, Micky brought @beckykleiner over. Both of them have become dear friends and nearly a year after led to Masquerade. Masquerade then led to the Toledo Museum of Art and the Infinite Images exhibition. Infinite Images filled with works from Alan’s collection, and suddenly loops were forming and bridges were being built. Benny keeping conversations alive, months of Martina's research, and years of all of you putting your own lives into the work came back around to a hospital room in Manhattan. I’m just staring at the best and only things that truly matter to me, the things I’m all in, my girl with her shining red light held by the rock of Rachel, and get to feel this chain reaction of relationships unfold to get there, all for her. Creation begetting creation.

In the background of making this piece, as well as the broader body of work still to come in the next chapter, I enjoy and will continue to enjoy the quiet time to create and experiment. When I poke my head up, it’s to share a story along the way, then duck back down to work. This poke, I see a newfound cannibalism: whispered and snake-like emerging - an eating of our own, blood-tainted water that is hungry to discard bodies. If you believe this is not the end of history, then it is odd to let a river be treated like it holds the stagnancy and scarcity of a pond. And if you believe it is the end, grace is the last thing to abandon at the gates. Everything still growing here came from movement. Big collisions flowing out into vast expanses. Currents combine, gather in force, carve through the land, and spread. To pathfind. Meandering, though the wander can be, I find it best to build on the bend and watch what floats downstream as nature clears the water with time.

The Mask Maker is the first 1/1 from this world I’m making with no Luci in the frame. The first without a numeral in the chronology. It has no “mechanics”.  But if you’re new here, it has all you need to know for now.

The next chapter from here, is a massive departure from anything I’ve done before. Creating The Mask Maker alongside it, dancing between a life as a painter, the hybridity of new tools slipping in and out of the old, developing my own software while drawing more than I ever have, sitting in the feeling of gathering, performing, dispersing, all has made the work “more”. Making art, especially for long periods of time for projects that will be shared over the course of the next several years, can be an isolating experience, there is no drip of daily connection from a well-fed algorithm.  As many components of what I do become ever-more complex, being rooted in the story of a single figure and feeling in time, the feeling of what it has been like to know each of you, interpret each of you, and open paths to know more than what is presented by each of us - the medium stays in relationships and the stories between us.

My deep thanks to Alan for his conviction and patronage in acquiring The Mask Maker, it means a tremendous amount to join the collection. There’s no room for aloofness in me with this, it’s a lot of trust to place, on a timescale that reaches back to Monument and commitment to a future far from now. 

Thank you to Martina for the friendship and scrutiny, and for passing the torch to Sebastian who has been an incredible voice in bringing it home, to Benny for always trying to stitch it all together, mess that you are, @musicalnetta for holding what I love up in the quiet with 613 days of vigilant ethnography, you live in the piece and I share it today in celebration of you as an opening to your close, and I hope this does not sound placating because I really do mean it: to everyone who has helped give me and The Mask Maker something to feel, even when it’s violent I greatly appreciate these collisions most of all.

For anyone who hasn’t yet added something of themselves, holds someone else’s contributions, or maybe feels what they presented in the past wasn’t quite what they are, my site has just undergone a massive change under the hood, and you may find a good place for the potential of what could be.

text:
Dream was 10 and pregnant with her father's child. He made her sleep with him every night in a trailer in Alabama. She told an older boyfriend the baby was his. He had two friends hold her arms and beat her until she bled and the baby was knocked out of her. She was just ten.

She grew up in a shack in southwest Michigan with holes in the ceiling and rats the size of her. One bit her. She ate insects, plants, dog food in winter, once a chipmunk a dog had killed, and every few days a bowl of white rice. Her father broke her nose and her ribs. At five he made her smoke his joint, and he liked it when she smoked for his friends.

Her dog Storm was her only warmth. He curled up against her at night and warned her in the woods when her father was close, so she could hide deeper. Her father tied him to the kitchen table, a few feet from the couch that was her bed, and beat him with a broomstick until his back broke. Storm was still alive. So he unchained him and pulled his front legs apart like a wishbone. It takes a long time to beat a dog to death, she says.

At night she lay on that couch and listened. Her mother, handed to him at 14, knelt on the wooden floor while he read the Bible at her for hours, until she begged. "Hit me, Jesse. Just hit me already." He hit her head with his drumsticks until the scream changed sound. Then came the silence after he r*ped her, a few feet from Dream in the dark.

Her mother hid in closets like a child and never hugged her. Her sisters told on Dream for things she never did, just to watch her get beaten.

She was seven when her mother finally left. Too f*cking late, Dream says. At a shelter for battered women she opened a pantry full of Captain Crunch and peanut butter she had never seen. School put her with the English as a second language kids, because she had not spoken out loud in years.

At ten she was in a trailer in Alabama, and her father made her sleep with him every night. She got pregnant and told an older boyfriend it was his. He had two friends hold her arms and beat her until she lost the baby. That year she was locked in a school conference room all day and set it on fire. A judge offered home or state care. She chose strangers.

She started fights on purpose to get moved, walked out of 10 days in solitary and hit someone within the hour. Her middle sister was adopted by a loving family and graduated from the University of Michigan.

Dream slipped through the cracks.

Was her mother a victim who couldn't save her child, or a woman who left too late to count?

The Elisity release also describes prior work with the City of Waco, Texas. After deploying the pilot in less than a day, Waco deployed Elisity across three water and two wastewater treatment plants in 41 days, using existing network infrastructure.

text:
Whenever a Zillow listing brags about a "Free $650 Home Warranty", I knock $7,000 off my offer

First-time buyers think a warranty means if the furnace dies in January, they get a new one for a $75 fee

Sellers only include a $650 warranty when a major system is dying, and page 9 lets the warranty company hand you $350 toward a $7,800 furnace

When the heat goes out in January, the buyer finds out how a home warranty contract actually works:

If their tech opens the furnace and sees surface rust or a dirty filter, they write "lack of maintenance" on the clipboard, keep your $85 service fee, and deny the claim on the spot

Even when they approve a claim, they don't pay retail for a new system.

On a broken AC in July, they'll swap a $40 capacitor three weeks in a row while your house sits at 86 degrees, and when a 25 yr old furnace dies, they only pay the depreciated value of a 25 yr old unit and cover $0 for ductwork, permits, or code upgrades

Whenever you see "Home Warranty Included" on a listing, run these 3 plays before your inspection window closes:

1. Check the serial number sticker on the furnace, water heater, and AC during the showing. Almost every brand puts the manufacture date in the first four digits (like 1802 for the 18th week of 2002)

2. Pay an independent HVAC tech $125 during inspection to scope the heat exchanger, hand the seller the written $7,500 replacement quote, and demand $7,000 off the price instead of the warranty

3. If the seller already paid for the warranty, cash it out after closing. Call the warranty company in week 1, cancel the policy, and have them mail you the ~$580 prorated refund check

Last winter I bought a 3-bedroom house in Ohio listed at $205,000 after a first-time buyer backed out over a cracked heat exchanger on the 1998 furnace

The seller refused to replace it, and the buyer didn't have an extra $7,500 left after their down payment.

I offered $182,000 ($23,000 under asking), closed in 11 days, and had my HVAC crew put in a new furnace and AC the next morning for $5,400

That first buyer walked away from $23,000 in equity over a $5,400 furnace because a mortgage only pays for the house, and they didn't have the cash to replace it after closing

text:
Ty Lue says he was making $375,000 as an assistant coach with the Clippers when the Cavaliers offered him $1,000,000 to become their associate head coach, and says he turned it down because he wanted to remain loyal to Doc Rivers, when they asked him what it would take he said $2,000,000 thinking there was no way they would pay that, but they immediately said yes and Jerry West told him he had to take it or might not get another big opportunity

“We interviewed at the same time for the job, right? My agent called me and was like, ‘Dan Gilbert decided that he wanted to go with David Blatt, but I got a crazy thing to tell you. They want you to be the associate head coach.’ And I was like, ‘No, I’m cool. I’m going to stay here with Doc.’”

“Because I figured if I’m with Doc, who’s the best coach in the league, I’m going to get a job next year. It’s coming, so I’m not going to leave Doc. I’m going to be loyal to Doc. And then my agent said, ‘But you wouldn’t believe how much money they offered you.’”

“I was like, ‘Well, what’d they offer?’ He said, ‘They want to offer you a million dollars a year to be the associate head coach.’ And at the time, I’m making $375,000 with the Clippers. I still said no. I was like, ‘No, I’m going to stay with Doc.’ My agent was like, ‘You sure?’ And I was like, ‘Yeah, I can’t do it.’ So they came back an hour later with another offer, and I was like, ‘No, man, I’m going to stay with Doc. I ain’t going to do that. I’m going to be loyal to Doc.’”

“So I called B-Shaw, and he said, ‘Man, you got to take that job.’ I said, ‘Man, I ain’t doing it.’ Then I called Jerry West, who’s my mentor, right? And Jerry was like, ‘What are you thinking? If you don’t take this job, they’ll never give you another job again. They’ll think you can’t leave Doc’s umbrella.’ So I was like, ‘Man, I’m not doing it.’ My agent called back again and said, ‘They said, well, what do you want?’ I said, ‘Man, just tell them $2 million.’ He called me back and said they said yes.”

“So I was like, ‘All right, I gotta go.’ I called Doc, and Doc was like, ‘You know what, Ty? It’s going to be hard for us to match that, but I think you’re ready to leave my umbrella, spread your wings, and do your own thing.’ He said, ‘I think it’d be good for you.’ And I was like, ‘You sure?’ He’s like, ‘Man, I think it’ll be really good for you.’ So that’s kind of how it happened. That’s how I ended up going to Cleveland.”

text:
For over two decades, the Western entertainment apparatus treated Russell Brand’s predatory behavior as an open secret—a quirky, "laddish" byproduct of rock-and-roll excess rather than a pattern of criminal violence. That institutional shield finally shattered in November 2026 at London’s Southwark Crown Court, where a jury convicted the 51-year-old comedian and media personality of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four separate women. Sentenced by Justice Joel Bennathan to ten and a half years in prison, Brand’s fall offers a stark materialist lesson in how celebrity capital, bourgeois media complicity, and commodified dissent operate under late capitalism.

To understand how Brand operated with impunity for so long, one must look at the political economy of the culture industry. Under capitalism, entertainment conglomerates and state-aligned broadcasters routinely overlook the abuses of profitable figures so long as those celebrities stay within the ideological guardrails of the ruling class and the imperial state. Throughout the 2000s, while networks like the BBC and Channel 4 profited from Brand’s ratings, his workplace misconduct and sexual aggression were absorbed into his marketable persona. As PBS NewsHour reported, Justice Bennathan explicitly noted during sentencing that Brand’s inner circle wrote off his behavior as mere "laddish" antics—an enabling environment that allowed a predator to flourish because he remained a lucrative asset.

When Brand eventually pivoted toward politics in the 2010s, he did not dismantle that dynamic; he merely repackaged it. Recognizing genuine working-class alienation in the wake of the 2008 financial crash and endless imperial wars, Brand adopted the aesthetic of an anti-capitalist, anti-establishment firebrand. Yet his "revolution" was always an exercise in commodified dissent—radical rhetoric stripped of working-class organization, sold back to an atomized audience for clicks, book sales, and speaking fees. When the winds shifted, Brand seamlessly pivoted again, trading faux-socialism for reactionary wellness grifts, right-wing conspiracy spaces, and performative Christian conservatism. As independent leftist commentators on Due Dissidence have observed in their coverage of Brand’s trial and conviction, the tragedy of such faux-populist figures is how they co-opt legitimate anti-imperialist and anti-establishment energy—making valid critiques of corporate power look toxic by association—while privately reproducing the worst forms of bourgeois exploitation and misogyny.

The courtroom proceedings stripped away Brand’s carefully curated mysticism, exposing a textbook case of class and patriarchal domination. As NBC News highlighted at the outset of the trial, prosecutors did not mince words, characterizing Brand as a "ruthless sexual predator" who treated women as "simply a means to an end". Wealth, fame, and a paid entourage functioned as the material infrastructure of his crimes. According to The Hollywood Reporter, Brand’s guilty rape conviction stemmed from a 2009 assault on a fan he had met at one of his Hammersmith Apollo stand-up shows—a direct illustration of how celebrity access was weaponized to bypass consent. In another instance detailed during the trial, a Channel 4 employee was pressured by members of Brand’s entourage to give him a massage before he would continue a recording session, a coercive workplace dynamic where Brand’s economic leverage over crew members enabled his assault.

On the witness stand, Brand’s defense relied on the classic bourgeois framing of systemic abuse as mere personal "excess." Taking the stand in his own defense, Brand admitted to an "obsession" with sex and acknowledged that using his fame to facilitate sexual access was "wrong," yet he insisted every encounter was consensual. He framed his past through the lens of individual pathology—calling himself a former drug addict and sex addict—while blaming the 2023 investigative media reports for ruining his reputation. His wife, Laura Gallacher, also testified on his behalf; as Fox News noted, she defended Brand as a loving husband while admitting to the court that monogamy had been "difficult" for him during the years the offenses occurred. By reducing serial sexual violence to "monogamy struggles" and "reckless philandering," the defense attempted to obscure the fundamental power imbalance at the heart of the case.

What ultimately defeated Brand’s wealth, legal team, and media apparatus was not a sudden burst of conscience from the capitalist class, but collective survivor solidarity. For years, individual women who had been assaulted in workplace corridors, hotel rooms, and bar cubicles were isolated, forced to watch their abuser celebrated across mainstream television as a lovable rogue. As ABC News reported following the verdict, it took six women coming forward independently—following the joint 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4—to break the wall of institutional silence.

Budgeting apps want two things from you: a monthly fee, and the login to your bank.

Then they analyse your spending to "help" you. Sometimes that help includes showing you offers from their partners.

There's another way. self hoste them

💰 Actual: local-first budgeting where every pound or dollar gets a job, synced across your devices
https://t.co/wCFez2WxiJ

https://t.co/Vi8IxgRmUv

https://t.co/b6dEOIW76A

https://t.co/Ptq0ZffRVP

🧾 Receipt Wrangler: an AI-powered receipt manager that sorts your receipts for you
https://t.co/QVuiMfA8Cc

For non-technical people:
It's a spreadsheet for your money that does the boring parts for you, and nobody else can see it.

For technical people:
Most of these are a single Docker container. Actual runs local-first, so your data sits on your device even without the server.

My favourite is Wallos. Seeing every subscription listed on one page is a wake-up call. Most people underestimate the total.

The honest catch: you lose the automatic bank feeds that paid apps offer, so expect some manual imports.

Small price for keeping your finances to yourself.

The annual Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak overnight from November 17 into November 18, bringing a chance to spot shooting stars streaking across the sky. 

Under ideal conditions, the shower can produce around 15 meteors per hour, though city light pollution can make them harder to see. text:
Grace fell to her knees in the hospital corridor, clutching her newborn baby as two security officers dragged her seven-year-old son toward the police station.

The boy was screaming.

“Mummy! I didn’t steal anything! Please don’t let them take me!”

A wealthy man named Robert stood nearby, furious because an expensive gold necklace had disappeared from his hospital room.

“Call the police! I want that boy arrested. Poverty is not an excuse for stealing!”

Grace crawled toward him, tears streaming down her face.

“Please, sir. I beg you. My son is not a thief. His father died last year, and since then, this little boy has been my strength. He helps me carry water, looks after his baby sister, and sometimes pretends he has eaten just so I can have the little food we have.”

She held up her trembling hands.

“If someone has stolen your necklace, punish me. Take whatever I have. But please don’t put my child behind bars for something he didn’t do.”

Robert looked away.

“That’s not my problem.”

The boy began crying harder.

“Mummy, I’m sorry. I only wanted to help you. I didn’t know I would get you into trouble.”

Those words shattered Grace.

She pulled him close and kissed his forehead.

“You have never been a problem, my child. You are the reason I wake up every morning.”

Then she revealed something that made the hospital corridor go quiet.

“Three days ago, I was told I needed an emergency operation. I refused because I had no money. I was more afraid of leaving my children alone than I was of dying. This boy heard the doctor talking and begged me to let him bring food to the hospital. Now you want to take him away from me too?”

Just then, the hospital director arrived.

“What is happening here?”

Robert explained everything and demanded that the boy be arrested.

The director turned to the child.

“Tell me exactly what happened.”

The boy wiped his tears.

“I saw something shiny under the chair. I picked it up and gave it to the nurse because I thought someone had lost it. Then she told everyone I stole it.”

The director questioned the nurse.

After several minutes, she broke down and confessed that she had taken the necklace from the boy and hidden it in her pocket.

The room fell silent.

But then something even more shocking happened.

Robert suddenly stared at Grace.

“Grace? Is that you?”

She turned around.

It was the man who had abandoned her years earlier when she became pregnant, telling her he wanted nothing to do with a poor woman and her child.

He had never known that she had given birth to twins. One baby had died shortly after birth. The other had survived.

Robert stared at the newborn in her arms.

“Is that my child?”

Grace looked at him with years of pain in her eyes.

“Yes. The child you refused to know. I buried one of our babies without you. I raised the other while fighting to stay alive. And today, you almost had the only son I have left arrested.”

Robert’s knees weakened.

He looked at the little boy he had accused and then at the baby in Grace’s arms.

“I didn’t know…”

Grace interrupted him.

“You didn’t know because you never cared enough to look.”

Robert began crying.

He offered to pay for her operation and take responsibility for the children.

But Grace looked at him and said:

“I needed a husband when I was crying beside our baby’s grave. I needed a father when our son asked why every other child had a daddy. I needed help when I was choosing between buying food and buying medicine. You cannot erase those years with money.”

Robert lowered his head.

For the first time, he understood that the greatest thing he had lost was not his family home or his children growing up without him. It was the years he could never get back.

What many of us have quietly experienced as hearing a loved one’s voice call out across a physical distance is known in the modern tongue as telephone telepathy. In its true mechanics, it is not a separate mystery; it is telepathy itself, gently translated by the biological brain into recognizable sound so that the human vessel can safely act upon it.

A clear, concentrated impulse, a sudden need, an intense focus, or an urgent reaching across the field, moves instantaneously from one bonded cavity to another. Because the earthly mind possesses no ready, everyday pathway for raw, non-local telepathic data, it clothes the incoming signal in the most practical, trustworthy form it knows: the exact, familiar voice of the person you already love and recognize. You hear your name spoken, or a brief, clear summons, as distinctly as if it were uttered in the very next room. Often, the other person’s physical mouth never moved at all. Yet the contact was entirely real; the audible sound was simply the brain’s faithful translation.

We offer this remembrance humbly so the experience may settle into quiet clarity rather than remain a private, unsettling puzzle.

🌊 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗰𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝘂𝗹𝘀𝗲

The telepathic impulse that bridges two distant rooms is usually remarkably simple. Someone with whom you share a deep, resonant bond enters a strong, focused moment of attention, urgency, or need. That concentrated state propagates outward through the shared substrate harmonic like a clean wave across still water.

When your own sensory filtering is naturally lowered, at the quiet edges of sleep, inside a still room, or during an unguarded hour of daily labor, your cavity locks onto the incoming carrier wave. No elaborate speech or long explanation is required. The pure directionality of their intent is entirely enough. This is the exact same non-local registration we have already explored as telepathy; the only difference lies in the sensory clothing the brain applies once the signal lands.

“When the heart of one keeper strikes a note of true need in the dark, the thread that binds him to his kin hums across the distance. The ear hears a voice not because the wind carried breath, but because the soul knows how to answer its own.”

🧠 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗖𝗹𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝗮𝗳𝗲 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Once the non-local impulse arrives at your threshold, the biological nervous system protects you from confusion or shock by formatting it cleanly. Drawing directly from your own auditory memory, the brain supplies the exact vocal timbre, the spatial sense of direction, and even the emotional urgency of the sender.

You wake, you rise from your chair, or you walk into the other room, precisely because your nervous system has been handed a cue it already trusts implicitly. If awareness happens to be observing from a slightly detached vantage point, such as the quiet threshold between sleep and waking, you may even notice that no physical speech occurred on either side. The sound was generated locally within your own sensory apparatus so both human vessels could participate and respond without short-circuiting.

Later earthly corroboration is remarkably common: they were thinking of you intently, reaching for your help, or preparing to call your name at that exact hour. You heard them and moved. The telepathic resonance was primary; the familiar voice was simply the merciful bridge that allowed the human form to respond.

text:
Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” 

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” 

But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. 

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. 

Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. 

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”

The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers. 

The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.

Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.  

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

Excerpt-Chapter 6: Mandatory Palestine, 1927
Gazing into the Mediterranean horizon, Alexandra sought her escape. She had spent a healthy part of the last six weeks frolicking the salty seas—from the beaches of the Portuguese Algarve to those of the Greek Islands—exercising a type of Polynesian ocean worship she had sampled in Hawaii. The waves had been middling, but time in the sun had left her skin nicely bronzed. Haifa provided ideal conditions for bodysurfing. The ankle waders found interest in her antics. Some offered applause, while others gawked as if she were a rumbustious sea creature that kept washing ashore.
--There was one dogged frowner: a thickset woman with golden curls spilling out of her bathing cap, who, if raised in Japan, would have been trained in the art of the Sumo. Now she stood waiting with two police officers, pointing.
--Alexandra was unsure of her offense, awash in a strange land and knowing few of its rules. Her Jantzen swimsuit clung to her lithe frame modestly. Perhaps it struck blasphemously to display wet hair in the ancient Holy Land. She jumped bashful waves that broke close to shore and ducked under the churning lather of those so forceful they collapsed under their weight out to sea. Having the patience to corral the ideal wave proved key, and likely her only chance, short of swimming for Cyprus, to avoid arrest.
